items.title: Why Are We So Good at Feeling Bad?
items.description: Charles Darwin was not a well man. As a youth, he suffered from scarlet fever and eczema. He couldn’t stand the sight of blood at medical school, and his five-year voyage on the Beagle brought seasickness, headaches, and infections. After returning to England,
items.author: Louis Menand
paragraphs: Charles Darwin was not a well man. As a youth, he suffered from scarlet fever and eczema. He couldn’t stand the sight of blood at medical school, and his five-year voyage on the Beagle brought seasickness, headaches, and infections. After returning to England, in 1836, he developed severe anxiety and gastrointestinal issues, including bouts of vomiting and flatulence. He also suffered from insomnia, fatigue, and depression.

In 1849, ten years before he published “On the Origin of Species,” he wrote to a friend of “dreadful vomiting every week” and reported, “I was not able to do anything one day out of three.” He thought that he was “rapidly going the way of all flesh.” In fact, he lived another thirty-three years, though the ailments never left him. Giving a scientific paper, or even attending a party, could overwhelm him. By then, he had moved to a village in Kent, rarely venturing out without his wife, Emma.

From 1849 to 1855, Darwin kept a “diary of health,” recording his conditions as “goodish,” “poorish,” and “very bad fl[atulence] with fright.” He consulted some twenty doctors and tried Victorian cures, including hydrotherapy, which offered some relief, and galvanism. Diagnoses included nervous dyspepsia, water brash (acid reflux), and “suppressed gout” (whatever that is).

What was the problem? Retrospective diagnoses range from Chagas’ disease, a parasitic illness he might have contracted in South America, to lactose intolerance. He may have suffered from some combination of diseases and allergies, and possibly Crohn’s. But some symptoms suggest a psychological condition. Agoraphobia with panic disorder is a plausible diagnosis.

Whatever the cause or causes, Darwin must, at some point, have asked himself, I got naturally selected for this? Of course, not every affliction has an evolutionary purpose. People get sick. But our extraordinary susceptibility to misery does raise a question about what kind of creatures natural selection has made us. We get depressed when we win the lottery; we lie awake worrying about whether the car needs new tires; we feel jealous when our girlfriend talks too long with the barista.

Anxiety might have adaptive utility when we are in danger of being eaten by a sabre-toothed tiger. But there are not a lot of sabre-toothed tigers around anymore, and we still get anxious, frequently for no very good reason. We don’t just react emotionally to things. We overreact. Why have genes for emotional overreaction, rather than genes for being cool, calm, and collected, been passed along? Wouldn’t we be reproductively fitter if we weren’t unhappy so much of the time?

These are questions George Loewenstein tries to answer in “The Opposite of Happiness: How Bad Feelings Make and Break Us” (Harper). Loewenstein, who teaches at Carnegie Mellon, is a leader in the field of behavioral economics. Neoclassical economics relied on the fiction of the rational actor, someone who makes decisions by way of a judicious calculation of self-interest. Behavioral economics, by contrast, emphasizes the nonrational factors in economic decision-making. Whatever human beings are rational about, it’s not money. We overspend it; we under-save it; we buy stuff on impulse. We generally don’t do the math. Why it took so long for this to dawn on economists is mystifying. Didn’t those people ever read a novel? Virtually every famous nineteenth-century novel is about people behaving badly around money.

Still, figuring out why we act foolishly when we could, or should, or want to act otherwise is a worthy academic pursuit. Among Loewenstein’s contributions is the identification of what he calls “empathy gaps,” our inability to imagine how we would feel or behave in an emotional state different from the one we’re in. When we’re pain-free, we can’t really remember what pain feels like. When we’re angry, we can’t imagine being calm. Emotions, Loewenstein argues, can reprogram our whole psyche. He gives a personal example: learning that it is better to wait a day before responding to an annoying e-mail.

Didn’t we know this already, though? Adam Smith made similar observations in “The Theory of Moral Sentiments” (1759). And some of Loewenstein’s work does seem to amount to a confirmation of common sense. One of his experiments, for instance, measured the effect of sexual arousal on judgment and decision-making in male students. Guess what? A sexually aroused young man reported a greater willingness to engage in morally questionable behavior to obtain sexual gratification.

Explaining how feelings affect our judgment is one thing. Why so many emotions make us unhappy is another. That’s the larger question Loewenstein takes up. His thesis is that these emotions “were built to keep us alive and reproducing, not to keep us happy.”

Loewenstein is hardly alone in proposing evolutionary explanations for misery. Randolph M. Nesse, a psychiatrist, made a similar case in “Good Reasons for Bad Feelings: Insights from the Frontier of Evolutionary Psychiatry” (2019), a work Loewenstein discusses. Such arguments recall the “selfish gene” model. Evolution is not about the reproduction of persons, is the idea. It’s about the reproduction of genes. And, from a gene’s point of view, the body is just a disposable gene container. It can fret about the tires, climb the Matterhorn, write “On the Origin of Species”—whatever, as long as the genes keep getting passed along. Darwin may have been wretched much of the time, but he had ten children. He checked the evolutionary box. Was he also farting and throwing up a lot? Sure. His genes didn’t care.

But Loewenstein thinks that negative emotions aren’t simply a design flaw or a regrettable by-product of natural selection. On the contrary, he thinks that we have good evolutionary reasons for being able to feel bad. Our ancestors would have been less “fit” to pass their genes along if they hadn’t been equipped with negative emotions. Fear could save us from predators; guilt could help us maintain the social bonds on which survival depended.

Knowing this, Loewenstein warns, won’t make us feel any less unhappy. “I offer in these pages no tips and precious little advice,” he writes. “This is not a self-help book.” (I wonder whether his publishers tried to talk him out of that.) Loewenstein describes the book as, instead, “one scientist’s bird’s-eye view of the subject, shaped by broad reading, personal experience, and, in many cases, my own research.”

“The Opposite of Happiness” is fairly nontechnical. There is no talk of neurotransmitters, and Loewenstein, who has himself conducted brain-imaging research, thinks that the interpretation of functional-MRI scans is often “not much more reliable than reading tea leaves.” The book is also quite personal, although selectively so. Loewenstein lets us know, for example, that he suffers from paruresis (shy-bladder syndrome) but neglects to mention that he is a great-grandson of Sigmund Freud, whose theories of unconscious drives bear some family resemblance to Loewenstein’s account of our emotional programming.

The problem with a lot of evolutionary psychology is that its explanations are hard to verify. It undertakes to explain an observable fact (we fret about bald tires) with an unobservable one (cavemen worried that a mastodon might trample them). Loewenstein is alert to the danger of producing “just-so” stories, accounts of human attributes based on unconfirmable hunches about what life was like in the Paleolithic era. But they’re hard to avoid.

Even if we accept these evolutionary explanations, they leave a further puzzle. Why do negative emotions so often persist long after they’ve served their purpose? Like the earworms of cheesy pop songs, they can get stuck in our heads. Our brains continue pumping them out even when the occasions for them have passed.

We also have the unfortunate ability to reëxperience some negative feelings just by remembering the occasions for them. We may find it hard to recall what physical pain felt like once it has stopped, but, when we remember something shameful we did, we can feel the shame all over again. Most of us could use an empathy gap there.

“At the heart of so many of our miseries,” Loewenstein says, “is not the fact that we feel bad, but the belief that we should feel otherwise.” Our brains fight with themselves. We feel ashamed of our shame, angry about our anger. The wish to escape an unpleasant emotion becomes another source of misery. Who’s running the show in there?

Not “us.” We may resolve, after firing off an intemperate e-mail, to respond more calmly the next time. But, when the next provocation arrives, our anger can make the resolution seem lame. As Loewenstein explains, we are adept at psychological self-sabotage. Sometimes our very efforts to gain control make things worse, as when athletes concentrate too intently on not trying so hard.

In the second half of “The Opposite of Happiness,” Loewenstein lets unhappiness sufferers speak for themselves. He has gathered their stories through what he calls the Misery Survey, in which more than five hundred respondents were asked about their experiences of negative emotions. Each was assigned an emotion at random and asked whether it had caused them misery. If it had, they were invited to describe the experience; if not, they were assigned another emotion. The stories make for fun reading (more or less), not so much because they hold surprises but because we recognize ourselves in so many of them. Misery, it turns out, loves company.

Loewenstein devotes a chapter to each of twelve varieties of misery. It’s a bit like Dante’s Inferno if Dante had modelled his work on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders rather than the “Summa Theologiae” of Thomas Aquinas. The first two circles in Loewenstein’s hell are Impatience and Boredom, followed by Anger, Envy, Jealousy, Rejection, Guilt, Shame, Anxiety, Regret, Loneliness, and, in the last circle, Depression, which he deems “a fitting finale to this Hieronymus Bosch underworld of psychic torments—not just because it is so supremely awful, but because nearly all the other miseries, when they persist and accumulate, can give rise to it.” (Hate, a resurgent political emotion across much of the planet, did not make the list. Neither did grief.)

Loewenstein suspects that depression, unlike some other negative emotions, has no adaptive function of its own. It arises, he thinks, as a by-product of other psychological systems in distress. That’s close to what Peter D. Kramer concluded in his 2005 book, “Against Depression,” where he defines depression as “a disease in which a host of injuries combine to cause a common downstream process that becomes self-sustaining.” It is hard to see how suicidality conduces to reproductive success. And depression can create what Loewenstein terms “the ultimate empathy gap”: people in its grip find it almost impossible to imagine what life without it would feel like.

At the other end of his inferno is boredom. We might not think of boredom as an emotion. It seems more like the absence of emotion. But, in a study tracking the daily feelings of some four thousand adults, Loewenstein and his colleagues found that boredom frequently accompanied strong negative feelings, including anger and anxiety. “We found that boredom was 4.2 times more likely to occur in the presence of another negative emotion than a positive one,” he says.

Two places where people commonly report being bored are doctors’ waiting rooms and airport terminals. We sit there fiddling with our smartphones, and with nothing else to do, running scary or angry scenarios through our heads—the medical news will not be good, the flight will be cancelled, they will close the gate while I’m in line at Starbucks—and composing powerfully cogent letters to the airline about the incompetence of the gate crew. We get mad when we are forced to wait for something for which there are no substitutes, and then we complain that we’re bored. (In a section titled “Why Are Dreams So Boring?,” Loewenstein says that one of the most “excruciatingly boring” things we can do is listen to someone describe a dream they had. This reads like a barely veiled put-down of his famous forebear.)

But how did we acquire the capacity for boredom? There don’t seem to have been airports or doctors’ offices back in Paleolithic times, when men just hunted and gathered (and, we hope, partied). Loewenstein suggests that the ability to become bored developed as a way of budgeting attention. “If early humans didn’t feel the urge to redirect their attention when staring at the same patch of woods,” he says, “they might have missed important opportunities—a rustle in the bush that signaled prey, or an approaching threat. Our ancestors who were better at reallocating attention had an adaptive advantage: they probably avoided more predators, found more food, and pursued more socially or intellectually engaging activities.” This might be a little just-so-y. It’s hard to see how the humans or proto-humans who never got bored were the ones who got selected out. Maybe sabre-toothed tigers ate them all.

Other evolutionary explanations seem more persuasive. Loewenstein agrees with many people who have written about negative emotions that feelings like shame and guilt perform a regulatory social function. They help enforce the norms of the group. Shame, in particular, encourages submission rather than confrontation, a response “designed to protect us from one of the greatest threats to our survival—being cast out.”

Explaining why negative emotions might have evolved, though, still leaves that problem of why they can become so consuming, so hard to toggle off. Why do we spiral? Is it because we inherited emotions like anxiety which evolved in response to genuine threats to survival and can now be triggered by the prospect of missing the bus? Or were our emotions always liable to become excessive? Did our Stone Age ancestors lie awake wondering whether they had remembered to put out the fire pit?

Loewenstein thinks that it’s at least partly the latter. Our emotional system, he says, “is prone, almost by design, to malfunction.” To protect us against threats, it has to be highly sensitive, prone to false alarms rather than risk missing a real danger. But this sensitivity also makes the system unstable. He believes our psyches are poised on a “razor’s edge” between negative feedback, which allows an emotion to subside when the threat has passed, and positive feedback, in which an emotion amplifies itself. Anxiety, for example, makes us more alert to threats, which can make us perceive more threats, which heightens our anxiety. It’s like driving on an icy road: the harder we brake, the more we lose control of the car.

Of course, an emotion that makes us miserable is not necessarily an irrational response to our circumstances. One question we can ask about psychological diagnoses is whether some states we classify as symptoms of mental disorders are responses to a world that’s genuinely frightening or depressing. What if life really is meaningless? What if other people really are out to get us? What if the barista really is hitting on our girlfriend? Then feelings like sadness, anger, and jealousy might be perfectly understandable, and the emotions that need to be explained are optimism, tolerance, and a sense of humor. Maybe it’s the optimists who are the crazy ones.

In the list of books that helped replace a theological understanding of the universe with a secular one, “On the Origin of Species” is near the top. One theory about Darwin’s poor health, in fact, was that he was horrified by the implications of his own discoveries—that our species was not a special creation and that no providence dictated its characteristics. Natural selection is a blind process. There is no being out there or up there that oversees its course.

Still, there is a way in which evolutionary psychology belongs to a religious tradition, the tradition of theodicy. This was the effort of theologians to explain why, given an omnipotent and beneficent God, there is evil in the world. Transposed to a Darwinian world view, this becomes the question: If natural selection has equipped us to survive and reproduce, why has it burdened us with so much misery? There is a temptation to assume that every form of suffering must have served some evolutionary purpose, just as God must have had a reason for earthquakes in Lisbon. The problem of why bad things happen kept intellectuals busy for centuries. The problem of unhappiness promises to do the same. It may be that both depend on a shared illusion: that it all makes sense. ♦

items.title: A Cartoonist’s Depiction of the Moment Things Got Weird
items.description: As a kid, Chris Ware loved collecting and preserving comics. He graduated from buying Batman and Superman at the nearby 7-Eleven to honing his taste at the local comic shop, where he revelled in the walls of comics, the smell of self-destructing woodpulp, and
items.author: Chris Ware
paragraphs: As a kid, Chris Ware loved collecting and preserving comics. He graduated from buying Batman and Superman at the nearby 7-Eleven to honing his taste at the local comic shop, where he revelled in the walls of comics, the smell of self-destructing woodpulp, and the polypropylene bags that protected his newfound treasures. That love of the physical object led the adult cartoonist to produce his own semi-regular experimental periodical, The Acme Novelty Library, whose serialized stories were later collected in hardcover graphic novels that bookstores were happy to misfile in their children’s sections.

When “Life Is Complicated,” a retrospective of Ware’s original drawings, finished touring museums in Europe and was about to land in Columbus, Ohio, at the Billy Ireland Cartoon Library & Museum for its only American stop, the artist didn’t want it to arrive without a printed souvenir. He returned to the traditional comic book, an ambition that soon metastasized into three comic books, a Sunday-sized comic section, and a cardboard model of a contemporary office building, all housed in a (compostable) keepsake box. Like “Building Stories” (2012), this twenty-first issue of Acme asks the reader to take the lead. Its three twenty-four-page booklets excerpt longer works that he told me he has been writing since the coronavirus pandemic began. This old-fashioned format delivers a thoroughly modern reading experience, one that parallels the disruptions of those years and the unravelling of reality we’ve endured since 2016. Shifts in scale allude to the fractal nature of the narrative, and characters and story lines make cameo appearances from booklet to booklet. It’s interactive in the truest sense: the reader, aware that she is building her own story, creates her own linearity and discovers her own rhymes, echoes, and harmonies.

In the pages below, excerpted from the broadsheet-size “Untitled,” Ware chronicles the end of the world and the disruptions brought on by the pandemic. “The vogue for baking, ukulele, and homes as places to actually live in rather than just come home to reflected a shift, however temporarily, to what really matters in life. It also seems to me to be the moment when everything started to feel really weird,” Ware told me.

items.title: “Wicker” and What Straight Women Want
items.description: “Being Straight Is Great, Actually” is the original title of an opinion piece published in the Times earlier this year, by Magdalene Taylor, a senior editor at Playboy. Timing is everything; the piece ran on May 31st, on the precipice of Pride Month, and that
items.author: Doreen St Félix
paragraphs: “Being Straight Is Great, Actually” is the original title of an opinion piece published in the Times earlier this year, by Magdalene Taylor, a senior editor at Playboy. Timing is everything; the piece ran on May 31st, on the precipice of Pride Month, and that gave it an incendiary lift. The essay was addressed to a certain kind of heterosexual woman, one with whom we’ve all become familiar. A loathing has rotted her heart, a loathing directed at the subpar men who surround her, and at herself. She is a smart woman. She is enraged by the recession of gender equality, she is appalled by the prominence of Andrew Tate and his misogyny gospel, and she is alarmed by the proliferation of the trad wife. She has removed herself from the apps, and perhaps from men altogether. And yet she still wants them, these men, or at least the idea of them. She keeps wanting them, all while not wanting them.

Taylor cheerily argues against this prevailing “bad mood” that is all the rage these days—that mood being heteropessimism, a cultural condition first explored, and named, by the writer and scholar Asa Seresin, in The New Inquiry, back in 2019. Seresin was trying to work out a knot. He used the framework of Afropessimism, which he described as “a school of thought that takes antiblackness to be the transhistorical structuring force of the world,” to understand an emergent form of internet-era ennui: “performative disaffiliations with heterosexuality, usually expressed in the form of regret, embarrassment, or hopelessness about straight experience.” Coinage is deadening. “Heteropessimism” had the appeal of new jargon, and it launched about a million confessionals that, maddeningly, had the effect of narrowing questions about desire—political desire, romantic desire, what have you—instead of opening them up.

The second title of Taylor’s essay, the Times’ fix after the initial blowback, is “There’s Nothing Wrong With Wanting Men.” This permissiveness—the permission to desire—is one theme of the new film “Wicker,” a romp directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. The movie’s essence is Chaucerian; the pacing is taut, jaunty, like a fairy tale, helped along by a twinkling score composed by Anna Meredith. In a medieval village, men are named by their occupations—the Tailor (Nabhaan Rizwan), the Bottle Washer (Gustav Lindh)—and the women, by their affiliation to their husbands—the Tailor’s Wife (Elizabeth Debicki), the Bottle Washer’s Wife (Marli Siu). The film delights in the slippage between satire and historical accuracy, laying out before us a wheat-colored, barely civilized civilization. Lewdness rules. The people are ritualistic. The men are boors. The women are sour. At marriage, the maiden bends her head and joyfully receives a collar, this universe’s version of a “ring,” and the union is pronounced “man and his wife.” At the reception for one such marriage, that of the Bottle Washer and his wife, the whole town spills out to celebrate. One woman, an outcast, the Fisherwoman, played by Olivia Colman—a performer whose gift of interpretation allows her to enliven the one-dimensional, matronly characters she often chooses to play—looks off scoffingly, but not uninterested.

“Wicker” is a hybridized movie, a comedy/horror/romance. It basically sustains itself on a pun, that of hard wood, but its recombinations of the joke don’t get old. We meet the Fisherwoman on the outskirts of town, by the water, where she expertly guts and cleans her fish, shelters in a modest hut, and pisses in a bucket by her bed. The women in town ridicule her for her fish stench, which is also the smell of being unchosen. But isn’t the Fisherwoman, a kind of sister to Chaucer’s working woman—the five-times married Alison, the beloved first sovereign woman of English literature—content to be alone? The film, which is based on a short story by Ursula Wills called “The Wicker Husband,” tees up a proto-feminist refusal: “Love seems more a burden than a prize,” the Fisherwoman replies to her bullies, who sarcastically ask if she has yet to catch a lover. What do they know about love? The time for the familiar beat, the wish-fulfillment moment, soon arrives. The Fisherwoman appeals to the Basketmaker (Peter Dinklage), a fellow-outcast, to cure her loneliness by making her a wicker husband.

The op-ed-informed mind luxuriates in the resonances that this movie continuously lobs at it. And the lightness of “Wicker” prevents us from ever feeling lectured at. For too short a time, it is a sexy movie. Alexander Skarsgård—his enormous form covered in an intricately knitted suit meant to mimic the wave and stroke of soft willow, all the way down to lashes drawn from flax fibre—takes the role of the Fisherwoman’s husband as his raison d’être, because it is. He is a dream man because he is not a man; he is made from earth, never baptized in the swamp of patriarchy. Wicker Husband and the Fisherwoman enter a haze of domestic bliss. Their sex breaks the bed. Wicker Husband is happy to fix it, and also to fix the roof, after he notices water dripping from the ceiling and onto the Fisherwoman’s foot, as she lies underneath him spread-eagle. The sound of their pleasure wakes up the whole town; it awakens a jealousy, confusion, and anger not only in the other women but in the men, with both camps amazed that marriage could ever beget something like pleasure. A culture war explodes. I won’t spoil the conflict, but know that it is not too dissimilar from the zealotry you might see on a manosphere message board.

The monster romance is as old as Pasiphaë tricking the white bull into bedding her, but a spate of recent offerings, across film and literature, especially, have come to form something less like a genre and more like a drug. The straight woman is in crisis, we’re told, and so she lightens her pain by engorging herself on works of romantasy, in which nonhuman creatures satisfy very human wants. The author Sarah J. Maas, known for her “A Court of Thorns and Roses” series, which devotees lovingly claim as fairy smut, has sold more than a hundred million books worldwide. In Hollywood, a certain ur-monster is getting notably and problematically hotter: Jacob Elordi’s Creature, as painstakingly imagined by the fable obsessive Guillermo del Toro, in his version of “Frankenstein,” is a soulful giant, with a shattered-pottery body and a long stare. In Maggie Gyllenhaal’s millennial update, “The Bride!,” Christian Bale reinvents the creature as a tall, dark, and handsome cinephile. You can imagine a version of “Wicker” that’s braver, accepting of the implicit queerness of its central couple, that does not make this monster so debonair and forthright and Skarsgårdian, to communicate something more real about the grotesque, and how, counterintuitively, it drives attraction.

The straight woman must find her love. I wasn’t expecting to think of Ingmar Bergman’s masterpiece “Scenes from a Marriage” after I watched “Wicker,” but, as I left the theatre, it came up. Bergman’s exploration of divorce, of the emotional alienation a marriage can bring, was blamed, in Sweden and elsewhere in Europe, for a spike in divorce rates. Causation seems dubious, but the point is about an outside force facilitating enlightenment. When the heteropessimist doubt begins to take over, in “Wicker,” when the Fisherwomen lets her mind be poisoned by rumor and gossip, the union starts to crumble. It’s the outside world, the ideological world, that introduces issues. “Wicker” ends with the promise of gender equality. As a marriage movie, it believes too deeply in the institution as a potentially liberating event in a woman’s life. The Husband is nothing more than hot; his undeveloped and cloistered psychology gives the marriage its ultimate peace. The film has to meet the needs of romance, but isn’t that the problem, the expectation that life moves like genre? ♦

items.title: Who’s the Real Victim?
items.description: What was to be done with the collaborators? In early December, 1945, a man and a woman in their thirties stepped onto a bus in Tel Aviv. Another passenger seemed to recognize the man; he went over to speak with him. “Are you Haim Molchadsky from Będzin?” he as
items.author: Paul Bloom; Azim Shariff
paragraphs: What was to be done with the collaborators? In early December, 1945, a man and a woman in their thirties stepped onto a bus in Tel Aviv. Another passenger seemed to recognize the man; he went over to speak with him. “Are you Haim Molchadsky from Będzin?” he asked. The man didn’t answer. The passenger repeated the question. More silence. Then the questioner shouted, in Yiddish, “You killed my family! You are responsible for the death of thousands of Jews!” Other passengers hit the man, and when the bus stopped and the couple fled, a crowd of riders and people from the street chased them, until they were rescued by police.

At the police station, the man confirmed that, yes, he was Haim Molchadsky, and, yes, when the Nazis took over Będzin, a town in Poland, they appointed him head of the “social department” of the Judenrat, or Jewish council. His job required him to select who would be sent to work camps, and, as he told the police, this made him many enemies. He was later promoted to head of the entire Judenrat. Then his luck ran out, and he was sent to Auschwitz.

This episode, recounted in Dan Porat’s book “Bitter Reckoning: Israel Tries Holocaust Survivors as Nazi Collaborators” (2019), was the kind of confrontation that led Israel to put on trial Jews who were accused of collaborating with the Nazis. As Porat tells it, the process carried its own agony, with heated public debate and shifts in popular opinion. At times, these men were treated as akin to Nazis. At other times, a softer view prevailed, and the collaborators were seen as Jewish victims trying, in extremis, to save themselves and their families.

In a classic essay, the Holocaust survivor Primo Levi explored the motives of these men—often it was self-interest, he argued, and sometimes it was a mimetic identification with their oppressors. Levi was interested in the difficulty of judging intermediate cases, those that lie in what he called the gray zone. He described how we are in the grips of a “Manichean tendency, which shuns half-tints and complexities”: a tendency reflected in Christian invocations of Judgment Day, which places the righteous here, the reprobates there, with no one in between.

That tendency has become the subject of considerable psychological research, most often on the reprobate side. Once someone is categorized as an enemy, their negative traits are exaggerated; they become a villain through and through. The pattern is most apparent in how we think about our political enemies. Surveys show that both Democrats and Republicans believe that sizable proportions of the other side favor wrongful imprisonment, tax fraud, embezzlement, adultery, animal abuse, and child pornography. (Only a few actually do.) In studies of “moral typecasting,” the psychologist Kurt Gray and his colleagues find that villains are seen as less capable of suffering; they become anti-victims of a sort. Villains like Ted Bundy are imagined to be relatively invulnerable to pain, even in a scenario as basic as stepping barefoot on a shard of glass.

There are clearly social forces at work here. Seeing complexity in villains can read as a worrisome softness, a lack of moral principle, or an indifference to victims’ suffering. Among Americans, there is little tolerance for people who talk sympathetically about the motives of the 9/11 hijackers. Likewise, anyone who talks with empathy about incels is liable to be mocked. But don’t incels also suffer? What about abusers who were themselves abused? Villain or victim? The proper response is “Why not both?” Yet such a response can feel unnatural, even repellent.

We’re as uncomfortable with moral ambiguity as with an awkwardly designed chair, and we react the same way—shifting and squirming until we find relief. We struggle to make sense of the Jewish collaborator or the Nazi guard who shows mercy, and so we simplify them reflexively, sorting them into distinct categories.

Much psychological research has focussed on the degradation of villains, but a symmetrical force works to elevate victims. In experimental studies, when we’re told about a character’s past misdeeds, we are later more likely to forget them if the character is described as a victim. When researchers tell stories about people who are victims of crimes—ranging from having an iPad stolen to being raped—such victims are seen as virtuous, more moral and more trustworthy than comparable people who have not been victimized. The researchers Jillian Jordan and Maryam Kouchaki describe this as the “virtuous victim” effect.

Maybe this is a good thing? It’s easy to see how vilifying villains poses a problem—it can motivate violent reprisal, cruel punishment, and cycles of violence—but, by contrast, elevating victims can serve certain social goods. Indeed, Jordan and Kouchaki argue that the main reason we morally elevate victims is to restore justice. We see victims as especially moral because that perception helps motivate both the punishment of perpetrators (we’re more outraged when those being harmed seem particularly innocent) and the aid offered to victims.

Yet there are downsides here, too. Once victims are imagined as near-saints, those who fail to meet the template can start to look suspect. Research on perceptions of victims of sexual assault finds that, even when there is indisputable physical resistance to an attack, people see the victim as less virtuous and less deserving of support if they had previously consented to sexual contact with their attacker, even a kiss. This perception holds even among the young and the politically and socially progressive, who would never consciously think that such acts are morally sullying. The same impulse that lifts some victims up can leave others, the imperfect ones, out in the cold.

If our psychological template of victimhood shapes how we judge and respond to victims, what happens in the heads of victims themselves? Many people have argued that victimhood enlightens, enriches, and improves. It toughens you up (“post-traumatic growth”) and makes you kinder (“altruism born of suffering”). On that view, the virtuous-victim effect becomes a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy: victims become virtuous.

This can certainly happen. The woman who founded Mothers Against Drunk Driving did so after losing her teen-age daughter to a drunk driver, and there are countless stories of rape survivors, or people living with spinal-cord injury or stroke, going on to work with organizations devoted to those who have faced similar adversity. Many of us carry narratives in which our own hardships helped make us the people we are today.

But it’s far from the rule. In a new book, “Is There Always Value to Adversity?,” the researcher Eranda Jayawickreme notes that, once you move beyond anecdote, the empirical support for such claims looks shaky. Some research even suggests that being victimized can make people mean. Individuals who were prompted to think about a time they had been victimized were less likely to offer help in an unrelated context. Moreover, people reminded of their own group’s victimization often show less sympathy for the suffering of other groups.

In a set of studies from Michael Wohl and Nyla Branscombe, Jewish Canadians tended to report a sense of collective guilt about the plight of Palestinians, but it diminished when they were reminded of the Holocaust. Another study found that Americans felt less collective guilt about harm done to Iraqis when they were reminded of 9/11—and even when they were reminded of Pearl Harbor. Primo Levi described how, in concentration camps, those who had suffered the longest sometimes met newcomers with something closer to cruelty than solidarity. The newcomers were derided and subjected to malicious pranks, resented for the lives they had led until their detention, for still having “the smell of home.” The logic seems to be: We have suffered, so why should we be obliged to care about anyone else?

Victimhood, then, offers two coveted benefits: moral absolution and moral license. By securing the role of victim in other people’s minds, we are absolved of perceptions of villainy. By securing it in our own minds, we license ourselves to act in ways we would condemn in others. Victimhood becomes a valuable moral currency, and the scramble for this privileged status is visible in debates over immigration and crime, free speech and “cancellation,” diversity policies and #MeToo. As Gray, the psychologist, has long argued, many of our culture-war battles can be read as fights over who counts as the real victim. Research suggests that some people are especially prone to this kind of “competitive victimhood,” including those with a stronger desire for power and less concern for others. In practice, though, it is a game anyone can play. As members of once privileged groups feel their status slipping, it is a short step to claiming victimhood themselves, sometimes to comic effect, as with talk of “white genocide” after a “Star Wars” film failed to cast white men in leading roles.

The inflation of victimhood comes at a cost. When we see victims, we start looking for villains. As we have widened the circle of people we feel bound to defend, we have also, as a consequence, swelled the ranks of those we seek to condemn.

How beholden are we to the pull of a villain-victim dichotomy? One can treat it as an indelible feature of human psychology, an unavoidable by-product of our appetite for simplicity and affiliation. Yet one of the revolutions in psychological research over the past decade or so has been a reluctance to treat localized observations as universal patterns, and a renewed attention to how much our psyche is shaped by cultural and historical context. Our typecasting may have a particular history.

The popular historian Tom Holland, in “Dominion: How the Christian Revolution Remade the World,” notes how novel it was for Christians to worship someone who suffered a humiliating death on the cross: “That a man who had himself been crucified might be hailed as a god could not help but be seen by people everywhere across the Roman world as scandalous, obscene, grotesque.” Friedrich Nietzsche blamed Christianity for the modern exaltation of victimhood, part of our “slave morality,” at the expense of what he took to be a more natural moral default: the celebration of mastery and power.

Whether or not Nietzsche was right about Christianity’s influence, the contemporary problem may be less about which moral categories we favor than about how crudely we apply them. In a recent article, the psychologist Joshua Conrad Jackson and his colleagues argue that the coarsening of moral categorization reflects the social dynamics of modern life, in which we deal so often with strangers and near-strangers, and lack the information for fine-grained judgment. In large correlational surveys in the United States, Singapore, Germany, and Brazil, they find that community size correlates with the bluntness of moral evaluation. The researchers also suggest a historical shift. An analysis of books over the past two centuries finds that judgments of moral character become more generalized; even in the course of the past two decades, blanket statements about “good people” and “bad people” have become more common.

Our social networks have expanded throughout history, moving from nomadic bands to agricultural villages to crowded cities to the disembodied multitudes of the internet. With so many people to evaluate—co-workers, politicians, historical figures, influencers, random people on social media—it’s hard to avoid moral shortcuts. Giving three dimensions to that many people asks more of our attention than we can reliably spare. Is it any wonder our moral culture drifts toward black and white, good and bad, victim and villain?

Yet we can push back and grant even strangers the nuance they deserve. Fiction provides one of the best laboratories for seeing how flexible our moral psychology can be. Some stories can harden moral perception, of course, pushing us to dichotomize the purely good and the purely evil, as in the moral pornography of superhero comics and revenge flicks. Writing in Aeon, the critic Catherine Nichols argues that this simplification is common in modern popular culture, which can end up “flattening all the deliberation and imagination of ethical action into a single thumbs up or thumbs down.”

But Nichols also asserts that older oral traditions often did better: Homer’s epics weren’t about good guys and bad guys. Plenty of fiction, across eras, does better, too, pushing us toward complex victims and villains, from the protagonists of Shakespeare’s tragedies to the classic antiheroes of cable TV. The worlds of Tony Soprano, Walter White, and Cersei Lannister become more compelling once we grant them the moral complexity we often refuse to grant the people on our side of the screen.

We should try harder. The truth is that we all live in the gray zone, a psychologically awkward reality in which villainy, victimhood, and heroism can mingle in a single person. In the turbulence of the real world, we will not find perfectly monstrous people or perfectly sympathetic ones. Not among our political enemies, not among our historical heroes, not among our martyrs, not among the incels, and not among the collaborators. They are as messy, as gray, and as imperfect as the people who judge them. ♦

items.title: Voters Reject the War in Iran
items.description: Watching from afar, Bruno Maçães, a Portuguese public intellectual and a former government minister, offered a pithy summation of the U.S. midterm elections. “So regime change came in Texas before Tehran,” he posted on X. The blue wave that crashed down on Pre
items.author: Ishaan Tharoor
paragraphs: Watching from afar, Bruno Maçães, a Portuguese public intellectual and a former government minister, offered a pithy summation of the U.S. midterm elections. “So regime change came in Texas before Tehran,” he posted on X. The blue wave that crashed down on President Donald Trump surged through America’s second most populous state and led to Democrats clinching every statewide race, turfing out the incumbent governor, Greg Abbott, and delivering a Senate seat to the Party for the first time since 1988. Late into the night in Austin, people were out in the streets, honking car horns and celebrating like, as one observer put it, “an Eastern European city that just overthrew a dictator.” Change came in Senate races across the country, including in South Carolina, where the seat long held by the late senator Lindsey Graham, a tireless opponent of the Iranian regime, was lost by his sister to a Democratic challenger.

The military mission to defeat the regime in Tehran that both Trump and Graham championed earlier this year ended up being the Republicans’ undoing. That was the view of Vice-President J. D. Vance, who on Wednesday morning fired the first salvo in what may develop into an internecine G.O.P. war over foreign policy in the months to come. He said in a long post on X that “the reason we lost is the war.” (According to an NBC exit poll, sixty-three per cent of American voters disagreed with Trump’s taking the country into the war.) Trump, of course, has spent much of the past year engaging in conflict with the Islamic Republic, bombing it repeatedly, in coördination with the Israelis, while piling on economic and political pressure. But his decision to launch a war of choice—one that remains hugely unpopular, and one that failed to topple the regime as initially promised, triggered a spiralling set of geo-economic global crises, drove up gas prices and other daily costs for Americans, divided his own MAGA base, and still may flare up again in the coming days—is at the core of the historic rebuke that his Presidency and his party received on Tuesday night.

The Iranian speaker of parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, offered his reading of events: “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” His assessment was curiously echoed by John Bolton, the former Trump and Bush Administration official who has advocated the bombing of Iran and the defenestration of its regime for two decades. But this effort is too shambolic for his liking. “Our lengthy operation against Iran is a direct consequence of Trump surrounding himself with a cadre of yes-men,” Bolton observed, referring to the small circle of White House advisers who backed Trump’s instincts in starting a conflict in the Middle East that no regional power outside of Israel wanted. “Americans are not happy to be in another seemingly endless war, and they are placing the blame squarely on Trump.”

In conversations with reporters as news of Republican defeats tumbled in, Trump waved away accountability for the wipeout and defended the war. “I am totally convinced that my decision in Iran, for the long term good of the country and even the world, was an absolutely correct one,” he told Politico. The day before, the United States had carried out what officials described as “limited” strikes for “defensive” purposes on Iranian targets on Qeshm Island, in the Persian Gulf. Trump did not dismiss speculation, amid his electoral losses, that he could resume full-fledged hostilities. In the days before the midterms, Qatari mediators had plunged into a fresh round of furtive diplomacy between the United States and Iran, but talks are still at an impasse. Trump insists that Iran’s military capabilities have been thoroughly degraded, but the regime remains defiant, and has vowed a wider arc of retaliation should the United States and Israel restart their offensive, even threatening to hit U.S. assets based in Europe.

At a regional forum in Bahrain over the weekend, senior officials from the Gulf states were frustrated about the path forward. The war has exacted a toll on their economies and shattered illusions about their security. “We find ourselves drawn within a crisis that we worked diplomatically very hard to try to avert,” Anwar Gargash, a top adviser to the President of the United Arab Emirates, said in a speech. He added that his country was “braced for the worst,” even as it worked for a regional solution to the ongoing standoff. Elsewhere, there’s no sympathy for the complexity of the challenge facing the American and Israeli strategists who instigated the conflict. In June of last year, the United States and Israel launched the Twelve-Day War, an intense period of bombardments and missile strikes that led to hundreds of civilian deaths and the supposed crippling of Iran’s nuclear program. At the time, the German Chancellor, Friedrich Merz, praised the military campaigns against Iran, telling reporters that “that is the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.” But that round proved insufficient from both Trump’s and the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s perspectives. In February, Trump, possibly goaded into action by Netanyahu, launched a more open-ended operation. The ensuing months of chaos and spiking prices have punished countries everywhere, including in Europe. This past weekend, Merz lamented that “businesses and consumers in Europe have paid more than 100 billion euros extra because energy has become more expensive as a result of this conflict,” and insisted that there was no military solution to the conflict. He seemed to have had enough of the “dirty work.”

The midterms have also reflected a shift in Americans’ views on Israel, with candidates such as Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s new senator-elect, not shying away from denouncing its war on Gaza and its apparent role in provoking Trump’s Middle East imbroglio. Democrats in Congress are likely to restrict military aid to Israel, which this week Trump, perhaps in anticipation, said that he was considering sunsetting by the end of the year, anyway—a declaration that surprised many analysts in Washington, given existing agreements between the United States and Israel, which extend into 2028. Republican voters, especially younger ones, also increasingly oppose Israel’s actions, and don’t want to engage in wars on its behalf. Officials in Tehran have been paying attention. “The American public is tired of and angry about the Israeli regime’s parasitic behavior toward the United States,” Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign-ministry spokesman, said ahead of the midterms. “The U.S. is devoting its credibility, wealth, and standing to a regime that thinks only about war.” Israel is itself in a political transition, with government-formation talks under way after an election last week delivered more seats to Netanyahu’s opponents than to his own party and its allies. Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats, a center-left Israeli faction, said that the U.S. midterms revealed “just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans,” and argued that a coalition led by the opposition could help “restore Israel’s standing in the world.”

Trump endorsed Netanyahu in his reëlection bid, but it’s been obvious to most analysts that the President’s interests do not fully align with those of the embattled Israeli leader. “Netanyahu clearly wants to go back to war with Iran. It would help him politically in this moment of government formation,” Rachel Brandenburg, a former Pentagon official now at the Israel Policy Forum, told me. For Trump, she added, that makes far less sense. “It will be more a question of how he wants to frame victory, and if there is actually a case to be made that another round of military strikes can lead to some better sense of victory. I have not seen that case.” On Wednesday, as Trump gave reporters a look at the construction site of his White House ballroom, he claimed that he had had “no choice” but to hit Iran’s nuclear facilities and was unapologetic about the conduct of the war. But he showed little enthusiasm for an extended effort to finish the job.

Still, maybe there was another way he could win. On the morning of the midterms, he mused on Fox News that, even if the elections proved a rebuke to his Administration, he was still at a “ninety-nine-per-cent approval rating” among Israelis. “If people ever got tired of me in the U.S.,” he said, “I’ll move to Israel and become Prime Minister.” ♦

items.title: The 7-Days-a-Week, 12-Months-a-Year School
items.description: On the first Saturday morning of the school year, Horacio and three of his children — Margoth, 8; Maithais, 6; and Noah, 5 — walked up 139th Street in the Bronx toward the charter school the kids attend. At the top of the hill, a pair of gray doors (which have
items.author: Lauren Hilgers
paragraphs: On the first Saturday morning of the school year, Horacio and three of his children — Margoth, 8; Maithais, 6; and Noah, 5 — walked up 139th Street in the Bronx toward the charter school the kids attend. At the top of the hill, a pair of gray doors (which have since been painted blue) swung open, and the family stepped inside. “I’ll be back around 2,” he told the safety officers sitting behind a desk in the lobby. One was Ellen Coleman, whom everyone knows as Ms. Ellen. She leaned back in her chair, grinned, and greeted each kid by name. “You sure you don’t want to leave them for longer?” she asked. “We’re getting dinner.”

The school, called Strive Charter School, opened in August. It was founded not with a lofty pedagogical mandate or unique classroom-behavior strategy but with the goal of making life significantly easier for working parents. The founder, Eric Grannis, takes pride in Strive’s academic offerings but knows that the school’s main selling point is its hours of operation. Horacio learned about Strive over the summer, when he was handed a pamphlet at the entrance to a subway station. “Open from 7am to 7pm,” the paper read. “7 days a week, 12 months a year.”

During the regular school year — from September to late June — class is in session five days a week, from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The extended part of the schedule (early mornings, evenings, weekends, and July and August) is optional and free of charge. Those hours will be filled with a variety of programming: tutoring, sports, art, music, viewings in a planetarium, and free play. In the summer, the full week will run like a classic day camp with some additional academic components, including required reading periods, tutoring, and enrichment. Dropping off and picking up a child outside of regular school hours, according to Grannis, should be as simple as stopping by Starbucks for a preordered cup of coffee.

In Strive, Grannis has embraced a dual role for schools as both centers of education and an integral form of child care that many teachers and administrators have long resisted. But the vast majority of working parents in America depend on schools to do their jobs, and Grannis believes educational institutions can and should do even more to help parents stay employed. Across the United States, there are about 23 million kids unable to access after-school programming whose families would enroll them if they had the option. And in New York City, the demand for free or affordable after-hours programming far outstrips the availability. In the 2023–24 school year, there were around 150,000 complimentary after-school slots for the over 643,000 children enrolled in the city’s K–8 public schools. The city comptroller’s office estimates a shortfall of more than 390,000 seats next school year. What’s more, around 30 percent of employed people work over the weekend, which makes Saturday and Sunday child care a necessity too. Strive, which serves grades K–4, aims to bridge these gaps and then some while sticking to a standard public-school budget.

Grannis started the school with assistance from his wife, Eva Moskowitz, co-founder and CEO of New York City’s largest and arguably most controversial charter-school network, Success Academy. The two met in high school and dated through college. He worked for Success Academy early on and explains, with some enjoyment, that when his wife was hired to lead the organization, his first and only recommendation for her was to fire him. (Grannis still does pro-bono work for Success Academy.) Moskowitz has spent years openly criticizing the city’s teachers union, and Grannis shares her sense of embattled disdain. Both say they are looking to serve students and this task has been impeded by complacency and bureaucracy. “This is how it is,” he wrote atop an email exchange he forwarded me between himself and the city Department of Education. “They always make things impossible for us.”

To create Strive, Success Academy’s board voted to transfer one of their charter-school licenses to Strive’s board of trustees, whose members Grannis had recruited. The move was then approved by the SUNY board of trustees — one of the governing bodies overseeing charter schools in the city. The transfer was subsequently challenged in court by the United Federation of Teachers, who argued that the license transfer violated a citywide cap on the number of charter schools in operation. Grannis, unbothered, expects a judge will throw out the case soon. With the school now open, he is focused on the practical challenges of delivering on the promises he made to the parents who took a risk on an untested enterprise and enrolled.

“I work anywhere from five to seven days a week,” Horacio said, straddling the doorstep at Strive that Saturday morning. “And even if it’s five, the weekdays are so crazy. Weekends are my only real time with the kids.” But on Saturday, he was using the school’s open-door policy to keep his older kids busy while he accomplished some errands with his youngest son. He just wanted a little bit of time. “Whatever you need,” said Ms. Ellen. “You run your errands. We’ve got them up there doing art.”

In the 19th century, the school calendar varied widely across America and even within individual states. Schools in one district might run for three months of the year, while those just a town over were in session for ten months. But one commonality all schools shared, wrote historian Kenneth Gold in his essay “The Myth of Summer Vacation and the Agrarian Calendar,” was that they were open in the summer. In fact, in many urban schools, attendance numbers during those months were the highest of the year. It is a fallacy that the modern-day public-school schedule — with its long summer break, weekends off, and early-afternoon dismissal time — came about to encourage seasonal farmwork. In reality, as the century progressed, the modern schedule arose from what Gold describes as a perceived “inferiority of summer term teachers” (the vast majority of whom were women); a series of summer illness outbreaks and heat waves that drove wealthy urbanites to flee cities for country homes; the need to expand, construct, and repair more school buildings as the city’s population grew; and eventually, a decline in student attendance, and a desire for standardization. By 1867, summer vacations in New York City were seven weeks long.

School leaders did worry about teachers’ skills growing soft over the break (concerns over a student “summer slide” didn’t take shape until the 1920s) but eventually justified it as a time for renewal and professional training. Summer education conferences flourished. By the dawn of the 20th century, the school-calendar model had become largely standardized: “A 180-day school held during the fall, winter, and spring; punctuated by a 2-3-month summer vacation,” Gold wrote.

By 1918, every state had some form of legislation making school compulsory, though what compulsory meant varied greatly. At nearly the same moment, early versions of after-school programs began springing up across New York, especially in immigrant neighborhoods. Settlement houses provided food and activities for children in lower Manhattan. A playground movement in the late 1800s prompted the construction of outdoor play spaces often overseen by city-employed supervisors who organized games and saw to the children’s safety. Starting in the 1930s, the city created what has become one of the largest publicly funded in-school after-school programs in the country. The school day began, almost universally, at 9 a.m. until the 1960s and 1970s, when some districts began to move the drop-off time earlier to accommodate parents who needed to commute to work afterward.

Schools across the United States have experimented with the calendar for decades, although none has gone as far as Grannis. In 2018, about 3 percent of public schools in the U.S. maintained year-round schedules. The Center for American Progress has been advocating for a school day that runs from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. for at least a decade (though without an even earlier drop-off and later pickup option, this tweak would still leave most parents scrambling for child care). KIPP Public Charter Schools used to have a program that required all enrolled students to attend school one Saturday a month, but it has mostly been phased out. No school has attempted the one-stop shop Grannis envisions. The closest competitor to Strive in New York City is the Harlem Children’s Zone charter-school network. It has an academic calendar that stretches from September into late June and offers a summer program in July and August, all in the hopes that truncated breaks will help limit learning loss. It also offers free after-school programming until 7 p.m. Monday through Thursday and until 6 p.m. on Friday. The schools aren’t open on the weekends, but they do offer Saturday programming at select central HCZ community centers. But overall, schools in the U.S. are almost uniformly closed over the weekends, which makes Strive’s Saturday and Sunday hours arguably its boldest, most appealing feature.

On the first Saturday of the school year, I followed Maithais and Margoth into Strive’s weekend programming. Grannis had warned me that he was still working out the kinks. For example, there had been problems with a missed bus stop, and the kitchen was still not operational; meals were sandwiches and other packaged foods that didn’t require cooking. The building Strive occupies is owned by St. Luke’s Catholic Church, which doesn’t allow the school to use the space on Sundays, and Grannis was still searching for an alternative. The DOE, he complained in an email, had been opaque and unhelpful. (In October, Grannis reported that the kitchen was now functional and that he had found a likely home for his Sunday programming— a Success Academy campus.) Grannis has hired a soccer coach for the weekends, but he’ll only work on Sundays. There will also be basketball, eventually, but the school’s gym has not yet been set up.

So far, Grannis has hired a staff of 40 teachers and assistants. Especially for experienced teachers, the school’s salaries are markedly lower than in New York City public schools. There, veteran teachers can earn more than $128,000 per year, and entry-level salaries range from $71,314 for those with no experience and no master’s degree to $80,166 for those starting with a master’s degree. Strive, by contrast, offers full-time assistant teachers $60,000 per year for 50 hours per week and $80,000 per year to lead classroom teachers with two years of experience; each subsequent year of experience adds only $2,000. And importantly, teachers at Strive are required to be at school for 210 instructional days, as opposed to the standard public school’s 180. The remainder of the extended hours at Strive are staffed largely by teaching assistants paid about $25 per hour. “There are lots of people who have experience in the world of education who don’t have Harvard degrees or a B.A., necessarily,” says Grannis. At most DOE schools, teachers leading after-hours programming or summer enrichment earn an additional $63.04 an hour. Its salary structure has all but ensured the Strive faculty will be inexperienced compared with that of a typical public school.

Grannis estimates that keeping the school open on Saturday and Sunday will cost Strive around $5,000 each week, or $250,000 over the course of the year. When I visited, Grannis pulled out his phone to check the math and informed me that, working from a budget of around $9 million a year, weekends will take up just 3 percent of his overall budget if he can attract 325 students to the school. “If we stick to the current enrollment,” he told me, “I will have to do some fundraising.” A shrinking student population is one of the most pressing difficulties city schools face.

Before I arrived that morning, Grannis sent me a barrage of emails. Among them was a message warning that attendance might not be high. “I honestly don’t care if you report that attendance was low because my view has always been that the point is to give parents optionality,” Grannis wrote. “Even if only a relatively small number of children come on any given optional day, that may be totally critical to that family.”

When Horacio arrived with his children at 9:15 a.m., there was a steady trickle of parents coming in and out, early proof that the demand Grannis predicted is real. One mother came in asking to order a school shirt for her son, another to retrieve a student who had gotten sick. “He’s not feeling his best,” Ms. Ellen told me sympathetically. A pile of boxes sat near her desk —all packages of books and LEGO sets Grannis had ordered. Myasia Ennis, the head of Strive’s after-school programming at the time (she has since left, and three lead teachers have taken over the project), came in and out of the lobby, keeping tabs on everyone.

Margoth and Maithais stood uncertainly in front of Ms. Ellen’s desk, both wearing their Strive polo shirts, as their father chatted with other parents. Margoth was quiet and wide-eyed as she followed Ennis, looking slightly unsure about what she had gotten herself into.

The first-floor hallway was quiet. The kindergarten classes were brightly decorated and carpeted; purchasing the rugs was a particular preoccupation for Grannis over the summer. Down the hall was the activity room, where the younger children built block towers and worked with Play-Doh under the supervision of Emprise Williams, a first-grade teaching aide and weekend teacher who sat on a chair at a slight remove. “You guys are doing great,” Williams told her charges. “Take a minute and kiss your brains.”

As Margoth settled in, an older group of children played Uno and drew with markers. She sat quietly on the rug while a teacher’s aide played name games with the kids. A group of girls watched in awe as Margoth pulled a pack of cheddar fries out of her backpack. “You got cheddar fries?” asked one girl, starting to play with Margoth’s hair. Margoth nodded.
“You’re lucky,” said the girl. She introduced herself as Emma. Her friend, she said, was named Phoenix.
The girls discussed whether they liked the school so far. They had heard rumors about a basketball program and soccer.
“I like it here,” said one of the girls. “I might just come every day.”
“You’re joking,” said Emma. “Who wants to wake up at 6 every morning?”
They squealed in horror at the thought. Then the aide told them it was time for lunch.

I first met Grannis in March in a coffee shop in South Harlem not far from his home. By the time I arrived, Grannis had parked his bike outside, ordered breakfast, and set out a copy of the book he co-wrote with Moskowitz, A+ Parenting, to give me. Grannis is an ideas man in the classical mold. He has theories about classroom layouts and teaching math, about meal plans, student engagement, and the value of the movie musical 1776. In a near-ubiquitous button-down and slacks, he doesn’t look like a fitness buff, but he is, in fact, an avid biker. Even when he’s not exercising, he is often slightly out of breath from either enthusiasm or activity.

Strive’s educational philosophy was shaped by Grannis’s own experience, what he likes to call “the tasting tour of American pedagogy” (or, more accurately, elite education). He went to the famous West Side Montessori School for nursery school and P.S. 145 and then Collegiate for elementary school. He transferred to the Bank Street School during middle school and attended Exeter and later Stuyvesant for high school. His fondest memories, he says, were at Bank Street, where he outpaced his classmates in math and the teacher gave him and another classmate a textbook so they could study independently. It’s an experience he says he wants to recreate for students at Strive.

Much of the curriculum Strive is using has already been tested at Success Academy, which has a track record of high scores on state tests but also a reputation for harsh discipline strategies and a fair amount of attrition as students move into later grades. The school’s math curriculum is based on a series called Context for Learning Mathematics and focuses on mathematical understanding rather than rote memorization. (Grannis happens to know the creator and author of Context for Learning, Cathy Fosnot, and on one of my visits to the school over the summer, she was there training teachers herself.) The literacy program, Grannis says, embraces a spirit of independent inquiry he hopes will set Strive apart.

The first principal Grannis hired, Rebecca Goodsell, previously worked as an assistant principal at Success Academy, but she left halfway through the summer to tend to a family emergency. Her replacement, Shaniqua Sonnee, was formerly the director of enrichment at Hunter College Elementary School, a highly selective K–12 school in New York. Sonnee has recruited several of her former co-workers from Hunter to lead, among other things, Strive’s science classroom and after-school programming. Grannis also hired a recent college graduate to help him build an app for families, called Strive Arrive, that he says will eventually enable parents to log on and alert the school they are on their way to drop off or pick up their child. Through location tracking, the app will estimate the parent’s time of arrival and, theoretically, with around ten minutes’ advance notice, enable staff to pack up the child’s backpack and get them to the front door for a seamless pickup. “Then they can just walk right out when you arrive,” Grannis told me. So far, the app is not fully operational and the school is handling arrival and dismissal in the usual analog way.

“What they’re offering us has been priceless,” Daniel Ramirez, a father of a Strive first-grader, told me over the phone when I asked how his daughter’s first month has gone. “This idea with this school, it’s just brilliant. And it’s not only brilliant, it’s considerate. It’s considerate of the lives of hard-working people.”

In the months I spent following Grannis as he got Strive off the ground, all of the parents I spoke with who were considering the school faced formidable familial and logistical challenges. More than one had to quit a job over the summer to care for their children. They told me about their children’s strengths, struggles, and interests; the quirks of their work schedules; and the impossibility of efficiently managing their days.

Ramirez lives in the Bronx and works in security in Yonkers, and he chose Strive after the charter school his daughter attended for kindergarten announced it would admit kids to the after-school program by lottery with no guarantee of admission. “My wife and I both work,” Ramirez told me. “I’m not in the business of ‘see if it happens or not.’ I need some certainty.” When a co-worker mentioned he was moving his daughter from Success Academy to Strive, Ramirez decided to follow suit. When I spoke to him in October, he was thrilled with his choice. “They give my daughter a lot of homework,” Ramirez told me. “And we are on top of what’s going on. We ask her a lot of questions. And Aria loves it. She loves her teachers already.” Ramirez and his wife have been using the school’s Saturday hours, although sparingly. “At the end of the day, she’s our child. She’s not the school’s child,” he said.

Raychelle, whose name has been changed to protect her children’s privacy, works a hybrid job in hospital administration. She moved back to the Bronx from upstate New York over the summer. “But working from home doesn’t mean the kids can stay with you. My mom used to help, but now my mom is older,” she explains. She found what she described as a perfect school for her son, who has autism, in the Bronx. But she wanted an academically rigorous fit for her 7-year-old daughter and knew she needed it to be convenient since she was handling both of her kids’ transportation to school herself.

A few weeks into the school year, Raychelle said she had come to love the Saturday program at Strive. Her daughter wanted to go every week, Raychelle told me. “She’s like, ‘No, I want to go to school. They have dance or soccer or Monopoly.’ One day, I was so proud, she was upset that I came to pick her up too early. She said, ‘Mom, I had four properties.’” But Raychelle also shared concerns about the school’s ability to smoothly deliver its curriculum and the meager class sizes in the older grades. “I worry about this learning process as they go through the kinks,” she told me. “I hope they can feed that gift that she has.” She confessed to me that she feels slightly guilty about picking a school primarily because it fits her own schedule, rather than her daughter’s interests and strengths. “That’s my greatest fear. I was up last night thinking about it. I couldn’t go to sleep thinking about it.”

Horacio, Margoth and Maithais’s dad, works in a bodega in the South Bronx. During our first conversation over the phone, someone in the background interrupted him, cursing. He politely asked me to excuse him. He put down the phone and I heard him telling the man to leave. “Get out of the store,” he said sternly. And then again, there was yelling. After some commotion, Horacio picked up the phone again. “I’m sorry for that,” he said.

Last year, as Horacio’s family went through a rough patch, his children did not attend school at all. “I’m just trying to create more stability for me and the children at the moment,” Horacio told me. “The best way we can is through education and keeping them busy.”

He believes in consistency. He believes that, while you may have all the talents in the world, you’re nothing without routine. He is proud of the fact that aside from a bout of the flu and hand, foot, and mouth disease, they’ve had perfect attendance at school this academic year. Horacio lives in a family shelter, where kids may not be left home without adult supervision. He is hoping to find housing somewhere in the South Bronx so his children can stay close to Strive.

He told me that his job as a parent — in addition to giving his kids love and a stable routine — is finding out what they excel at and encouraging them. He wants them to know how to be with other people in the real world, rather than online. Margoth loves to draw, so Horacio fosters it. His youngest, he predicts, will end up in construction or demolition because of his tendency to take things apart. “He’s my little bull in the china shop,” Horacio laughed. His middle child is, at the moment, obsessed with dinosaurs.
“I can see already that Strive is taking care of the academic needs that the babies have,” Horacio told me.

In an idealized America, parents would be available to collect their children when the school day ends and to then oversee their kids at home with the benevolent calm of the mothers of our imagined past, watching them play as the afternoon light dwindles, no iPads or Xboxes in sight. For real working parents, however, the search for child care — after school, on weekends, in the summer, when the babysitter calls out sick, when camp is too expensive — is perpetual and stressful.

Teachers may be wary of conflating education with child care; they may feel the association denigrates or mischaracterizes their expertise and impact. But as the pandemic and its exodus of mothers from the workforce demonstrated, schools function as the most widely used and most effective form of child care we have in America. The overlap of education and child care doesn’t have to look exactly like Strive. The program could be teacher-led or built through partnerships with community organizations. It could be implemented in established and better-funded public schools that give enrolled families more confidence in their infrastructure and academics. But Grannis’s notion to expand in-school child care into the weekends and summer is so intuitive that it’s hard to believe he’s the first to get it off the ground.

On Strive’s first free Saturday, lunch (sandwiches and fruit) was followed by recess. After that, Grannis gathered all the kids, younger and older, and had them help unpack the LEGOs he had ordered. The last student left at 7 p.m., after dinner. By the end of the day, just over 40 of the school’s around 200 students had passed through the doors. He sent an email afterward thanking parents for dropping off their kids and included a video of the unboxing. “We didn’t have a lot of formal programming because we haven’t gotten everything in place yet, so children engaged in a lot of informal play, but that can actually be very educational,” he wrote. “If you ask a class of students if any of them want to help with something, all of their hands shoot up. It is so important to give children opportunities to do work.”

There is a part of me that is loath to see children spending time in any single institution for a 12-hour day. Watching students go in and out of Strive on a Saturday was bittersweet; although they looked excited and their parents relieved, I was struck by the fact that none of these families could afford, as Grannis put it, to “buy time” with their children. “Lower-income parents can’t afford to free up their time the way more affluent families can,” Grannis told me when we first met as he explained why a school like Strive is necessary. Parents, for example, may not have the resources to move closer to their jobs or hire help for time-consuming chores, nor do many have the autonomy to set a work schedule that accommodates their children’s needs. In situations like these, a flexible and familiar school where children feel safe and comfortable is an obvious and ideal child-care solution. Unlike many charter schools in New York, Strive does not weed out kids and families unable to meet attendance expectations or strict homework requirements. Any child who wants to enroll at Strive is welcome (though Strive is currently unable to accommodate students with certain individualized education plans), and in fact, the school is seeking more students.

Grannis is aware of the challenges involved in keeping the school running and funded. While the parents and teachers I interviewed attributed the difficulties of the start of the year, including faculty resignations and facility problems, to growing pains, outsiders — especially those opposed to charter schools in general — have questioned the scrappiness of this kind of venture and the benefit of extending the presence of a new, untested school in any child’s life. There were moments when I, too, strongly questioned whether Grannis and Strive could succeed. On one sparsely attended school-tour day at Strive, the operation had the feel of a start-up venture. A welcome video for touring parents, played inside an inflatable planetarium, featured a Star Wars–style yellow scroll and AI avatars of then-principal Goodsell and her vice-principal. Grannis hired a video editor in the Ukraine to help him produce it. He told me Goodsell moved too much in the regular recorded version, rendering it unusable.

The parents I spoke with early in the year have had somewhat mixed experiences in the time since. By the end of October, Raychelle, the parent who had been worried about the school’s academics, had moved her daughter to another school. “It wasn’t a fit,” she told me. “But I still believe in the school’s mission. I’m still a fan.” Ramirez and Horacio, however, remain happy with their choice. Their kids are settling in, doing homework, and learning.

And within the school, Grannis’s optimism has proven contagious. With Sonnee, he has managed to recruit a staff of aides and teachers who, when I spoke with them, were overtly enthusiastic about the school’s aims. Strive’s assistant principal and science department chair, Andrea Coleman, told me she has arranged a partnership with the Bronx Zoo. “We’re going to do real data collection,” she said. “We’re trying to create the scientists of the future.” Williams, the weekend teacher, said she felt blessed to have found the place. Ms. Ellen told me her employer, a security company, tried to relocate her to another school, but she refused to go. When she’s at work, she likes to imagine how much a school like Strive would have helped when her own children were still at home.

With school well into its second month, Grannis says he has already stepped away from classroom operations, which are now in the hands of Sonnee and an assistant principal. Sonnee smiles patiently while he talks. “We work well together,” she told me as the two reviewed a color-coded weekly schedule.
