items.title: Balming Tiger - Kinfolk
items.description: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
paragraphs: An hour with the alternative K-pop group.
- Hair & Makeup Mahito Ohtani

My Zoom interview with Balming Tiger is chaotic. Five of the eleven members are on the call, each in a different location in Seoul. Omega Sapien is at a salon, dyeing his hair green for a music video. Leesuho is munching on a snack with a soda. Unsinkable is strumming a guitar, on mute. bj wnjn is lying in bed in sweatpants. Mudd the Student sits calmly, his long wavy hair dyed like a lion’s mane. There are multiple conversations all happening at once as we wait for the other members, some of whom never show up.

When the interview starts, however, the group is focused and attentive. A self-described “alternative K-pop group” from South Korea, Balming Tiger is composed of two women and nine men. They’ve been described by critics and fans as pioneering, experimental, an artist collective beyond music and, last but not least, “a group of hairstyles that elderly Koreans would definitely hate,” a running joke among fans online. In their two studio albums and a debut mixtape, released in 2018, they sing about alienation, absurdist humor, friendship and love, pigeons and frogs.
“We want Balming Tiger to be its own genre,” says Omega Sapien, a rapper and singer-songwriter, holding up the phone as his hair, now fluorescent green, is being rinsed out in the sink.

Ironically, Balming Tiger’s alternative identity depends on its proximity to South Korea’s best-known cultural export. K-pop, literally Korean popular music, is itself less of a distinctive genre than a cultural phenomenon. Within South Korea, it can refer to a wide variety of styles including ballads, EDM and hip-hop. Abroad, K-pop most often means idols: entertainers whose music and image are strictly produced by massive entertainment conglomerates, such as mega-groups like BTS and Blackpink, or soloists such as Somi and G-Dragon. However you define it, K-pop is a glittering symbol of Korean soft power. The stratospheric success of different Korean musicians in the past decade—especially BTS on the US charts—has catapulted K-pop into a household name everywhere.
“Honestly, we don’t really think about what genre we are, other than during interviews,” says Leesuho, one of Balming Tiger’s producers and video directors.

True as that may be, the label they have chosen—alternative K-pop—is a strategic choice, devised by the group’s founder and creative director, San Yawn. With K-pop’s international popularity, Balming Tiger has smartly positioned themselves as adjacent to something familiar to the global audience—giving themselves a wide playground to try anything and everything.

“It’s always more fun when the possibilities are open,” San Yawn later explains over email. “Whatever we are now won’t be ‘the final version’ of us. We have no idea what we’ll be in the future, but we want to continue to express the little joys of the world in our own language.”

It’s true that the structure of Balming Tiger is wildly different from a conventional K-pop idol act. Idols are usually conceptually defined by an agency, with clear roles differentiating members, for example “lead vocalist” or “lead dancer.” Idol wannabes train, sometimes for years, to audition for a role. Once the group is formed, the performers are the faces of a much larger and more intricate corporate structure.

There were no trainees in Balming Tiger. And no auditions—think more “Wanna join?” conversations at waffle houses and barbecue joints. Nor are all of Balming Tiger’s members performers—their 11 members include producers, photographers, music video directors, A&R managers and DJs. Some faces are more familiar, like those who sing, rap and dance in the music videos (usually Omega Sapien, bj wnjn, Mudd the Student and Sogumm, with cameos by others), but behind the scenes, everything is more collaborative and collective.

Balming Tiger can be seen as less a band with a signature sound than a creative universe, a rainforest of different species colliding and coexisting with each other. From their critically acclaimed debut mixtape, Homie304, to their first studio album in 2023, January Never Dies, to the 2026 album, Gongbu, Balming Tiger’s music defies classification—as does their creative direction. Their videos embrace Hong Kong noir (“SOS”), a ’90s boy band parody (“Big Butt”), and the industrial-era alleyways of the Euljiro neighborhood in Seoul (“Sexy Nukim,” featuring BTS member RM). Their sounds traverse old Korean pop, EDM, psychedelic rock and—of course—hip-hop, many of the members’ first love and forays into music.
“We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

The origins of Balming Tiger can be traced to Itaewon, one of the most culturally diverse neighborhoods in Seoul. It’s a place where the city’s only mosque towers over a hill, next to mom-and-pop stores and cockroach-filled villas, the US military base and ritzy alleyways that are home to the Samsung family and BTS members.

“Balming Tiger is basically a meeting of people that are full of holes,” San Yawn once said on the Korean talk show Moneygraphy. These “holes”—loneliness, for instance, and the desire to fill them through music and art—were what brought together this cacophonous collective through a random series of events starting in 2017, when San Yawn began looking for a crew.

They met at San Yawn’s home in Itaewon and spent much of their time together at Trans 201, on the second floor of a run-down villa in an area popularly known as Transgender Hill. The members started connecting in various ways: through friends of friends, an Instagram message, a chance listening to a future member’s SoundCloud account. “Trans 201 was Omega Sapien and bj wnjn’s house,” recalls Mudd the Student. “The space was very damp and full of dark energy.”

“After a heavy rain, the ceiling in my room was bulging with water, like a giant pimple,” Omega Sapien adds. “We had horrible mold problems. bj wnjn and I split the rent, which was like 600,000 won [approximately $400], and I didn’t even have that money, so my older sister helped pay half of my 300,000. It really was an awful time.”

“Not for me,” says bj wnjn, a vocalist, singer-songwriter and producer. “That space is one of the most memorable moments of my youth. Even with the cockroaches and all that noise from the clubs outside, there was a joy particular to that time.”

Memories like this are specific to Balming Tiger, to Seoul, and permeate their art in ways that can’t be manufactured. The evolving members remain consistently curious about their own experiences and the world around them. There have been some member changes over the years, including the exit of Byung Un, a beloved front man in the early years. But the joy—and the DNA—from that early, formative period is still alive, holding everyone together 10 years later. “There’s a childlike attitude that we never lost as a group,” Sogumm, a singer-songwriter and vocalist, says in an email. “A simplicity that feels honest.”

Often, Balming Tiger’s childlike experiments feel much deeper than mere fun and play, resonating like a sharp resistance against the norms imposed by others. Sometimes this critique feels particularly Korean—like in the 2023 music video of “Kamehameha,” where exhausted office workers are forced to drink with their superiors at a hoesik, an after-work company gathering notorious for heavy alcohol consumption. And at other times it feels fantastically delocalized, like in “UP!” where a cashier at a mega supermarket climbs up the mountain of objects he must clear, reaching for the sky.

“It’s different for me,” says Omega Sapien, who grew up in Korea, China, Japan and the US. “I’m not trying to be rebellious. But I do like provoking a sense of discomfort in others. I like creating differences of opinion through what we do.”

“I’m less interested in making others uncomfortable than in creating a sense of wonder,” says Mudd the Student, who is from Busan, down south. “I love art that makes me feel things for the first time. I suppose that can sometimes make people uncomfortable.”

Despite their almost tongue-in-cheek label as alternative K-pop, Balming Tiger is grateful to the K-pop industry for opening doors for other Korean musicians. The group has performed at major music festivals including SXSW in the US, Primavera Sound in Spain and Fuji Rock Festival in Japan. Their creative orbit is similarly wide-ranging: they’ve collaborated with artists including Japanese girl group ATARASHII GAKKO! and RM of BTS, while independently creating content celebrating figures they admire, such as Korean artist Lee Bul and Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Their music video with RM, “Sexy Nukim,” remains Balming Tiger’s most viewed, with 20 million views.

“People often think of idols as these puppets, who only do what they’re told,” says Omega Sapien. “But creative languages within the idol industry are changing too. I really love groups like CORTIS. I think their work is raw and fantastic.”

“I’m really interested in girl groups,” says Unsinkable, a producer and DJ. “These days we see groups that are more like crews, with more creative independence from their company. I sometimes wonder if new idol acts are inspired by what we do.”

In Gongbu, Balming Tiger explores themes of Korean and Asian identity. The single “Home” is absurdist and nostalgic, evoking Korean folk music while mixing synthesizers, rap and ritualistic chants. The music video is black and white, reminiscent of a Park Chan-wook film or a Lee Gap-chul photo. It’s inspired by the architecture of Kim Chung-up and the traditional marriage ritual hamjinabi.

“What does it mean to be Korean? To be Asian? When we were younger, we looked up to American hip-hop,” says Omega Sapien. “I wanted to be like J. Cole. But now I see that that’s his thing. We have our own thing: We’re Balming Tiger, young people living in South Korea, exploring our identities. Doing this is what’s Korean, what’s true to ourselves.”

items.title: Taking Play Seriously - Kinfolk
items.description: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
paragraphs: - Words Ellen Peirson-Hagger
A conversation with the National Institute for Play.

In 1966, psychiatrist Dr. Stuart Brown was appointed by the governor of Texas to investigate a mass shooting at the state university—at the time the deadliest in American history. Brown realized there could be a connection between the gunman’s actions and his oppressive childhood, which had been dominated by his controlling father. He would go on to spend the following decades showing that the need for play is biologically hardwired into the brain stem—the part of the nervous system that governs our essential functions like breathing and heart rate.

“When we’re deprived of play, it can be similar to being deprived of sleep and nutrition and connection—the things that fundamentally make us human,” explains Mia Sundstrom, Dr. Brown’s granddaughter and the CEO of the National Institute for Play—a nonprofit organization Brown established in 1994 to champion play as a public health necessity. “I grew up through play,” she says, “and have firsthand seen the benefits of it.”
Appointed to her role earlier this year, her mission at the institute is to show “how people can incorporate play into their lives to promote cognitive, social, emotional and physical health.”
Ellen Peirson-Hagger: Why is play important?

Mia Sundstrom: Here’s the paradox—and it’s why it’s so difficult to convince people that play matters: One of the core definitions of play is that it’s purposeless, that it’s not done for any specific outcome. Yet there’s a ton of purpose in the outcomes we get. We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.
EPH: What are the benefits of play?

MS: When we are in a state of play, it boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which is the neuroplasticity protein that helps to create new neural connections and strengthen existing pathways. Play also calms down our amygdala—our emotional processing center—meaning it takes us out of a stress response, which is great for emotional regulation. And in the case of social play, our mirror neurons—which light up when we observe the motor activity of someone else—allow us to develop the basic foundation of attunement, which is the first seedling of connection with another human being, and which in time leads to trust, to community, to belonging. So on a neurobiological level, play promotes our cognitive health, our emotional resilience and our social competence.

Physical play is obviously good for us: Exercise is healthy, whether we enjoy it or not. But we’re a lot more likely to sustain it when it’s something we enjoy, so we might as well try and find a form of physical exercise that feels like play.
EPH: If we don’t play, are those things lost?

MS: When we’re play-deprived, there can be really severe consequences. It can lead to cognitive rigidity, which is when you can’t think outside the box and solve problems creatively. We have seen that a lack of play can lead to susceptibility for anxiety and depression, and toward addictive behaviors, because we try to find those things that we need from play in other forms—alcohol, drugs, social media, sugar—all these things that offer short-term relief rather than long-term benefit.

And then there’s social incompetence: As my grandpa’s research showed, when we don’t play it’s hard to build tolerance and empathy for each other because we miss that fundamental level of attunement. This leads to diminished well-being.
EPH: How does our need for play change as we become adults?

MS: There’s a misconception that it has to change like crazy, that what you do as a kid is not what you should do as an adult. But we don’t ever lose the desire to play, we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways. For example, as you go through grade school, the playgrounds change—there is no longer the opportunity to go down a slide at recess—and then all of a sudden you forget that you love to do that, and you might never do it again.

I don’t think adults should stop swinging, or playing at parks, or jumping on a trampoline in the backyard. We often think that we outgrow these things, but we really shouldn’t. Lego is a breaker of this rule: Lego adult sets are selling so well right now because of their connection to nostalgia and childhood. And what’s great about moving from childhood to adulthood is that the possibilities to play open up significantly: Instead of exploring your backyard with a stick and turning your cardboard box into a rocket ship, you have access to a car and a plane.
EPH: Is play different to different people?

MS: Everyone is born with a deep natural predilection for play, but that looks different for each of us. There are people who love to make things—art, music, building, tinkering with objects. There are people who love to dream or get lost in a book or movie and create imaginary worlds in their mind. There are people who love to compete, who play through mastering. There are people who love to organize—collecting new things, arranging social gatherings, even cleaning out a junk drawer. These are all different play styles, and one of the greatest gifts you can give a child is to notice what those natural tendencies are and help nourish them.
EPH: Do you think we need to take a broader view of what play is or can be?

MS: Yes! Most of the time, when I ask people “What is play to you?” they say “a board game” or “my kid’s sport.” We have confined play to this really narrow scope, when actually play is any activity that brings us into the play state, which is an altered state of being, almost dreamlike, that takes us out of the usual experience of time and space and evokes positive emotions like joy and awe. It is intrinsically motivated, not coerced, so it’s done for its own sake, and it’s self-reinforcing, so the benefits of a play state last beyond the time we’re playing.

Any activity that meets that criteria can be play—that could mean coding for someone who loves to code, or cooking for someone who loves to cook. Heck, that could even be cleaning if you put on a great song and you turn your broom into a microphone.
EPH: Why is society so resistant to play?

MS: Well, the psychologist and play researcher Peter Gray would answer by taking us back to the 16th century, when the Protestant Reformation taught us to believe in the moral virtue of work and that play, by contrast, is the breeding ground of sin. And then you throw capitalism into the mix which calls for more production, more consumption: that’s what defines success in the capitalist dream, right? Then you add in the compounding effects of automation and AI. Of course play isn’t celebrated in a world that prioritizes those things.
EPH: Has digitization played a role?

MS: We can’t prove causation, but our screens do seem to be factor in why we’re not playing. Scrolling on your screen disguises itself as play because you lose track of time, and it feels fun in the moment. But it has long-term detriments in terms of our attention span and our loneliness. If we’re scrolling, we’re not connecting with each other on a human level.
EPH: What kind of society would we have if we all played more?

MS: Play dissolves our differences and reminds us of what we have in common. Our world is so polarized, but play brings us together and is one of the most powerful ways to create a better society. Play lowers our inhibitions—I want to shout that from the rooftops. If you disagree with someone and go play with them, you’ll see the humanity in one other. It can also help combat the trends that we’re talking so much about right now—loneliness, disengagement, burnout—because play brings us back to that deep intrinsic drive to do something for a sustained period of time that makes the time pass more quickly.
EPH: What should adults do to help recover their love of play?

MS: We help adults rediscover their natural spark—their thing that makes them most curious and fully alive—and then think about small ways to reintegrate that into their life. The first step is to think back to your earliest memory of play: What was that thing you loved to do before the world told you who to be? Second, based on that, what do you love to do now—is there something that you’ve forgotten about and haven’t done for ages? Third, nothing ever works when we try to create massive changes all at once. So we say that 30 seconds is enough. See if you can add a burst of play into your morning or evening routine, based on those two things you reflected on. What’s great about play is that it’s self-reinforcing, so as soon as you give yourself that permission, it will keep you coming back for more.
“We have taught ourselves that play is the opposite of work, but actually play is productive, play is learning; it is not a waste of time.”

items.title: Kyle Kuzma - Kinfolk
items.description: The NBA forward is playing the long game.
paragraphs: The NBA forward is playing the long game.

Kyle Kuzma is enjoying himself. He’s about to catch a flight for the south of France, where he’ll be attending the Cannes Film Festival, and is midway through the long, complex and, for him, extremely pleasurable process, of picking out what to wear. “If I’m going somewhere in three days, I may already be in my closet, just trying on clothes, seeing what I want to wear, thinking about what type of events I’m going to,” he says over a video call from his home in Miami. He’s planning ahead for the films, parties and red carpet events.

If a lot of this sounds like fun, Kuzma thinks so too. “Everything is play—unless, you know, it’s your profession,” he says. This is the challenge because Kuzma’s job is, after all, a form of play. He is in his 10th year in the NBA. A first-round draft pick in 2017, he’s currently a power forward for the Milwaukee Bucks; in 2020 he won the NBA national championship with the Los Angeles Lakers in only his third year in the league.

items.title: i-D X New Balance, Straight-Up!
items.description: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheeseca
items.author: Tiffany Lai
paragraphs: Last Thursday, the great and the glamorous descended on One Club Row in Shoreditch to enjoy a three-course dinner at the New York-style bistro. Guests like Aminé, Sainté, Chopova Lowena, and Coco Capitán tucked into shrimp cocktail, roast chicken, and cheesecake before the party continued downstairs at the Knave of Clubs for pub drinks and a boogie.

At 8 p.m., a new billboard was unveiled outside the pub, celebrating version 7 of New Balance’s iconic 990 silhouette, set to release globally on November 6. Made in the USA, the 990 has been a proud “dad shoe” since 1982, so naturally, we had to ask our guests: who is your favorite American? And which celebrity dad has the best style?

Who is your favorite American? Kim Kardashian or Adam Sandler. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Rey Mysterio from WWE. What’s an album that’s on repeat right now? The new Worldpeace DMT album. What are you doing this weekend? Spreading optimism and premature Christmas cheer!

What do you do? I’m a stylist. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Ford Bronco cars. What are you wearing today? Mules, which aren’t very practical for walking in the rain, an old pair of Our Legacy jeans, a cashmere jumper to keep me warm, and a vintage bomber. My hat is made by my friend Biddyish. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Brad Pitt.

What’s an item of clothing you’d never part with? My 1960s vintage McGregor jacket that I picked up in Paris a few years ago. What are you drinking tonight? Guinness. Who’s your favorite American? Jim Carrey. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My granddad, actually. What’s your favorite form of exercise? Running, because of the mental clarity and the long and steady journey I’ve had with New Balance.

What do you do? I’m a photographer, director, and DJ. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? A secondhand leather jacket from a market in Paris. What album is on repeat right now? Choke Enough by Oklou. What’s a color that you’d love to wear more of? Green.

What do you do? I make music, but I like saying my job is just connecting the dots because there’s no laws or limits to art. Tell us about your outfit. My outfit’s steady but also flex-y, smart-casual. What are you doing this weekend? I’m always creating. I’m working on some new music, shooting cool videos, fun stuff. Who first taught you to tie your shoes? My mum. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? I’m in a black era right now.

What do you do? We’re freelance stylists. Which celebrity dad has the best style? Jacob: Jeff Goldblum. His personality is the style. If you had to run between two Tube stops, which ones would you choose? Jacob: Bethnal Green and Mile End because they’re the closest ones together. Lauren: Custom House to Canning Town. Nice scenic run. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? Lauren: A big fur coat.

Who’s your favorite American? Fred Hampton. He was one of the leaders of the Black Panther Party. What’s your side hustle? I’m rebranding my friend’s fashion brand. Doesn’t mean I give it less attention than a main hustle, but that’s the thing that I’m supporting right now! What’s your favorite form of exercise and why? Push-ups and pull-ups at home. I hate going to the gym. What are you doing this weekend? I’m seeing my friend who’s leaving for Australia. I’ve got to sort his Moonpig out ASAP!

What do you do? I’m the editor-in-chief of i-D Magazine. What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Me. Which celebrity dad has the best style? My dad. He’s modeled in the Chopova Lowena show, he wears New Balance 990s, and he loves a Ralph Lauren polo. Best grail? This Prada scarf. Who’s your favorite TV dad? Michael Bluth from Arrested Development.

What do you do? I’m a fashion designer. What’s an item of clothing you’ll never part with? This pair of jeans that my boyfriend gave me. What’s a color you’d love to wear more of? Gray. What’s your favorite form of exercise? I go to the gym, but I want to pick up tennis.

What’s your favorite thing that’s made in the USA? Black music. What are you wearing tonight? Made in the USA 2040 V5 New Balance shoes, Supreme Made in Japan denim, and a Bleue Burnham ring. What are you drinking tonight? Chili margarita, some red wine, Guinness, and water. Got to stay hydrated. What are you doing this weekend? This weekend, it’s the Amsterdam Dance Event where I live. My partner’s going clubbing, so I’m taking care of the kids.

What do you do? I’m a musician, and I play the harp. What’s an item of clothing you would never part with? My 1800s Victorian body that is falling apart, but I’ll never let her go. Who first taught you how to tie your shoes? My dad. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a cemetery walk date with my girlfriend in Abney Park. Who’s your favorite American? Lana Del Rey.

What are you wearing? Hysteric Glamour boots with pink studs, a skirt that my ex-boyfriend gave me, a nice, warm Supreme jacket, and a Goldwin jumper. What are you drinking tonight? Two spicy margaritas, a glass of white wine, and a glass of red wine. Who’s your favorite American? Martine Syms. I like her exhibition at Sadie Coles. What are you doing this weekend? I’m going on a first date to a wine bar in Hoxton. Do you have a side hustle? Hustling!

What do you do? I work for Homer Jewellery and Louise Konrad Jewellery. Who’s your favorite American? The Tiger King. What’s your favorite thing to wear with trainers? My sweatpants. What’s an outfit that lives rent-free in your mind? Zendaya’s Mugler outfit for the Dune premiere. What are you drinking tonight? Vodka soda.

items.title: Gisele Bundchen Interview: Motherhood, Happiness, Modeling Career
items.description: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
items.author: Steff Yotka
paragraphs: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
photography COLLIER SCHORR

When she was 15 years old, Gisele Bündchen left Horizontina, Brazil, and moved to Tokyo to become a model. It was 1995. She didn’t speak Japanese or English. To reach her parents, grandparents, and five sisters, she used an international calling card on a landline phone. She would speak to them every 15 days, exactly.

“It was, in a way, liberating because I felt like I was living life,” Gisele says, thinking back to getting lost on the subway, navigating teenage growing pains, and learning how to integrate into a foreign reality. “I was experiencing life.”

Thirty-one years later, there is little of life Gisele hasn’t experienced. She walked her first major runway show for Alexander McQueen in 1998, and for the next decade was a regular on the catwalk for Gucci, Dolce & Gabbana, Versace, Valentino, and Marc Jacobs. She signed an advertising contract with Dior, posing for Nick Knight amongst bubbles and saddle bags, then another with Dolce & Gabbana for its glittering perfume The One, and then another with Victoria’s Secret. She routinely wore the brand’s Red Hot Fantasy Bra—estimated to be worth $15 million in 2000.

Gisele was the Forbes highest-paid model for 12 years in a row, from 2005 to 2016. Her own website estimates she has appeared on an unprecedented 1,200 magazine covers (this issue will be her seventh for i-D). She walked the runway during the 2016 Olympic Opening Ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, released multiple singles, and has appeared in a handful of movies, from Taxi (2004) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006). Gisele has fundraised for Lotus House, Save the Children, The Red Cross, and more. In 2016, Taschen published a book commemorating her 20 years of modelling, retailing for $700 and selling out in one day. The cover shot is by Irving Penn of a nude Gisele. (“I still have the note from him saying that it was wonderful. ‘You did great.’”) Inside are now-legendary photographs by Steven Meisel, David LaChapelle, Inez and Vinoodh, and Juergen Teller. Gisele has published one autobiography and one cookbook, which is to say nothing of the digests she posts on Instagram to her 22 million followers. She is so famous and so known, from Brazil to Tokyo to New York to Mars, that it would be impossible for any one of us to calculate exactly where we know her from or how many times we’ve seen her face.

And yet, for Gisele, who turned 46 in July, those wandering Tokyo days are among her most special. “My whole thing is going back to that,” she tells me, tucked into an armchair in a white tank and jean shorts. “How can I create more of that reality in my life?”

You see, despite being the object of so many gazes, Gisele prefers to set hers on the sun, the sea, the sky. She was born on a farm in Brazil, surrounded by her grandparents, parents, sisters, and pets. Now, 6,900 kilometres away, she’s recreated that paradise in Northern Miami with her children Benjamin (16), Vivian (13), and a baby boy (16 months), her husband Joaquim, and a pair of dogs.

“Life is a gift,” she says. “I think I have so much joy in my life because I really see the ordinary as the extraordinary… The sun rises every day. You can walk around and be grateful for it, or you can just be disconnected from all these incredible things. You can be robbed of your life if you think life is this”—she mimics looking down at her phone—“and you forget life is so much more.”
She smiles, sipping from her room-temperature water. “Anyway, I’m sure you have more questions for me.”
Because we got into the meaning of life and Gisele’s very philosophy of being so quickly into our first meeting, here’s what happened in the lead-up—minutes one through seven:
1. I enter Gisele’s small ranch home a couple blocks from her larger, beachfront estate. I am promptly served her homemade granola and her proprietary tea (warming, like dark chocolate and honey).
2. Alfie, her gigantic German Shepherd, comes in first and gives me the once-over. “He’s my protector,” Gisele smiles, kicking off her sandals and wrapping me up in a hug.

3. “You smell amazing,” she says, and I just give her the bottle of perfume in my purse. She asks if it has parabens, and I say I don’t know, and she tells me never to use anything with parabens, especially on your wrists or neck. It’s been three months and I am still too embarrassed to research: Does Maison Louis Marie’s scent Aboukir have parabens?
4. She checks my astrological vibe to make sure this interview will go well: “What’s your sign?” she asks squarely.
“Cancer. I knew we’d talk about it. I read you’re a Cancer, Scorpio Moon. What’s your rising?”

“Oh, go girl! I don’t even know how I ended up doing this job. If you let me, I would just never leave my house, because I’m a crab. And with the Scorpio Moon, for me, if it’s not deep, I don’t want to talk about it.”

That’s the guiding premise of being Gisele: Always searching for depth, connection, and meaning. In some way, modelling was the perfect job for her—homey, crablike tendencies notwithstanding—because it allowed her to find connections the world over. The high-low of the industry, which led to anxiety attacks in her mid-20s, was the impetus for Gisele’s soul searching. “Shit happens to all of us, but I think I don’t stay there,” she says of the down days. “I learned how to meditate. It’s like you can take a step back: You can be having an experience and observing yourself having that experience at the same time.”

Meditation led her to yoga, which she practises routinely, and then to Pilates and then to jujitsu. Recently, she has added weight training. “I do weights three times a week. I do Pilates once or twice a week. I do yoga two or three times a week. I work out every day because, for me, working out—I don’t see it as something I have to do. I see it as something I get to do,” she says. “It doesn’t matter if I’m surfing, if I’m playing volleyball with my daughter, if I’m paddleboarding. Whatever it is, I feel like it’s a moment of being.” She bares a bicep. “Now for the first time in my life, I can do pull-ups.”

Early this summer morning, she took her baby to the park. Much like his older half-siblings, he has picked up on Gisele’s connectivity and generosity. “I have to show you this video.” For the first time, she whips out her phone and opens her camera roll. As she scrolls through—I promise I’m not trying to peek!—I realise almost every photo is of her kids. “He’s so funny,” she says of her son, captured waddling around the park with a paper towel. “I mean, he’s 16 months and he saw that I was cleaning the park—because Miami, it’s so damp all the time!—and he wanted to participate and he felt really good about it,” Gisele beams, watching her tiny son dry off the slide, the seesaw, the swing.

“Kids give us this opportunity to live again, to be more present and to experience life again. To do it maybe differently than we’ve done it before.” She pauses. “I don’t know. I find every little thing so amazing.” Gisele goes on to show me videos of Benny DJing in his bedroom, his baby brother dancing by his side. She has pictures of Vivi playing volleyball (“She’s amazing!”) and dancing with friends. She scrolls to a dancing video. “I mean, what is better than this? This is my daughter and she’s like, ‘Mum, let’s do a dance class.’ So this is us doing a dance class. I’m not so great,” Gisele laughs, “but look at her and her friend—and that’s her mum’s friend.”

She quickly scrolls through about 20 more videos before she chucks her phone away. “By the way, I don’t know if you noticed, my phone doesn’t ring. There’s no alarms. It never rings. It’s liberating.”

A silenced iPhone and spending all day with her family is a far cry from the past 30 years of Gisele’s life. To briefly summarise the lore: Her mother enrolled her, her twin sister Patí, and younger sister Gabriela in modelling classes in Brazil. Gisele was later scouted to participate in the Elite Model Look competition, and in 1995, she placed second. From 1996 to 2016, life didn’t stop—she spent the better part of her 20s and 30s at the white-hot centre of it all: Fashion, fame, celebrity, paparazzi, and money. She was signing bigger contracts than other models, getting bigger media attention, becoming an entity bigger than Gisele Bündchen from Horizontina, Brazil. She was, by 2004, a supermodel, capital S. Everything about her sparkled.

“I’ve experienced the rat race. I was on the hamster wheel in my early 20s,” she says. “I won Model of the Year at 19. I worked so hard from 14 to get to that place, I felt like I couldn’t say no [to major jobs].” And sure, Gisele encountered so much of the bullshit so many models of the ’90s and ’00s did. She tried not to let her industry’s lack of protection faze her. “Even though I wasn’t going to the parties, I was doing 360 days [of work a year]. I wanted to be the best that I could be every day. I wanted to bring my best.”

We start to look through some of her runway fits from her catwalk days and she sparks up with delight. “Girl, it was very tight inside. You couldn’t really move so much—but, I mean, look how he made you look!” she cheers of a supersized Fall 2004 Christian Dior look by John Galliano. “I’m forever grateful to McQueen, I’m forever grateful to John. I was always so excited to do the Dior shows because I never knew what I was going to look like.”

She singles out a Galliano show for Dior held at Versailles. “This was 60 years of Dior and I wasn’t even doing shows anymore. John was like, ‘Please, Gisele. This is all my muses and it’s going to be the 60 years, it’s to be in Versailles.’ I was like, ‘I must do it,’” she remembers. “Look at these shoes. It was like a platform without a heel. I was walking on cement, like bricks. It was crazy. I was like, ‘Am I going to fall and break my ankle?’”

But that’s the thing about Gisele: Even if she’s struggling to walk or struggling to feel beautiful—as she often recounts of that first-ever McQueen show, where she hit the runway topless with a trompe l’oeil white tank painted on by Val Garland, rain falling and her lashes dripping into her eyes—she is always going to do her best. “I didn’t say no or complain because people were giving me the opportunity,” she reflects. “I came in, I did my job, I went home… and I think what I really appreciate and really enjoyed about fashion is that it got me to access and experience different sides of me. I really wanted to be the best canvas for the creatives. I felt like it was my way of contributing.”

But working in the oil-slick glossy world of new millennium modelling meant that few people saw Gisele as a full person—because of her beauty, her chameleonic qualities, and her prowess, she was quickly regarded as an idol. Nice to look at, nothing to say. The first time she appeared in i-D, on the cover in December 1998, she wasn’t interviewed. Instead, the photographer who took the picture was, and here’s what he had to say about the smart and vibrant Gisele: “She’s certainly gorgeous. I’d marry her.”

Her “godfather” in the turbulent fashion industry was Steven Meisel. (Are you surprised that the greatest model of her generation would find kinship with the greatest photographer of his?) In one of the earliest pieces of press about Gisele, a New York Magazine article from 1999, Meisel already saw her as more than a body to stand in front of his lens. He felt her spirit. “Gisele is able to change because she wants to—it’s not in her looks; it’s in her mental process. She is malleable and is willing to be a silent screen star because she understands that modelling is acting,” he told the mag. He later wrote the foreword for her Taschen book, and she still speaks of him as her guardian angel. “I’m grateful for him. I don’t think I would have been the model that I was if it wasn’t for him, for real. We got to play together. I shot with him every week.”

And yet, after weekly Meisel shoots, over 130 Vogue covers, and decades on billboards and TV ad spots, Gisele wanted more. Well—maybe not more in the way you and I might think of it. She wanted to actually enjoy what she’d accomplished, and that meant leaving the fracas behind. After a decade in Boston, she relocated here, to Florida, to co-parent her older children and set up a new world of sea and sun and sand. Being mum, practising gratitude, taking care of herself and her community have become more valuable than any seven-figure ad job: “I say no to 99 percent of the jobs I’m offered because, when I put it on the scale, I’m like, ‘Am I going to miss my daughter’s volleyball game? Am I going to miss going to the park with my son? Am I going to miss my son DJing?’”

That’s why, with the exception of a few trips to her home in Costa Rica, to see family in Brazil, and recently, to Tahiti, Gisele rarely leaves Florida. “Having a baby at this moment of my life is such a gift, because I’m in a different place. I don’t have anything to prove. I don’t feel like I really, quite frankly, care.”
“I’m not defined by other people’s opinions,” she continues, firmly. “I feel like I get to choose how I want to live my life.”

Being alive today can feel like a quest for more: Make more money. Diversify your portfolio. Get PRP+ to be more beautiful and then Ozempic to be more svelte. Become a brand and use that brand to become more famous. Every day of your life can be used to sell something or say something or self-improve. I don’t think I have ever encountered a person more satisfied with exactly how her life is than Gisele. She has a lot, sure, but it’s long been enough. She’s done a lot, sure, but she’s not looking back. She’s been everywhere, yeah, but she isn’t driven by getting in your face.

She’s not a brand. She’s not an entrepreneur. She’s not a self-help guru—even though I tell her she should have a podcast. She’s not forcing Gisele-dom down our throats and, in some way, it seems like she doesn’t really want to be famous at all. That she’s financially well-off, she tells me, is just an opportunity to take care of her sisters and her family. She doesn’t want fancy clothes. She hasn’t been to New York in over two years and she’s not eager to come back.

“At the end of the day, this is your temple, this is your life, this is your journey. How do you want it to look? What do you want it to be? Who defines success?” she asks, as concerned in that moment with my well-being as with her own. “What is success? Some people say success is power, money, fame, more. Some people say success is being able to spend time with your kids, to have food on your table, to have a home to live in, to have great relationships and actually enjoy every day. I find that, quite frankly, much more successful than…” she trails off, not eager to point a finger. “It’s up to each person to define, because when I was in my 20s, success was different than what I feel today.”
“What do you want your legacy to be?” I ask as we’re wrapping up our conversation.

“In the end, I ended up having the best time. I ended up enjoying it all, staying in it, learning from it, and growing up in it. It’s been a blessing. However people see me, that’s okay with me. I want to look back and think, ‘I really enjoyed this journey. I really loved fully. I really experienced every emotion. I really had meaningful relationships. I tried to make the world a better place, and I made my surroundings more harmonious and loving and beautiful.’ I want my kids to feel like I was a great mum and that I helped them become the best version of themselves. I want to feel like I lived striving to be the best version of myself. Hopefully, I can look back and say I did it.”

Today, after I pack up my things and head for Miami International Airport, she’ll go to a birthday dinner. It’s a rare night out for Gisele, and after decades of no carbs and no dairy, she might have some of her friend’s homemade sourdough. “What’s better than bread and cheese? Oh my god, I don’t know!” she laughs. Tomorrow, she’ll wake up early to paddleboard. She’s worried about me not seeing the sea one last time before I get on a plane back to New York, but she’s calmed when I tell her I spent two hours on the beach this morning. As I wheel away my little suitcase and say goodbye, she pops her head out the front door with a final blessing. “Live the life you want to live! Everything else is going to shake out.”

items.title: Madonna Really Does Love New York
items.description: There I was minding my business (by not minding my business) when I get the email of a lifetime: "What are you up to Thursday night? Wanna spend it with Madonna?"
items.author: Paper Magazine
paragraphs: There I was minding my business (by not minding my business) when I get the email of a lifetime: "What are you up to Thursday night? Wanna spend it with Madonna?"

You know me by now... and if you’re pretending you don’t: I’m Linux, New York’s premiere downtown it-girl. I spend my nights either attending or throwing Scene City’s hottest parties. This week in particular is madness, being New York Pride. It's the Thursday of NYC’s Gay Marathon and, "What are you up to Thursday night?", was a question I'm more than prepared to answer.
At the end of the day, I’m a human being on planet Earth. And around these parts, when Madonna calls... you answer!

So I did just that (after waiting about 30 minutes to respond, of course... I didn’t want to come off too desperate). They told me to meet at the Moxy in Chelsea at 10 PM. A bus would be there waiting to take me and a hundred drag queens to a very proud and very gay night with Madonna at Terminal 5.

My Uber pulled up to the trendy hotel to a Jean Paul Gaultier-emblazoned double decker bus already boarding the world’s hottest gaylebrities: Symone, GiGi Goode, Shea Coulee, Aquaria, Gottmik, Detox and Kylie Sonique Love all posed for photos as the Gaultier team smoked cigarettes on the sidewalk. The bus driver honked his horn and we all screamed, knowing that noise meant it was time to leave towards Hells Kitchen to party with Madonna.

A DJ on the bus blasted Madonna's deep cuts as we drove through Times Square — a moment when all of us asked ourselves, "Is this real life?" Once we pulled up to Terminal 5, the marquee with Madonna’s name in flashing lights made it all too real that we were really about to see the Queen MDNA herself. So, what was this Madonna event all for anyways?

Madonna, who has been a leader in the NFT space, partnered for another time with WoW (World of Women), a thriving community celebrating representation, inclusivity and equal opportunities. The entire event was sponsored by The Sandbox, who has partnered with WoW to create the WoW Foundation, which will invest $25 million over five years in education and mentorship through programs across the metaverse.

Finally Enough Love, Madonna's 16-track career-spanning remix compilation album, was also released on streaming at midnight. To put it in simpler terms: Madonna was doing God’s work for the LGBTQ+ and wrapped it all up into a sickening Pride party.

As I entered the venue, I was immediately welcomed by teams of artists from MAC Viva Glam, who were offering guests Madonna-inspired touch ups (MAC Viva Glam has raised more than a half billion dollars to end HIV/AIDS). My makeup was already flawless, so I didn’t need anything done, but it's always nice to kiki with a MAC girlie.

I scammed my VIP bracelet from Geordon Nicol of the Misshapes, who was helping produce the night, and ran upstairs to Terminal 5’s VIP rooftop. I needed a cocktail and, luckily, Belvedere was offering free vodka, keeping the kids all liquored up. Next to the bar sat boxes and boxes of pizza from Made in NY (so Italian). But we’re not here for Pizza, we’re here for Madonna! So I ran back downstairs to get a good spot for the show.

Bob the Drag Queen served as MC. The icon Laganja Estranja performed "Vogue," where she was joined by Jose Xtravaganza, one of Madonna's dancers on the Blond Ambition tour. After that, we were all blindsided by Saucy Santana appearing on stage to perform "Walk," before "Material Girl" started playing and Madonna came out to perform it with him. Girl, when I tell you the crowd went wild! Herstory in the making. Madonna then premiered a "Hung Up" remix with Tokischa, which ended with the two of them making out on stage... it was really hot.
Joined by all of the performers, Madonna ended the night with a show-stopping performance of "Celebration" while rainbow confetti flooded the venue.

It was the best way to celebrate Pride imaginable. There was only one problem: I didn’t want it to end! Luckily, Madonna didn’t want it to either. For those with VIP bracelets, the party continued on the third floor of Terminal 5, where all the Ru Girls, it-kids and fashion peeps partied until the early morning.
Photography: Ricardo Gomes

items.title: As Donald Trump's Handpicked Candidates Flop Nationwide, the President Accepts Reality
items.description: As the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections began to roll in, Donald Trump’s mood seemed to darken, especially when it came to coverage from his network of choice, Fox News. But after a few posts complaining about the cable news channel, the president fell s
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: As the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections began to roll in, Donald Trump’s mood seemed to darken, especially when it came to coverage from his network of choice, Fox News. But after a few posts complaining about the cable news channel, the president fell silent for hours, before telling the New York Times that he will accept the results of Tuesday's election.

As polls closed in Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. ET, Trump termed the end to the latter state's election day “A BIG DEAL!” The president was likely aware of the closure as he was “Watching the Pre-Election Results on FoxNews,” he wrote, before complaining that he can't stand the voice of one of the network's few liberal leaning commentators, Jessica Tarlov.

“DUMB AS A ROCK,” Trump complained, his mood apparently turning. “Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I'll be back later!” After less than an hour, he returned, his anger at Fox increasing. “The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask,” he wrote. “Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLSHIT!’ This has been going on for years.”

A few minutes later, he returned again, this time with a longer rant about the cable channel. “FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats! All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me — My numbers are better than they have ever been.”

“No wonder FoxNews Ratings are collapsing, and they’re going to go down a lot further,” he continued. “They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me! This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”

In Georgia, Trump had earlier stumped for gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson and US Senate nominee Mike Collins, who lost his race against incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff. When that race was called, Trump made no comment. The same was true as Democrat James Talarico's lead over Texas Senate hopeful Ken Paxton continued to grow. Those who checked Truth Social after CNN projected that the Democratic party would capture the House of Representatives were also set up for disappointment, as the president has yet to comment on those results as well.

Instead, he returned some hours later with a post not about any candidate, but his own popularity. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!,” the president wrote. Shortly thereafter, at around 10:30 p.m. ET, the president spoke with the New York Times, where he struck a conciliatory tone. “I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” he told the paper. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”
And, minutes later, another Truth Social post. “I'm going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” (Capitalization his own.)

items.title: James Talarico Flips Senate Seat In Texas, While Gina Hinojosa Takes Governor's Race
items.description: The polls closed in Texas at 7 p.m. local time (the state is split between Central Time and Mountain Time) Tuesday, and within hours, one of the state's most contentious battles in the 2026 midterm elections was over, with Democrat James Talarico prevailing ov
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: The polls closed in Texas at 7 p.m. local time (the state is split between Central Time and Mountain Time) Tuesday, and within hours, one of the state's most contentious battles in the 2026 midterm elections was over, with Democrat James Talarico prevailing over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, giving Democrats their first statewide victory in Texas since 1994.

As part of a campaign in the state's most closely watched race, Paxton embarked on a whirlwind tour across Texas, joined by President Donald Trump along the way. Given Trump's slumping approval, combined with popular discomfort around Paxton's scandal-plagued career, Talarico's lead continued to grow even as Elon Musk pumped cash into the Republican side.

In June, political advisor Mark McKinnon described Talarico in a piece for Vanity Fair as “a rare talent.” “He’s an eighth-generation Texan, a former middle school teacher, and a Presbyterian seminarian. In a state where the Scriptures amount to a kind of civic fixture, Talarico out-Bibles many Republicans,” McKinnon wrote. "What’s more, he is preaching a new kind of message that is not along partisan lines. Here’s a sample: ‘The biggest divide in this country is not left vs. right. It’s top vs. bottom. Billionaires want us looking left and right at each other instead of looking up at them.’”

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas's governor's race, becoming the state's first Latina governor, as well as the first Democrat to hold the office in more than 30 years. The last one was also a woman: Democrat Ann Richards, who served from 1991-1995. Richards was the mother of Cecile Richards, the longtime president of Planned Parenthood.

items.title: In Ohio, Amy Acton Defeats Vivek Ramaswamy for Governor
items.description: Ohio was home to one of the nation’s most competitive races for governor in the 2026 midterm elections, as entrepreneur and former Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat physician Amy Acton battled to replace term-limited GOP governor M
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: Ohio was home to one of the nation’s most competitive races for governor in the 2026 midterm elections, as entrepreneur and former Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat physician Amy Acton battled to replace term-limited GOP governor Mike DeWine. But on Tuesday, Acton defeated Ramaswamy, according to the AP.

The Buckeye State, which is also home to Vice President JD Vance, hasn’t elected a Democrat to its highest office since 2006. But rising concerns regarding affordability and data centers boosted the campaign of Acton and running mate David Pepper, the former chair of the Ohio Democratic Party. Ramaswamy’s running mate, Rob McColley, is currently the Ohio Senate president.

A $4 million ad campaign from Ramaswamy had also split Republicans. The commercial featured Acton’s mother, from whom Acton has been estranged since her stepfather was reportedly arrested and charged with raping Acton when she was 12 years old. (According to The New York Times, the stepfather, who died in 2004, pleaded not guilty to the charges and then fled the state before trial.) In the ad, Acton’s 82-year-old mother, Donna Arthur, says, “Don’t let her become your governor,” prompting GOP members, including DeWine, to repudiate the commercial.

Meanwhile, Ohio’s US Senate race also went to the Democrats, further cementing their grip on the House. Over $500 million has been spent in the battle for the seat currently held by Republican senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to the role by DeWine in 2025 to replace JD Vance. Husted has been singled out for praise by President Donald Trump in recent weeks, especially when it comes to his physique, but trailed in the polls behind Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his previous seat in the US Senate to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. The Associated Press and CNN have projected Brown as the winner, giving his party a major win in one of the country's most closely watched Senate contests.

items.title: As a Blue Wave Washes Across the Country, Democrats Take Control of House and Senate
items.description: The long-predicted blue wave hit shores Tuesday, as results from the 2026 midterm elections indicated that Democrats have captured both the House of Representatives and the US Senate.
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: The long-predicted blue wave hit shores Tuesday, as results from the 2026 midterm elections indicated that Democrats have captured both the House of Representatives and the US Senate.

“The face of American politics just changed,” CNN's Stephen Collinson said Tuesday. “MAGA's monopoly on Washington will end. Trump will face relentless multi-front investigations from Democratic House committees.”

While polling had predicted a House flip in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections, until Tuesday night, the fate of the Senate was less clear: Democrats had to flip at least four seats held by Republicans to win control of that body. With the projected victories of James Talarico in Texas, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, and Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Democrats are on track to wrest the Senate from Republican control.

items.title: The Art of the Deal: Jared Kushner’s Hacked Phone Revealed More Than $700 Million in Transfers
items.description: In late spring 2020, a source I knew to be reliable called me with a story. The Dutch government had hacked into Jared Kushner’s phone and monitored him as he accessed a Dubai-based bank account. What was odd, the source said, was that the money in the account
items.author: Matthew Cole
paragraphs: In late spring 2020, a source I knew to be reliable called me with a story. The Dutch government had hacked into Jared Kushner’s phone and monitored him as he accessed a Dubai-based bank account. What was odd, the source said, was that the money in the account—hundreds of millions of dollars—had come from a bank in Azerbaijan. Most importantly, Kushner appeared to have transferred significant amounts of money from the Dubai account to other individuals, including a warlord, a mercenary and a one-time hit man. The story sounded preposterous, I told my source. And yet.

Six months later, I found myself speaking with someone else about the UAE government and their use of mercenaries in conflicts around the Middle East and Africa when I asked, on a whim, whether they knew anything about Kushner and bank transfers from a UAE account. My acquaintance grew quiet. Then they replied, “Yes.”

Over the next four years, I came to learn that, sometime in late 2017, the Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) made a startling discovery. A General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (GRU) operative, a dark web hacker specializing in stolen bank data, was traveling to the UK for an espionage mission. They reached out to the British government for permission to apprehend him when he arrived. The British agreed.

When the Russian national arrived in England, the Dutch informed him that he had two options: he could work for them against the GRU, or the British would arrest him. Once in UK government custody, the operative would be charged with espionage. If convicted, he would spend years in a British prison. The Russian chose to change his employer.

Later that year, the Russian operative gave the Dutch spies access to one of the GRU’s most sensitive assets. Located in Rostov, Russia, the GRU’s hacking and cyber team operated a remote server on which they stored some of their bounty. During their search through these secret files, the Dutch found something astonishing: screenshots of Jared Kushner’s iPhone.

In The Hague, the MIVD hacking team tried to reverse engineer the Russian penetration of Kushner’s iPhone. Kushner owned what was then the latest model, the iPhone X. Released in November 2017, it featured Face ID, a state-of-the-art security feature that Apple had promoted at its launch. The Dutch team had been trying to pick the phone’s door lock, so to speak, when it occurred to them that the Russians may have found an unlocked window to gain entry instead. Their hypothesis was correct. By early 2018, the MIVD had found a vulnerability in the iPhone that gave them access. The security exploit wasn’t perfect, however. Some malware allows a hacker to turn a victim’s phone into a microphone and video camera, turn the phone on or off, and pull and add files. The Dutch solution did not provide that level of access. Instead, when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner’s screen as he used it, filing their own cache of surveillance on their internal computer servers.

As they monitored Kushner’s phone, they discovered he used it to log in to a UAE bank account. By the time the Dutch spies had visibility into the phone, the account had received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan. Their initial assessment was that the bank account was affiliated with the government there.

For the MIVD hackers, the bank account became an intelligence mystery to unravel. Nearly everything they worked on had a tinge of Russian conspiracy. A little over a year into Trump’s first presidency, the MIVD, like FBI agents and federal prosecutors in Washington working on the Robert Mueller investigation, had only part of the story.

Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept. Despite the perception of his wealth, Kushner was not entirely financially independent of his parents, and the family business, Kushner Companies, faced a billion-dollar loan coming due on their trophy property, the Manhattan office building at 666 Fifth Avenue.

Early in the first Trump administration, MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals. The idea was to help pay for Trump’s promised wall between Mexico and the US, for example, in an effort to secure a second term in the White House. The two Arab royals initially discussed with Kushner putting more than $10 billion into the effort. Within months, though, as MBZ pushed the Trump administration to help back MBS’s effort to become his country’s crown prince—and future king—the broader foreign policy slush fund idea fizzled. Instead, MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2 billion into at least two bank accounts for Kushner. It is unclear how the royals organized their $2 billion in combined payments, but they effectively split the cost. For the purposes of explanation, it is best to understand where and how each bank account was controlled.

Bank account Alpha was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in the UAE, and was overseen by MBZ’s brother, Tahnoon bin Zayed, who served as the bank’s chairman. Beginning in 2017, the Saudis and Emiratis transferred roughly $750 million into the Alpha account. Alpha would be used as a foreign policy fund. This money would be overseen and partially managed by Kushner and MBZ, who, in their effort to strike a grand bargain to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, believed the region’s map needed to be redrawn.

“Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” a source who knew of the UAE’s deal with Kushner said. This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. “Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off.” A slush fund—a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives—was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption, this person explained. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.”

The Alpha account looked like the funding source of a UAE government program, by which MBZ paid his bureaucrats their salaries or funded government-run schools. But how and through whom the money flowed into the Alpha account revealed that it was intended to remain secret, more akin to a covert and illicit scheme, given that it was managed in part by a senior advisor to the president of the United States.

The Dutch spies who monitored the Alpha account noted that all of it was sent by a bank in Azerbaijan in American dollars. Azerbaijan plays a unique role in money laundering. Its central bank maintains high levels of US dollars in its reserves but does not adhere to the highest standards of bank transparency. As a result, Azerbaijani banks have well-established but unadvertised practices of serving as way stations for large transfers, in which a foreign currency is exchanged for an equal amount in dollars. For a roughly 6 to 7 percent fee on the transaction, some Azerbaijani banks will accept a transfer from a client who wishes to move Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. The Saudi or Emirati client sends the money to the Azerbaijani bank, which then uses a different internal bank account to transfer the equivalent US dollars to the client’s requested destination. For auditors, this shadow trade can’t be discerned.

A shallow audit, as the Dutch tried while monitoring Kushner’s iPhone, revealed nothing more than what appeared to be an Azerbaijani government–linked bank account that sent hundreds of millions of dollars to an account in Dubai. But there was another aspect of the Alpha account that the Dutch couldn’t see or understand, one that helped reveal the secret purpose of the money. Kushner did not own the bank account at First Abu Dhabi Bank. He was a signatory for an account managed and owned by an Emirati charity.

When MBZ and MBS first began contributing to the Alpha account in 2017, the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a UAE government-funded charity, was run by Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi. Al Falasi was a technocrat and a member of the Federal National Council, and friends with one of MBZ’s closest friends and advisors. As a result, Al Falasi and the Watani Foundation had a second mission. The charity was used as a cover to move money in support of the country’s secret military and intelligence operations overseas. Under the Watani cover, Al Falasi helped facilitate the UAE’s secret weapons-purchasing programs, one confidential source who had direct knowledge of the charity’s proliferation program revealed. This source said that the Emiratis believed that the program’s status as a charity made its international transactions less likely to be scrutinized and therefore served as a useful cover for funding MBZ and his brother’s secret wars.

MBZ and Tahnoon made Kushner a signatory on the Alpha account with Watani. As a signatory, Jared had access to it and could, in theory, make transactions, but it technically wasn’t his account. One way to view what Kushner did with the Alpha account is to imagine him as the director of the CIA. Had he been running the government entity that managed and ran secret foreign programs, maintaining the account, again, with presidential approval and congressional disclosure, Kushner’s conduct would have been within his job’s responsibilities. But he was not the director of the CIA, whose position is approved by the Senate and whose operations are overseen and accountable to Congress. Instead, Kushner was overseen only by his father-in-law, who, according to four senior Trump administration officials—two national security advisors, a White House chief of staff, and a former CIA director—were unaware of any presidential authorization for Kushner to access a foreign government bank account. (Kushner’s counsel, however, said Kushner did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed to by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.)

Regardless of whether he was a signatory or the owner, Jared was required by federal government regulations and the Internal Revenue Service to disclose his access to the account. Unless disclosed to and approved by the US government and reported on his tax returns, Kushner’s access to the Alpha account may have violated US law. (A lawyer for Mr. Kushner denied that his client had any knowledge of or connection to Al Falasi, the Watani charity, or a UAE bank account and stated that he had complied with all legal requirements when dealing with foreign governments.)

In addition to the Alpha bank account, MBZ put money into at least one other account intended for Kushner. By the spring of 2018, the crown prince had moved roughly $1 billion to Israel via Azerbaijan for Kushner. We will refer to this account as the Beta bank account. It is unclear how Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu first learned of MBZ’s money for Kushner, but a person briefed on the Beta account told me that the prime minister encouraged Kushner to have the money deposited in the Israeli Central Bank, in what would appear to be a government account. It is also unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him, but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit. But as with the Alpha account, there were clues in the way the Beta account was managed.

Israel’s Central Bank does not operate personal accounts. The bank holds and transfers only government funds. The government accounts use a dual-key system, which requires two authorized individuals to make any transfers from the account as an oversight mechanism. Netanyahu required Kushner to inform him before making any transactions from the Beta account.

To do so, Kushner passed his messages through Ambassador David M. Friedman, who frequently met with Netanyahu. With the money in the Central Bank, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to connect MBZ’s payment to Jared. It is unclear if spies in the Netherlands had any indication of the Beta account. (Ambassador Friedman denied that he had any knowledge of, or involvement with, any UAE money made available to Kushner, or that he passed messages on Kushner’s behalf. “I know absolutely nothing about any of these allegations,” Friedman said, “and the specific allegations about me or my alleged involvement in this alleged scheme are 100% false.” Kushner’s counsel also said Kushner “has no idea” about any such account, and insisted that “there are no accounts and never were.”)

Apparently, Kushner faced the challenge of moving money from the Beta account in Israel to other accounts where he could have untraceable access to the funds. One person who worked with Kushner to move the money out of Israel said that much of it went to bank accounts in Cyprus before being moved elsewhere.

During Kushner’s secret financial arrangement with MBZ, he helped negotiate a third, altogether distinct account. As part of what was, at the time, a secret warming of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE, Kushner helped negotiate an agreement by Israel to help defend the UAE from a major Iranian military attack. The UAE needed to cover the cost of the emergency defense, however, and the government secretly made another transfer to Israel’s Central Bank. This was something like a rainy-day defense fund. Combined, the three accounts represented a secret foreign policy negotiated by Kushner with the leaders of Israel, the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

Although Kushner’s position as senior advisor to the president was unpaid, he was an official government employee. Not only did his position require financial disclosures for ethics regulations, but each year he worked in the White House, he had to file both a public and confidential financial form, known as the Executive Branch Personnel Public Financial Disclosure Report, also known as a 278e disclosure. Because he had access to classified government secrets, Kushner was required to disclose any bank account to which he had signatory—or beneficiary—access.

Kushner’s apparent betrayal of the public trust, however, went further than his failure to disclose the secret Alpha account in the UAE or the Beta account in Israel. By giving him access to roughly $2 billion, regardless of how the money was used, MBZ and MBS were paying for his influence within the US government. Any efforts he made to shape US policy that came from a foreign government that had provided him with money would make him an agent of a foreign power. US law requires citizens who lobby on behalf of a foreign power to declare themselves and the country they are working on behalf of to the Justice Department.

One former prosecutor who worked on the Mueller investigation said that if Kushner promised anything to MBZ and MBS in return for the money they offered him—even if it was just speaking to his father-in-law—he may have violated federal bribery laws, as well as the foreign agent statute. (Mr. Kushner’s lawyer denied that Kushner violated any laws while serving in the White House.)

From PRINCES AND THIEVES: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East by Matthew Cole. Copyright © 2026 by Matthew Cole. To be published by One Signal Publisher/Atria Books, an Imprint of Simon & Schuster, LLC.

items.title: Russell Brand Survivors Deliver Impact Statements: The Rape 'Affected Almost Every Aspect of My Life'
items.description: Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison Monday following his conviction on rape and sexual assault charges. During the sentencing hearing, survivors of his sexual assault gave harrowing testimony.
items.author: Althea Legaspi
paragraphs: Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison Monday following his conviction on rape and sexual assault charges. During the sentencing hearing, survivors of his sexual assault gave harrowing testimony.

One of the rape victims, who was anally raped in 2009 by Brand at his home one week after she met him at his show at Hammersmith Apollo, said the attack impacted her life pervasively. She had to live with her parents for some time; took time off work, which impacted her career; it seriously affected her “intimate relationships,” and also her daily life. “It’s something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending,” Her impact speech said. Her statement was read by the prosecution’s lead barrister, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, as Sky News reports.

The statement continued: “I doubt my ability to make good decisions and no longer trust my instinct in the way I did.” Brand being in the public eye made it difficult for her to speak about it. “I felt that if I reported him I would not be believed,” she said, adding, “His fame, wealth, and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless.”
It has “affected almost every aspect of my life,” she continued. “Even now, I continue to experience anxiety, difficulties with trust, reduced confidence, and the lasting effects of trauma.
“What happened is not something that I have simply been able to move on from.”

Another one of the victims who Brand sexually assaulted in the summer of 2004 during a party in a bar in Soho where he grabbed her breasts, said she initially felt in “shock and turmoil” after the attack. The woman delivered her impact statement herself in court.

She said, via Sky News, that she “literally lost any love for myself for a long time, thinking I was damaged goods” and that turmoil over what she “should” or “could” do has remained with her for more than 20 years. Seeing Brand in the press made her feel “physically sick” while he was “parading around thinking he can get away with anything.”
She told the court, “It really affected how I viewed myself, I didn’t have any respect for myself and got into situations with toxic men as I didn’t have any self-worth.
“For many years, as his star was rising it was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke,” she continued.

As she read her impact statement, Brand reportedly did not show emotion. “Seeing the front pages of the newspaper talking about what happened to me caused me to have the only panic attack I’ve ever had in my life,” she added. “It was a truly terrifying experience.
“Even more terrifying was seeing my character be torn apart on social media by people believing all of us women were making it up.”

The woman voiced concerns about her identity being revealed as she has been receiving “accusations and death threats from manic supporters” on social media, which have “installed a genuine fear that my name will somehow get out there and some crazy person will come after me or my family.’

A jury in London found Brand guilty on four of the seven charges against him, including one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was found not guilty on two additional counts of rape, as well as one count of attempted indecent assault. The allegations against him were tied to claims made by six women between 1999 and 2009.

Judge Mr Justice Bennathan, who presided over the trial and sentencing, commended the victims for their “determination and bravery” for presenting evidence at the trial. He also nodded to the Metropolitan Police for taking “great care” of the victims and for their “hard work” collecting evidence.

“I do not increase your punishment because of it, but all those women had to face being confronted and being told they had lied or twisted the truth and/or they had agreed to your sexual demands,” he told Brand in court, per Sky News. “That was all done because of you, on your instructions.”
The judge emphasized that women “retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts” from predators like Brand, whatever they wear, “wherever they go, whatever they drink.”
