items.title: The 200 Greatest Rock Songs of the 21st Century So Far
items.description: “Rock & roll can never die,” Neil Young sang deep in the 20th century. Guess what: Neil wasn’t lying. Nearly 50 years later, rock is thriving the way it always has — by mutating, diversifying, evolving into the future. Now that we’re deep into the 21st century
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: “Rock & roll can never die,” Neil Young sang deep in the 20th century. Guess what: Neil wasn’t lying. Nearly 50 years later, rock is thriving the way it always has — by mutating, diversifying, evolving into the future. Now that we’re deep into the 21st century, it’s a perfect time to celebrate the songs that have made this a golden age for rock fans. But as always, rock & roll keeps moving too fast to get pinned down, which is why it remains defiantly, unrepentantly vibrant a century after Chuck Berry was born.

That’s the spirit behind this list — the 200 best rock songs of the 21st century so far. It’s a companion piece to our recent Reasons to Love Rock feature. The list is a wide-ranging mix of different rock styles, different generations, different voices. Some of these tunes are universally beloved classics, known and sung worldwide; others are deep cuts or underground cult faves. But from Bruce to Boygenius to Bombino, from Dylan to D’Angelo to Deftones, from Wilco to Wednesday to the White Stripes, we’ve got artists from around the world and all over the stylistic map.

This is an era when rock can’t be contained — it travels everywhere. In our Top 10 alone, we’ve got the blues, we’ve got dance-floor glam, we’ve got gritty punk and psychedelic jams and high-tech dystopia and acoustic storytellers, along with loads of air-guitar riffs. We’ve got metal warriors from Black Sabbath to Mastodon. We’ve got pop-punk and emo. We’ve got sex and drugs and black leather jackets. We’ve got riot grrrls, rock en español, indie upstarts, rootsy twang, African desert grooves, virtuoso guitar heroes, garage bands, electro experiments, grunge, deep soul. We’ve got Nineties legends from Fiona Apple to Sonic Youth. We’ve got the grizzled veterans who learned new tricks instead of going quietly: David Bowie, Prince, even Neil “Time Fades Away” Young himself.

We’ve got country rebels. We’ve got hip-hop headbanger anthems from OutKast and Jay-Z. (You know, the guy who called himself “rap’s Grateful Dead.”) We’ve got ambitious pop rockers from Olivia Rodrigo to Harry Styles to Taylor Swift, who’ve kept their unabashedly rock moves at the top of the charts. We’ve got the skinny-tie postpunk club commandos of the Meet Me in the Bathroom era. We ramble from the U.S.A. to Colombia, Tokyo, Versailles, Niger, Dublin, CDMX, and YYZ. Some of these songs are innovative and complex; others are three-chord bangers to make you jump up and down. Their only thing in common is that they rock. You can listen to it all here.

It’s a list of songs, not artists, so we mostly avoid repeating songs by the same artist. But a handful of legends simply had too many classics to deny. (How could you pick just one Radiohead song from this century?) The toughest part was cutting it down to a mere 200, with so many more worthy artists than we could cram into one list. But it’s a tribute to the vitality, diversity, and energy of rock in our modern age. There will always be folks asking why it can’t stay like the old days, but that question has been around since Buddy Holly’s plane went down, and the answer is the same as it ever was — rock keeps growing because rock keeps changing. The only way to deny the music’s irrepressible health is to stop listening, and what fun would that be? Keep reading for 200 excellent reasons to pump up the volume and let it blast.

- Yellowcard, ‘Ocean Avenue'(2003) Yellowcard managed to capture the ephemera of teenage summers of yore — and the angsty yearning for those days — in this violin-driven pop-punk classic. It wasn’t an easy feat. As the band finalized recording its debut, Ocean Avenue, lead singer Ryan Key couldn’t find a melody for the title track’s chorus. “One day I walked in, exhausted and almost defeated … and I sang, ‘if I could find you now, things will get better,’” Key told Rolling Stone for Ocean Avenue’s 20th anniversary. It was just what producer and pop-punk architect Neal Avron was looking for. “I tracked it on the spot, and our lives were changed forever.” —Maya Georgi

- Noah Kahan, ‘American Cars’ (2026) On his 2026 album, The Great Divide, Vermont songwriter Noah Kahan broadened his palette beyond the indie-folk magic of “Stick Season.” On “American Cars,” he dug deep into heartland rock, channeling Bruce Springsteen, John Mellencamp, and the War on Drugs. He likens drinking to a profession (“If drinkin’ was a day job/I’d be askin’ for more money”), while begging his sister to come fix the latest kerfuffle in the family. “The song was basically like, ‘You’ve got to get your ass home, we really need you this time,’” Kahan told us in his Rolling Stone cover story. It’s a propulsive stunner unlike anything in Kahan’s catalog — and proves he’s a genuine rock star. —Angie Martoccio
- Speedy Ortiz, ‘The Graduates’ (2015)

Sadie Dupuis’ pen was never sharper than on this 2015 song, which spins an alt-rock anthem out of a complaint about feeling overlooked: “I was the best at being second place, but now I’m just the silver you dread.” Her witty, literate lyrics and her twist-and-turn chords somersault over one another until she hits the bridge and flies even higher. (“Someone tweeted that I looked bored onstage,” she told RS. “I’m like, ‘I’m just focusing so I don’t fuck up this guitar part!’”) It’s a gem from a moment when indie rock was heating up again, and it seemed like all you needed was a distinct perspective and a distortion pedal to get the world’s attention. —Simon Vozick-Levinson

- Mogwai, ‘2 Rights Make 1 Wrong’ (2001) Thirty years in the noise game, and the Scottish punk lads in Mogwai have yet to go stale. They rose up in Glasgow, after getting their minds blown by My Bloody Valentine and Slint, blasting their own massively emotional — yet ear-bleedingly loud — style of worshipful feedback devotionals on their 1997 debut, Young Team. “2 Rights Make 1 Wrong” is their apex, from the 2001 gem Rock Action, around the time Stephen Malkmus was declaring them “the best band of the 21st century.” It’s a swirl of banjos, a vintage 1970s Vocoder, heavy guitar fuzz, distorted strings and horns, barking dogs — a psychedelic hymn, building for nearly 10 cathartic minutes. —Rob Sheffield

- Incubus, ‘Circles’ (2001) Incubus broke through in the final breath of the 20th century with Make Yourself in the fall of 1999 — a cosmic rock odyssey that featured their meditative acoustic hit “Drive.” They carried that momentum into the 2000s with Morning View, an ultra-chill California masterpiece that glistened with rockers like “Wish You Were Here” and “Mexico.” The album’s hardest-rocking moment was the head-banging kiss-off “Circles,” complete with guitarist Mike Einziger’s fiery riffs. When they rerecorded Morning View in 2024, the songs were less an exact replica of the originals and more a reflection of how they’d evolved in live settings over the years. Unsurprisingly, “Circles” sounded more ferocious than ever. —Angie Martoccio

- The Mountain Goats, ‘This Year’ (2005) Singer, songwriter, and guitarist John Darnielle’s look back at “playing video games in a drunken haze” when he was “17 years young” and acting out against an abusive stepfather brims with the sort of warts-and-all autobiography that feels uncomfortably intimate. And then you get to the chorus, in which the Mountain Goats founder vows that “I am going to make it through this year/if it kills me.” This track from the Goats’ stellar The Sunset Tree has long been a fan favorite before becoming an unexpected viral hit in 2020, when the notion vowing to make it through a shit time became unexpectedly resonant. —David Fear

- Old 97’s, ‘Rollerskate Skinny’ (2001) Dallas’ Old 97’s were initially lumped in with the alt-country scene, but by 2001’s Satellite Rides, they had turned into something else: an ace pop-rock band. Inspired by a brief romance with Winona Ryder, “Rollerskate Skinny” finds frontman Rhett Miller piling up lines both boyishly endearing (“You’re pretty as a penny”) and caustic (“Wouldn’t be here if the Athenia hadn’t sunk”). It’s joyfully buoyant, but with an ache at its center, summed up by its final line, which Miller stretches out till it sounds almost like an affirmation: “I believe in love, but it don’t believe in me.” —Jon Dolan

- Momma, ‘Speeding 72’ (2022) The Brooklyn-by-way-of-Los-Angeles band Momma was born out of the tight-knit friendship between childhood pals Etta Friedman and Allegra Weingarten, who met in grade school. Their longtime connection is all over the group’s wistful melodies, often hidden in under blankets of distortion, as no song might be as reflective of what they’re good at than “Speeding 72,” off their 2022 album, Household Name. It’s a dreamy, riff-heavy joy ride that brings in more and more overlapping guitars, swelling into a bit of chaos that sounds like the whole band moving around each other without ever stepping on each other’s toes. —Julyssa Lopez

- Juanes, ‘Es Por Ti’ (2002) Back in the late 1990s, Medellín, Colombia native Juanes left Ekhymosis, his heavy metal band, and decamped in Los Angeles in search of pop-rock stardom. He found it almost immediately thanks to a superlative ear for comforting hooks, and the guidance of producer Gustavo Santaolalla, By the time his second album, Un Día Normal, dropped in 2002, Juanes was a Latin Grammy winner and concert favorite. “Es Por Ti” sums up the Zen beauty of his spiraling, guitar-based melodies, the supple comfort of his guy-next-door vocals, and a sunny cosmovision of disarming sincerity. —Ernesto Lechner

- Wolf Parade, ‘I’ll Believe in Anything’ (2005) Spencer Krug’s baroque and surprisingly hopeful rock anthem has had a few lives now, the most recent being the endlessly charming needle drop from HBO’s Heated Rivalry. Krug actually wrote the first version of the song, a low-fi take on an upright piano, for his side project Sunset Rubdown back in 2005, calling it a “kooky” experiment. “For me, it was a scrappy little love song about two people willing to take a chance on their young relationship,” Krug said. He eventually rerecorded it into the billowing version that’s become the enduring Wolf Parade classic that saw a 2,650 percent steaming jump and peaked at Number Seven on the Billboard U.S. rock chart 20 years later. —J.L.
- Alex G, ‘After Ur Gone’ (2014)

Alex Giannascoli was a college kid making music in between term papers when he wrote, recorded, and produced this two-and-a-half-minute stunner. Released as the first track on his breakthrough album, DSU, it has all the qualities that would make him a star — the haunting falsetto, the piercing guitar lead, the cryptic words alluding to an unnamed loss. “I guess some kids do model cars or skateboarding,”  Giannascoli told Rolling Stone at the time, describing how he developed his DIY methods. “I’d go to the basement after everyone was asleep and record all fuckin’ night.” Many years later, he’s still doing more or less the same thing, for an audience so huge you can hardly call it a cult anymore. It all starts here. —S.V.L.

- Baroness, ‘Isak’ (2007) A surface read of the lyrics to “Isak” makes this song seem to be about living an unfulfilling existence on a farm. But singer-guitarist John Baizley hollers couplets like, “Isak, tender the swine, carry the hare and barrow home,” in a way that suggests there’s something deeper going on. Ultimately, it’s the overall feel of this Red Album standout that made “Isak” an instant classic. Baizley and Brian Blickle play swinging blues-metal riffs, each guitarist dutifully stacking his part over the other’s, with two great solo breaks — the first echoing Pink Floyd space rock, the second summoning Tony Iommi–like metal miasmas. And drummer Allen Blickle somehow holds them together with unusual, jazzy rhythms.—Kory Grow

- The Raconteurs, ‘Steady, As She Goes’ (2006) “Steady, As She Goes” was the first song Jack White and Brendan Benson wrote together before forming the Raconteurs in 2005 with Patrick Keeler of the Afghan Whigs and Jack Lawrence of the Greenhornes. They had an alt-rock hit with “Steady, As She Goes,” a catchy garage-blues tune with a bassline that recalled Joe Jackson’s 1979 hit “Is She Really Going Out With Him?” This song has two very different videos, each directed by notable filmmakers. The first was more traditional, directed by Jim Jarmusch, with the band playing in a barn, and another directed by the Malloys that featured Paul Reubens as a cartoonish villain. —Alison Weinflash

- Slipknot, ‘People = Shit’ (2001) “I’m in this band because of everything that I hate about everything in the world,” Slipknot drummer Joey Jordison told Rolling Stone in 2000. Actual children of the corn, the nine mutants of Slipknot came out of Iowa in the late Nineties with their scary masks and bone-breaking live shows, and made their eye-popping extremism the most explosive attraction on Ozzfest. They summed up their hate-everything worldview with succinct fury on the nu-metal maelstrom “People = Shit,” an undeniable statement of tribal misanthropy and outcast self-determination. —J.D.

- Tame Impala, ‘Elephant’ (2012) On “Elephant,” Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker took some of rock’s most familiar pleasures — fuzzed-out Sabbath chug, high-heeled glam stomp, mind-melting psychedelia — and fused them into a sonic funhouse of his own. The lead single from his sophomore album, Lonerism, builds a whole world around Parker’s supersized riff. The song’s wonderfully wiggy midsection — a fantastic voyage of proggy synths, heavily distorted guitar, and burbling electronics — blasts into the cosmos before snapping back into its big dumb riff, showing Parker’s knack for indulging headphone listeners without losing the arena crowd. —Jason Roth

- Velvet Revolver, ‘Slither’ (2004) Unlike so many other Frankenstein bands, the mashup of Stone Temple Pilots and Guns N’ Roses known as Velvet Revolver wasn’t a cringey lark. The group actually turned out kick-ass, relevant hard rock songs, and “Slither” is chief among them. Driven by the river-bottom bass of Duff McKagan, the song twists and turns like its serpentine title, with Scott Weiland’s keening vocals cutting through the din. It climaxes with an eruptive Slash solo that ranks right up there with the guitarist’s best. Even Axl Rose seems to like the song: It’s become a staple of the reunited GNR’s set list. —Joseph Hudak

- Mudcrutch, ‘Crystal River’ (2008) After an incredible run of in the 1990s, Tom Petty hit a creative rough patch in the 2000s, with underwhelming albums like The Last DJ and Mojo. But he rediscovered something in 2008 when he made the unlikely decision to reform his pre-Heartbreakers band Mudcrutch and record a new album with them. Unlike Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, this was a democratic unit where all members wrote songs and even sang lead. But their best song, “Crystal River,” was a Petty original that clocked in at nearly 10 minutes. (In concert, it stretched out to 15.) Though considerably longer than just about anything else in Petty’s catalog, it’s a mellow journey that never gets boring or repetitive. —Andy Greene

- Bombino, ‘Amidinine’ (2013) A member of the nomadic Tuareg people, singer and guitarist Omara “Bombino” Moctar traveled from Niger to the Nashville studio run by Black Keys frontman Dan Auerbach and recorded the searing 2013 album Nomad. It kicks off with the anthemic “Amidinine,” which bridges West African “desert blues” and the pyrotechnics of Jimi Hendrix, whom Bombino discovered as a child living in exile with his family in Algeria. As he told Rolling Stone, “The freedom that Jimi expressed through his guitar sent me to another world, where I was also free.” You can hear that freedom in every note he plays.—J.D.

- Avril Lavigne, ‘My Happy Ending’ (2004) Following the spunky one-two punch of breakout hits “Complicated” and “Sk8ter Boi,” Avril Lavigne had something to prove on her sophomore effort, 2004’s Under My Skin. Though barely 20 years old, the Canadian pop-punk star had already seen her share of challenging relationships, channeling her disappointment into a singular line — “So much for my happy ending” — at the top of the album’s breakup ballad. She’s a co-writer on the song, with producer Butch Walker, and Lavigne’s lament is achingly felt in the bridge, “It’s nice to know we had it all/Thanks for watching as I fall/And letting me know we were done.” The success of “My Happy Ending” confirmed the opposite, as Lavigne’s star continued to rise.—Shirley Halperin
- Yungblud, ‘Hello Heaven, Hello’ (2025)

While he hadn’t yet turned 30 when his fourth album, Idols, came out in 2025, British agit-rocker Yungblud had already blazed a singular career path by the time of its release, and he used its opening cut to reintroduce himself to the world. The nine-minute, three-part rock opera, he told Rolling Stone, was inspired by him realizing the parallels between stadium rock and concert-hall classical; Yungblud added a dollop of 21st-century angst to the mix, cementing the song as his own. “Hello Heaven, Hello” veers from propulsive rock to swaggering post-glam to cavernous neo-power-balladry; it’s audacious and triumphant, with Yungblud’s tightly wound yawp sounding ready to conquer the world. —Maura Johnston

- Downtown Boys, ‘Monstro’ (2015) Providence, Rhode Island’s Downtown Boys combined refreshingly confrontational left-wing politics and a refreshingly confrontational punk attack on their excellent second album, Full Communism. The album’s peak cathartic moment was “Monstro,” a roaring critique of sexist, racist stereotypes and celebration of revolutionary power. With a blaring Lora Logic-style sax leading the charge, the song builds and builds until it combusts, as frontwoman Victoria Ruiz repeats the line “She’s brown! She’s smart!” like a battle cry. It’s political punk rock primed for the DSA era. —J.D.

- Moses Sumney, ‘Virile’ (2019) Moses Sumney is no stranger to challenging our expectations, whether he’s making your jaw drop with his ocean-deep, sky-high vocal range or creating spellbinding visual worlds to complement his otherworldly music. On “Virile,” a standout from his 2020 album, Græ, Sumney raises his glass to masculinity and smashes it on the ground. Sumney does rock music his way, alchemizing cavernous drums with spritely harp, industrial rock with classical music, heaven with hell. “Dear son,” he screeches to the stars, before slinking into his lower register, “We pick our own prisons.” “Virile” is evidence that we’re only confined to the boxes we lock ourselves into. —Jaeden Pinder

- Sleigh Bells, ‘Rill Rill’ (2010) A band birthed both in the belly of MySpace and peak-hipster Williamsburg, Sleigh Bells became a huge hit with blog-era tastemakers. This breakout track — off 2010’s Treats — sounds like your heart beating its way out of your chest, a tidal wave of guitars, booming drums, and electro sleaze, all showcasing Alexis Krauss’ almost too-sweet vocals. If you ever saw them perform live, you’ll know the feeling of all those amps buzzing in your chest as the crowd pogoed along. The track just sounds like 2010: languid and hopeful, a party before the world burns. —Brenna Ehrlich

- Alejandro Escovedo, ‘Castanets’ (2001) No one is better at merging the worlds of country-roots and punk than Alejandro Escovedo, and no song of his embodies his New York Dolls meets Austin roadhouse sound than “Castanets.” Escovedo storms and stomps his way through his deceptively nuanced tale of “a woman people don’t understand,” as he later explained. When George W. Bush was reported to have liked the song in 2005, Escovedo retired it from his set lists for several years, even though it was his most well-known tune. Then, more than two decades later, Escovedo deconstructed his cowpunk anthem with an entirely new arrangement and Spanglish lyrics on 2024’s “Castañuelas.”—Jonathan Bernstein
- King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, ‘Rattlesnake’ (2017)

The marvelously prolific Australian psych-punk shredders King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard have released a slew of songs that could potentially be on this list, but the opening track from their 2017 exploration of alternate guitar tunings Flying Microtonal Banana has taken on a life of its own. Chugging guitars and huge gales — as well as a Vibraslap that echoes the titular serpent’s warning sound — give “Rattlesnake” an ominously windswept, while lead Gizzard Stu Mackenzie’s constant repetition “rattlesnake” (he says it 54 times on the album version, according to fans) and the microtonal tuning make it feel like a fever dream that won’t — and shouldn’t — end. —M.J.

- Red Clay Strays, ‘Wondering Why’ (2022) Though ostensibly a country band from Alabama, the Red Clay Strays sure can rock: Songs like “Ramblin’” and “Down South” have all the punch of Lynyrd Skynyrd. In the case of their breakout song, “Wondering Why,” however, they display more of a slow burn. There’s no big riff, no bombastic intro — just Elvis-adjacent frontman Brandon Coleman’s smoldering croon, which blazes near the song’s end as drummer John Hall plays an understated beat with a few choice cymbal hits. For the really ferocious version of “Wondering Why,” check out the band’s Live at the Ryman album.—Joseph Hudak

- Future Islands, ‘Seasons (Waiting on You)’ (2014) The idiosyncratic Baltimore indie band had a surprise hit with the high-drama synth-pop of “Seasons (Waiting on You),” a song about how time may pass but some people remain frustratingly the same. Singer Samuel T. Herring delivered his heartbroken lyrics with an uncanny emotional force, going from a forlorn croon to an overwrought rasp that was hard to shake once you heard it. His ungainly dance moves were unforgettable too; when the band performed on The Late Show With David Letterman, the host’s floored reaction helped seed the song’s viral success. —J.D.

- Blondshell, ‘Salad’ (2023) “Gonna get big,” Blondshell’s Sabrina Teitelbaum declares. She accomplishes all that and more on “Salad,” the deliciously dark centerpiece of her 2023 self-titled debut. It’s the indie-rock version of “Goodbye Earl,” as Teitelbaum sets out to get revenge on a guy for abusing her friend — specifically by poisoning his greens. She lays out her plan across thrashing, restless riffs, inspired by Hole’s “Doll Parts” and Nirvana’s “You Know You’re Right,” a move that proved she was carrying the furious torch of the Nineties into a new generation. “Look what you did/You’ll make a killer of a Jewish girl,” she sings. It was one of the first startlingly great Teitelbaum lines — and certainly not the last. —A.M.

- The Monkees, ‘Me and Magdalena’ (2016) The idea of a brilliant new Monkees album in 2016 seemed about as likely as the Archies making a major musical comeback. But for their 50th anniversary, Monkees superfan Adam Schlesinger recruited an incredible slate of songwriters, including Noel Gallagher, Paul Weller, and Rivers Cuomo, for the comeback LP Good Times! Dead Cab for Cutie’s Ben Gibbard contributed the gorgeous ballad “Me and Magdalena,” which Schlesinger arranged as a duet between Micky Dolenz and Michael Nesmith. Their voices blended as seamlessly as they did back in the 1960s, finally giving them a new classic they could play in concert alongside “I’m a Believer” and “Pleasant Valley Sunday.” —A.G.

- Mdou Moctar, ‘Afrique Victime’ (2021) Equally inspired by Eddie Van Halen as he is by the Tuareg guitarists of his native Niger, Mdou Moctar is one of the 21st century’s greatest guitarists — and his hypnotizing solo on the desert blues track “Afrique Victime” is a perfect example why. Across the song’s seven-minute run time, the tempo rises and rises as Moctar laments French colonialism’s eternal scar on Niger. He plays the song’s guitar solo as if he’s vehemently typing away on a computer, sliding back and forth and drumming along the strings, warping the instrument’s tones to mimic a wailing siren. “Afrique Victime”’ is frenetic yet liberating — it’s no wonder he’s often called the Hendrix of the Sahara. —J.P.

- Sum 41, ‘Fat Lip’ (2001) “Fat Lip” is so immaculate, you’d never know Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley cobbled it together from disparate parts: a monster riff, a howl-along chorus, a tender bridge, and, most daringly, a rap-rock verse with the pass-it-off stylings of the Beastie Boys and Run-D.M.C. By Whibley’s admission, the demo stunk, but producer Jerry Finn saw the vision. “Fat Lip” remains one of the great achievements of the early-aughts pop-punk boom: an undeniable hit that’s sneakily inventive in construction and execution; a brilliant loser anthem that’s defiant, deprecating and degenerate, funny and furious. Still, to this day, it’s guaranteed to get the pit going. —J. Blistein

- The Rolling Stones, ‘Whole Wide World’ (2023) At the start of the 2020s, Rolling Stones fans had resigned themselves to the idea that they were simply a touring band at that point. Fortunately, producer Andrew Watt didn’t share this viewpoint and managed to coax them into the studio for 2023’s revitalized Hackney Diamonds. The LP’s climax is “Whole Wide World,” where Mick Jagger sings about a broke-down Londoner convinced his best days are long behind him: “When the whole wide world’s against you/And that’s got you on the run/And you think the party’s over/But it’s only just, only just begun,” he sings. The song was also a tribute to the Stones themselves, who managed to extend the party longer than any rock band in history. —A.G.
- Electric Six, ‘Danger! High Voltage’ (2002)

All together now: “Fire in the disco! Fire in the Taco Bell!” (Yes, it rhymes with “gates of hell.”) “Danger! High Voltage” was an insanely catchy floor-filler in the indie-sleaze days of the early 2000s — if you were a drunk girl and this song came on in the scuzzy rock bar at 2 a.m., you were legally required to dance on a table and kick the DJ’s drinks over. Detroit conceptual mastermind Dick Valentine groans about the agonies and ecstasies of physical love for a global left-field hit. But he gets a big assist from his duet partner: Jack White, uncredited but unmistakable, wailing “danger, danger!” in his high-pitched sex yelp. —R.S.

- Jason Isbell and the 400 Unit, ‘Cumberland Gap’ (2017) Before his name became synonymous with the best in detail-rich Americana songwriting thanks to albums like his 2013 opus, Southeastern, Jason Isbell was one of the three singer-guitarists in this century’s top literate bar band, Drive-By Truckers. On this rocker from his 2017 LP, The Nashville Sound, Isbell showed how hard he could still bring it, singing about working-class angst and desperation in the heart of coal country over the roaring backing of his band the 400 Unit. “Maybe the Cumberland Gap just swallows you whole,” he wonders. That sense of fatalism is deep in his bones, but so is the dream of punching your way out. —J.D.

- At the Drive-In, ‘Arcarsenal’ (2000) At the Drive-In’s third album, Relationship of Command, truly felt like a band firing on all cylinders. Their sound was sharper, crisper, and more adrenaline-surged than ever — some of that a result of producer Ross Robinson finding ways to capture the musicians at their most heightened state. And the first song, “Arcarsenal,” offers the best introduction to the power coursing through the album, functioning as a forceful call to action to break from societal conformity. It’s also a solid example of Omar Rodríguez-López and Cedric Bixler-Zavala’s almost telepathic connection, with Bixler-Zavala howling out the lyrics (“I must have read a thousand faces”) to Rodríguez-López’s blistering riffs. —J.L.

- Louis XIV, ‘Finding Out True Love Is Blind’ (2005) Deliciously sexy and sleazy, this track epitomized why Louis XIV were once banned in Alabama. What other band can make “carrot juice” sound dirty? The standout on 2005’s The Best Little Secrets Are Kept, this song encapsulates a truly horny era replete with flat-ironed bangs, that first foray into skinny jeans, and a solid lacquering of eyeliner. The song may have an STD or two, but singer Jason Hill is an equal opportunity letch: smart girls, short girls, tough girls, girls of all races and creeds, he’s down to wind you up and make you crawl to him — even 20 years later. —B.E.

- Deerhunter, ‘Desire Lines’ (2010) On their space-rock epiphany “Desire Lines,” the Atlanta band Deerhunter found a happy place somewhere between moody Velvet Underground drone poetry and languid, stretched out, eat-a-peach transcendence. The peak moment on their great LP Halcyon Digest, the song begins as a hesitant reflection on twentysomething coming-of-age ambivalences, then lifts off into a mind-meld monster jam between guitarists Lockett Pundt and Bradford Cox, who make like shoegaze ninjas for three dazzling minutes. It’s a modern psychedelic bounty that brilliantly undercut trippy escapism with real-life ambivalence. —J.D.

- Sturgill Simpson, ‘Call to Arms’ (2016) After the release of his breakthrough album, Metamodern Sounds in Country Music, it was clear that Sturgill Simpson was in a category all his own, far beyond just the bounds of traditional country. He cemented that on 2016’s A Sailor’s Guide to Earth, which ends with the furious “Call to Arms,” where Simpson, alongside a wailing horn section, bemoans our modern discontents. “They serve up distractions and we eat ‘em with fries, until the bombs fall out of our fucking skies,” he sings. When Simpson appeared on Saturday Night Live, he finished the song with the ultimate rock star move: smashing his guitar.—Marissa R. Moss
- Ought, ‘Beautiful Blue Sky’ (2015)

The Montreal post-punk rebels Ought racked up a string of cerebral records in the 2010s, eventually evolving into the new band Cola, which put out one of 2026’s finest rock statements with Cost of Living Adjustment. “Beautiful Blue Sky” is a life-affirming staccato guitar groove, building under Tim Darcey’s acerbically witty voice, as he narrates another boring no

items.title: The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time
items.description: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks. So we’ve updated the list. We kept the update light; the 2021 list covered many decades of popular music, and was the result of a vote among more than 300 artists, writers, producers and industry figures; this update covers three years, from 2021 to early 2024.

In 2004, Rolling Stone published its list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. It’s one of the most widely read stories in our history, viewed hundreds of millions of times on this site. But a lot has changed since 2004; back then the iPod was relatively new, and Billie Eilish was three years old. So we’ve decided to give the list a total reboot. To create the new version of the RS 500 we convened a poll of more than 250 artists, musicians, and producers — from Angelique Kidjo to Zedd, Sam Smith to Megan Thee Stallion, M. Ward to Bill Ward — as well as figures from the music industry and leading critics and journalists. They each sent in a ranked list of their top 50 songs, and we tabulated the results.

Nearly 4,000 songs received votes. Where the 2004 version of the list was dominated by early rock and soul, the new edition contains more hip-hop, modern country, indie rock, Latin pop, reggae, and R&B. More than half the songs here weren’t present on the old list, including a third of the Top 100. The result is a more expansive, inclusive vision of pop, music that keeps rewriting its history with every beat.

- Harry Styles, ‘As It Was’ The lead single from Harry Styles’ third album balances its agitated inner monologue, where the shape-shifting pop star picks at the details of a relationship in crisis, with spun-sugar synths that give cover to his torment. From its playful opening — Styles’ goddaughter Ruby giggling “Go on, Harry, we want to say goodnight to you!” — to its singsong bridge, during which Styles’ thoughts are ping-ponging around his head at “high-speed internet” velocities, “As It Was” paints an unusually vivid picture. Everything might seem fine on first glance, but it all becomes more troubling (“What kind of pills are you on?”) with each repeated glimpse.

- Townes Van Zandt, ‘Pancho and Lefty’ An epic story-song about a bandit and the friend who betrays him, “Pancho and Lefty” became a country hit thanks to Willie Nelson and Merle Haggard’s 1983 duet. But it’s the songwriter’s own forlorn reading, on 1972’s The Late Great Townes Van Zandt, that best conveys the doomed fates of the main characters. It begins with what might be one of the most descriptive opening verses in the country-folk canon: “Living on the road my friend/was gonna keep you free and clean/now you wear your skin like iron/your breath as hard as kerosene.” “It’s hard to take credit for the writing,” Van Zandt said in 1984, “because it came from out of the blue.”

- Lizzo, ‘Truth Hurts’ “That song is my life and its words are my truth,” Lizzo wrote at the time. She had to tack on a writing credit to British singer Mina Lioness, who had tweeted its iconic line “I just took a DNA test, turns out I’m 100 percent that bitch,” but the power of this gale-force breakup banger was pure Lizzo, uproariously swaggering and endearingly soulful. “Truth Hurts” was originally released in 2017, but the song got a big boost two years later, when Gina Rodriguez day-drunkenly sang it in the Netflix show Someone Great, and it became Lizzo’s signature hit.

- Harry Nilsson, ‘Without You’ “We did it because my career was on the wane and we wanted something to make a hit,” Harry Nilsson bluntly told an interviewer when asked why he covered Badfinger’s near-despondent ballad: “I heard it and searched through every Beatles album for two and a half weeks, trying to find out which one of their tunes it was.” Producer Richard Perry agreed, piling on the strings to showcase Nilsson’s desperate lunge of a vocal. Both were right — the song went to Number One and earned a Grammy nomination for Record of the Year.

- Carly Simon, ‘You’re So Vain’ The holy mother of all diss tracks, “You’re So Vain” contains one of the most enduring musical mysteries of all time. Just who is so vain that he probably thinks the song is about him? Simon previously revealed that actor Warren Beatty inspired the second verse of the song (“Oh, you had me several years ago/When I was still naive”), but speculation abounds regarding the other man (or men) behind the ire. Either way, the track — boasting omnipresent Seventies arranger Paul Buckmaster’s orchestration and Mick Jagger’s background vocals — is pure soft-rock fire.

- Cyndi Lauper, ‘Time After Time’ Cyndi Lauper was nervous about “Time After Time” — the aching ballad she wrote in the studio with keyboardist Rob Hyman to finish off her blockbuster solo debut, She’s So Unusual. “I asked them to please not put ‘Time After Time’ out as the first single,” Lauper said. “People would never have accepted me. If you do a ballad first, and then a rocker, that doesn’t work.” Her instincts were right: Following the jaunty “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” “Time” became her first Number One.

- The Pixies, ‘Where Is My Mind?’ No song typifies the freakish pop instincts that made the Pixies stand out in a sea of gloomy Reagan-era bands better than “Where Is My Mind?” Joey Santiago’s lead guitar is catchier than most Top 40 hooks, and by the time Fight Club made this song iconic a decade after its release, it had already formed part of the DNA of countless alternative-radio hits in the years between, from Nirvana to Korn. When an interviewer in 1988 asked about his unique ability to crank out great songs, Black Francis’ answer was typically cryptic: “It’s nice to have space. How much can one brain deal with?”

- Kanye West, ‘Stronger’ Explaining the tighter, broader-reaching songs on his third album, Graduation, Kanye West said, “I applied a lot of the things I learned on tour [in 2006] with U2 and the Rolling Stones, about songs that rock stadiums. And they worked!” West found the inspiration for his most grandiose statement to date from Daft Punk’s “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger,” which he sampled and reshaped. West is a big fan of the French duo: “These guys really stick with the whole not-showing-their-faces thing. Just amazing discipline — that’s straight martial-arts status.”

- Miles Davis, ‘So What’ It’s likely that no song on this list has soundtracked more dinner parties than Kind of Blue’s warm, welcoming first track. But at the time it was a jarring departure, trading bebop chord changes for a more open-ended modal style. According to pianist Bill Evans, the trumpeter worked up his material just hours before recording dates, but the all-star band here sounds like it’s been living with “So What” for years: Saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley turn in solos that have since become as iconic as any in jazz history, and the rhythm section of Evans, bassist Paul Chambers, and drummer Jimmy Cobb swings like it’s dancing on air.

- Bad Bunny, ‘Titi Me Pregunto’ “Tití Me Preguntó” is a showcase for Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny’s unbridled creativity and eccentric pop genius, mixing frantic dembow beats, a classy sample by bachata master Anthony Santos, and a coda with a dash of Latin psychedelia to the global mainstream. He does it all with panache and a healthy sense of humor. Using the archetype of the concerned Latin American aunt asking about her nephew’s potential girlfriends as a starting point, he launches into a hilarious tirade of salacious puns to a bouncy party vibe that — in typical Bad Bunny fashion — unexpectedly morphs into moody self-reflection.

- Lil Nas X, ‘Old Town Road’ Montero Hill was an Atlanta college dropout sleeping on his sister’s couch and looking to break into music when he came across a track he liked by a Dutch 19-year-old called YoungKio that was based around a banjo sample from a Nine Inch Nails track. “I was picturing, like, a loner cowboy runaway,” he told Rolling Stone. Within a year “Old Town Road” was the longest-running Number One song of all time, seeming to sum up eons of American cross-cultural love and theft in just one minute and 53 seconds.

- The Breeders, ‘Cannonball’ Notified by fax that her services in the Pixies were no longer required, Kim Deal called up her twin sister, Kelley, to be her new guitarist (never mind that she didn’t know how to play guitar) and had the last laugh when this absurdist gem became an MTV phenomenon in 1993. “When people were talking about the Breeders being a one-off,” Kelley told Rolling Stone, “I was like ‘No, actually … the Pixies are a side project.'” A little over a year later, the Breeders were on an extended break of their own, but the effortlessly fun trampoline bounce of “Cannonball” is one for all time.

- The Weeknd, ‘House of Balloons’ Far from the international superstar he’d become, Toronto singer-songwriter Abel Tesfaye didn’t even send out photos or do any interviews when he released the first Weeknd album. “The whole ‘enigmatic artist’ thing, I just ran with it,” he said. “No one could find pictures of me. It reminded me of some villain shit.” But the title track of House of Balloons nevertheless set the course for his career, both thematically — drugs and sex, meet depression — and musically, with its sample of Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “Happy House” announcing a new direction for R&B.

- Solange, ‘Cranes in the Sky’ In an interview with her sister Beyoncé, R&B innovator Solange Knowles described how this song was inspired, in part, by overzealous real estate development she noticed around Miami: “This idea of building up, up, up that was going on in our country at the time, all of this excessive building, and not really dealing with what was in front of us.” She turned the metaphor inward to examine her own feelings about change, self-doubt, and aspiration, finishing the song years after it was originally conceived with producer Raphael Saadiq to create a lavish moment of neo-soul introspection.

- Lil Wayne, ‘A Milli’ Producer Bangladesh looped the opening chords from Gladys Knight and the Pips’ “Don’t Burn Down the Bridge,” then segued to a drill-like volley of trap drums. He gave the beat to his friend Shanell — a onetime R&B singer on Wayne’s Young Money Entertainment — to pass along. Wayne initially had grand plans for “A Milli”: He wanted to use the instrumental as skits for rappers like Tyga, Hurricane Chris, Corey Gunz, and Lil Mama. In the end, though, “A Milli” is just Weezy solo, blacking out in the booth and dazzling everyone who hears him.

- Azealia Banks, ‘212’ In 2011, Azealia Banks was a teenage rapper-singer whose clear talent yielded a development deal with XL Recordings but little else. “She had been working on a collection of tracks and there was one Dutch house-sounding one that was just absolutely insane,” producer Jacques Greene recalled. Banks freestyled ferociously about her New York hometown and, uh, cunnilingus over the jittery beats of Belgian house duo’s Lazy Jay’s “Float My Boat.” Initially released in 2011 as a viral track, “212” was a hip-house banger that earned Banks a deal with Interscope and served notice that this uninhibited provocateur would not be constrained.

- Weezer, ‘Buddy Holly’ Never has geek been so chic as in Weezer’s 1994 breakout single, “Buddy Holly.” Written for frontman Rivers Cuomo’s girlfriend, the poppy ode to nerdy romance was almost left off the band’s self-titled debut, also known as the Blue Album, due to Cuomo and now-ex-member Matt Sharp’s reticence. “We had the sense that it could be taken as a novelty song, and people aren’t going to take the album seriously,” Sharp told Rolling Stone. After producer Ric Ocasek heard the receptionist at the recording studio humming it, he insisted they keep it in.

- The Four Tops, ‘I Can’t Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)’ One of Motown’s most rousing anthems, “I Can’t Help Myself” was inspired by songwriter Lamont Dozier’s grandfather, who’d call the women his hairdresser wife fixed up “sugar pie” and “honey bunch.” During the recording, engineer Harold Taylor recalled, “People were banging on the door of the studio; they were so ecstatic about what they heard.” Nevertheless, Levi Stubbs asked Brian Holland if he could do another take. Holland promised him they’d do it soon — and Stubbs’ first pass hit Number One.

- Lady Gaga, ‘Bad Romance’ Shortly after Gaga had established herself as a star, she catapulted to a next level of weirdness with this Nadir “RedOne” Khayat production, which drew upon the electronic music Gaga had been inundated with while touring Europe. “I want the deepest, darkest, sickest parts of you that you are afraid to share with anyone because I love you that much” is how she summed up the idea behind the song. Fittingly, she debuted the hit-to-be at Alexander McQueen’s show at Paris Fashion Week.

- Robert Johnson, ‘Cross Road Blues’ The primal terror in the Mississippi bluesman’s voice, and his mystifying slide guitar playing, transfixed the Sixties generation of British rockers: “I could take the music only in very small measures because it was so intense,” said Eric Clapton. Recorded during a session at a San Antonio hotel room in 1936, two years before Johnson was murdered at 27, “Cross Road Blues” is a mythmaking statement of spiritual desolation and scorched-earth betrayal — even if the legend that it’s about Johnson selling his soul to the devil in exchange for his monster guitar chops is, as far as we know, apocryphal.

- Biz Markie, ‘Just a Friend’ Nobody beats the Biz (1964-2021), an impossibly good-natured DJ, rapper, producer, human beatboxer, and hip-hop personality who broke big with this ode to the friend zone off his second album. Built on a fat beat, plinking piano, and his charmingly off-key singing, “Just a Friend” interpolates Freddie Scott’s 1968 song “(You) Got What I Need” as Biz warbles about a love that will never come to pass. It was based on real life. As he told Rolling Stone in 2000, “I was talking to this girl from L.A., and every time I called her, this dude was at her house, and she’d say, ‘Oh, he’s just a friend.’ I hated that.”

- Santana, ‘Oye Como Va’ Growing up in San Francisco, Carlos Santana was shaped by the city’s psychedelic explosion. “You cannot take LSD and not find your voice,” he once claimed, “because there is nowhere to hide.” And while his early heroes were bluesmen, he changed history with this foundational Latin-rock reworking of a 1962 salsa number by Cuban percussionist Tito Puente. Santana kept the original’s cha-cha pulse but replaced its horns with Greg Rolie’s organ and Carlos’ lysergic guitar flares. Said Puente years later, “He put our music, Latin rock, around the world, man.”

- Juvenile feat. Lil Wayne and Mannie Fresh, ‘Back That Azz Up’ In the late Nineties, Mannie Fresh’s diamond-sharp productions for Cash Money Records helped put New Orleans in the center of the hip-hop map. The title of this hit was so reminiscent of local artist DJ Jubilee’s single “Back That Thang Up” that Jubilee sued (unsuccessfully) for infringement, and the beat rode the “Triggerman” rhythm that is foundational to New Orleans bounce. Juvenile freestyled his best shit-talking bounce rhymes, and Lil Wayne shut it down with a “drop it like it’s hot” hook. As Mannie said, “[He] immediately was just like, ‘Shit, I’m getting a piece of this.’”

- The Go-Gos, ‘Our Lips Are Sealed’ The radiant first hit of the Go-Go’s was influenced, according to writer Jane Wiedlin, by “the Buzzcocks and Sixties girl-group stuff.” It was also inspired by a clandestine relationship she was having with Terry Hall, of U.K. ska group the Specials, who got a co-writing credit because Wiedlin based the lyrics on some poetry he’d written her in a letter. “It was pretty personal,” Wiedlin recalled. “I mean he had a fiancee at the time — nowadays I wouldn’t touch that with a 10-foot pole, but I was 19, and I was like ‘fiancee shmiancee.’”

- Kris Kristofferson, ‘Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down’ The desolation of spirit in Kris Kristofferson’s “Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down” is so heavy, so apparent, that it’s almost hard to listen to. But that despair is exactly what drew Johnny Cash to sing it on his TV variety show in 1970. Kristofferson cut his own stunning studio version that same year for his debut album, Kristofferson. Cash’s interpretation, more shuffling and accessible, is the one most listeners turn to, but listen to them back-to-back if you can, and marvel at how Kristofferson’s lyrics about being hung over, alone, and desperate shake your soul.

- Janet Jackson, ‘Rhythm Nation’ Jackson’s socially conscious Number Two hit came together late in the sessions for her blockbuster LP Rhythm Nation 1814. Co-producer Jimmy Jam recalled being in the studio and “switching between MTV and CNN. Watching music videos on one side and watching atrocities on the other. Somehow they all merged together. The idea for ‘Rhythm Nation’ was you can dance, but we can also do something more intelligent.” When Jam heard Sly and the Family Stone’s “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)” at a restaurant, he raced to the studio to sample it.

- Curtis Mayfield, ‘Move On Up’ Mayfield’s irresistible “Move On Up” was politically empowering, morally demanding, and effortlessly propulsive, powered by swinging horns and tangy congas — the nine-minute LP version, with its powerful drum break, laid a foundation for disco and hip-hop alike. Mayfield’s message was just as steadfast: that pride and dignity were paramount for Black America to rise. “I’m not trying to say anything to make you think, ‘Well, this is the way, this is the only way,'” Mayfield said. “I’m trying to cover the whole subject.”

- Tammy Wynette, ‘Stand by Your Man’ From the start, this pledge of wifely devotion, the first song Wynette ever co-wrote, was a cultural lightning rod. Feminists recoiled from its pledge of unquestioning fidelity in the Seventies, and Hillary Clinton defined herself a modern woman by slamming the song during Bill Clinton’s first presidential run. But the recording itself steamrolls over ideological objections, as the catch in Wynette’s voice on the verses gives way to a vocal swell that rises to meet the epic sweep of Billy Sherrill’s production.

- Peter Gabriel, ‘Solsbury Hill’ Shortly after Gabriel quit Genesis in 1975, he climbed to the top of Little Solsbury Hill in Somerset, England, to reflect on his life-changing decision. It inspired his debut solo song, in which he explained to fans why he felt the need to go out on his own. Musically, it was a departure too, a pastoral tune with a 12-string acoustic guitar lead that was pointedly different from Genesis’ prog-rock. The song has since become ubiquitous in movies and film trailers. “Maybe I’ve let it go too much,” he admitted to Rolling Stone in 2011.

- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.title: Cupertino Recap: Drivin’ ’n’ Testifyin’
items.description: A lot of people consume network television via streaming services these days, and often in batches rather than one episode a week. So it’s probably not that meaningful that Cupertino’s sixth episode debuted on a Sunday night, rather than at the show’s usual Th
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: A lot of people consume network television via streaming services these days, and often in batches rather than one episode a week. So it’s probably not that meaningful that Cupertino’s sixth episode debuted on a Sunday night, rather than at the show’s usual Thursday time. But I still find the switch interesting, if only for what it says about CBS’s faith in this show. The network put this episode in a prime slot, after a day of football and 60 Minutes. Then they followed it with reruns of two more Cupertinos. Clearly they’re hoping to hook some new viewers.

CBS picked an especially hooky episode for this too. “Harper” is named for an uncommon Price, Siffre & Associates client: a young woman who is one of Christy’s many roommates, and not someone who has been recently harmed by a tech company. Michael and Olivia represented Harper in an insurance claim, convincing Judge Hornstein (Peter Riegert) to order her insurer to pay for a liver transplant that had already been scheduled.

But then, seconds before the operation is about to begin, another patient cuts the line. The purported reason? The algorithm that generates the transplant list ruled against Harper. Now that’s a case for PSA!

This plot is classic TV courtroom drama fodder. With the clock ticking on the donated liver — which needs to be transplanted into someone within four hours — two sets of lawyers hustle to make their arguments. In one corner: Harper Irvin, a young woman with her whole life ahead of her. In the other: Albert Ensler, a middle-aged husband and father who runs a hugely successful business as a venture capitalist. Both have a fair claim on the organ. But that’s not what the attorneys are debating. Their respective cases have to do with whether an AI-driven algo can be trusted.

Because this is a Michelle and Robert King-produced show, there are, of course, multiple twists — and I don’t just mean in the plot. The credited screenwriter Keith Eisner and director Rosemary Rodriguez stage this case-of-the-week cleverly, with nearly all of the testimony and arguments happening on cell phones via Zoom, while the judge and the lawyers are stuck in post-49ers game traffic. Complicating matters further: Judge Hornstein is in a ride-share car that picks up another passenger along the way, while Ensler’s lead attorney, the sleazy Ry Vance (in his first appearance since the series premiere), is in a self-driving taxi.

Eisner and the Cupertino writers don’t miss many opportunities to work technology into this story at odd angles — often making fun of the nagging inconvenience of all of our modern conveniences, from the noisy GPS devices that don’t seem to know where they’re going to the cell phone that dies in the middle of crucial testimony. (Judge Hornstein has to leave his car to find a charge and ends up in a noisy auto body shop, where the first they ask him is, “USB or lightning?”)

But again: The main technology under debate here is AI, and whether it’s capable of properly determining who should get a human organ. And what’s ingenious about this episode is that before the hearing’s four hours are up, both Ry Vance and PSA will end up arguing both sides of the issue.

When the case begins, Olivia and Michael are putting their former client and occasional employee, Vik Malhotra, on the virtual stand to claim that AI is biased against young women with a modest income. PSA also tears apart Vance’s witness Dr. Marjorie Wellington for phoning in her testimony from a nudist colony at Burning Man. Then another witness — who is in the actual courtroom! — testifies that the AI actually picked Harper, and that a human doctor overruled it. Suddenly, PSA is siding with Dr. Wellington and accusing Vic of being an unreliable druggie. (“I micro-dose!” Vik protests. “So does Elon Musk!”)

What eventually sinks the Ensler team is the testimony of Dr. Dexter Stimson, the man who overrode the algorithm. He claims to Judge Hornstein that he considered things the AI couldn’t, like the patients’ respective recent medical histories and the size of the donated liver. Sounds reasonable, right? Unfortunately, Stimson is undone when one of his disgruntled former assistants mentions that the doctor overrules the algo a lot, for patients who always end up dying. Oh, and before making this particular decision, Stimson’s cancer research program got a huge donation from the Ensler Charitable Foundation.

There are — somehow — two subplots running through this episode, even though nearly every major character is inside various cars for nearly the whole time. Olivia is in traffic because she just picked up her brother Jacob (Gilles Geary) from the airport. During the ride, she discovers that Jacob is very likely the victim of a pig-butchering scam, as he has sent thousands of dollars overseas to a girlfriend he’s never met.

Meanwhile, Michael’s in a car with Nichole, his ex (and lately his greatest legal rival), who is trying to find a moment to talk with him about an offer she just received. A boutique Silicon Valley law firm named Pandas & Associates — which handles “reputational” cases for all of the “Magnificent Seven” tech companies — wants her to come on board and become their dedicated anti-PSA attack dog. (And this company apparently loves dogs, given that every touchy-feely employee Nichole meets there has a pooch by their side.)

Both of these subplots in their own way speak to what Cupertino has been up to through its first half-dozen episodes — what those Sunday night CBS viewers might’ve been missing, in other words. In one storyline, we see how deep fakes and social media have led to a nice young man getting fleeced. In the other, we see how the friendly face of a Silicon Valley business masks ruthlessness. In both cases, the utopian promise of technology has curdled into crass money-making.

What’s been fascinating about all this over the past month-plus of Cupertino is that Michael seems to think that the only way he can sell his firm is to act as though PSA’s “standing up for the little guy” pitch is also just about profit, ultimately. When he tells Nichole that prosecutions of white-collar crime have dropped from 350 a year to 95 a year over the past decade, he says he sees that as an untapped market. Idealism be damned.

Does he really believe this, or is he just speaking the language of his peers? I think Michael’s body language may be telling us what we need to know. After Harper’s surgery finally begins, her mom hugs Christy, who brings Olivia into the embrace, who then reaches out to Michael, who stays stock-still. The ladies have to scoot over to him. He’s not doing this job for the hugs.
• Alas, any viewer whose first Cupertino episode is “Harper” will be deprived of Busy Philipps’s delightful performance as PSA’s rich benefactor Natalia — absent from this story.

• We also didn’t get as much of Christy as usual in this one, although it was a good running gag to have the nurses constantly snapping at PSA’s chief assistant for being on her cell phone while racing through the hallways.

• Olivia explains the presence of condoms, lube, and a sex toy to her brother by saying that one of her roommates borrowed her car. I’m not sure I buy that. I believe there’s much more to Olivia’s backstory and personal life than we’ve been told. For example, doesn’t she seem unusually hard-bitten when she warns Jacob not to trust every needy person?

• I’m glad Nichole Ferebee is sticking around, and that she will apparently be working for a firm that plans to aggressively and proactively antagonize PSA. I enjoyed Nichole and Michael’s bickering banter in her fancy rental car this week, poking at each other over who’s had a more privileged upbringing and whose legal strategies are more effective. (I also like how, when they part ways, Nichole says, “Come work with me!” and Michael answers, “At the Panda Express?”)

items.title: Saturday Night Live Recap: Druski Struggles to Do It Live
items.description: Druski is the most famous comedian in the country whom you possibly haven’t heard of. The host of last night’s episode of Saturday Night Live, who made history as the first “digital creator” to host the show, is undoubtedly on the rise. His self-described “ski
items.author: Charu Sinha
paragraphs: Druski is the most famous comedian in the country whom you possibly haven’t heard of. The host of last night’s episode of Saturday Night Live, who made history as the first “digital creator” to host the show, is undoubtedly on the rise. His self-described “skits” have amassed millions of followers on Instagram and YouTube and garnered him a multiyear deal with Netflix. It tracks that SNL would seek him out to host, given the show’s commitment in recent years to recruiting internet-famous comedians to join the cast. It’s a logical move on Lorne Michaels’ part, likely rooted in a desire to keep the show’s finger on the cultural pulse.

But what works on Instagram is not necessarily what works on live television. Though Druski brought a palpable enthusiasm and energy to this hosting gig, it became increasingly clear throughout the night that he is not a seasoned live sketch performer. Which, to be clear, is not a requirement by any means of an SNL host — there are myriad ways that the show can work with and around a host’s natural talents and abilities, whether or not they include live comedy. However, the show’s insistence on having every sketch of the night revolve around Druski only made more obvious the fact that this type of performance is not his strong suit. It became difficult, in fact, to keep track of the flubbed lines and awkward comedic timing that plagued so much of the episode, from the monologue right down to the last sketches of the night. It makes sense that the strongest moments of the show came in the pre-tapes, which perhaps share more DNA with Druski’s internet comedy than the live sketches.

The middling nature of last night’s episode also has something to do with the fact that the show didn’t do much at all with the current events of the week. Despite the writers having plenty of topical political material to mine with the midterm elections, the episode didn’t do or say anything interesting with it. Nowhere was this more evident than the cold open, which was weirdly inert, again featuring James Austin Johnson’s Trump and Colin Jost’s Pete Hegseth saying a bunch of nothing. And while I love JAJ’s Trump with all my heart (and will not comment on Jost’s Hegseth), the whole open felt like a missed opportunity to comment meaningfully on the blue tsunami. Even a cameo appearance by newly elected Senator James Talarico couldn’t save the thing.
Nonetheless, here are the highlights…

Far and away the high point of the evening, this pretape saw Druski donning whiteface (one of his favored bits) to play Elizabeth Holmes in a parody of You Can See Everything. Druski delivered his funniest performance of the night as a deadeyed Holmes opposite Jane Wickline (who also nailed it as Holmes) and Ben Marshall as Billy Evans. Druski’s understated delivery of “You trying to fuck me?” perhaps proves that he’s at his best when he’s not doing too much. Prepare to see this sketch clipped on Instagram Reels for the foreseeable future.

Another pretape that made good use of the night’s host. This sketch has a sort of convoluted premise (the weird guy on your corner gives you updates on your health by making unwanted comments on your body), but it works regardless. Maybe it’s because of the good character details— like the corner guy always having a fully charged Beats pill.
Weekend Update: Democrats Win Control of Congress, Trump Blames Poor Quality GOP Candidates

Update had a lot to work with this week, and while it didn’t quite knock it out of the park, Jost and Che still got some jokes in (though I’d like to note that the bits about Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed felt lazy). Special shout-out to the Epstein reference, “Infinity Watergates,” and the observation that Trump will live on in all of us in the form of long COVID.
Two People Who Just Hooked Up

This recurring Update desk bit remains a favorite, even if it follows the same beats every time and doesn’t really ever break its form. Is it possible that I just want to watch a romantic comedy starring Andrew Dismukes and Ashley Padilla? Yes! It is purely a delight to see these two onscreen together, and I hope we see them again.

The last sketch of the night made the smart choice of placing the host in an ensemble, as part of the socially conscious hip-hop group Lenny & The Street Smart Crew, played by Druski, James Austin Johnson, Ben Marshall, Kam Patterson, and Tommy Brennan. The sketch is smartly heightened, and the music doesn’t overstay its welcome.

• This episode had a number of cameos (Talarico in the cold open, Emma Stone during the monologue, and Walton Goggins during The Strokes’ performance). The goodnights revealed that apparently Dave Chappelle, Chris Rock, Austin Butler, and Michael B. Jordan had also been there, though they didn’t appear in the actual episode for some reason.
• Jeremy Culhane stopped by Update with an Elon Musk impression, which was solid, though not as memorable as his take on Tucker Carlson.

• The clearest example of the weird comedic timing of this episode appeared at the end of the Wedding Photographers sketch. I don’t know if there was a cue card flub or a missed line, but the ending of that sketch was truly odd.
