items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Recap: Attention Economy
items.description: Change has never been Dexter’s strong suit. The O.G. series’ familiar formula turned it into a serialized show with a distinctly procedural vibe — not that there’s anything wrong with that. After several years, however, a series that had once kept us on our to
items.author: Louis Peitzman
paragraphs: Change has never been Dexter’s strong suit. The O.G. series’ familiar formula turned it into a serialized show with a distinctly procedural vibe — not that there’s anything wrong with that. After several years, however, a series that had once kept us on our toes became surprisingly predictable. How many times did Dexter take on a burgeoning serial killer partner while another Miami Metro cop tried to pin him as the Bay Harbor Butcher? And then came Dexter: Resurrection, a radical revamp that actually recaptured the joy of the show’s glory days. Sometimes change is a good thing! It’s fitting, then, that the second episode of the season sees Dexter learning that the best way to counter a midlife crisis is by doing something different.

Harrison is also all in on change, having evolved from impulsive murderer to police officer working homicide. And while some might consider that a lateral move, he does get to spend more time with his one-night stand, Fiona, who turns out to be his field training officer and Captain Mixon’s daughter. This makes for a delightfully awkward moment at Brooklyn Diner when a clueless Dexter asks Harrison, “Is your officer one of those old-school types who’s gonna ride you hard day and night?” Double entendres aside, Dex is right to rain on his son’s parade about Harrison’s plum homicide assignment. It does seem more likely that Wallace wants to keep a former suspect close than that she was simply impressed by his test scores. Harrison’s frustration soon gives way to fear with the sudden arrival of Charley Brown, crashing their dinner and sporting a much calmer demeanor than when she was Prater’s right-hand woman. “Be cool, I’m not a threat,” she says when Dexter instinctively reaches for his knife. It’s such a thrill having Uma Thurman back, and the chemistry between her and Hall is electric from the jump.

Once Charley assures both Morgans there’s no need for police intervention, Harrison leaves so she and Dexter can have a one-on-one. “I’m here to help tie up some loose ends,” Charley explains. If we take her at her word (and that’s a big “if”!), she’s had a dramatic change of heart. Before her mother died, Charley confessed all of her serial killer-wrangling in the hope of absolution. Instead, she got the appropriate amount of judgment, and now she’s determined to make things right — which starts with eliminating the last remaining members of Prater’s club. Charley has no interest in hunting down the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger and the JawSplitter herself, but she can coax them out of hiding and into Dexter’s crosshairs. “I have no reason to trust you, so forgive me if I don’t jump at this opportunity,” Dex answers. He’s right that Charley could be lying, but what would her end game be? And on some level, he wants to believe her. While she can’t sway him with cash, Charley is probably right that these killers will strike again if Dexter doesn’t take them out first.

Back at home, Dex debates his next move with Harry, who has become a lot more open-minded between seasons. (Given that Harry is not an actual ghost but a reflection of Dexter’s psyche, I think that makes sense.) When you’re stuck in a rut, Harry reasons, it’s good to try something different. As hard as Charley may be to trust, there may be worse ideas than partnering up with her. Dexter points out that Harry has advised against this sort of arrangement in the past, and that’s certainly true of Lumen, Hannah, and Mia, among others. “That was true then, but things feel a little different now,” Harry notes. “Maybe being alone all the time has become part of the problem.” As it turns out, Dexter won’t be alone for long. Right on cue, there’s a knock at the door from none other than Joey Quinn. Both men look like they’ve seen a ghost.

Over drinks at a nearby bar, the former colleagues catch up. Quinn has left Miami Metro — does anyone still work there? — and he’s now a private investigator. Because the NYPD has not made any progress in finding Prater (good luck with that), Quinn is now working to find him and his serial killer pals on behalf of their victims. Last week I mentioned my concern that the Quinn storyline was going to play out exactly as Batista’s did last season, so I’m encouraged by a different angle here. At the same time, I don’t buy that Quinn isn’t also suspicious about Dexter, who famously faked his own death after Deb died. That’s not a normal thing to do! Quinn also makes a point of mentioning that Prater had a ton of memorabilia from notable Miami serial murderers like the Ice Truck Killer, Arthur Mitchell, and Travis Marshall, but nothing for the Bay Harbor Butcher beyond a James Doakes nameplate. Dexter smartly realizes he needs to keep Quinn close, and to that end, suggests working together on finding Prater. The theme of this episode may be change, but there’s a throughline of unlikely partnerships, too.

As Dexter mulls over Charley’s offer, he decides it’s worth trying to get the ball rolling on the New York Ripper. When he spies on Don Framt, he discovers that the octogenarian has groupies — though he’s not fessing up to his crimes, Framt has been publicly identified as the city’s most brutal serial killer, which has the hybristophiliacs out in full force. It’s fun watching Dexter wrestle with his complicated feelings here, balancing his repulsion toward the Ripper with his jealousy at another serial killer getting so much adulation. Dex follows Framt into a strip club, where he fans out over the New York Ripper and presses him for details that Framt is smart enough to hedge on. One thing Framt is clear about, however, is how much he’s loving his new fame. “Attention, adoration… that’s awesome, man,” an envious Dexter says. There’s a flash of the Ripper’s dark side when he harasses a waitress, a reminder that he’s likely still more dangerous than he looks. After Framt gets kicked out of the club, Dex fantasizes about doing what the cops can’t.

The problem, of course, is Harrison, whose admiration for his superior, Detective Wallace, means he can’t let Dexter take out the Ripper — she needs to be able to put Framt in prison herself. Thankfully, Harrison is accepting of the fact that Dex will have to get his jollies going after the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger and the JawSplitter instead. As much as I don’t need to see these two at odds again, I have doubts that a loving relationship between a serial killer father and his homicide detective son can last. On the other hand, it’s possible Harrison sees real value in what his dad does, especially given how much the NYPD is struggling to find the Five Borough Killer. The department is in hot water for not warning baseball game attendees about the first threat FBK called in — especially after Oliva’s daughters share on TikTok that their dad tipped them off — and Wallace’s casual remark that the killer could be a one-off prompts FBK to deliver his next warning. “I promise you, I’ve barely gotten started,” he says. “Someone will die on Broadway tonight. A very special show.” The cops have nothing to go on, beyond that the suspect is of average height and wearing smart glasses, so they take the drastic step of shutting down the theater district. It’s that or risk the cast of Other Desert Cities.

Elsewhere, Dexter decides he’s ready to accept Charley’s offer. “Maybe Harry was right,” he reasons. “Maybe I can change more than I think.” In this case, that involves discussing plans for offing the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger over a very expensive bottle of wine. (Charley has been draining Prater’s bank account, which she counts as her severance.) Dex’s one condition is that he needs to do the killing on his turf, which means Charley will have to be more involved than she’d intended. Under the pretense of a Prater dinner party, she will invite the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger (real name Ray Ballard) to a new venue, where she’ll introduce him to “Red Schmidt.” Dexter will take care of the rest. As part of the plan, Charley rents a townhouse that isn’t quite as upscale as Prater’s mansion, but will work in a pinch.

Ballard seems like a worthy next target for the Bay Harbor Butcher. Charley details his M.O.: watching his victims while they sleep, gaslighting them with barely perceptible changes to their home over multiple nights, and finally stabbing them to death with an ice pick. She also admits he creeps her out more than the others. “I think if you were to peel back the layers, you wouldn’t find an actual human in there,” Charley says. Even as they discuss a homicidal sociopath, there’s no denying the spark between Charley and Dexter, who quickly fall into a mutual respect that sure looks a lot like attraction. “It’s nice to work with a professional,” she tells him. Dex, who has spent these first two episodes desperate for attention, responds, “It’s nice to be recognized.” Kiss already!

To be clear, I love a slow burn, and I’m here for whatever course the relationship between Dexter and Charley takes. But the show is clearly leading us in a specific direction, as evidenced by the final scene of the episode, in which the two meet again at an outdoor restaurant and get mistaken for a couple by the waiter. When Dexter says it might be safer to let people think they’re a couple, Charley grabs his hand. (A “fake dating that leads to real feelings” trope? It’s almost like the Dexter writers knew AO3 would be down.) Charley asks what led Dex to agree to work with her, and he shares his new outlook. “I think I just finally came to a point in my life where I felt like it was okay to do things a little differently,” he says. “Be open to change.” They look like they’re about to lock lips for real after Charley learns that she and Harrison are the only two people alive who know Dexter is the Bay Harbor Butcher. “I’m honored,” she tells him, which is a funny way of saying, “I’m horny.” Am I falling into an obvious trap? Is Dexter? Before anything can happen, though, they’re interrupted by a body being thrown off the roof above them and splattering on a nearby newsstand. Nothing like the next FBK murder to kill the mood.

• FBK hasn’t earned the serial killer title yet, because, as Dexter repeatedly notes in frustration, it takes three kills. Earlier in the episode, he tells Harrison, “He’s killed one person, putting him in the same category as Aaron Burr and Phil Spector.”

• Was anyone else thrown when Wallace mentioned that the Ryan Foster case was a few years ago? I clearly hadn’t been paying enough attention to the timeline. For fellow confused folks, there was, indeed, a three-year jump between seasons.
• Harrison gets to flex some of his Spanish, along with a reminder that he grew up in Argentina with Hannah. Fiona looked pretty impressed!
• The song playing at the strip club while Dex buddies up to the New York Ripper is, hilariously, “Pony.”
• Speaking of Brian Cox, the sequence of the Sleepy-Eyed Stranger casing his next victims’ house reminded me of the Tooth Fairy in Manhunter, which feels deliberate.

• Care of Charley, Dexter finally has a new boat to dispose of bodies with, and he’s named it the Slice of Life Too. As Harry taunts, “You expect me to believe this isn’t part of your midlife crisis?”

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: The Price of Loyalty
items.description: Just when Henry and Julia think they have a little breathing room to figure out how to get back to the 1900s, a new wrinkle appears to blow up their plans. And this wrinkle, whether it actually happens or not, is surely going to have some major ramifications f
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Just when Henry and Julia think they have a little breathing room to figure out how to get back to the 1900s, a new wrinkle appears to blow up their plans. And this wrinkle, whether it actually happens or not, is surely going to have some major ramifications for Blood of My Blood going forward. Friends, Lord Lovat is totally going to try to kill Julia.

Let me back up a quick second: The lairds of loyalist clans — including Uncle Grant and Lovat — have gathered at the Duke of Sandringham’s Scottish Estate to meet with King George I. They are being celebrated and thanked for putting down the Jacobite rebellion. Lord Gerard Grey, who isn’t in attendance because he’s out hunting Dougal MacKenzie, gets elevated to Duke of Pardloe. Lovat gets his title and lands back and is named Governor of Inverness. Lovat could not be more smug about being the guest of honor. He’s especially thrilled to clock that Uncle Grant is bestowed with only a bronze medal, not a silver like him. And that’s not the only thing Lovat’s clocking: He meets Margaret Grant and is immediately taken by her.

You’d think this would be welcome news for Julia. It is initially, mainly because when Lovat makes up an excuse about Julia not feeling well to signal that he wants her to scram, it means she gets to sneak off with Henry. It does seem wild that everyone is cool with Julia being even remotely close to the dude they all think just tried to kidnap her, but I guess that just shows you how little Lovat actually cares about her. Sure, he makes a joke about demanding his head, and Henry gets big mad and begs him to try, which is objectively hot, but other than that, kidnapping, schmidnapping.

Julia and Henry do use Lovat’s fixation on Margaret and Uncle Grant’s fixation on Lovat’s fixation to their advantage. They sneak into a spare room so Julia can drop that bomb she discovered at the end of last week’s episode: According to Maisri, who has been right about everything else, Julia only traveled through the stones because she was pregnant with William, who does not have the power to travel. Leaving Julia behind is a nonstarter for Henry. It doesn’t take long before he’s like, Well, why don’t we just get you knocked up again? It sounds like an obvious conclusion to make, but Julia immediately shuts it down. She reasons that they shouldn’t have a child just to use it for their own needs, but I’d think a bigger reason is that there’s no guarantee the baby will be able to travel, and if not, they just brought another child into a very dangerous situation. But these two have never really concerned themselves with the nitty-gritty of time travel.

The next option they have is, of course, to grab William and run away together. But Lovat wants that baby — his future king — and if they run, he will never stop hunting them. Instead of feeling overwhelmed by the current situation, they take a moment to dance like they used to, remember how much they love each other, and remind themselves that for now, both of them are in safe situations and they have those gemstones ready to go in case of emergency. They have time to figure out what to do next.

Meanwhile, Lovat and Margaret have found a quiet place to make out. Uncle Grant bumps into them and is mostly disgusted by the whole thing, but it doesn’t take long for both Margaret and Grant to take control of the situation. Lovat wants to have sex with Margaret immediately, but she refuses to let Lovat do anything until he promises to marry her. She seems like the only woman he’s ever kowtowed to — and he likes it. God, he really is the worst.

We know that Uncle Grant has been looking to off-load his sister, so when Lovat sidles up to him, he starts talking about how Margaret would make a good wife, what with her sizable dowry and connections to some powerful people in London (she knows the king’s mistresses), but wow, isn’t it such a shame that Lovat’s already married … to his former maidservant. Whatever Grant is up to here, he’s good at it. Twisting the knife about how low-class Lovat’s wife is plays right into Lovat’s insecurities about his status. You see his wheels — okay, it’s like, one wheel — turning now. He wants Margaret, and he’s a man who gets what he wants. So he decides to build a little trust with Uncle Grant: He “lets” it slip that Ellen was handfasted to Brian before her wedding to Malcolm and the MacKenzies lied about it. Something tells me Uncle Grant isn’t just going to move on with his day after learning that piece of information.

Now that Lovat knows Grant is onboard with him marrying Margaret, he just starts spending time with her out in the middle of the room, for all to see. And “all” includes Julia. The moment she sees the two standing so close, she knows exactly what is happening here. Thankfully, Henry is nearby so she can tell him, too: Lovat wants to get rid of her, and the only way to do that and keep the baby without any type of scandal is for her to die. Seems like their whole plan to take a breath and figure things out, since they’re both safe for the moment, just got tossed out the window.

There are some death threats happening over at Castle Leoch, too. Lord Grey — now Duke, it seems — has arrived at Leoch looking for Dougal. (You’d think that would’ve been his first stop, but never mind me.) When Colum plays dumb about his brother’s whereabouts, Grey decides to arrest him. He doesn’t care that Colum stayed neutral in the rebellion — it’s still treason by omission and punishable by death. He agrees not to commandeer Leoch for the crown since the deed is under Ellen’s name and she had no power to fight for the king or stop Dougal from joining the Jacobites (Ellen’s plan worked!), but when Dougal rushes in to nobly save Colum from having to pay for crimes that aren’t his own, Grey takes it as an opportunity to kill two MacKenzie traitors.

Once again, Ellen has to clean up her brothers’ messes. At least this time, she’s going to take a little something for herself, too. She calmly gets Grey to agree to give Colum and Dougal time to pray before they’re taken off to be executed and then pays those boys a visit in the chapel. She will bargain for their lives — and she’ll get Grey to agree — but with a few conditions. First, Colum is going to be the sole laird of the clan. Dougal put them all at risk, and he can’t be trusted with any decision-making. Second, she’ll sign Leoch back over to Colum, but only if he agrees to give her the parcel of land that abuts Fraser land — the exact piece of Fraser land where Brian will be building their home. Colum and Dougal are livid that she’d even ask these things, which is especially rich because she could just let Grey take them, and Leoch and all the land and money that comes with it would be hers. These two are the biggest ding-dongs to ever ding-dong, and it is a wonder that they’re still around decades later in Outlander. Dougal can call his sister “a black-hearted bitch” all he wants, but they really have no choice but to agree to Ellen’s demands.

And Ellen makes good on her promise. She meets with Grey, and after flattering him for a bit, she reminds him that if he does go along with these executions, the story behind them will get out too. That story is, of course, that a rebel Highlander escaped Grey’s prison, killed a bunch of his men, and remained hidden and then gave himself up to save his family. Dougal will become a legend to the cause, and Grey will be humiliated. She also tosses in a bunch of money for good measure. It remains as true as ever: Ellen is the only MacKenzie really suited to be laird.

With Grey satisfied and Colum and Dougal saved, Ellen has one final condition for them: They are never, ever allowed to set foot on her and Brian’s land. At first, both of her brothers react to the rejection with anger. Colum refuses to pay her dowry, and Dougal makes a dig at Brian (who just saved his life, by the way) before storming out. But it becomes quite clear that they’re feeling more than anger, and if I had to guess, it would be that they’re embarrassed and heartbroken. Everyone on this show needs therapy, but especially the MacKenzie brothers.

You know what? There is one caveat to my previous statement. You know who is almost fully self-actualized? Ned. Sweet Ned! Colum may hide his tears when Ellen walks away from him, but not Ned. He finds Ellen one more time to say a real good-bye. He’s not afraid to tell her that he’ll miss her. The two used to sit by the fire and read and perform plays, and so, tearfully, he gives her a bit of Titania’s monologue from A Midsummer Night’s Dream — a bit in which he can tell her he loves her. “I do love thee,” she returns. She makes sure he knows he isn’t just the family lawyer and adviser to her. And hey, she never said Ned had to keep off her property. Fingers crossed these two best buds will get to perform Shakespeare again someday soon. Honestly, Brian would make a great Bottom.

• Have we been too hard on Colum? When Ellen tells him he’s not allowed to set foot in her home, he quietly tells her that she is always free to return to Leoch. When Ned remarks that he was actually worried Colum would turn Dougal over to Grey, he responds with a small but adamant “never.” Is he a secret softy inside, worried that he’s becoming a monster?

• Gah! John Cameron is headed to the West Indies (without Jocasta) to manage a sugarcane plantation he just bought, and he’s forcing Grace to go with him. Murtagh is beside himself when he finds out. He gets very Daniel Day-Lewis in The Last of Mohicans with his whole “I will board a ship! I will find you!” declaration. This can’t be the end for these two, can it?

• When Murtagh first goes to surprise Grace and she refuses to kiss him out of fear of them getting caught, he tells her that he’ll settle for his name on her lips. Murtagh is such a goddamned dreamboat. Nobody hurt him!!

items.title: Black Doves Season-Finale Recap: It’s So Hard to Find a Good Nanny
items.description: There’s a moment in “Murder Mix” that I barely noticed on my first watch and that I now think reveals a vital aspect of Laila’s character. She’s a mouthy smartass who amuses herself by launching peanuts into finance bros’ beers with stunning accuracy, sure. An
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: There’s a moment in “Murder Mix” that I barely noticed on my first watch and that I now think reveals a vital aspect of Laila’s character. She’s a mouthy smartass who amuses herself by launching peanuts into finance bros’ beers with stunning accuracy, sure. And yes, she can vanquish a van full of would-be kidnappers single-handedly. It’s likely Helen will be making choices to counteract the spy-wife label Laila slapped on her well into a hoped-for third season. But it’s the sincere “Mrs. Reed, are you okay?” when this teacup-size one-woman cavalry rolls up that points the way to Laila’s pivotal role in “Peace Summit.” It’s less of a softening detail — it does soften her a bit, but the character doesn’t need it — than a reminder of how focused Laila is on the purpose of the mission.

Everyone else is somewhere on the scale of checked out to what’s next. Helen’s locked in to being a supportive spy-wife for Wallace’s summit (and seemingly locked out of whatever he’s thinking — his face when she sees him in the kitchen the next morning, surrounded by the busy hive of his team, may as well be a closed door); Eleanor and Williams are figuring out what life after “I love you, too, you twat” looks like; having turned Reed over to Kestrel, Sam is doing penance by attending Jerry’s funeral. But Laila’s Spidey sense is tingling. She knows Sam didn’t walk Reed home, and she can feel something terrible is going to happen. Even if Sam had walked Reed home, I’m not convinced that home is safe anymore. What reason do we have to think the Black Doves are going to leave Reed alone now?

And Laila’s point about Reed’s safety and whereabouts is well taken. What was the point of all of them “risk[ing] our necks breaking her out of Downton fucking Abbey” if Sam was just going to put her right back into someone’s crosshairs? There’s not enough time, and goodness knows Sam doesn’t have the energy or inclination to explain the whole sordid story, but it turns out there’s no need to do so, anyway. Kestrel strikes on several fronts simultaneously with agents swooping into Wallace’s peace summit to kidnap Katya Chernov before she can deliver her late husband’s pre-opening remarks. They swarm his motorcade, snatching Cecile Mason and exploding her SUV (Helen has Wallace’s security team get them out of there immediately), and thanks to some very foolish IT assistance by Dani, they take over all of the security systems in the Black Doves’ main office.

It’s time to get the band back together! Yes, again! Laila explains she doesn’t just have a gut feeling that something is going down at the Black Doves’ offices; she knows because she has access to their computer network and saw the offices’ security system is down. And how does she know that? Well, remember how Laila was booted from active duty a few months back? It’s because she told her higher-ups their security system was inadequate and then hacked it after no steps were taken to improve it. So it took them three days to bring the system back up? Well, that only proves her point! The bosses do not like being made to look foolish (although right now would be a perfect time for a scathing “I told you so,” followed by a snotty, fully justified “Fuck around and find out”).

Meanwhile, Wallace and Helen are being whisked to a more secure location in a seemingly empty parking garage. This would be fine were it not for a couple of problems that make it completely not fine. Aside from the immediate threat of kidnapping, violence, and possibly death, I mean. Wallace can’t help but notice Helen’s effortless calm in a terrifying situation. She’s breathing normally and directing their team to contact the twins’ school so they can be secured as well, while Wallace is shaking like a leaf. Who is she? Who is Lily Morris? Why is the only photo of her as a girl the one Officer Perryman gave him? Helen puts in a decent performance with her usual lies, but it’s Katya, of all people, who provides the opportunity for Helen to start to come clean.

Katya was not kidnapped at all, as it turns out, because Katya is Vita. Storming the Black Doves’ offices was always the plan, as was having her mother frog-marched in and forced to sit through a very classic Bond-villain monologue about Franz eventually rescuing her from a Soviet orphanage and their pact to exact vengeance from everyone involved in the 1988 Berlin operation that nearly ruined their lives. She really shifts into high gear when she gets Helen on the line, taunting her about Nanny Marie’s years of service as a mole and current mission, having kidnapped Ollie and Jacqueline. Oh, dear. Katya, this is amateur-hour nonsense! I know you’ve spent years poring over the Black Doves and collecting details about Helen’s life and work; how are you going to stand there with all those hours of game tape under your belt and threaten her children to get her to convince her to shoot Wallace? Bush league!

Helen’s response is worth watching twice — first just to enjoy the scene in the flow of the episode as a whole, and then to see it through Wallace’s eyes. They’ve been together for over a decade, but in some ways, this is his first time seeing her. While she doesn’t confess any specific misdeed, she acknowledges the toll of the many secrets she’s kept from him and things she’s done, right alongside her love for him and their children. This may blow up their entire relationship and scuttle their planned future, but the score playing under this scene is the same bit of music that used to play under scenes of Helen’s reminiscences about Jason. It’s lovey-dovey and dreamy, and it could be a glimmer of hope. And then she pulls the trigger. Not on Wallace! Get real, this is a fake-out — she’s got children to rescue!

Chaos erupts immediately at Black Doves HQ once Eleanor, Williams, and Laila arrive. Kestrel is in immediate disarray, though Patrick manages to escape. Reed calmly grabs a gun and walks purposefully away, while Dani runs out of bullets and makes a run for the elevator, only to be blown to smithereens by the grenade Laila, Williams, and Eleanor relay to her. She really wasn’t going to get back to field work, was she? Reed finds an injured, bleeding-out Katya on one of the empty office floors below and confesses what we all knew: that she never went looking for her daughter because she didn’t want to find her. She was both selfish and generous in her restraint, expunging Vita from the mission records to save her own skin and to protect her child from any further fallout from the misfortune of being born to a Black Dove.

I can’t help thinking that this is a bit of a prelude to a similar conversation Helen must eventually have with her twins, not because she’s going to abandon them but because she’s murdered their nanny. What’s she going to tell them? Ollie and Jacqueline have known Marie their entire lives, then one day she takes them to the London Zoo for a treat and is never heard from again? They’re going to grieve and have all sorts of questions. They’re going to wonder if they’re to blame somehow! Therapy for all, stat.

So at the end of this mad week or so, where do we stand? Katya and most of her foot soldiers are dead, but Patrick survived and Kestrel is still well-funded. Black Doves have had to find new offices and deal with a staggering amount of paperwork, so they’re down but not out, and perhaps Reed will be able to bring Laila, Williams, and Eleanor on board. That might be over Helen’s objections: As Keira Knightley put it in our interview, Helen’s “whole life is about not knowing any of these people, and she really doesn’t want to have to be anywhere in such close proximity with them.” Then again, she may develop different notions about who should be on staff with the Black Doves because she finds herself needing their help. Regardless of future staffing issues, Knightley firmly believes that Helen is “going to take over the Black Doves, obviously,” reasoning that “if you are betraying your husband and the prime minister of your country, it is because you want to feel more powerful than them, right? I don’t think that kind of personality could just fade off into the distance.”

For now, Sam and Helen bid a loving, rueful good-bye as he heads back to that little town in Italy where it seemed like he’d found some peace (but he promises to come back if she sends up the Bat-signal). Most intriguing, Wallace does a bit of improvisational lying on Helen’s behalf in his follow-up meeting with Officer Perryman. There’s no CCTV footage from the parking garage or a several-block radius to compare to Wallace’s incredibly flimsy story about him and Helen dashing away to hide in a stairwell (where the armed men he references took their car but left them alone?) and Helen running off to some other hidey-hole until backup arrived. No mention here of Ollie and Jacqueline or of Sam. I assume all CCTV footage between the garage and the zoo is also gone. The real stars of this scene are the successive waves of micro-expressions crossing Adam Best’s face as Perryman is forced to perform calm acceptance of the obvious pack of lies that his prime minister is feeding him. I can’t wait to learn what Helen makes of Wallace’s freelancing, but first they’ll need to discuss her real name.
Strange Times to Be Nefarious

• So it turns out Cecile Mason was just there to be an insufferable American blowhard (fair, honestly) and then to get shot in the head? This piece of the story feels very rickety, though it does give us Reed’s “Well, you don’t hear much about Chechnya these days, do you? Thought it might be fun to bring them back,” so maybe it does balance out in the end.

• Jerry’s funeral was appropriately devastating and a vital reminder that, whatever assassins and their handlers tell themselves to justify their work, the grief and wreckage they leave behind in the lives of their victims’ loved ones is immense. Jerry’s best friend’s eulogy isn’t sad; she’s furious, and his murder will probably never be solved. The lavish, exuberant floral arrangement on top of his casket, reflecting his sunny personality and the way he made the world more colorful and beautiful, absolutely did not make me tear up.

items.title: ‘GTA 6’ Presales ‘Far in Excess’ of Expectations Ahead of Next Week’s Launch, Take-Two CEO Says
items.description: Rockstar Games‘ “Grand Theft Auto VI” presales are “running far in excess of our expectations,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said Monday.
items.author: Jennifer Maas
paragraphs: Rockstar Games‘ “Grand Theft Auto VI” presales are “running far in excess of our expectations,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said Monday.

“That’s a good thing. That said, we never claim success before it occurs,” Zelnick told Variety in an interview ahead of the company’s earnings release. “So we’re just days away from from beginning to see the fruits of our labor.”

“GTA 6” will launch Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S and X devices priced at $79.99 for the standard edition and $99.99 for the ultimate version. While Rockstar has yet to confirm exact pre-order results for the title, despite some rumors floating around regarding sales, Zelnick assures the company will “certainly be giving more information about how ‘GTA 6’ performs post-launch.”
The results are in line with what Zelnick and Rockstar previously disclosed after pre-orders began in June and reached “unprecedented” levels at that time.
On Monday, SAG-AFTRA released a statement in support of Rockstar Games workers’ decision to unionize, which Zelnick declined to comment on when speaking with Variety.

As for if and when “GTA 6” will make it onto other platforms, like PC and Nintendo Switch 2, or see a full physical disc release, Zelnick says that “information always comes from our labels” and will leave those potential future announcements to Rockstar.
Take-Two’s game revenue for the July-Sept. quarter was $1.38 billion. Ad sales reached $121 million. Sales for “NBA 2K” were softer than anticipated.

Wall Street forecast a loss of earnings per share (EPS) of 86 cents on $1.66 billion in revenue, according to analyst consensus data provided by LSEG. Take-Two Interactive reported a loss per share of 29 cents and net bookings of $1.6 billion. The company reported a loss of $54 million for the quarter.

items.title: DC Shocker: James Gunn, Peter Safran Out as Co-Chairmen, Marvel Veteran Jeremy Latcham to Lead Comic Book Studio
items.description: In a surprise executive shuffle, James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as CEOs and chairmen of DC Studios. They will be replaced by Jeremy Latcham, who will serve as president and chief creative officer.
items.author: Rebecca Rubin
paragraphs: In a surprise executive shuffle, James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as CEOs and chairmen of DC Studios. They will be replaced by Jeremy Latcham, who will serve as president and chief creative officer.

Gunn and Safran’s exit is unexpected because they were named as part of David Ellison’s business leadership team at the newly renamed Skydance when Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery had closed in October. After four years as heads of DC, resetting the studio’s comic book division to mixed commercial results, Gunn and Safran will return full time to creative work.

Gunn and Safran were appointed in 2022 by former Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav, with an edict to fashion a true rival to Disney’s Marvel Cinematic Universe. Under their direction, the duo rebooted the languishing DC Universe with last summer’s “Superman,” a relative success with $618 million globally, and then stumbled with July’s “Supergirl,” a massive bomb with $126 million on a $170 million budget. “Clayface,” a darker, R-rated body-horror thriller, performed modestly this fall with $109 million on a $44 million budget. Meanwhile, they expanded the comic book empire to streaming with its “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns” shows for HBO Max.

DC’s upcoming big-screen endeavors include next summer’s “Superman: Man of Tomorrow,” written and directed by Gunn, and 2028’s “The Batman: Part II,” starring Robert Pattinson. On the television front, there’s the 2027 series “The People v. Gorilla Grodd,” anchored by Skyler Gisondo as his “Superman” character Jimmy Olsen and Jimmy Tatro as Gorilla Grodd.

“Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore ‘Superman’ to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with ‘Peacemaker,’ ‘Creature Commandos,’ ‘Lanterns’ and ‘Clayface,'” Gunn and Safran said. “We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in ‘Man of Tomorrow.'”

Gunn posted a statement to social media after the announcement, saying “What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job.”
Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz praised Gunn and Safran for “[launching] a new era for DC Studios and [leading] it through a period of real transformation.”

“We’re grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand,” Ellison and Kreiz said in a statement. “Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans.”
Ellison also posted a statement to social media welcoming Latcham.

Latcham, a Marvel veteran whose credits include “Iron Man,” “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Spider-Man: Homecoming” and “The Avengers,” will lead DC’s film, television and animation slate, overseeing the creative pipeline, along with production, talent and strategy. He will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

“Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” said Goldberg and Greenstein. “Under his leadership, every film and television show will be ushered from start to finish through the prism of the legions of fans who love and champion it. Jeremy’s track record exemplifies the excellence he will bring to building out DC and the many beloved characters within it.”

Latcham joined Marvel Studios in 2004 and rose to senior VP of production and development, working closely with president and CCO Kevin Feige to launch the MCU. Latcham was associate producer on “Iron Man,” a co-producer on “Iron Man 2,” and executive producer on “The Avengers,” “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Avengers: Age of Ultron” and “Spider-Man: Homecoming.”

Latcham left Marvel in 2017 to found Latcham Pictures, which held first-look deals at 20th Century Fox, Hasbro and Wonder Project and produced “Bad Times at the El Royale” and “Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves.” Recently, he held an overall deal at Hasbro Entertainment, where he was developing a “Dungeons & Dragons” sequel and an “Action Man” film, and was also producing the Lionsgate adaptaton of “Naruto” from director Destin Daniel Cretton.

“DC’s pantheon of characters is among the most iconic in American popular culture. I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era. The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility that I do not take lightly,” said Latcham. “I am grateful to Dana and Josh for putting their trust in me. I can’t wait to work night and day alongside filmmakers, comic book creators, artists and storytellers of every kind, across film, television and animation, to build something ambitious for longtime DC fans and newcomers alike.”

items.title: Russell Brand Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison After Rape, Sexual Assault Convictions
items.description: Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being convicted of rape and sexual assault in his London criminal trial last week.
items.author: K J Yossman; Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being convicted of rape and sexual assault in his London criminal trial last week.
He was facing a potential sentence of 19 years to life in prison for the rape conviction. The maximum sentence for sexual assault is 10 years.

In relation to the sexual assaults, Judge Bennathan handed down a sentence of nine months for Count 3, 18 months for Count 5 (reduced from two years) and eight months for Count 7, which would be served concurrently. He also imposed a sentence of nine years imprisonment for the Count 6 charge of rape. The judge said Brand must serve two thirds of the sentence before he can be released on licence.

The former actor and comedian was found guilty Thursday on three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape. He was found not guilty of two other rape charges and a count of attempted indecent assault.

At the sentencing hearing on Monday morning, the women in the case told the judge of the ongoing impact Brand’s crimes had on them. One victim, who was sexually assaulted at a radio station in 2005 (Count 5), said in a statement read by the Crown Prosecution Service’s lawyer the attack had had a “lasting impact” on her life.

The victim of Count 3, who was sexually assaulted in a Soho bar in 2004 said that after the attack it was “impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke,” while the victim of Count 7, who was assaulted by Brand during a shoot for Channel 4 in 2009, said she “lost trust in people and felt that my working environment wasn’t safe” in the aftermath. She also said the incident was “brushed under the carpet by senior management.”

The victim of Brand’s most serious crime, who was anally raped by Brand at his home in Hampstead before he ordered her to change the sheets and had her escorted out by his driver (Count 6), said she feared she had contracted HIV after the encounter. The judge said that Brand removing the condom and ejaculating inside the victim without her consent were aggravating factors in his sentencing decision. “The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect and your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live,” said the judge.

“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous,” Judge Bennathan began his sentencing remarks. “You were clever and, in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”

Of the radio station sexual assault, in which he forcibly kissed the victim, pushed her against the wall and ran his hands all over her body after encountering her in the corridor, the judge said: “No doubt your companions thought it was outrageous laddish behavior that only you could get away with: It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offence, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it.”

Brand, who stood as the sentence was handed down, did not react although his wife Laura Gallacher clasped her hands and was supported by friends. Brand’s father Ronald was also in the gallery to watch his son’s sentencing.

Brand’s sentence began on Thursday when he was taken into police custody after the judge refused to grant him conditional bail following the jury’s verdict. As Brand was taken to the cells, he mouthed “I’m OK” and “I’m good” to his lawyers and gave a thumbs-up sign, according to Sky News.
Brand did not visibly react when the verdicts were read out. His wife, Laura Gallacher, rushed out of the courtroom when Brand was taken to the cells to wait before his bail application.

Brand was accused of raping three women at various locations between 1999 and 2009. One of the alleged victims also accused him of sexual assault in addition to oral rape. He was also accused of one count of attempted indecent assault at MTV’s U.K. offices in 2001 and one count of sexual assault in 2009. After the trial concluded, the Metropolitan Police confirmed that he is being investigated on further allegations of rape from two other women.

Allegations against Brand went public in 2023 with a docuseries from the Sunday Times and Channel 4’s “Dispatches.” Before then, he was best known as a comedian and for his roles in films like “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.”

items.title: Maya Jama Strikes Deal With Netflix (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: British multi-hyphenate Maya Jama has signed a Netflix deal with a number of new projects in the works, Variety can exclusively reveal.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: British multi-hyphenate Maya Jama has signed a Netflix deal with a number of new projects in the works, Variety can exclusively reveal.

The news follows Jama’s announcement on Sunday night that she has exited her “Love Island U.K.” hosting gig after nine seasons. “I’ve always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then, and now is my time to throw myself into something new,” she wrote on Instagram.

The pact marks an exciting new chapter in Jama’s relationship with Netflix after she made her acting debut in “The Gentlemen” Season 2 earlier this year. Jama played Aisha, a business acquaintance of Kaya Scodelario’s Susie, and will be returning to the role next season. Jama also recently competed on “The Celebrity Traitors,” which broke ratings records for the BBC.
As for Jama’s upcoming projects, details are being kept under wraps for now.

“Maya is fabulous,” Anne Mensah, Netflix’s vice president of U.K. content, said in a statement to Variety. “She has an infectious energy and an ability to captivate audiences. We adored working with her on ‘The Gentlemen,’ and we’re absolutely delighted for her to be an even bigger part of the Netflix family.”

Added Jama, “I’m absolutely buzzing to be working with Netflix! There are some really exciting things coming and I can’t wait for everyone to see what we’ve been working on. I can’t give too much away just yet, but I’m so excited for this next chapter. Watch this space!”

Jama got her start as a presenter for MTV and BBC Radio 1, before moving to television with “Love Island U.K.” and “The Masked Singer U.K.,” on which she serves as a panelist. “The Celebrity Traitors” recently gave her another boost, as she was a fan favorite and the only original Traitor to make it to the final episode.
Speaking with Variety about her time on the series, Jama said she “was reminded about how resilient I am.”
“You don’t really know what you’re capable of in some situations until it actually happens,” she added. “And I’m really proud of myself for just holding it down despite the stress all around.”

items.title: Kanye West Breaks His Own Record for Biggest Rap Concert in U.S. History — Again — With 83,132 Fans
items.description: Kanye West broke his own record this past Saturday as his show at Dallas’ AT&T Stadium became the most-attended hip-hop concert in U.S. history, with 83,132 fans, and the fifth-highest-grossing concert in U.S. history, with more than $18 million in reported gr
items.author: Jem Aswad
paragraphs: Kanye West broke his own record this past Saturday as his show at Dallas’ AT&T Stadium became the most-attended hip-hop concert in U.S. history, with 83,132 fans, and the fifth-highest-grossing concert in U.S. history, with more than $18 million in reported gross revenue generated in a single night, according to his rep.

It is the third time this year that West, who has legally changed his name to Ye, has broken his own record: His concert at Houston’s Reliant Stadium on Halloween night brought in around 80,210 fans, and his two April shows at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, which saw him sell over 74,000 tickets on each of its two nights.

The concerts have continued Ye’s long history of dazzling spectacle: The setlist is filled with hits from his golden era, he’s brought out many guests, and he performs atop a stunning half-orb illuminated to look like the Earth, a progression from earlier sets that saw him performing atop a fake mountain, or on a moving stage suspended from arena ceilings. Read Variety’s review of Ye’s first Los Angeles concert here.

The SoFi concerts were Ye’s first in the U.S. since 2021, as his shocking antisemitic comments and posts over the last few years alienated many fans and especially business partners. He apologized for those comments in January, via a full-page ad in the Wall Street Journal asking for forgiveness and attributing his behavior — which included baldly declaring “I am a Nazi” and releasing the single “Heil Hitler” — to his bipolar type-1 diagnosis, which prompted a “four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behavior that destroyed my life.”

While many people have not accepted or believed his apologies, clearly many thousands of fans have forgiven him. By contast, the most-attended of Jay-Z’s three July concerts at New York’s Yankee Stadium was just under 46,000.
Significantly, Ye’s concerts are independently promoted, without a major partner like Live Nation or AEG Presents.

items.title: The Hollywood Reporter's latest cover stories from its magazine.

items.title: James Gunn “Incredibly Relieved” to Leave DC Studios: Job Was “Trying, to Say the Least”
items.description: James Gunn wasn’t entirely happy as DC Studios co-chief anyway.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: James Gunn wasn’t entirely happy as DC Studios co-chief anyway.

That’s according to Gunn, who posted a farewell message on Instagram in the wake of the surprising news that he and Peter Safran were exiting the top studio roles and Marvel veteran Jeremy Latcham was taking over.
The Superman and Guardians of the Galaxy director expressed eagerness to return to full-time creative work rather than split his attention with managing a studio.

“What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” he wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that) … And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head … So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking.”

Gunn also had praise for some of the “high points” of the job such as releasing Superman and Clayface, and making the HBO series Peacemaker — though notably didn’t mention the box office disappointment Supergirl.

“That’s not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes,” Gunn added. “We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that.”

The exit news came in the wake of Skydance completing its purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery last month and despite Gunn being apparently reassured that he would continue at the studio. Latcham has credits on many MCU titles (including Gunn’s first Guardians) and has been considered Marvel head Kevin Feige’s right-hand man.
Gunn’s full note is below.
Oh, boy. What a four years.
Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios.

When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job.

There have been so many highs along the way — releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to [The People v. Gorilla Grodd], the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments.

The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people I’ve worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran, the smartest and most competent person I know. You’ve been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend.

But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from Oath myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I’m sorry and you don’t need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I’m no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head.

So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That’s not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on.
Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we’ve put on screen.

items.title: DC Studios Shocker: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down with Marvel Alum Jeremy Latcham to Take Over
items.description: In a major shakeup that will send shock waves throughout Hollywood and the comic book world, James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-CEOs of DC studios.
items.author: Borys Kit
paragraphs: In a major shakeup that will send shock waves throughout Hollywood and the comic book world, James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-CEOs of DC studios.

Skydance, which now oversees the division thanks to its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, has appointed former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham to the post of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios.

Gunn and Safran are stepping down from their leadership roles effect Dec. 1, four years after taking over the job to much fanfare. The duo released three movies during that time (Superman, Supergirl and Clayface), as well as three live-action TV shows (The Penguin, Peacemaker season 2 and Lanterns), and had a decade’s worth of plans in the works. In an Instagram post in which he talked about the highs and lows at DC, Gunn acknowledged that being an exec was “trying, to say the least.” He added: “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that.).”

The duo will still be in the fold creatively, at least on a few projects, as Gunn has Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow in post-production for a planned release next year, with the TV spinoff The People v. Gorilla Grodd also in post. Gunn and Safran remain producers on The Batman: Part II as well, for a 2028 release date. With their executive days done, the plan is for them to return full time to their creative work. Gunn rose to fame as the blockbuster filmmaker behind Guardians of the Galaxy, while Safran is a prolific producer on numerous DC and horror titles. Gunn revealed in his Instagram post Monday that he is writing one more secret DC movie, and that the characters they set up will live on beyond them.

“James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of,” Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said jointly in a statement. “We’re grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand.”

Regarding Latcham, the duo stated, “Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans.”

Latcham returns to his executive roots with the role. He was one of the earliest employees of Marvel Studios, joining the company in 2004, and ultimately rose to senior vp of production and development. As a protégé, and then right hand man for Marvel head Kevin Fiege, he gained credits on Iron Man, Iron Man 2, The Avengers, Guardians of the Galaxy, Avengers: Age of Ultron and Spider-Man: Homecoming. He worked with Gunn on Guardians, the 2014 movie that made the filmmaker an A-list director.

Per Skydance, Latcham will lead DC’s film, television and animation slate, overseeing the creative pipeline, along with production, talent and strategy. He will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group. That’s a change from the days of Gunn and Safran, who reported directly to Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav before the merger, and prior to their exit, reported directly to Ellison.

“DC’s pantheon of characters is among the most iconic in American popular culture,” said Latcham in a statement. “I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era. The chance to steward the incredible cast of DC characters to the screen in a way that excites lifelong fans while introducing their timeless stories to the next generation is a massive responsibility that I do not take lightly.”

Hollywood observers will be looking to discern if Gunn and Safran decided to move on, or if they were pushed out. Before the merger, Ellison flew to the set of Man of Tomorrow, which was seen as a vote of confidence for the duo, and in recent weeks, the pair presented their long-term plan to the mogul. Sources previously told THR Ellison told them to keep doing what they were doing. “David knows everything… he’s been great with us,” Gunn told THR last month of keeping Ellison informed of their larger vision.

The exit now puts into question the vast plans the duo announced when they took over and tried to steer the DC movies beyond the long shadow cast by the Zack Snyder era. Gunn and Safran started off with the successful launch of a new Superman movie last year but then stumbled big with Supergirl, a critical and commercial bomb. Their third movie, Clayface, has generated strong reviews and is a moneymaker.

“Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker, Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface,” The duo stated regarding their tenure. “We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with.

On the Latcham front, they enthused, “We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow.”

items.title: Russell Brand Sentenced to Over 10 Years in Prison for Rape and Sexual Assault
items.description: Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault.

He’ll be expected to serve around seven years of that prison sentence before being released on licence. Brand was silent as the sentencing was read out and mouthed “I love you” to his wife, Laura, as he was led away.

The judge, Justice Bennathan, took Brand through all of his crimes in extensive detail, citing the witness impact statements from the four victims before handing down the sentence. He said Brand operated with “staggering arrogance” during the attacks and that his entourage often “indulged” his “dreadful behavior.” He said toward the end of his statement: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say ‘no’ and to demand justice from criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”

After a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court, the jury delivered the verdicts on Thursday, finding the disgraced comedian and presenter guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was found not guilty on two other rape charges and not guilty of attempted indecent assault.
The Met Police has also confirmed Brand is under investigation over further rape allegations from women not connected to the trial.

The victims, who have been granted lifelong anonymity, spoke from behind a curtain at the sentencing hearing. “I wanted to express how this crime has impacted me,” said one during her witness impact statement according to BBC News coverage. “I’ve been in shock and turmoil for weeks. I was extremely upset and traumatised. I didn’t have any respect for myself… I was thinking I was damaged goods — scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way.” She continued that there were many times she felt “physically sick” seeing Brand in the media. “I just want to say, a leopard may change its spots, but it’s still a leopard,” she added.
Another victim said in court on Monday: “Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse. […] I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women.”

But the star’s defence argued that he is “a fundamentally different person today” and said his wife is experiencing “total devastation” from the convictions. Journalists inside the court noted Laura Brand was shaking her head as one victim read her witness impact statement. Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter, said the couple is “wrestling” with how to explain to one of their children, aged 10, what has happened.
The trial — and verdicts — captivated the country, leaving not just the industry but the entire British public with questions over how Brand went unreported for so long.

Thursday’s guilty rape verdict relates to a woman who met Brand at a Hammersmith Apollo gig of his in 2009. “I was expecting to have sex with him,” the victim told police about going to Brand’s house a week later. After consensual vaginal sex, Brand turned her onto her front and anally raped her. She recalled feeling as though “she couldn’t speak or breathe” and said she was in pain. When finally able to speak, the woman told Brand to stop “a few times quietly and then really loudly.” The anal rape lasted “minutes,” and Brand “looked absolutely fucking horrified” when it was over, she said. She expected him to apologize, but he only told her: “You need to clear up the mess you made.”

Brand was also found guilty of three sexual assaults. One was his grabbing a victim’s breasts at a bar in Soho in 2004; another was an incident in 2004/2005 at Capital Radio where he pushed a victim up against a wall, kissing her and grabbing at her body, breasts, sides and buttocks “aggressively”; and lastly, an incident where he put his head and nose in the “vaginal area” of a female colleague in 2009.
