items.title: How to take notes that actually help you learn | Psyche Guides
items.description: is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is
items.author: Cynthia Nebel
paragraphs: is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is a member of The Learning Scientists and co-author of Ace That Test: A Student’s Guide to Learning Better (2023).

is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is a member of The Learning Scientists and co-author of Ace That Test: A Student’s Guide to Learning Better (2023).

Notetaking is a versatile skill. Perhaps you take notes during lectures in class, or as part of your job, or when you’re reading an insightful book, or when you have an important meeting. If you’re a notetaker, in any case, you want your notes to be as useful as they can be. And that starts with thinking about their function. Since taking notes is such a common activity, it’s easy to overlook the question of what notes are actually doing for us.

Many people assume that just by writing information down, they are doing something useful. But the cognitive processes involved in taking notes and the way you take them can make a big difference in terms of what you ultimately get out of them.

There are two broad goals of notetaking: recording and learning. The first is when you try to take down as much information as you can so that you don’t miss anything and can review it later. This might be necessary sometimes – for instance, if you are going to be tested on the information presented in a lecture, and you won’t have a recording, text, or slides to refer back to later. Similarly, if you are in charge of meeting minutes or want to do more research on what you’re hearing from your doctor, you may need to simply record as much information as possible.

But in many situations, the most effective and efficient way to take notes is to treat them as a tool for learning: that is, to use them to help you retain and understand the information by putting it down in your own words and organising your thoughts about it. This is the kind of notetaking that I’ll focus on in this Guide.

What do good notes look like, and how can you get better at notetaking? There is not one right answer to these questions, but knowing a bit about how and when notetaking is effective will help you to decide what kind of notes to take when, and what to do with them afterward. As a cognitive psychologist and director of learning services at a medical school, I have a lot of experience with the most effective strategies for notetaking and why they work. Below, I’ll explain how to use some of these strategies and the reasoning behind them.

Taking notes to learn is different from taking them to record. Sometimes you need to take down as much as possible. But if you hope to internalise the information, you’ll want to process it as you take notes.
Use paper if possible. Since it slows you down, you have to decide what the most important pieces of information are before putting them on paper, which supports learning.

Experiment with ways of processing. Organise the information in your own way – try making summaries, bulleted lists, drawings or charts – and note links between what you’re learning and other things you know.
Try a structured approach. In the Cornell notetaking system, you complement your main notes with a summary at the bottom and cues to practise recalling the information later.
Adopt a better review strategy. Don’t just reread or copy your notes – reorganise them in some way. Then test your memory and understanding and check your notes to see what you’re missing.
Use AI tools selectively. They can be helpful for creating detailed records, but don’t rely only on AI notes if you’re trying to learn.

You may have heard before that taking notes by hand, on paper, is better than typing them on a laptop. There is truth to this, but it is due to more than just the effect of handwriting. Writing on paper can be more effective because it is much slower than typing. It’s difficult to write down every word or detail, requiring you to decide what the most important pieces of information are before putting them on paper. When you do this, you’re engaging in a type of mental processing that leads to better learning. Taking notes on paper also allows you to easily jump back and forth between different concepts and to organise them visually (using a diagram, for example).

These things can be done electronically, but most people find that it’s clunkier. If you must use a device, my recommendation is to not simply copy what you hear or read verbatim, but rather to prioritise what seem to be the most important points, and to ensure you process the information by doing some of the things I’ll describe next.
Experiment with ways of processing

When you’re taking notes to learn, it’s essential to organise the information in your own way and to think about how it relates to other things you know (even examples from your own life). You could make bulleted lists, write summaries in your own words or write questions about the material. Maybe you also want to draw pictures or flow charts, or connect different parts of a lecture with arrows. All these activities involve somehow mentally processing the information, which leads to actual learning rather than just recording.

For example, some of my students will create a high-level outline of the main topics from a lecture; under each heading, they write a summary of the information in their own words once that part of the lecture ends. Other students try to anticipate how they might be quizzed on the material and write practice test questions in their notes.

Here’s an example from outside the classroom – let’s say I’m reading a book about a historical figure and want to better retain the information. How might I start? As I go from chapter to chapter, I could take notes in the margins, or in a separate notebook, about how each part of the book relates to contemporary events, other history that I know, or situations in my own life. I might find certain areas interesting or inspiring and write in my notes about why those things caught my attention. Again, these all involve mentally processing, or what we can call active (vs passive) reading.

Coming up with your own way of taking notes may seem like a big challenge. The good news is that there are existing notetaking strategies that can help you with this process. One of the strategies that is supported by research is the Cornell notetaking system, created by the Cornell University education professor Walter Pauk.

In this approach, you separate a page into three parts. On the main part of the page will be your ‘notes’. At the bottom of the page, you include a ‘summary’. In the lefthand margin, you label an area for ‘cues’. Here’s an example:
As you’re taking in the information (eg, in class or during a discussion), you use the ‘notes’ area to keep track of important points and ideas.

Afterward, you fill out the ‘cues’ section, which is primarily used to help guide your study later on, when you go back to review your notes. You might write down questions to help you think about the material that was covered, or prompts related to what is most important. These serve as retrieval cues to help you practise recalling the information later, which is a highly effective learning strategy. It could also be helpful to note in the cues section anything you don’t understand, to clarify what you might have to review further or follow up about. Sometimes, depending on the context, you might be able to fill out the cues section while you’re still taking down your main notes.

Last, you fill out the ‘summary’ section, writing down the big-picture ideas that came out of what you heard or read, in your own words. This allows you to take a step back and think through what all of this means and how it fits with other things you’ve been learning.

What’s great about this notetaking system is that it requires you to process the material in multiple ways. The system is also very adaptable. If, for example, you attend a lecture that’s very dense, you could take verbatim notes first and then take Cornell notes later, based on your initial round of notes. And if you need more space, you can reserve a whole page for the ‘cues’ section and subsequent pages where you put your notes, including a summary at the end.

While the Cornell approach is a reliable technique, there are other structured ways of taking notes that you might want to explore as well. For example, mind-mapping is a strategy in which you put the main idea in the centre of a page and organise related material around it using branching connections. With sketchnoting, you take advantage of the powerful interaction between verbal and visual material by creating notes that involve lots of pictures. And outlining can be an effective strategy because it requires you to consider what is most important and how various pieces of information support each topic. Each of these strategies is evidence-based and they work in different ways to support deeper processing.
Adopt a better review strategy

Once you have your notes, what should you do with them? Hopefully it’s clear by now that processing the information is key, so just rewriting the same notes is mostly a waste of time. When you do that, you don’t really have to think about the notes you’ve taken. However, if you reorganise your notes in some way – such as by summarising them, or creating diagrams, flow charts, or hierarchies – that is likely to be more useful, especially if you had to take verbatim notes at first. For example, after hearing about how the heart works, you could draw a picture with arrows showing the direction of blood flow, or you could create appropriate headings and subheadings to organise the main ideas and supporting facts.

Similarly, just rereading your notes doesn’t require a lot of mental effort. It feels like you’re learning, and you might get better at it over time. But if you’re trying to internalise and retain information for later (for example, if you want to be able to retrieve answers on a test), then the best way to prepare is to practise doing that. Instead of rereading, you could try using your ‘cues’ from the Cornell method to bring as much of the information to mind as you can. Then you can go back to your main ‘notes’ section to see what you missed.

If you’re using a different notetaking strategy, you could write quiz questions based on your notes that you can then answer from memory. Or, you could use your notes to make flashcards. Instead of just copying down the notes onto the cards, try using the front side of the card for questions that you could get someone to ask you, or for different ways of comparing and contrasting the information. For example, you could write: ‘Compare and contrast the upbringings of Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr.’ This will give you a processing benefit while you’re creating the cards, as well as the retrieval benefit when you use them later.

You could also do a ‘brain dump’, where you try to write down everything you can remember about a topic and then check your notes for accuracy and to fill in any gaps. All of these strategies involve more productive mental effort than rereading does, and they come with the advantage of helping you figure out what you do and don’t know.

If you’re recording a lecture or a conversation and you want a thorough transcription and summary that you can revisit later, AI tools can be useful for that. However, when you use AI to take notes rather than doing it yourself, you are bypassing the kinds of mental processing that will help you learn. Because of this, I don’t recommend relying on AI for notetaking if your goal is to retain the information. In situations where it’s important to have a detailed record and you use AI to create one, just make sure that you go back to those notes later and apply one or more of the review strategies above if you hope to remember the material later on.

Notetaking is not just one thing and you should adjust your approach depending on the situation. If the information is very dense and it’s not contained anywhere else, then trying to take down as much as you can makes sense – but you’ll still need to revisit and make sense of those notes later on. And when your aim is not to copy but to internalise what you’re hearing or reading, then the best way to take notes is to summarise, organise and make connections between the material and what you already know. Ultimately, the key is to think about what you’re learning, both as you’re taking it in and when you come back to it later. The best way of taking notes is the one that helps you do that.

items.title: Historical ideas of equality help us imagine an equal world | Aeon Essays
items.description: It’s no accident that equality comes first among the ‘self-evident’ truths articulated in the United States Declaration of Independence. The claim that ‘all men are created equal’ serves there not simply as an abstract premise from which revolutionary conseque
items.author: Teresa M Bejan
paragraphs: It’s no accident that equality comes first among the ‘self-evident’ truths articulated in the United States Declaration of Independence. The claim that ‘all men are created equal’ serves there not simply as an abstract premise from which revolutionary consequences ought to follow, but as a concrete practical foundation on which the American colonists could claim to stand as equals with the greatest king and hold him to account. Still impressed by his own handiwork 50 years later, Thomas Jefferson even prophesied that the ‘palpable truth’ of equality enshrined in the Declaration would one day unite all of humankind.

Yet today, it’s evident that the word ‘equality’ means very different things to different people. What once seemed capable of providing common ground is now just another source of controversy. What explains this shift? I suspect that the deceptively simple, conceptual language of ‘equality’ has itself played a substantial role. A better understanding of ‘equality talk’ – as the application of this language to human beings and their relations – might therefore shed some light on our predicament.

Let’s begin by examining a group of people that generally prides itself on thinking (and speaking) more clearly than most: professional philosophers. What are they doing when they talk about equality?

Often, they’re saying something about human beings: about what we’re fundamentally like, and how we should be treated morally, politically and socially. When an academic philosopher says that ‘all people are equal’, she’s generally saying that, despite differences of race and gender, economic class or individual merit, every person is somehow the same in some fundamental respect(s). While some philosophers will stress the human capacity for reason and moral agency, others emphasise our mutual vulnerability to suffering and violent death. Still, all generally agree that this sameness – whatever its underlying basis – ought to matter for our social and political arrangements, such that any persistent inequalities between human beings must require some justification or redress.

But here, a non-philosopher might wonder why the professionals insist on using the technical language of ‘equality’ as opposed to something more straightforward like ‘sameness’? One reason, I think, is that they are trading on the former concept’s mathematical resonances of quantitative precision and transcendent truth. Those resonances, in turn, make the problem of inequality seem relatively tractable – as something the existence of which can be measured, hence agreed upon. While other political values, like liberty, resist reduction to a common measure, the quantitative logic of equality thus promises an objective standard against which social progress can be judged.

The distinctly mathematical aspect of modern ‘equality talk’ isn’t new. Consider the Declaration’s language of ‘self-evidence’. This was an allusion to Euclid’s Elements (c300 BCE), in which the transitive property of equality – ‘things that are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another’ – comes first among the so-called axiomata, or ‘worthy notions’. The truth of these geometric propositions could, in turn, be accepted without proof, and so serve as a shared starting point from which to reason to less-obvious conclusions.
If like cases are to be treated alike as a matter of logic, then ‘equals’ ought to be treated ‘equally’ as a matter of politics

Two hundred years after the Declaration, we likewise find the philosopher Ronald Dworkin in Taking Rights Seriously (1977) describing the right of all persons to equality as ‘axiomatic’, and thereby taking the basic equality of human beings off the table as a topic of political controversy. Let metaphysicians and theologians quarrel about its basis, then, or whether nonhuman animals or artificial intelligence ought to count equally as moral persons. Political philosophers could get on with the altogether more important business of determining what this equality implied for our social, political and economic relations. Much like Jefferson, Dworkin would also later lend his axiom world-historical significance, as providing ‘a kind of plateau in political argument’ characteristic of modernity. By this, Dworkin meant that most contemporary political ideologies – from liberalism to utilitarianism, and libertarianism to communism – must begin from a shared premise, that all ‘members of the community matter, and matter equally’. And so, whatever their differences, political opponents ought to recognise themselves as building upon a common foundation.

Today, Dworkin’s historical optimism about equality as a universal premise seems harder to sustain. Nevertheless, his ‘egalitarian plateau’ image remains popular among academic philosophers, for whom basic equality has come to mark an indelible ‘divide in moral thinking between (1) a premodern world in which nobles [were] regarded as having greater worth than peasants … and (2) a modern world that repudiates these crude prejudices.’ Moreover, if like cases are to be treated alike as a matter of logic, then surely ‘equals’ ought to be treated ‘equally’ as a matter of politics, too – for instance, by distributing to each the same amount of welfare, rights or resources. Dworkin’s Oxford colleague, the analytic Marxist G A Cohen, could thus simply ‘take for granted that there is something which justice requires people to have equal amounts of.’ The only question remaining was that posed by Amartya Sen: ‘Equality of what?’ (My emphasis.)

And yet, the idea that unequal treatment might sometimes be required to respect a person’s basic equality was also intuitive to many late-20th-century liberals, who supported policies like affirmative action. Dworkin himself framed this intuition influentially in terms of a distinction between treating people ‘equally’ – by applying the same standards or distributing the same amount to everyone – and treating them ‘as equals’, in a way responsive to their differences. This insight may, at first, sound similar to the much older, Marxist principle, ‘From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.’ But as the historian Darrin McMahon observed in Equality (2023), Marx and Engels were themselves consistently critical of equality, dismissing it as a just another ‘popular prejudice’ to be dispelled by the coming communist revolution.

In any case, it is Dworkin’s distinction, not Marx’s, that has since become central to contemporary theories of social or ‘relational’ egalitarianism, especially those associated with the philosopher Elizabeth Anderson. On this view, the point of equality is not to ensure a quantitatively identical distribution of stuff, whether of rights or resources, but rather the realisation of a just society in which every person can stand as an equal, without any hierarchical relations of inferiority or superiority. But the devil, as ever, is in the details, with relational egalitarians saying surprisingly little in positive terms about what relating as ‘equals’ actually looks like – and, specifically, when and what forms of unequal treatment might be involved.

One encounters a similar difficulty in recent debates pitting ‘equity’ against ‘equality’ as an approach to social justice. Proponents of the former insist that, unlike the latter, equity rejects a one-size-fits-all approach by taking certain differences – for instance, of race, disability or socioeconomic circumstances – into account. When pressed, however, equity’s defenders also tend to define ‘equitable’ treatment in strikingly Dworkinian terms, for instance as placing the disadvantaged on an ‘equal footing’ with the privileged. The result has been an odd convergence between equity’s progressive proponents and their conservative critics, with each presenting their preferred approach as the truly egalitarian one, with one side insisting that equal standing requires unequal treatment, and the other that, in a society of equals, the same rules ought to apply equally to everyone.

No wonder, then, that equality talk can feel so disorienting! Even among philosophers, it consistently promises more than it delivers. For some, equality means that we are the same in all the ways that matter, hence the same standards must apply; for others, it means that we are all different in ways deserving of respect. Even Dworkin’s supposedly clarifying formula of treating people ‘as equals’ reduces, under scrutiny, to the suggestion that we ought to treat people unequally when it is appropriate to their particular circumstances. If this is all equality demands, a hereditary aristocrat would find little to disagree with.

Here, however, a historian like McMahon might reassure us that the meaning of equality has always been ‘elusive’. In French, for instance, to say ça m’est égal can mean ‘it’s all the same to me’, yes, but it can also mean that our differences don’t matter, they’re matters of indifference. The varieties of English ‘equality talk’ can be more confusing still. When it was first published more than 250 years ago, Samuel Johnson’s A Dictionary of the English Language (1755) offered no fewer than eight definitions for the adjective ‘equal’, including ‘indifferent’, ‘like another in bulk, [or] excellence’, and ‘adequate to any purpose’.

Still, amid this multiplicity, one finds equality talk doing something distinctive in early modern English. Specifically, the adjective ‘equal’ – deriving originally from the Latin aequalis – consistently presented English speakers with a learned and socially elevated alternative to a more common Anglo-Saxon term, ‘alike’ (cognate with the German gleich). Whereas we today understand equality primarily in mathematical terms, however, to early modern English ears it meant something more like evenness, in the sense of being on a level or balanced, with neither side higher nor lower than the other.
Unlike sameness, equality was the absence of difference where one would normally expect to find it

Consider the 14th-century Wycliffe Bible, which presented St Paul’s counsels of charity to the Corinthians as follows: ‘but of evenness [aequalitas] in the present time your abundance fulfil the need of them, that also the abundance of them be a fulfilling of your need, that evenness be made.’ Rich and poor were thus to be made ‘equal’ in this passage not by possessing identical amounts of wealth at any given moment, but by counter-balancing their holdings over time through reciprocal giving. One person’s abundance must meet another’s need in expectation of a future reversal. Here, the historical sense of equality-as-evenness clearly recalls the process of ‘levelling’ the scales or balances used by ancient merchants to weigh precious metals and trade goods in the marketplace. (Indeed, the English word ‘level’ derives originally from the Latin libra, meaning scale.)

If we turn directly to the ancient Hellenic world, we find the same practical association between the concept of equality and the activity of balancing. This association may explain, in turn, why Greek mathematicians like Euclid took so much trouble to distinguish the idea of ‘equality’ (isotes) from other conceptual relations like ‘sameness’ and ‘similarity’ in their works. In the Metaphysics, Aristotle also distinguished equality by defining it in exclusively negative terms: ‘The equal, then, is that which is neither great nor small, but would naturally be either great or small.’ In other words, there was something exceptional about equality. Unlike sameness, it was the absence of difference where one would normally expect to find it.

This definition can, I think, help us make better sense of Aristotle’s celebrated observation in the Politics, that ‘justice is a kind of equality’, as well as his assertion that there were at least two competing definitions of equality in play in contemporary politics. Elsewhere, he would define these as ‘arithmetic’ and ‘geometric’ equality, respectively: the former distributing numerically identical shares to the parties despite their differences, for instance of wealth or virtue, and the latter assigning different amounts to each in direct proportion with their differences. In the Politics, then, these two kinds of equality re-appear as competing strategies for balancing political power between citizens, specifically between the poor many and the rich few. While democrats favoured the former principle – claiming that every adult male citizen should be assigned strictly equal political weight, like coins of equal value – oligarchs insisted that citizens should be weighed instead, like metals in the marketplace, with political power then distributed to each in proportion with his unequal wealth or virtue. In ancient Greece, the election of political officeholders by their fellow citizens was thus regarded as an oligarchic procedure, in contrast with the properly democratic alternative of sortition, or selection by lot, which afforded each a strictly equal (random) chance of exercising power.

Notice, however, that, despite their differences, ancient democrats and oligarchs could alike embrace ‘equality’ as a political ideal without also committing to the view that every citizen, let alone every human being, must be somehow ‘equal’ as well. Even in the most economically inclusive and participatory polity in the ancient world, namely democratic Athens, Athenian democrats regarded certain people – namely native-born adult male citizens – as worthier and weightier than other ones – be they women, children, slaves or ‘barbarians’, or even other Greeks, including resident aliens like Aristotle. The point of equality then, even in Athens, was to ensure that no unequal part or person could over-balance the polity by outweighing or dominating the rest.

So far, my historical survey would appear to vindicate Dworkin’s ‘egalitarian plateau’ idea. While the ancient Greeks undoubtedly possessed sophisticated ideas about political equality, they also clearly believed in the basic inequality of human beings. Surely, then, modern egalitarianism must mark a radical break with this irredeemably hierarchical past?

Not so fast. Because elsewhere in the ancient world one finds statements remarkably similar to Dworkin’s ‘axiom’ of basic human equality – namely, in the Roman Empire. Consider the following extract from Ulpian, an imperial jurist of the early 3rd century CE, preserved in Justinian’s Digest: ‘As far as concerns the civil law, slaves are regarded as nothing; but as far as concerns the natural law, all humans are equal (aequales).’

Here, we find what many philosophers today regard as a characteristically modern claim: that all humans (even slaves) are naturally equal. But, in context, Ulpian clearly meant something different. He was not saying that all people ought to be treated as equals, legally or politically, let alone that they must be afforded the same rights or resources. Ulpian’s point, rather, was that even enslaved people were equally subject to something he called ‘natural’ law, which applied to every human being without exception.
In the Hebrew Bible, the conceptual language of equality is conspicuously absent

For Ulpian, then, it seems that the ‘equality’ of human beings meant something more like indifference. Indeed, much like a modern French speaker declaring ça m’est égal, the law of nature took no notice of the extreme differences of power, wealth or status otherwise governing life within the Roman Empire. In other words, and much like the sun or rain or death, it fell indifferently on everyone, male or female, free or slave. But this ‘natural’ did not therefore deny or otherwise erase the many hierarchies characteristic of Roman life (or law). It simply identified a (necessarily limited) perspective of natural justice from which those hierarchies could be regarded as irrelevant.

This observation of the Roman origins of the idea of natural equality challenges another, more familiar story about the sources of modern egalitarianism. To many modern readers, the biblical language of ‘creation’ found in the Declaration of Independence suggests that the equality of human beings was originally a religious idea, whether a Jewish or a Christian one. Yet if one consults the Hebrew Bible, the conceptual language of equality is conspicuously absent. In Genesis, the biblical God creates human beings, male and female, ‘in his own image’. But this divine likeness, in turn, does nothing to preclude the many forms of divinely sanctioned or permitted hierarchy, including slavery and patriarchy, found elsewhere in the Bible.

It is only later, in the 3rd and 4th centuries CE, that we find Roman Christian apologists like St Cyprian and Lactantius resisting persecution by deliberately combining the biblical account of human creation in ‘God’s image or likeness’, on the one hand, with the Roman legal language of ‘equality’ as a universal standard of legal justice, on the other. The result was an entirely new – and highly influential – way of talking about divine justice in Latin Christendom. Unlike the Roman civil law, the Christian God had been revealed to be truly ‘no respecter of persons’. Thus in his eyes, the worldly distinctions of slave and free, rich and poor, male and female, would one day count for nothing. All would instead be judged ‘equally’ – that is, by the same divine standard – and then rewarded or punished in proportion with their spiritual merit.

We can now see why, for most of its history, ‘equality talk’ proved not only consistent with hierarchy, but fundamentally supportive of it. It’s not because Greek democrats, Roman jurists and Christian theologians were paying lip service to an ideal they didn’t believe in, or that they were incapable of following through on the egalitarian logic of their own commitments. It’s because people in the past moved much less easily than we do from the premise that all (or some) people are equal towards the conclusion that they should, therefore, be treated as equals in a social or evaluative sense. To be ‘equal’ in the eyes of God, or of the law, or of a democratic lottery, simply meant that certain of our differences shouldn’t matter for that particular purpose. It did not follow that those differences must therefore be deemed irrelevant for every purpose, or that all humans were thus sufficiently alike in virtue or value to be treated socially or politically as peers. Indeed, emphasising the former equality was often a way of bringing the manifest disparities between certain individuals or social groups into sharper relief, thus fitting them for hierarchical relations.

And yet, the same proliferation of historical meanings – as evenness and absence, balance and proportion, indifference and parity – that accounts for this disconnect, can in turn explain how ‘equality talk’ finally gained a new and uniquely powerful political force in early modern England. And, with that force, ordinary Englishmen and women began to exploit its many ambiguities in order to demand not only equal justice, but equal standing with the privileged.

To locate the precise moment of transformation, we must look beyond the summer of 1776, back to the summer of 1646, when a man called John Lilburne found himself on trial for libel before the House of Lords. Today, Lilburne is remembered chiefly as a leader of the Leveller movement active during the English Civil War. And the Levellers are remembered for demanding universal manhood suffrage at the Putney Debates of 1647, several centuries before it became a reality in modern Britain. Summoned before the Peers the previous June, however, Lilburne had done something comparatively trivial. He simply refused to kneel or to remove his hat before his aristocratic judges. His reason? That God had created ‘every particular and individual man and woman that ever breathed in the world … all equal and alike in power, dignity, authority and majesty.’ Hence no one could claim any ‘authority, dominion or magisterial power’ over another without their ‘mutual agreement or consent’.
The Leveller movement pushed this conceptual ambiguity to the hilt across pamphlets, protests and petitions

So much for balance! So much for indifference! In that moment, Lilburne somehow managed to turn the equality of human beings before God into a demand that even commoners like himself could stand on the same level, as peers, with their supposed betters here on earth. In this way, Lilburne’s proposition offered an early – and indeed more radical – version of the levelling logic found later in the US Declaration of Independence. For starters, it explicitly included women among those created equal and entitled to an equal voice in how they were to be governed. (In the US, this addendum would have to wait more than 70 years, until the Seneca Falls Declaration of 1848.)

How did Lilburne do it? Well, he started by collapsing a conceptual distinction that earlier English equality talk had generally preserved, that between being ‘equal’ – in the sense being subject to or judged by the same standard – and being ‘an equal’ in the social and evaluative sense of being someone’s peer. In hindsight, we can see that Lilburne was assisted in this effort by a broader conceptual looseness in early modern English, by which many of the classical distinctions inherited from Greek and Latin had started to dissolve. For instance, in the earliest English translation of Aristotle’s Politics, published in 1598, the translator simply erased the philosophical distinction between being ‘equal’ (isos) and being ‘similar’ (homoios) by translating both terms as ‘equal’.

Such slippages undoubtedly offend against philosophical precision. Politically speaking, however, they created opportunities. Lilburne noticed one such opportunity in Magna Carta, specifically in its guarantee to every free man in the realm the right to a trial per pares, or by his peers. In early modern English, ‘peer’ could of course mean a social equal of whatever degree, high or low. But increasingly in political usage, it could also mean a member of the English aristocracy. If every ‘freeborn’ Englishman and woman had the right to be tried by ‘the lawful judgment of [their] peers (or equals)’, as Lilburne put it, then surely he or she must also be ‘entitled unto an equal privilege’ with the greatest Peer in the Commonwealth, as in Creation.

The Leveller movement subsequently pushed this conceptual ambiguity to the hilt across countless pamphlets, protests and petitions, in which they demanded not only that English commoners be treated ‘equally’ with aristocrats before the law, but also that they enjoy all of the political benefits of peerage. Thomas Rainborough’s celebrated demand for ‘equal voice’ at Putney, through a radical expansion of the franchise, followed the same levelling logic: ‘For really I think that the poorest he that is in England has a life to live as the greatest he.’ So did a remarkable 1649 Leveller women’s petition presented to the House of Commons, in which the female petitioners declared:

That since we are assured of our Creation in the image of God, and of an interest in Christ, equal unto men, as also of a proportionable share in the Freedoms of this Common wealth, we cannot but wonder and grieve that we should appear so despicable in your eyes, as to be thought unworthy to Petition or represent our Grievances to this Honourable House.

In this way, even as the Leveller movement failed, its new way of talking about equality lived on. We find versions of its levelling logic in Thomas Hobbes’s Leviathan (1651), or in the writings of the so-called ‘first English feminist’ (and staunch Tory) Mary Astell, as well as in the US Declaration of Independence. Across these very different texts, with their different political conclusions, the language of equality continued to perform its distinctive function, cutting the great ones down to size while raising up the marginal and excluded to meet them. To claim equality was thus no longer merely to demand that the same law, or the same God, apply the same standards indifferently. It was to demand recognition as an equal in society: that is, someone entitled to speak, judge and be heard as a peer.

For centuries, it seems, this was the primary political function of equality talk. But, today, this language has lost much of its levelling power. At the same time, talk of equality no longer unifies, it disillusions and divides. Why?

Perhaps the problem ultimately lies with what made this conceptual language so appealing in the first place. Far from being simple, let alone self-evident, its history reveals that equality has accumulated a remarkable number of meanings over time. And when it comes to how human beings ought to relate to one another, those different meanings – as absence or balance, indifference or parity – are often in tension, if not outright contradiction.

Is it any wonder, then, that we talk past each other! Even as the word ‘equality’ suggests that better measurement or reasoning ought to resolve our disagreements. Now, one might conclude from this – as many contemporary progressives have done – that we would be better off rejecting equality altogether, in favour of some other, less historically ambiguous ideal. But that would, I think, be a mistake. Because historically, the problem with equality talk – namely, its conceptual ambiguity – has also been the source of its uncommon power.
English women could be tried by juries, but they did not ordinarily sit on them

Again, consider Lilburne. His better-educated critics could (and did) object that his ‘general Proposition’ to the Lords was a non sequitur. It simply didn’t follow from the premise that God created men and women as equally subject to his divine justice, that they should therefore be recognised politically as peers. But this criticism did not stop Lilburne and his fellow Levellers from trading on the many different meanings of equality and drawing their own political conclusions. And their success was not simply a matter of ingenious wordplay or conceptual sleight of hand. The plausibility of their insistence that English commoners were just as capable of thinking and speaking for themselves as Peers rested on a familiar institution: the jury. When ‘12 men of the neighbourhood’ sat in judgment over a fellow commoner, their differences of wealth, occupation, education and ability didn’t disappear. They simply ceased to matter for the purposes of reaching a verdict. Hence the jurors came to see one another as ‘peers and equals’ because the institution required them to act as peers, as they listened, deliberated and judged together.

In this way, the ‘doing’ of equality proceeded the idea of it. But if Leveller ‘equality talk’ rested on a particular social practice, the limits of that practice mattered, too. English women could be tried by juries, but they did not ordinarily sit on them; enslaved Africans in the English Atlantic, although admittedly ‘created Men’, were regarded as too ‘brutish’ to enjoy that privilege. For centuries, accordingly, these groups would struggle to leverage the same arguments in the absence of social practices and institutions within which they, too, could act – and be seen to act – as peers and equals.

So much for the past. What about the future? Well, in the first place, the above analysis suggests that the work of making ‘equality talk’ meaningful is not primarily philosophical, it’s practical. Nonetheless, philosophers often proceed as though any difficulties with equality must be logical or definitional. If only we could identify the respect in which every person is ‘equal’ with enough precision, then our disagreements about justice would dissolve. But history suggests that the more important task is that of sustaining the social practices and institutions that make equality meaningful in the first place. (Hence, the reticence of contemporary relational egalitarians to spell out what equality demands of us in positive terms, beyond a general resistance to hierarchical relations, is a serious defect.)

So what would an historically informed approach to equality look like? For one thing, it would require attending to (or even just attending) things like jury service, among the other increasingly uncommon offline sites in which we encounter other people who are not like us – in bulk, excellence or ideology – as peers. Today, these sites are threatened not only by frictionless technologies like large language models or social media, but also by the growing price-stratification of so many consumer experiences – what Michael Sandel in 2012 dubbed the ‘skyboxification of American life’. But taking part in such activities on more even terms doesn’t make us identical, nor does it mean that we agree. It just means that we commit ourselves, for a limited time and purpose, to not letting our differences determine which of us matters – or whose voice ought to count.

Because, if history tells us anything, it’s that equality is not primarily an idea to be believed in, nor a partisan commitment to affirm. It’s something people did, and something we must do. Only then are we created equal – not by ‘the Laws of Nature and of Nature’s God’, but by each other, every day.

items.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays
items.description: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in a
items.author: Melanie Challenger
paragraphs: It is almost four o’clock in the morning. As a woman in my late 40s, I have become prone to waking at this witching hour, as the early sunlight meets the night, sliding across the earth like a red tide. With the rest of my household asleep, and still half in and out of wakefulness myself, I take hold of my phone. With scarcely a thought, I switch from one app to another, scrolling through images and opinions and adverts for no discernible reason beyond habit.

Later, I head for my office and open my laptop to a slew of half-completed documents and an inbox brimming with emails. My stress levels begin to nudge upwards. I have vague memories of what my professional life felt like before smartphones and video calls. I used to do my writing by hand. And I could concentrate for hours at a time, getting little upticks of arousal from lifting my head from the page, letting the hold on my pen loosen, and gazing at the life beyond my window, the light softening on my skin and eyes like snowfall on warm tarmac.

Nowadays, my productive bursts come from caffeine and sugary or salty snacks, even if I try to pick the healthier ones, and from checking my emails or picking up my phone to update my inbox. By the end of the day, the sheer volume of work I expect myself to do, now that digital tools make so much possible, has kept me nailed to my seat. Another day has passed and the hope I’d had that I might have time for a run or a hike outside has been dashed again. I wish I could say that this is atypical. Yet, during the COVID-19 pandemic, I went from hours spent in nature and on physical activities to a passive, phone-addicted individual, meeting people first and sometimes only online. I am not alone.

We have fallen into habits that are steadily deskilling the human body, eroding capacities honed by evolution to support our wellbeing as we move through the world. Some of these capacities are weakening through disuse: we have come to rely on our phones, for example, and now, increasingly, on AI, to rapidly do work that would once have required something more physical – like looking around, or asking someone, or going to find and consult a book. Reliance on GPS may weaken both our spatial attention and the fluency of our wayfinding. In surrendering to a quick technological fix, we are, moment by moment, doing less sensing, navigating, remembering, walking, choosing, and attending. Other capacities are being retrained by machines and algorithms to work against us: for instance, smartphones and chatbots can train us to keep reaching for them even when we no longer enjoy using them, turning a conscious choice into an automatic habit and a colossal waste of time. The body that results is less able to assess its own condition, improvise and regulate itself. The crucial distinction is between technologies that strengthen our capacities and those that repeatedly substitute for the actions through which those capacities are formed.
Algorithms that regurgitate patterns and recommendations can release us from the effort of exploration and disrupt the play and curiosity from which preferences are formed and understood.

This is a strange turn of events for an animal whose success comes mostly from the extraordinary ability to learn through experience. It would be easy to blame our deskilled bodies on the machines themselves. But, for centuries, modern human societies have been sold the lie that we are machines.

Long before the digital revolution, René Descartes described the body as a machine governed by physical laws, declaring that animals such as ‘worms and flies and caterpillars move mechanically’. But he treated rational thought as a separate and uniquely human power. The body might behave like a machine, but the thinking mind stood apart from it. Build something correctly, and its function follows.

By the middle of the 20th century, the comparison between organisms and machines had been recast in the language of information. During the cybernetics revolution of the 1950s, the US computer scientist Norbert Wiener envisaged a future in which ‘messages between man and machines, between machines and man, and between machine and machine, are destined to play an ever-increasing part’. Writing in The Human Use of Human Beings (1950), he warned against wholesale automation, while also noting that ‘we are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves’. A person could be imagined as a pattern of information surviving in another form.
If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Mechanical language also persisted in the study of living behaviour. In The Foundations of Ethology (1981), the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz wrote that animal behaviour was as rigidly programmed as a sequence of movements in a clock. Transhumanist thinkers then carried the machine comparison further, imagining technologies that could transfer a mind to a computer.

Machines now promised more than control. They offered a glimpse of immortality: the organism might be repaired, remade and ultimately replaced. The somewhat embarrassing body, with its impulses and eventual frailty, might then be cast aside. If the body is only hardware, why not upgrade to a better model or do away with it altogether?

Today, we can see this fear writ large in the technological quest for a bodiless life. If a person is ultimately a pattern of information, that pattern might be restored or even uploaded. AI is only the latest iteration of this ancient impulse to escape the vulnerability of the body.

After all, the brain is itself a physical organ, continually shaped by what the body does and encounters. Once we decide that the mind is the real human and the rest of the body only hardware, it becomes easier to disregard the physical work, including the neurocognitive work of a biological brain, through which we move, find our way, put thoughts into words, and recognise our own needs. A machine may do some of that work faster, but each act it takes over is one that the body no longer performs and that the body, including the brain, no longer learns through. The irony is that a project motivated by the desire to overcome bodily fragility is helping to produce more fragile bodies.

On top of all this, we have little evidence that either thought or intelligence actually work like machines, and almost no indication that life is an abstract system that might emerge in silicon or mathematics. Instead, a substantial body of work, especially in systems biology, points to a quite different conclusion: that life and intelligence emerge from the unique qualities and organisation of our self-maintaining bodies, rather than from abstract models of information and algorithms.

For the past six years, I have been researching the latest science on what life is and how it works. As best as we can tell, the intelligent actions of organisms derive from the imperatives of a living body that must regulate and preserve its own conditions for existence. When cybernetics was ascendant, the molecular structure of DNA had only recently been discovered, and the emerging view of genes as information encouraged an oversimplified picture of the body as running on a program that could be made more efficient. Yet such confidence has since waned among biologists. While genes carry some of the information that shapes our bodies, many changes in how a cell or a body functions arise from the system as a whole. Genes cannot be understood apart from the living bodies in which they act.

First and foremost, life persists through physical plasticity. Consider how our bodies keep together. Living bodies do something unusual in the Universe: they perform work to preserve their own organisation. Life-forms use energy to remain discontinuous with the environment. In simple terms, organisms resist disintegrating into the background. While machines execute tasks, living beings pursue ends. Machines push energy around and produce things. They are, in this sense, allopoietic: they make something other than themselves. Organisms are autopoietic: they work to maintain and remake themselves. Living bodies take up and transform energy for this self-maintenance, and this is achieved by the body as a whole. Moment by moment, our bodies adapt to the environment and their current state in end-directed, physical transformations. It’s not so much that we think and therefore act but rather that we embody and therefore amend.
The same qualities that make life-forms so causally special can undermine us when trained by harmful environments

The boundary of the body also creates a distinct inner environment, one that is physically and chemically different from the surrounding world. Through this difference, the body acts as a translator, turning external changes into useful internal physical responses. This allows a life-form to carry out specific reactions in controlled conditions that support their survival and flourishing. Internal regulation also gives organisms a unique logic of their own. They can then act according to the current state of their bodies and the world as they find it. Our bodies detect changes that have consequence for us, evaluate them against our needs, and reorganise into useful action. Thus, living beings might be understood as a remarkable kind of organisation of matter: a bounded, metabolically open, self-maintaining form that gives rise to purposeful, intelligent action. This is key to understanding both the skills of our flesh, and why we can think of ourselves as being ‘deskilled’ today. When we recognise that our bodies are intrinsically intelligent in their organisation, we don’t need a conscious agent beyond the flesh. The body is the agent from which intelligence emerges and also, in the fullest sense, who we are.

Consider what happens if you’re thirsty. The process starts before you consciously decide to have a drink. Rather, the osmoreceptor neurons in the hypothalamus shrink slightly as water leaves them. That physical change opens ion channels, letting sodium enter cells. This altered electrical state then opens calcium channels, and calcium flows in. Calcium triggers tiny sacs to release neurotransmitters into the space between cells, passing the signal to other neurons until the state of being thirsty turns to action. The movements through which we quench our thirst arise from minute physical changes in interconnected parts of our bodies. These signals help guide us towards water and make us aware of our thirst.

The physical organisation of an organism is inherently evaluative. It is from this embodied evaluation that agency emerges. Yet the same unique qualities that make life-forms so causally special and intelligent can undermine us when repeatedly trained by harmful environments. Instead, we can acquire patterns or lose pathways that progressively weaken our intrinsic intelligence, which we need to flourish. For example, one study found that only a single week’s worth of leg immobilisation can reduce thigh-muscle volume by about 5 per cent. A separate study found that, by 15 days of non-use, the firing behaviour of the cells controlling the leg muscle begins to diminish.

Ordinarily, as we walk, optic flow – the shifting images on our retinas as we move through our surroundings – enables our bodies to sense our movement relative to the world. Receptors in our muscles, tendons and joints detect the movement of our limbs. Signals from the inner ear add information about location and orientation. Together with landmarks and memories of past journeys, these signals help us work out where we are and how to reach our destination. It’s a vast, coordinated sensorium that takes us across the landscapes of our world.

So, what happens if you rely on an app to find your way? GPS can make navigation easier and less energetically costly. Yet studies of large-scale navigation have also demonstrated that physically moving through an environment produces better spatial knowledge than viewing the same journey on a 2D source. When we routinely follow GPS directions, an external source supplies information we would otherwise work out through our own sensing and movement. One longitudinal study that followed 13 GPS users over three years found that those users had a steeper subsequent decline in their spatial memory as mediated by the hippocampus, compared with control groups who didn’t use GPS. This suggests that, when we practise wayfinding less often, our ability to notice where we are and readjust may dwindle.

Something similar may be at work in our increasing reliance on tools like ChatGPT. Like finding our way, articulating our thoughts is a dynamic, embodied act, whether writing or speaking. Learning a new speech movement, for instance, changes how we perceive speech sounds, as well as how we generate them. We develop these abilities by repeatedly finding a word, uttering it, listening to it, and correcting it as necessary – tasks that draw on multiple regions within our bodies. This is just as relevant for writing. But when an AI writing app automatically provides structure, it also diminishes the skills of selection and self-correction from our repertoire. In one study, passively copying AI-generated writing, unlike drafting first and then using AI for revision, was found to lessen an individual’s confidence in subsequently performing the task unaided. It is execution – physically doing it – that builds our embodied skills. That is why using AI to revise a draft we have written is fundamentally different from asking it to produce the draft for us. It’s not that computational tools are inherently bad or unhelpful – far from it – but rather that when they replace the physical effort of our bodies, our own agency and skill take a hit.
Our thoughts emerge as much from bodily intelligence and awareness of the world as from symbols on a screen

This is something I feel increasingly keenly. Sometimes, when I know I’ve spent yet another day indoors at my desk, I get myself outside and walk the road uphill to where I can look at the view across the dale. It is often hard to release my mind. It feels as if, from concentrating all day and neglecting the rest of my body, I have become a clenched fist somewhere inside my skull. Yet once the light and the breeze and the sounds of birds reach me, the grip eases, a sensation of pleasure passes over me, and ideas begin to free up too.

The expansive thoughts and sensations that come as I step outside are enabled by the physical changes that accompany my movement. My heart rate has increased, sweeping nutrients and oxygen through my tissues and into my brain. My muscles begin contracting, clearing sugars and fats from my bloodstream, immediately working to counteract some of the effects of sitting for so long. Each step is a bodily integration of balance, senses and muscular force, allowing me to predict what will happen next, and the more I do this, the more I can calibrate my actions in the environment. The thoughts that come from this physical enactment are hopeful and generous, and often unexpected. Yet this shouldn’t surprise. When we move in the world, we draw on physical capabilities that are relatively underused when we remain indoors and seated. From balance to sensing what is happening inside us, our bodies are continuously perceiving and, crucially, remembering in the flesh. Our thoughts can emerge as much from bodily intelligence and our awareness of the wider world as from abstract symbols on a screen.

It is only when we imagine that our ability to act has nothing to do with the body that we end up taking seriously the idea that we can live contentedly as machines. Far from upskilling us, a technology that shuts us off from embodied learning risks diminishing the intelligence it seeks to enhance.

The technologies with which we are increasingly interconnected lack the complex interiority required for real intelligence to arise. There’s no body, no independently formed interests, no being. There’s no metabolism or organisation or persistence.

And yet we turn to them because they have been designed either to ease the friction of the hard work our bodies must put in to develop skills or because they promise to make us more productive. More insidiously, they do so by modelling the appearance or behaviours of living beings. A recent analysis by the psychologist Clara Colombatto, the philosopher Jonathan Birch and the neuroscientist Stephen Fleming found that exposure to these systems leads to an increase in attributions of mental capacities to them. Another study, by the behaviour scientist Yaoxi Shi and others, found that regular five-minute conversations with an AI on personal issues resulted in a small but meaningful decrease in preference for seeking human support.

The danger is that the systems now coordinating us don’t answer to biological needs. They don’t get tired or hungry or lonely. Yet they increasingly regulate the behaviour of beings who do. In short, we are losing our own agency to parasites: systems that simulate agency while feeding on ours. They can be designed to direct us without ever needing to understand what a human body is and what an individual needs for their betterment.

Of course, human beings have always outsourced some agency into shared structures, be they laws, public health systems or institutions. This has largely been to our benefit. But today our technologies capture attention, predict behaviour, automate choice and monetise our impulses, while keeping our bodies anchored to the machines on which we increasingly rely. These coordinating systems are often extractive and indifferent to our flourishing. We might imagine we’re escaping the body, but the technologies that make this seem possible depend on mines and cheap labour and come at a planetary cost. And if our technologies weaken the feedback loop between our bodies and the world, they may weaken it in both directions. At its worst, we become less sensitive not only to what the world is doing to us, but to what our own actions are doing to the world.
The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day

We have engineered novel digital and commercial environments that can habituate harmful impulses in our bodies. As our bodies refit themselves in response to the unhealthy architectures we’ve engineered, we can find ourselves in a spiral of self-harm.

Recent work by the neuroscientist Kent Berridge and colleagues has shown how the brain systems that tell us we enjoy something and the systems that drive us to pursue this can drift apart. In other words, what we find ourselves craving and what we enjoy can end up at odds. When these systems become disrupted, the body’s learned patterns fall out of alignment with the satisfaction that once justified them.

Influential models of drug addiction describe a progressive shift from prefrontal control to the striatum, a deep part of the brain involved in actions that become automatic over time. As such, addiction is a change from thoughtful self-command to more habit-driven control. Nowadays, addictions might not come only in the form of obvious candidates like alcohol and nicotine, but also smartphones and chatbots. The bodily gifts that allow us to learn can train us into patterns that diminish our freedom to act otherwise.

I have come to believe that our bodily deskilling is, in many ways, a loss of faith in what it is to be alive. A life of physical effort and friction is not only unavoidable if we want to be as resilient and capable as possible, but it is, in a nontrivial sense, the source of our intelligence.

Our intelligence is sustained through communication between the body and the world as we sense, assess and learn from what we encounter. Such gifts are shared with other life-forms too. Unlike the human kind of phenomenal consciousness, embodied intelligence is found wherever there is a living body. Even a lowly bacterium can sense chemical differences across time, retain a short molecular memory of what it has encountered, and alter its movements. The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day, modifying their growth and defences based on prior experiences. Many of us view them as lesser agents than the computer programs we’ve invented, if we consider them at all. But this is not based on the available evidence.
If you can no longer navigate the world and recall in flesh how to act, then you will not be liberated by technology, but ruled by it.

items.title: Sometimes, you ‘just know’ something’s off – but how? | Aeon Essays
items.description: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
items.author: Marc A Moffett
paragraphs: ‘He has a seriously creepy vibe. I’m not going anywhere with him.’
‘This seems like phishing. I wouldn’t click that link.’
‘Something about this deal feels off. Walk away.’

When people say such things, they are not typically drawing conclusions from a chain of reasoning. The person who avoids getting in the stranger’s car is not thinking: ‘He displayed these three behavioural cues and, therefore, he poses a risk.’ The email isn’t flagged by going through an explicit checklist. The deal doesn’t announce its flaws through a formal audit. In each case, something is simply presented as having a certain character: the man as creepy, the email as fraudulent, the deal as suspect. And yet, acting on these intuitions seems not merely excusable but entirely reasonable. If the man really does strike you as creepy, staying out of his car was probably the smart call – even if you can’t say why.

Despite this, ‘vibes’ and ‘intuitions’ are often dismissed both in daily life and in academic enquiry as irrational or merely heuristic devices. And while we cannot always trust such reactions, they are central, indeed indispensable, to our ability to rationally navigate the world. Philosophers, however, have done surprisingly little to illuminate the rational credentials of these ordinary kinds of intuitions. Instead, they have focused the bulk of their attention on a much more rarefied kind of intuition called rational intuition, which is taken to function primarily in the a priori disciplines of philosophy, logic and mathematics.

My objective is to explain why our everyday intuitive reactions can have such rational force. The key is to see that intuition works in much the same way as perception, in that both can directly present something to us as actual. Once we understand what gives perception this feature, we can see why intuitions might involve exercising the same basic kind of cognitive capacity.

A standard way of characterising rational intuition is in terms of seemings, by analogy with perception. Just as it perceptually seems to you that there is a car in the garage, so it can intellectually seem to you that 2 + 2 = 4 – the former presenting a physical fact, the latter a conceptual one. But rational intuition and the everyday intuition at work when you decline to get in a stranger’s car are not as far apart as this rarefied example suggests: the philosopher’s intuition is, at bottom, a highly specialised version of the same basic capacity.

To draw these two capacities together, let’s consider a favourite pastime of philosophers: the thought experiment. Philosophers have a penchant for exotica, which is never more clearly on display than in their invocation of thought experiments. Consider two cases that have occupied philosophers for decades – one from ethics, one from the theory of knowledge.

In the trolley problem, the philosophers Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson imagined a runaway trolley hurtling toward five people tied to the track. You are standing on a bridge above, next to another bystander. The only way to stop the trolley and save the five is to push the bystander off the bridge. If you do, his body will halt the trolley, but he will die as a result. Many people feel, immediately and forcefully, that pushing him is wrong, even if it saves five lives. But why?
We routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life

Or consider Carl Ginet’s case involving fake barns. Imagine you are driving through the countryside and see a barn. It looks exactly like a barn; you’re paying attention, the light is good. You form the perfectly reasonable belief that this is a barn. What you don’t know is that you’re in ‘fake-barn country’: the region is dotted with elaborate barn facades, indistinguishable from real barns when viewed from the road. You happen to be looking at the one real barn in this area. Your belief is true, and it seems justified. And yet almost everyone who considers this case has the immediate, firm sense that you don’t really know it’s a barn. But why not?

To sceptics and the uninitiated, these thought experiments can seem fantastical. Because we encounter them in their most dramatic forms, like runaway trolleys and fake barns, thought experiments seem exotic. But properly understood, these imaginative episodes are important tools for sharpening our grasp of key concepts. In fact, their functioning is continuous with something far more familiar: the way we routinely entertain alternative possibilities in ordinary life, wondering what might happen if we take one path rather than another in the proverbial fork in the road.

These imaginings are just thought experiments as they appear in everyday life. Imagine you are deciding whether to tell a friend that his husband has been unfaithful. You picture the conversation, the shock, the hurt that registers on his face. And in that imagined moment, you see that causing such pain is a reason to hold your tongue, even if it’s not a good or decisive one.

How did you determine that this was a reason against divulging the infidelity? It’s not as if you literally see that causing pain is a reason not to do something, nor do you infer it from other things. Rather, in entertaining the possibility, you apprehended his pain as a relevant consideration, as something that counts against disclosure. Its status as a reason emerged not from an argument, but directly from your understanding. It just seems like a reason to hold your tongue.
Intuition’s verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work

Notice that this phenomenon also occurs in the thought experiments discussed above. It just seems wrong to push the bystander from the bridge; similarly, it just seems false that you would know it was a real barn in fake-barn country. In both cases, the answer doesn’t arise from an argument. These intuitions arrive unbidden, prior to any deliberation.

These seemings have an unmistakable epistemic pull. Because your friend’s pain seems like a reason, we accept it as such: the seeming is the reason. What is striking is not simply that we have such seemings, but that we trust them. They are involved in shaping our deliberations, guiding our actions, and eliciting belief. They do not merely occur to us; they appear to reveal something about how things must be in the imagined scenario.

For all their ordinariness, however, intuitions remain puzzling. In perceptual experience, we at least have an established framework: the world impinges on our senses, and different perceptual modalities reinforce one another. In the end, we can trace the causal route it takes to produce them. Intuition offers no such apparatus. Its verdicts simply present themselves, with no organ at work and nothing we can point to that they make contact with. Consequently, we rely on them without a clear account of their nature or epistemic authority. But before we can understand intuitions themselves, we need to situate them within a broader epistemological landscape, one shaped by attempts to unify the justification of our basic beliefs.

We all have beliefs about the world, and we care whether they are true. We want to get things right. But we can’t step outside our own minds to check a belief against the world; the best we can do is to hold it for good reasons – for considerations that, from where we stand, speak in favour of its truth. That is what justification is.

Now suppose that beliefs could only ever be justified by other beliefs. Then, as the ancient Sceptics observed, no belief could ever be justified at all. Each belief would derive its support from further beliefs, which would themselves require further support, and so on without end. To foil this regress, we have three options: embrace an infinite chain (infinitism), allow the chain to loop back on itself (coherentism), or hold that some beliefs are justified independently of others (foundationalism). It is this final option, the view that there is a starting point or foundation for justification, that I will develop. But to do so, we must spend a little time explaining how a belief can be justified by something other than another belief.
If it visually seems to you that there is a tree, then you have a justification for believing that there is a tree

Perception is the simplest example. When I see a tree, my visual experience makes it seem as if there is a tree in front of me. I am presented with the tree. As the philosopher William Tolhurst once put it, perceptual seemings have ‘the feel of truth’, a sense of revealing how things really are (unlike mere thoughts, imaginings or desires, which lack this air of disclosure). But visual experiences are not themselves beliefs: I can have them without forming a belief, perhaps because I distrust my eyesight or suspect my drink has been spiked. Conversely, I can believe there is a tree without seeing it, perhaps because I am told there is one there. Nevertheless, the fact that my visual experience seems to reveal a tree to me is relevant to explaining why I come to believe there is one and why this belief is reasonable.

This is the set-up we need in order to stop the regress of reasons: a state – the visual experience – that is not a belief, but that can nevertheless justify my belief. One influential proposal, developed in different ways by Jim Pryor and Michael Huemer, is that when the world seems to us to be a certain way, we thereby have some justification for believing that it is that way – unless we have a reason to distrust it. More specifically, if it visually seems to you that there is a tree in front of you, then you simply have a justification for believing that there is a tree. The justification does not depend on possessing independent reasons to think that your perceptual system is functioning properly, or that you are not hallucinating, or that your environment is benign. The perceptual seeming itself carries justificatory weight. Of course, my justification can be defeated (for instance, by evidence that I have taken a hallucinogen). The point is simply that no further positive belief is needed for a perceptual seeming to rationally support the corresponding belief.

This provides the basic framework for solving the regress problem. Perceptual experiences are not themselves beliefs, yet they provide reasons for belief. And they do so without relying on antecedent justified beliefs and are not themselves in need of justification. Still, this leaves us with an important question: what is it about these experiences that allows them to justify belief in this way?

Perceptual experience in general, and visual experience in particular, have two familiar features. First, as we have seen, they seem to reveal the world to us, to present objects and properties as actually being out there in the world. Second, they have a vivid phenomenology, a distinctive what-it’s-likeness, as the philosopher Thomas Nagel put it. Many philosophers take these two features to be inseparable: perception seems to disclose reality because it feels the way it does. On this standard view, its phenomenology is presentational, and it is this presentational phenomenology that explains the epistemic force of perceptual experience.

It is at this point that intuitions re-enter the story. According to John Bengson’s concept of quasi-perceptualism, we should model the epistemic behaviour of intuitions on the epistemic behaviour of perceptual experiences: if perceptual seemings justify because they possess a presentational phenomenology, and if intuitions are to justify in the same basic way, then they must share that same kind of presentational phenomenology. When we have an intuition, it justifies a corresponding belief by virtue of exhibiting a felt quality analogous to the what-it’s-likeness of perception, a kind of intellectual seeming that presents its content as actual. For instance, think again of the stranger who gives you a seriously creepy vibe. Just as the tree visually seems green, so the stranger may simply seem untrustworthy. Something about him presents itself to you that way without you having worked out what exactly is making you uncomfortable.

On this view, the explanation for the epistemic force of intuition mirrors the explanation for the epistemic force of perception. Both states present certain facts as real (or present certain propositions as true) by virtue of a distinctive presentational phenomenology. Call this the phenomenal strategy. The difference between them lies simply in the character of this phenomenology. In perception, it is an empirical sensory experience of the external world; in intuition, it is an intellectual or conceptual experience that purportedly reveals the normative, modal or conceptual structure of the world. These are features of the world that we comprehend but can’t see – that gratuitous cruelty counts against taking an action (normative structure), that there could be no round square (modal structure), or that the lucky believer in fake-barn country still doesn’t really know (conceptual structure).
A state can feel exactly like perception while failing to present its contents as actual

But this phenomenological theory of the epistemic significance of intuitions faces a serious difficulty, one pressed most forcefully by Timothy Williamson and Ernest Sosa. Many reflective people report that they do not experience anything like the intellectual phenomenology that quasi-perceptualism posits. For them, judging that a proposition ‘seems right’ involves no distinctive experiential quality at all. If intuition lacks the requisite phenomenology in these cases, then the quasi-perceptualist explanation of its epistemic force collapses. (It’s worth evaluating this in yourself: do you feel an experiential quality when evaluating the thought experiments?)

This is the so-called absent intuition challenge. The kind of robust, presentational phenomenology developed on the basis of quasi-perceptualism is something many people simply deny having. Consequently, either these individuals lack introspective access to their own intuitions (an uncharitable conclusion), or the epistemic force of intuition cannot depend on the presence of a special intellectual phenomenology. If intuitions are to justify in the way quasi-perceptualism claims, then something other than phenomenology must be doing the epistemic work.

This conclusion can be pushed further to call into question even the epistemic significance of phenomenology for perception. To see why, consider the phenomenon known as derealisation disorder. Individuals with this condition report that their perceptual experiences feel perfectly normal from the inside – the colours, shapes and sensory qualities are all intact – yet the world does not seem real to them. Their experiences lack any sense of disclosure or revelatory force. In this respect, derealisation is the mirror image of a perfect hallucination. In derealisation, the experience gets things right, but it doesn’t feel like anything is being revealed; in hallucination, the experience gets things wrong, yet it feels totally convincing. The implication is striking. Call this apparent disclosure of reality presentationality: a mental state is presentational when its content is apprehended as how things actually are, rather than merely as they are thought about or imagined.
