As Jackson turned onto the Maine Turnpike, with a stale cup of Aroma Joe’s coffee and a Killers CD in the console, he grabbed one of three pairs of sunglasses from the visor above the driver’s seat and started to tell me that running for office made him feel “scared to death.” As a labor activist, he’d learned that in “every action, every strike, somebody always gets made an example of—and that’s so that people will remember, so that they’ll be less likely to break ranks, to get out of line,” he said. Politics was no different. “You’re going to go to Exit 7,” the aide interjected. Anyway, he continued, at some point he became less afraid and decided to run for office—first as a Republican, and later as an Independent. Exit 7 came and went. He tried to swerve but couldn’t make it. “Coming back!” Jackson exclaimed, laughing heartily.

Earlier this summer, Jackson, a fifty-eight-year-old former logger and president of Maine’s state Senate, replaced Graham Platner as the Democratic Senate nominee running against Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent. Jackson accepted the nomination at a convention in Bangor, though on the campaign trail, he can occasionally sound as if he wishes he hadn’t. At a meeting with graduate-student workers in a co-op house in Orono, Jackson, who finished third in this year’s gubernatorial primary, emphasized that he didn’t expect to be the Senate nominee. “I didn’t know that I’d be the person,” he said. “I didn’t want to be the person, but I’m happy to be that person now with all of you because we really can do this.” At a town hall in Jay, he told about a hundred supporters that “it could have been anyone else.” Reading through his bio, he said, half jokingly, “I don’t want to make you have to listen to it again. . . . Obviously, I’m a fifth-generation logger. People are getting sick of me saying that.”

When Jackson finished high school in Allagash, a town near the Canadian border, his father was adamant that he shouldn’t continue in his family’s trade, but “I was an idiot, and I went to work in the woods,” he told the crowd. Throughout his career, he said, his critics seized on that background to deride him as a rube. “I went back to school at Fort Kent and finished with a 3.87 G.P.A. I’m a member of the National Honor Society. I mean, whatever,” he told me. “I don’t give a fuck what people think about if I’m educated enough.” Recently, Collins had referred in an interview with Politico to the fact that he and his partner were second cousins. “Me and Lana are consenting adults,” Jackson told me, adding that they have been together since they were in middle school. “I got two awesome sons that I’m so fucking proud of it’s not even funny, and that right there to me means that there ain’t nothing wrong with it.” He thinks that an implied classism runs through the attacks coming from Collins, a daughter of politicians, who grew up in the same county as he did. “She’s what I would consider management, and I’m the employee,” he said. “You know, with people like her, I should know my place.” Shawn Roderick, a spokesman for Collins’s campaign, pointed to Jackson’s twenty years in the legislature and his six years as state Senate president: “For him to pretend that he is a rank and file employee is ridiculous.”

Jackson’s self-effacing rhetoric might come from knowing his place with Mainers, who gave Platner more primary votes than any other Democratic Senate candidate in history. Dave Harvey, who attended one of Jackson’s events, said, “I think Troy’s got the same message” as Platner. “He certainly doesn’t have—I mean, Platner was a once-in-a-lifetime orator. This guy’s a hard worker.” Many supporters and allies have said that Jackson would have to work hard to match, let alone overcome, Collins’s fund-raising and enormous name recognition. But Jackson has notched multiple union endorsements, and there’s a sense that he could have cross-party appeal. “I think there are a number of Republicans—I’ve heard this anecdotally from people—that say, ‘Hey, you know, this guy’s worth considering because he’s speaking my language,’ ” Liz Shuler, the president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., who came to Maine to help canvass for Jackson, said. “And, to be honest, Donald Trump did the same thing, right?”

Tim Vitanza and Jay Porter are the kinds of Mainers whom Jackson might have an in with—both are three-time Trump voters who have grown dissatisfied with the President’s performance in office, particularly this year. “ ‘Drill, baby, drill’—how come he ain’t fucking drilling?” Vitanza said. Porter, a retired truck driver, liked the idea of having a nonpolitician in the White House, but he didn’t understand why Trump “had to have a statue of himself in every damn town.” “It’s been garbage,” he added. Both men live at the Blueberry Ridge mobile-home park, in Wells, which is owned by a real-estate holding corporation, and had come to the back yard of a neighbor to talk about the water issues in the community. (Brown liquid has been coming out of faucets and showers.) Vitanza was furious at how the company that he rents his lot from doesn’t seem to care to fix the problems, and yet the rent keeps going up. Jackson, addressing the residents from a plastic chair on the back yard’s deck, decried the greed of private equity and told them that he’d try to help; Collins has never shown up to their neighborhood, as far as they know. “It’d be nice to find somebody that gave a crap,” Porter said.

There was one thing holding Vitanza back from voting for Jackson, and he waited until the candidate was leaving to talk to him about it. “I’m a Republican. I’ve voted both ways. I work for the Maine Turnpike. I’m union,” Vitanza told Jackson, crossing his arms. “You don’t like ICE, you want to abolish ICE. Why?” “Well, because I think they’re just wrong right now,” Jackson replied. “I mean, we used to have Customs and Border Patrol do that.” What about “all these undocumented people who are here—you think, Oh it’s no big deal?” Vitanza asked. “No, I don’t,” he replied, raising his hand. Jackson thought ICE’s money could be invested elsewhere, and that the Border Patrol could do the job of conducting immigration enforcement. By this point, Jackson was surrounded by aides; it was time for him to go. He thanked Vitanza for being there, before adding, with a laugh, “Stay workin’, brother!”

It wasn’t exactly what Vitanza, who has many relatives working in law enforcement, wanted to hear. “I like ICE, I’m sorry,” he told me. Of the Border Patrol, he said, “Obviously, they’re not doing their job.” (Later, Vitanza saw a Collins ad that claimed that Jackson had raised taxes for seniors in the state legislature and told me that he wouldn’t vote for him “no matter what.”) Porter said he was keeping an open mind. “This is just the first date,” he said. But both agreed on one thing: Jackson had a better chance of winning than Platner did.

Platner, the combat veteran and oysterman whose Senate campaign unravelled after he was accused of various forms of misconduct, including sexual assault (which he denies), is credited with infusing the state’s middle-of-the-road electorate with enthusiasm for a progressive campaign. At a town hall in Jay on Saturday afternoon, Jayne Costa, a retired English teacher, told me that she thought the Democrats’ chances of flipping the seat would have “probably” been better if Platner had stayed in the race; she felt that the Party had gotten scared. The town hall, she added, would’ve had a bigger crowd if Platner was the host. “He drew in a lot of new voters, and he drew on a lot of young people, and that’s what we need,” Costa, who is in favor of revitalizing the town by putting an A.I. data center in an abandoned mill, said.

Jackson wants to convince his doubters that the messenger doesn’t matter as much as the message. “Look, all these things you care about are still right in front of us,” he told me. “They’re still on the table.” In Jay, he attempted to do that, touting how he would push for Medicare for All, how he “wouldn’t be opposed” to adding members to the Supreme Court, and how he “wouldn’t be opposed” to term limits. He got emotional as he spoke about spending little time with his father because of how much he worked, and how the time that work took away from family seemed to him like “the biggest robbery I’ve ever seen.”

Sitting in the front row, a retired paper-mill worker named Linda Deane used her question to steer Jackson toward the dwindling days before the election. She and some guys who met at the union hall every day for coffee had been worrying about Collins’s attacks against him—and the possibility that they could sway voters. “When are you going to start pushing back on these attacks and setting the record straight?” Deane asked. Jackson rubbed his face. “So, I mean, it’s been real fun,” Jackson said facetiously, and the crowd laughed. “I’m not sure right now if I want to vote for myself, either. But honestly, I mean, I don’t know that, you know, we’re gonna answer them.” It was worth correcting the record on the trail, he said, but he wouldn’t be able to keep up with Collins’s spending.

Elsewhere, he could seem more sure-footed. Jackson has said that he won’t support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to lead the caucus, and he described a meeting in Washington, earlier this summer, during which Schumer raised this with him. “ ‘I understand you’re not going to support me,’ ” he recalled Schumer saying. “Senator, I’ve been through enough leadership elections,” Jackson replied, shaking his head. “ ‘Well,’ ” he recalled Schumer saying, “ ‘We need to have Maine. I just want to work with you.’ ” Jackson said that he did, too. (Schumer did not respond to a request for comment.) Although Jackson wouldn’t have the seniority that Collins accumulated over thirty years, he believes that he will be able to wield power for working-class people in a closely divided Senate. Otherwise, “I don’t know that I’m super excited about going to Washington,” he said. “What I’m super excited about is standing up for people that I believe, you know, have been left behind by our federal government.”

Jackson isn’t a newcomer to politics, but he has never won a statewide race, let alone one as gruelling and nationally scrutinized as this one. On Saturday night, upstairs at the Baxter Brewing Company in Lewiston, Jackson sipped on a Moscow Mule and got on the dance floor at “labor karaoke” as soon as the jumping piano chords of Dolly Parton’s “9 to 5” came on. He was making his way out an hour later when a young man started chasing him with a phone, recording a video with the flash on. He screamed questions at Jackson, such as why he had endorsed a “communist” local official, or whether he would denounce Hasan Piker, the leftist Twitch streamer.

“I would love to know what your karaoke song is, Jacob!” a staffer accompanying Jackson said, addressing the heckler by name. “Wow! Thank you so much for coming to karaoke!” She had recognized him as a tracker—an operative hired by the opposition to create such spectacles as fodder for social media—and interposed herself between Jackson and him while also trying to shout him down. Jackson, seeming unbothered by the ruckus, made for his minivan and then drove away, honking twice. ♦
An earlier version of this piece mistakenly said that Troy Jackson’s father was deceased.

items.title: The Cruise That Never Ends
items.description: Some time ago, while daydreaming about tossing out my to-do list and becoming a Buddhist nun or a berry farmer, I signed up for a newsletter called New Escapologist, which advocates freeing oneself from “the overbearing world of work, consumerism, and anxiety.
items.author: Shayla Love
paragraphs: Some time ago, while daydreaming about tossing out my to-do list and becoming a Buddhist nun or a berry farmer, I signed up for a newsletter called New Escapologist, which advocates freeing oneself from “the overbearing world of work, consumerism, and anxiety.” The June edition included the story of a couple who met on a cruise ship, sold all of their belongings, and embarked on back-to-back voyages. Soon afterward, I watched a short documentary, “The Happiest Guy in the World,” from 2018, about a man who’d been on cruises continuously for nineteen years. I also read news stories about a voyage called the Odyssey, a cruise that started in 2024, and that was never supposed to end.

I posted a message on cruisecritic.com, the largest online cruise-reviewing platform, explaining that I wanted to talk to people who had decided to live at sea indefinitely. In July, Starr Davis, a retiree from Florida who was living aboard the Odyssey, e-mailed me. “I heard you were looking to find people who sold everything to do life on board,” she wrote. “Well, that’s me!” When we talked, by phone, she was in Thailand and her voice was chipper and clear. She told me that since 2024 the Odyssey had already taken her to dozens of countries, and that during excursions in East Asia, she’d taken advantage of inexpensive medical care. She talked as if she’d found the ultimate retirement hack, and said that I could visit her on the ship, if I liked. Of her fellow-passengers, she said, “We’ll be friends for life.”

Around the same time, however, I got a cryptic e-mail about the Odyssey from someone who asked to remain unnamed. “It is quite important to at least allude to current issues and risks,” the e-mail said. Positive coverage of the Villa Vie Residences, the Florida-based company that launched the Odyssey, might “jeopardize the finances of your readers by falsely creating the impression that VVR is a secure, low risk cruise line.” The tipster warned that a small number of enthusiastic residents tend to appear over and over in media coverage, skewing public perceptions. This person was not a resident of the ship but claimed to have been harassed on Facebook by a co-founder of Villa Vie. When I searched for the company there, I quickly found a very active group devoted to discussing it.

The Facebook group had its own lexicon. High-profile residents had nicknames such as “the pirate” and “the mermaid.” Villa Vie’s co-founders, Mikael Petterson and Kathy Villalba, were “the Florida Couple.” I found A.I.-generated images that depicted the Odyssey as a kind of floating dictatorship in which “leakers” were punished for telling the truth. On August 1st, my anonymous source e-mailed me again: “Very disturbing insider news occurring right now on Odyssey in Singapore.” It seemed that the ship was supposed to have left the country, according to its itinerary, but Villalba, via a Zoom call from Florida, was asking passengers for more than a million dollars—thousands of dollars per person—in order to buy fuel. Residents were booing her. The ship’s internet had been shut off; it was unclear whether the crew was being paid.

When I e-mailed Davis, asking her about the fuel issues and delays, she replied, “We are sailing now. Yeah!!!” But she told me that she was getting off the ship for a while, to do some tours on land. I started to check the Facebook page every morning, and I sent direct messages to several passengers, but I didn’t hear back. Then, on a Friday evening in September, I was at a brewery in Brooklyn when an e-mail popped up on my phone with a curious subject line: “Villa Vie Odyssey is sinking.” The sender, Toni Trombecky, owned a cabin on the vessel but had left the ship after the Singapore debacle. “I’m one of the few that didn’t sign the NDA so I don’t mind talking about it,” she wrote. I was puzzled. Why would a residential cruise ask residents to sign a nondisclosure agreement?

Soon, I heard from Wade Rand, another resident who had recently left. He told me that my inquiries had caused a stir on board. Residents had been informed that anyone talking to a journalist would, in his words, “incur severe wrath.” One morning, I found an A.I.-generated image of me in the Facebook group. Details from my résumé had apparently been scraped from the internet, and commenters were debating my intentions. I mentioned to Rand that I hoped to visit the ship. “At this point, it may be impossible to get on the ship except undercover,” he replied. “It could be dangerous even. Apparently . . . everyone knows who you are.”

Before Petterson and Villalba founded Villa Vie, they worked for a failed cruise-ship venture called Life at Sea. In 2022, Petterson, a former financial planner for cruise companies who described himself on his résumé as a “cruise start-up entrepreneur,” dreamed of a cruise that would last longer than any other. He signed a contract with Miray Cruises, a Turkish company, to develop and market Life at Sea, which would offer a three-year voyage with stops at hundreds of ports. The story attracted widespread news coverage, and more than half of the cabins were reserved within a month. Rates started at ninety thousand dollars for interior cabins and just under a million for a suite. (The most successful multiyear residential cruise, the World, has been sailing for more than two decades; it operates essentially as a nonprofit co-owned by ultra-rich passengers, who pay millions for cabins that can be as large as town houses. “The only thing that’s similar between the World and a cruise ship is they float on the water,” one resident said in 2024.)

Many of Life at Sea’s customers invested significant portions of their savings into the cruise; some sold their homes. But Petterson’s relationship with Miray deteriorated. He told the New York Times that the head of the company owned a pizza parlor and wanted him to route customer deposits into its bank account, because Miray Cruises didn’t have an account in the United States. (The company said this was a temporary solution.) Petterson left the company shortly before passengers travelled to Istanbul to board the three-year cruise; there, they learned that a deal for the ship had fallen through. Miray then cancelled the voyage altogether. A year later, some passengers were still trying to get their money back. Miray did not respond to requests for comment.

Petterson didn’t want to give up on his concept, however. He attacked Miray online, and the company sued him for tortious interference and defamation. (The lawsuit was voluntarily dismissed.) He announced that he was working on his next project, Villa Vie Residences: “With total transparency and integrity, we will make the dream come true stronger, better than anything else on the market today. Stay tuned explorers.” Villalba, his romantic partner and colleague, joined him as a co-founder and the C.E.O. of Villa Vie. Public records show that both of them had declared bankruptcy in the past; Petterson had done so only a few years before.

The Odyssey was advertised as the “first truly affordable residential World Cruise.” In March, 2024, one couple paid a hundred and seventy-nine thousand dollars to buy a cabin. For an additional maintenance fee of six thousand dollars a month, which was supposed to hold steady in perpetuity, they would both receive three meals a day, housekeeping and laundry services, basic medical attention, and wine or beer at every meal—forever. Passengers who paid more up front would not owe a monthly fee. “There are no surprise costs going forward,” Petterson told Fox Business.

A former employee of Villa Vie told me that Petterson was a skilled public speaker who appeared to know what he was talking about, but that his business plan “seemed like a guesstimate.” The former employee remembered Petterson and Villalba saying that, as long as the Odyssey sold out of cabins, the business would be financially sustainable. The employee worried that they were “really just trying to wing a multimillion-dollar project.” Still, the company managed to purchase and retrofit a four-hundred-and-eighty-five-cabin ship that had been built in 1993.

The Odyssey was scheduled to set sail in May, 2024, from Belfast, Northern Ireland, with a portion of the cabins filled. Claude Sadovsky, a retired emergency-medicine physician from Illinois, was one of the passengers who travelled to the area before departure. He’d previously put down a small deposit with Life at Sea, which was refunded, and he’d paid a hundred thousand dollars for an interior cabin on the Odyssey. But residents soon learned that the departure would be delayed for repairs, and because of problems with the ship’s certifications. The Odyssey needed a new rudder stock, a vertical metal shaft that helps with steering, but when the rudder arrived staff members didn’t seem to know how to install it. An expert was called in. “The first thing the expert said is, ‘Why are you trying to fit it horizontally when it’s going to sit vertically?’ ” Sadovsky told me. Another incoming passenger, Jenny Phenix, complained in a WhatsApp group about the setbacks. Villa Vie informed her that her contract for a cabin was cancelled. Phenix is currently suing the company in U.S. district court.

The Odyssey finally departed in early October of 2024. It was different from other cruises that Sadovsky had been on. Residents were invited to give PowerPoint presentations on topics of their choice; a retired forensic psychologist gave a lecture on nature versus nurture, and a retired coroner spoke about resuscitation. The furnishings were simple and the pool seemed to be closed for maintenance just as often as it was open. The food was decent, but not decadent, with a rotating menu that frequently repeated. And yet Sadovsky started to have a wonderful time. He was meeting people and seeing the world. The itinerary changed constantly; Villa Vie eliminated about half of the ship’s planned stops in Alaska, instead spending ten days sailing back and forth along the coast, and the Galápagos Islands had to be skipped because ships with more than a hundred people couldn’t stop there. But Sadovsky grew to appreciate the chance to visit lesser-known spots. At one point, over dinner with some fellow-residents, he realized that he’d gladly pay twice the twenty-five hundred dollars a month that he was being charged. “That’s what I think the value of this thing is,” he told me. If anything, his worry was that he wasn’t paying enough. “How could you guarantee that you will never raise the monthly rate?” Sadovsky said.

When Toni Trombecky retired from a federal-government job, thirteen years ago, she and her husband moved to Las Vegas. They liked to travel, but as they got older long flights were harder to recover from. She was thrilled when she read about the Odyssey online. “You don’t have to pack your bags,” Trombecky told me. “And your whole neighborhood goes with you.” The couple spent a hundred and fifty thousand dollars on a fifteen-year contract for a porthole cabin, and in January, 2026, they boarded the ship in Australia. After eight weeks, they upgraded to a large-window cabin, for an additional twenty thousand dollars. Their room was only a hundred and forty square feet, but Trombecky thought of the Odyssey’s two restaurants as her dining room and the ship’s library as a living room. There were onboard exercise classes and games. She bought wallpaper, furniture, and new tile for the cabin. Fellow-passengers often invited her and her husband to join them for meals. “This was not a vacation,” she said. “It’s a life style.”

Trombecky told me that Villalba, who came on board periodically, had a gentle manner and seemed conflict-averse. When Trombecky and her husband upgraded rooms, they asked for the perks that had come with their first room. “We’ll let you keep them, but don’t tell Mike,” Trombecky remembered Villalba saying. But the former employee said that Villalba had a temper, and that she occasionally complained about guests to her employees. A couple of months after Trombecky boarded, Villalba announced that a temporary fifteen-hundred-dollar fuel surcharge would be added to monthly fees. Israel and the U.S. had recently launched a war on Iran, and oil prices were sharply up. Residents pushed back; they had been promised set rates. Villalba soon apologized and said that the fuel surcharge was voluntary. Tensions emerged between those who did and did not pay, however. A resident told me that the ship was like “junior high school during spirit week.” Trombecky, who paid, said that a neighbor hung a flyer that said, “We paid—how about you?”

Petterson and Villalba blamed the media for negative news coverage of Villa Vie, especially after the delay in Belfast. The ship’s viability depended on sales, which weren’t going as well as planned. Facebook allows users to flag harassment, hate speech, spam, and misinformation; Villalba started to flag groups and posts that discussed Villa Vie in an unfavorable light. Some residents were on her side and referred to the Facebook group I’d found as a hate group. Villalba facilitated a separate Facebook group called Mythbusters, but it became inactive after Villalba complained bitterly about leaks. “Every leak narrows what can be shared next time,” she wrote. “That’s not karma. It’s cause and effect.” A travel journalist wrote in Cruise News about the odd air of censorship on board: “Sometimes I’d feel like Bob Woodward meeting with a Watergate informant in an underground parking garage as a resident whispered his or her disappointment.” A resident told me that some passengers started checking others’ phones in search of alleged leakers.

Passengers who had invested extra money up front had special status as “Founders,” and each tier had a designated color. “Black” members had paid three hundred and fifty thousand dollars; “Gold,” a hundred thousand; and “Silver,” twenty-five thousand. A resident who requested anonymity told me that Petterson and Villalba shared more updates on the status of the ship with the Founders. After they began to suspect that one of the Silver Founders was a leaker, however, they cut the entire Silver cohort out of the loop. “We knew that there was a financial incentive for everyone to be quiet if we were going to attract more people to the cruise ship,” the resident said. “I do feel a little bit, like, Should we have been bigger whistle-blowers all along? Probably. But they had turned the community so against each other that if you were a whistle-blower, the other passengers would have made your life miserable. You would have had to leave.”

Trombecky told me that, as Villa Vie’s money issues became increasingly evident, the subject became as taboo as “politics and religion. “You didn’t talk about it,” she said. In April of this year, Villa Vie taped letters to the door of each cabin, asking for emergency loans and promising between twelve and twenty-four per-cent interest in return. Trombecky gave fifty thousand dollars. When the first interest deadline arrived, however, she wasn’t paid. At the end of July, she left the ship for a friend’s wedding, in Bali, and while she was gone she heard about the fateful meeting in Singapore. After passengers signed the N.D.A.s, Villalba, via Zoom, told them that the ship could be detained on behalf of creditors if they did not contribute. There was apparently no money left for fuel, provisions, or crew salaries.

A passenger with Founder status, Shirene Thomas, told me that they had been getting such requests since early in the voyage. “I don’t think we ever went two or three months” without one, Thomas said. Because the money covered basics such as hot water and air-conditioning, Founders felt pressure to help their fellow-passengers. At one point, a Founder paid off a Starlink bill so that internet service could be restored. I spoke with a passenger who had attempted to tally up all the extra money that residents had contributed during the trip; the figure was easily in the tens of millions. Villa Vie Residences did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

In Singapore, the residents came up with the money in two days, but Trombecky and her husband decided to give up thousands of dollars in belongings and leave. “We just felt like we’re throwing good money after bad here,” she told me. According to Trombecky and to passenger contracts that I reviewed, Villa Vie had guaranteed that it would buy back cabins at a reduced rate. When Trombecky invoked this policy, however, she was told that the program was suspended.

The Odyssey managed to sail to Hong Kong and then to Hạ Long Bay, in Vietnam. In early September, at another emergency meeting, Villalba, on Zoom, asked passengers for even more money. “She was crying,” Susan O’Brien, a ballroom-dance instructor who was working on board told me. She remembered Villalba saying, “This is my baby, and you don’t know what I’ve been through.” According to O’Brien, one passenger stood up and yelled to the crowd, “Do you want the whole ship to go bankrupt? Because if that happens, we all lose.”

In late September, I received a surprise WhatsApp message from Villalba, whom I had yet to contact. She’d heard about my outreach. “Villa Vie has had an extraordinary couple of years . . . some wonderful chapters and some extremely difficult ones,” she said. “If you’re writing about us, I’d rather give you the opportunity to see the ship for yourself.” We discussed a visit while the Odyssey was docked in Ho Chi Minh City, but then Villalba backtracked: Vietnamese regulations would not allow visitors on board the ship. She said that I could come aboard for lunch in Bangkok but then declined a Zoom meeting, citing the time difference. When I followed up, she said that she was “slammed” and asked to talk when she was back in the U.S. I continued to reach out, and she delayed each time. Finally, she sent me a screenshot from what looked like a WhatsApp group of residents. Trombecky was asking others if they wanted to speak with a journalist. “Is this your story?” Villalba said. I didn’t hear from her again, not even when I e-mailed her a list of detailed questions about the cruise.

On September 30th, the passengers who remained on the ship celebrated two years of sailing. “Many doubted she’d ever make it out of Belfast,” a resident wrote about the Odyssey on Facebook. “201 ports, and 2 years later, she’s still sailing.” He also shared a photo of a “Happy Anniversary” sheet cake. At the beginning of October, there were rumors that Oneil Khosa, a hotel-and-banking entrepreneur, was considering an investment in the ship. Residents were hopeful that he might offer an influx of cash. But Petterson wrote to residents that discussions had effectively ended. In a separate message, Villalba wrote, “I will readily admit that we underestimated the financial demands of this venture. We wanted to make residential cruising affordable. Looking back, we made it too affordable.” The ship’s monthly operating costs were exceeding its revenues from fees by more than two million dollars a month, she said. As usual, she requested money. This time, though, residents were reluctant to contribute.

On the evening of October 26th, the ship’s hotel manager, Rodrigo Lopes, addressed passengers in an announcement that eventually ended up on YouTube. He noted that residents had been forming groups that could theoretically take over ownership. “Guys, it doesn’t matter,” Lopes said of these plans. “If there is no resolution by Tuesday, all residents will be asked to leave the ship.” Passengers spent Monday night emptying their liquor cabinets at a ship-wide party. They gathered at the bar and in the dining rooms. They hugged one another and danced. On Tuesday morning, they received the final notice from Villalba. The roughly two hundred residents who were left had to disembark at an industrial port on the outskirts of Sihanoukville, Cambodia, by 2:00 P.M. In a press release from Villa Vie, the company blamed rising fuel prices for the demise of the cruise. Yet many residents I spoke to rejected this claim. The company was also in debt to COLUMBIA Cruise Services, which paid the crew; VIKAND, which provided medical staff; various provisioning companies; port authorities; internet providers; and, of course, to the passengers who had loaned the ship money.

On the day of disembarkation, shuttle buses pulled up alongside the Odyssey and passengers shuffled out. Each shuttle seated sixteen, but many of the seats filled up with luggage. Dana Teton, a seventy-one-year-old passenger who had been renting from the owner of a cabin, felt grateful that he’d lost only eleven thousand dollars. One of his friends had bought into the Endless Horizons program, paying three hundred and fifty thousand dollars to secure a cabin for life. When the Odyssey stopped sailing, the friend had spent less than a month on the ship. “Anybody who contributed money might as well have taken a Zippo lighter and just set it on fire,” Teton said. Villa Vie had been trying to sell cabins up until passengers disembarked, and many people who had purchased one never even got a chance to board. Desley Thomas, who had already booked her travel and paid for a four-and-a-half-year contract, was supposed to start her voyage in early November. She found out about the Odyssey’s demise on Facebook.

As of early November, some crew members were still on board. According to passengers, some had not been paid in weeks. Teton talked to a senior crew member who said that many hadn’t been given transportation off the ship or help with their visas. Passengers also heard that the air-conditioning and much of the power were shut off. Villa Vie said in the press release that it would attempt to restructure its debt. In a message to residents, Petterson wrote that the ship was now under the control of a lender. It would be moved to Singapore, where it might be sold. But he was still looking for a way to regain authority. “It’s not like you get your car repossessed and you can’t get it back,” he told CBS. He did not respond to e-mails from The New Yorker.

Before Trombecky boarded the Odyssey, she had sold her house. On the day she left the ship, in Singapore, a crew member asked her where she would go. She started to cry. She’d expected to spend the rest of her life on board. “I was going to throw my ashes out to sea,” she said. She and her husband were able to afford a new house and car in Las Vegas, near family, and for this she considers herself lucky. “There are a lot of retired women who have put their entire retirement savings into this ship,” she said. “Not only do they not have anywhere else to go; they don’t have the money. The ship has taken it all.”

Thomas, the passenger with Founder status, had lived on the ship with two cats since 2024. After disembarking, she and her cats checked into a hotel near the port in Cambodia, along with other passengers. Some residents will continue travelling in East Asia by land, she said, and others will go home—if they have one. Thomas had given up her place in Wilmington, North Carolina, to participate in Petterson’s previous cruise-ship venture, Life at Sea. When she decided to invest in a cabin on the Odyssey, a friend asked her, “Why would you put your faith in something like this again? Haven’t you been burned already?” She replied, “I’ve already lost everything. There’s nothing more to lose.” Thomas wasn’t sure what her next destination would be. While she made up her mind, she was spending time sitting by the hotel’s infinity pool, which had a view of the Cambodian coast. She could see the Odyssey in the distance. ♦

items.title: “Paper Tiger” Views Family as Deadweight
items.description: There are no ticking clocks or flipping calendar pages in James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” but it’s nonetheless a drama of time implacably passing. Call it a September song: the story opens on Labor Day in 1986, in Queens, at the home of the Pearl family.
items.author: Richard Brody
paragraphs: There are no ticking clocks or flipping calendar pages in James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” but it’s nonetheless a drama of time implacably passing. Call it a September song: the story opens on Labor Day in 1986, in Queens, at the home of the Pearl family. Early in the morning, the jovial, still youthful paterfamilias, Irwin (Miles Teller), has his power tools going in the narrow driveway beside the house, waking his sons—Scott (Gavin Goudey), who’s about to turn eighteen, and Ben (Roman Engel), maybe five years younger—on their last day of summer vacation. As Jerry Lewis’s annual telethon blares from a TV in the kitchen, Irwin and his wife, Hester (Scarlett Johansson), tell the boys that they’re all going to visit Hester’s mother, Iris (Cindy Katz), at a country club near her home, in the prosperous and largely Jewish Long Island suburb of Great Neck.

From this banal beginning, Gray launches a tale of fear and violence, criminal conspiracies and paranoia. That night, after the family gets back home, Irwin’s older brother, Gary (Adam Driver), arrives with princely pomp, bringing a takeout feast from the venerable steak house Peter Luger. A former high-ranking cop now earning a grand living as a security consultant—and basking in the admiration of his former N.Y.P.D. colleagues—Gary, who drives a Mercedes and is seemingly sewn into sharply tailored suits, is as dashing as Irwin is staid. The fancy meal is the prelude to a proposition: he wants Irwin, an environmental engineer, to team up with him as a co-consultant to the owners of a grossly polluted site on the Gowanus Canal, in Brooklyn, which is about to undergo a federally funded cleanup. Gary is sure that the job will be lucrative and tells Irwin that the owners, recently arrived Russians whom he describes as scientists and engineers, are in need of Irwin’s regulatory and technical expertise.

At a preliminary meeting in Gowanus, little about the prospective clients’ rough manner and crude appearance bears out Gary’s claims. And a few days later, when the overeager Irwin, following his usual procedure, visits the site to take stock—proudly bringing his sons along to see the world of his work—he finds that he’s dealing with gangsters of rare ruthlessness and brutality. By this time, though, he and Gary are in too deep: the gangsters beat Irwin and menace Hester and the boys. To protect the family, Gary goes into heavy debt to the syndicate; the movie’s title comes from the description he offers of his gangland creditors to allay Irwin’s fears. “I’m N.Y.P.D.,” Gary says, adding, “They’re not gonna touch me.” “But they can touch me,” Irwin skeptically retorts. As the days until payment is due tick grimly by, Irwin and Hester grow increasingly fretful and angry, and their widening divisions wrench the family apart, to intimately catastrophic effect.

Such lovequakes are a through line of Gray’s directorial career, which began in 1994, with “Little Odessa.” Gray, one of cinema’s great homebodies, grew up in Queens, and most of his movies are set there or in Brooklyn and deal bruisingly with the financial tensions, thwarted dreams, and frayed bonds of middle-class Jewish families like the one in which he was raised—stressed, streetwise, and crime-proximate. His previous film, “Armageddon Time,” from 2022—to my mind, his hitherto most accomplished one—is, like “Paper Tiger,” set in his home neighborhood, Fresh Meadows. That film takes place in 1980, with frequent allusions to Ronald Reagan’s ongoing Presidential campaign, and it focusses on a family very similar to the one in “Paper Tiger”: a father named Irving, who is a contractor; a mother named Esther; and two sons, the younger of whom transfers from public school to a nearby private day school dominated by a wealthy local family—the Trumps.

Gray conceived “Paper Tiger” as a sequel to “Armageddon Time” but altered his plans when the actors who played the parents in the earlier film, Anne Hathaway and Jeremy Strong, were unavailable. The two works remain cognate, but their differences are crucial. Strong’s Irving was tougher, more abrasive than Irwin is; conversely, Hathaway’s Esther, a teacher, was relatively refined and educated, whereas Johansson’s counterpart sleeps with rollers in her hair, like a vestige of the pre-Beatles sixties; speaks in a Queens accent that could cut metal; and holds the family together with her life-worn smarts and iron will. Yet she’s as unworldly as the nerdy Irwin, looking up to him with his fund of “facts and figures.”

But fires of rage burn below the surface of “Paper Tiger,” exemplified in the opening visit to Great Neck. Iris wants Hester and her family to move there; Hester demurs, explaining that college tuition for the boys must come first, but Irwin openly scoffs: “Everyone here was born with a silver spoon in their mouth, or stole one.” Iris, seeing suburban luxury as her daughter’s birthright, thinks that Hester’s marriage has been a comedown. The Pearls aren’t poor, but they’re burdened by expenses and tantalized by comforts just out of reach, especially now that their sons’ heads have been turned by Gary’s flashy success. (Comparing his uncle’s Mercedes with his parents’ cars, Scott whines, “Why do we always have to buy crappy stuff and live crappy?”)

Irwin’s run-in with the Mob dispels the fantasy of easy money; instead, he packs suitcases and makes plans to get the family out of town for their safety. Yet “Paper Tiger” is far more than a tale of criminal violence piercing the domestic bubble. It’s a story of silences, ones that form a conspicuous contrast with its precursor. “Armageddon Time,” with its expressly political context, is a film of rich discourse, filled with rhetorical expositions of ideology and history, reminiscences and commentaries. In “Paper Tiger,” there’s plenty of talk throughout, but hardly any of it involves cultural context, broader observation, or deeper reflection; it’s not a film of ideas. Instead, the heated dialogue is an expression of the inner life of the family and its time.

Interviews with directors have become a familiar part of movie promotion, but Gray’s interviews are different, often less like conversations than like performances. He’s among the most publicly funny of filmmakers, a gifted impersonator; I’ve long hoped that he would direct a comedy (he hasn’t yet) and appear in it. But his talent for mimicry comes across thrillingly in the dialogue of “Paper Tiger”—Gray wrote the screenplay himself—which adds an extra dimension to the story’s autobiographical elements. Both in ordinary chitchat and in big confrontations, the dialogue plays like a musical score of language built from a trove of memories. The film’s wondrously street-lyrical patter, its emblematic phrases and inflections, amount to a vast act of world-building—a lost milieu brought back to life in bygone clichés.

Much of this evocative talk also proves evasive. Just as Gary’s forecast for the Gowanus venture turns out to have been misleading, the fallout from that calamitous misadventure quickly brings on further elisions and secrets, transforming a happy home and a stable marriage into a curtained stage of furtive designs, hidden agendas, and stealthy exploits. Gary’s Mephistophelian temptations break the façades of business, law, and marriage, revealing the profound and irreparable solitude that lurks beneath life’s fundamental bonds.

Gray has always displayed a probing visual style, boldly confrontational yet painfully tender. In “Paper Tiger,” he refines these tendencies into lapidary images—spare, taut, and precise—that evoke the fierce solidity of the family circle and the fearsome emptiness that’s left when it shatters. With a quietly dazzling repertory of shadows and reflections, fragmented glimpses, truncated vistas, and blocked perspectives, he conjures everything the film keeps hidden, the illusions and limitations that inhere in frank gazes and point-blank views. I’ve seen “Paper Tiger” on the big screen but am looking forward to its streaming release in order to rewatch it as a silent film. Amid all its chatter, Gray has found the space to let images be eloquent, too. And their eloquence is greatest when expressing the silence and solitude of Hester.

In this regard, Gray’s movie resembles a pair of recent classics by Martin Scorsese, “The Irishman” and “Killers of the Flower Moon,” both of which feature women who respond to betrayal by men with silences deafening enough to rend the films’ finely textured surfaces. In “Paper Tiger,” the cycle of tragedy finds its definitive voice in Hester’s reproachful silences, which turn out to be radical rejections of the tight little world she inhabits. Determined and relentless, Hester, as incarnated by Johansson, dominates the action and steals the film with a decisive form of passive aggression—one that Gray condenses into a breathtakingly rapid, boldly symbolic special effect. By the time September winds down, Hester is on a timetable all her own, out of synch with her family, detached from its cares, paradoxically and bitterly free. ♦

items.title: Trump Publicly Begs Dana White to Be His New Press Secretary
items.description: Any hope that Donald Trump would respond to the Republicans’ midterms wipeout by quietly redecorating the White House and trying strike deals with his Democratic “friends” died on Friday when he announced that Stephen Miller would be the new White House chief
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Any hope that Donald Trump would respond to the Republicans’ midterms wipeout by quietly redecorating the White House and trying strike deals with his Democratic “friends” died on Friday when he announced that Stephen Miller would be the new White House chief of staff.

But rest assured that Trump’s lame-duck years won’t be totally focused on enacting cruel policies and seeking revenge on his enemies either. There’s also going to be plenty of previously unfathomable absurdity, as evidenced by Trump’s Saturday afternoon announcement on Truth Social that he wants Dana White to be his next press secretary:
While one aide told CNN that the president was joking, White House communications director Steven Cheung promoted his post on X:

White is Trump’s good friend. Their business and political ventures have been deeply entwined for decades, culminating in White staging an Ultimate Fighting Championship event on the White House lawn for the president’s birthday last June.

But still, why would White walk away from his role as as UFC president and CEO to be White House press secretary? Well, maybe he wouldn’t. While Trump’s Truth Social declaration initially looks like a hiring announcement, he’s actually just publicly begging White to take the job. The post says he’s merely offered White the role, and closes by begging, “Dana, please take the job!”

Maybe White is so loyal to Trump that he would step away from his day job. Or perhaps he thinks jumping fully into one of the most difficult roles in politics — perhaps for as little as five days — isn’t great for business.

White’s account has been active on X and Instagram in the hours since Trump’s post went up, and he posted what appears to be an AI-generated photos of himself as White House press secretary with the caption “On to the next chapter” to Instagram Stories:
It’s unclear if this is trolling or confirmation that he’s taken the job. A CNN source suggested it’s the former, telling the outlet that White declined Trump’s offer.

Whether he’s accepted or not, White is probably looking to add to the drama ahead of UFC Vegas 124, which takes place on Saturday. Tune in to tonight’s cage match to learn the identity of the next White House press secretary!

Another theory: this is all a huge mix up. Someone on Team Trump suggested hiring a different Dana White, a woman who’s actually highly qualified to serve as press secretary in a Republican administration. But Trump got confused and wound up publicly inviting his Dana White to take the role:
Whatever is actually going on here, it seems the next two years are going to be stupider than we could possibly imagine.
This post has been updated.
- Is Trump Trying to Save the Oval Office From Himself?
- Trump Tests Out Gentler, Bipartisan Rebrand on Truth Social
- ‘Watch the Beam Go Up’: Trump Goes Full George W. Bush

items.title: My Favorite Pen Is Cheap, Beautiful, and Writes Like a Dream
items.description: For those of us who journal, draw, jot, and scribble, finding the perfect pen is a personal and sometimes lifelong endeavor. I have made many pen quests, delving deep into the veritable ink well of options and coming out with stained fingers and dashed hopes o
items.author: Michael Hession
paragraphs: For those of us who journal, draw, jot, and scribble, finding the perfect pen is a personal and sometimes lifelong endeavor. I have made many pen quests, delving deep into the veritable ink well of options and coming out with stained fingers and dashed hopes of the perfect tool. After amassing a trove of expensive fountain pens, I was surprised to find my absolute favorite daily writer in the Uniball Zento gel pen. It’s cheap, beautiful, and writes like a dream.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I’m no stranger to gel pens. They are a logical choice for someone like me who became frustrated with the maintenance and messiness of fountain pens. Although it remains true that nothing comes close to the feel of a fountain pen for pure writing bliss, you have to be willing to put up with refills, cleaning routines, ink mishaps, and smears. After a while, I got fed up. I just wanted something without all the fuss.

Despite the wide variety of gel pens and roller-ball pens out there, each with their own base of superfans, I never found the perfect fit for me. Some that promised smooth, deep, bold lines ended up stalling and skipping after only a couple of weeks of use (those would be the Pentel Energel line, Papermate Inkjoy, and Uniball Signo). Others were more reliable but felt too “sticky” with that classic ballpoint resistance (the Uniball Jetstream). Others seemed to check all the boxes but were sadly housed in a simply hideous form-factor that didn’t get me excited to use (the Pilot Precise V5 RT).

When I saw the Uniball Zento being hyped in stationery blogs and Instagram ads, I was skeptical of yet another overpromising pen. But I was immediately taken with its aesthetic. It’s friendly, modern, and dispenses with the typical dated marketing imagery. It even comes in tasteful colors as opposed to flashy metallics plastered with logos. The Zento has a smooth barrel, rounded at the end and sheathed in a grippy rubber that extends from the tip halfway up the length of the pen, smoothly transitioning to a velvety plastic. For us fidgeters, there are fewer protrusions to pick and pry, making it easier to keep the pen in one piece. It has a familiar push-button clicker and one of my favorite clips of all time. As someone who compulsively breaks off pen clips, the Zento’s lovely metal design is much harder to destroy than most.

The Zento was released in 2025 and was supposedly the result of years of development at Uniball. I’m not sure how much of that is marketing hype, but I do know the Zento writes beautifully. It glides smoothly across the page, leaving a bold, uniform line in its path. I can write fast without too much pressure and come away satisfied with consistent, dark strokes. My fast scribbly sketches are no problem for the Zento. The ink dries fast, so smudging is a rare occurrence, and it doesn’t bleed through most papers, even after some manic layering. You can get the Zento in .38-, .5-, or .7-mm thicknesses. I prefer the boldness of the .7-mm nib.

A pack of four Zento pens will run you about $6 on Amazon. They are widely available in various-size packs. If you fancy blue or red ink, those variations are available, though harder to find as cheap as the standard black. Other variations include the Zento Flow, which simply features a metallic bottom portion of the barrel, and the Zento Signature, which has a premium design with a postable cap (i.e., you can stick it on the other end of the pen while writing). These are in high demand and often marked up significantly when they’re in stock.

After years of babying precious fountain pens, the basic and budget nature of the standard Zento suits me perfectly. If I lose one (which I have and will), it’s not a big deal. I can toss it in a bag carelessly and still be confident that when I dig it back out I will be served with excellent feel and reliability. More than that, because of its considered aesthetic, it’s a pen that is always satisfying and a delight to use.

items.title: The Iran War Didn’t Decide the Midterms, It Just Made the Wave Higher
items.description: Within hours of the GOP’s midterms walloping, Vice President J.D. Vance was quick to assign blame. “The reason we lost was the war,” he argued in an X post. The new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is apparently blaming the war, as well. Both men, f
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Within hours of the GOP’s midterms walloping, Vice President J.D. Vance was quick to assign blame. “The reason we lost was the war,” he argued in an X post. The new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, is apparently blaming the war, as well. Both men, for slightly different reasons, are intensely concerned about the views of the most ideological of Trump’s MAGA base, who were never that jazzed about the Iran War to begin with. Vance hopes to become the MAGA movement’s candidate for president in 2028 and Miller wants to toss the war and those who backed it over the side so as to protect his own wildly unpopular agenda.

It’s not so clear, however, that it was the most important issue in the minds of midterm voters. The best evidence that it mattered quite a bit comes from a pre-election Gallup survey in which 77 percent of Americans said “the situation in Iran” was “extremely” (47 percent) or “very” (30 percent) important to their vote. That ranked it behind the 87 percent who said “the economy” (50 percent “extremely important,” 37 percent “very important”); even with the share that said “health care” (50 percent “extremely important,” 27 percent “very important”); and slightly ahead of “gas prices” (42 percent “extremely important,” 30 percent “very important”). Similarly, the exit polls showed 74 percent of voters reporting that the war in Iran was “crucial” (34 percent) or “a major factor” (40 percent) in their votes, as compared to the 89 percent who said the cost of living was “crucial” (49 percent) or “a major factor” (40 percent) in their votes.

But the question is why the Iran War is so unpopular. An October 2026 Pew Research survey asked this question, and the top concern was its contribution to “higher gas and fuel prices” (50 percent said they were “extremely” concerned about this economic byproduct of the war and another 23 percent described themselves as “very” concerned). That’s more than the percentage of people worried about U.S. military casualties (41 percent “extremely” concerned and another 30 percent “very” concerned), traditionally by far the biggest expressed source of anxiety about sending our forces into harm’s way.

One’s suspicion that voters viewed this more as an economic than as a foreign policy issue was strengthened by a comparative exit poll finding. When asked which of six issues is the “most important facing the country,” 39 percent cited “the economy,” 33 percent “the state of democracy,” 14 percent “immigration,” eight percent “healthcare,” and a mere four percent “foreign policy,” just ahead of “crime” at three percent.

To put it simply, voters were very concerned about Trump’s record on the economy, with the cost of living (and specifically the cost of health care and gas or fuel) their biggest economic concern. The Iran War absolutely aggravated those concerns, and in that sense may have made the GOP’s midterm losses worse than they would otherwise have been. But unhappiness about Trump’s economic record (and before that, Joe Biden’s) predated the war.

Attributing the loss of Congress to the war is just wishful thinking on the part of Team Trump members who want to insulate themselves and the rest of their administration’s unpopular agenda from blame.

items.title: Stephen Miller’s Promotion Is a Chilling Sign for Final Trump Years
items.description: Talk about a weave. Donald Trump’s reactions to his party’s midterm-election disaster have been all over the place. He signaled right away that he accepted the terrible results (a first for this sore loser) and even mumbled about working with the Democrats who
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Talk about a weave. Donald Trump’s reactions to his party’s midterm-election disaster have been all over the place. He signaled right away that he accepted the terrible results (a first for this sore loser) and even mumbled about working with the Democrats who will now control Congress in January. Yet he deflected blame for the debacle everywhere other than to the man he sees in the gilded mirrors of the White House every day. Would he drift toward retirement quietly and somewhat passively, much like George W. Bush, who was similarly rebuked by the electorate in a second midterm election? Or resort even more to wild theories of unlimited executive power to get his way without any significant involvement from Congress?

We didn’t have to wait long for the answer. Trump has now taken the step that best explains his take on the midterms and where he intends to lead his party and the country, announcing on Truth Social that Stephen Miller is his new White House chief of staff:

I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job! President DONALD J. TRUMP

Blaming Susie Wiles for the midterms isn’t totally surprising since she was part and parcel of the 2024 Trump campaign team that moved into the White House and oversaw the midterm effort, to the limited extent that they were able to do anything other than following the boss’s orders. But putting Miller into her place is a pretty clear signal of defiance to Democrats, to Republicans who wanted a change of direction, and to the electorate.

For one thing, Miller has overseen policy for the White House with an extremely broad portfolio that extends beyond his signature obsession with immigration. As The Atlantic explained earlier this year, he has placed his distinctive stamp of rigid ideological fidelity across the full range of controversial issues:

Steve Bannon, a former Trump adviser and a Miller ally, describes him as Trump’s “prime minister.” Miller has a role in nearly every area about which he cares deeply: immigration and border security, yes, but also national security, foreign policy, trade, military action, and policing. He may draft a flurry of executive orders one day, lead a meeting on lowering domestic beef prices the next, and travel to deliver a fiery speech of his own — think Trump at his angriest and most dystopian, without any of the president’s impish humor — the following week.

Yes, dating back to the reputation he earned as a nativist crank while working for Jeff Sessions in the pre-Trump Senate, Miller is especially devoted to the task of mass deportation of undocumented immigrants and, beyond that, to eliminating to the maximum extent possible avenues for legal immigration, too. He has famously lashed subordinates in all the federal agencies involved in immigration policy to meet tight quotas for deportations, and he clearly has no problems with the enforcement excesses that have made ICE widely regarded as an American gestapo. That Trump is promoting rather than firing Miller shows he doesn’t understand or doesn’t care about the loss of support among Latinos that, more than any other individual factor, fed the midterm debacle. Miller is deeply responsible for losing 2024 Trump voters who supported border control and deportation of violent criminals but never bargained for the terror ICE has inflicted on immigrant communities or the unapologetic racism that underlies Miller’s approach.

And that may be the scariest thing of all about his new base of power: He has two more years to act on his deep belief in the Great Replacement theory. This is the idea that traitorous liberals are deliberately destroying the country through a conspiracy to drown native-born white Americans in a sea of shiftless immigrants who trade illegal votes for welfare benefits and the opportunity to commit crimes. Trump talks about this nightmare scenario all the time as part of his demagogic pitch to the MAGA base. But for Miller, it’s an article of faith.

Some Trump defenders will try to rationalize Miller’s elevation as insignificant, a semi-automatic move up the ladder for the Trump loyalist who was technically Wiles’s deputy. It’s true that he may bring more discipline and fewer leaks to the White House staff. But it will likely be the discipline of sheer fanaticism and intolerance for dissent.

Trump’s big decision in the wake of the midterms is whether to learn something from his party’s setback and seek to wind down his final term in office in a dignified manner or instead try to implement the worst and most divisive elements of his agenda come hell or high water. There’s little question Miller would take the administration down this second path, and his promotion will give him that chance.
