items.title: That feeling of values crumbling has a name: civic grief | Psyche Ideas
items.description: If reading or watching the news feels less like staying informed and more like a daily horror or heartbreak, you’re not alone. Many of us are carrying a kind of civic homesickness. It’s what happens when the truths we presumed were universal start to crumble.
items.author: Rebecca Lewandowski
paragraphs: If reading or watching the news feels less like staying informed and more like a daily horror or heartbreak, you’re not alone. Many of us are carrying a kind of civic homesickness. It’s what happens when the truths we presumed were universal start to crumble. Sometimes, differences of worldview so profound have emerged that even dinner conversations feel like foreign policy negotiations.

How do we give shape to this disquiet? We might call it fatigue, burnout, or ‘just needing a break from the world’, but often it’s grief – mourning for a faith we once had in fellow citizens to recognise a certain decency or sense of fairness. It isn’t partisan; it’s human, and it has a name. Civic grief doesn’t care which side of the table you sit on. It can visit anyone who has seen their values of citizenship and belonging abandoned or even opposed by their neighbours or friends or country.

If this sounds familiar, take heart. The ache itself is proof of care, a sign that some part of you still believes we can do better. Around the world, survey after survey shows people losing faith in institutions, leaders, and even each other. Freedom House’s 2026 report found that global freedom declined for the 20th consecutive year in 2025, with political rights and civil liberties deteriorating in 54 countries and improving in only 35. Those numbers have lived counterparts: military coups, efforts to weaken constitutional safeguards, violence against peaceful protesters, attacks on courts and journalists, and families increasingly unable to discuss public life without treating one another as hostile witnesses. The grief, in other words, is not floating above reality. It is responding to it. In naming civic grief for what it is, we can find a more honest place to begin, and perhaps a way to see what is still in common even across bitter divides. First, civic grief needs to be understood more clearly.

The first stage is denial, a most civilised coping mechanism. It wears a suit, reads editorials, and insists that things are not as bad as they look. We might remind ourselves that democratic government has survived worse: wars, recessions, demagogues, corruption. We use history like a sedative, and call the system ‘resilient’, confident the pendulum will swing back. We vote and try to convince ourselves that the institutions are working as they should. Denial has its uses, but slowly we begin to absorb the scope of the crisis in small, unavoidable doses.

The trouble comes when denial hardens into complacency. In places where the erosion of our civic life is subtle, it is easy to believe that real breakdowns aren’t a crisis. If we decide events are a ‘temporary disturbance’, nothing fundamental has to change. Scaled up, it turns into a false, reassuring voice saying ‘institutions are basically fine’ long after the evidence disagrees.
The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality

When denial cracks, anger usually walks in, puts its feet on the table, and opens a social media account. Biologically, it is the nervous system in fight or flight. The amygdala turns up the volume on threat, stress hormones spike, and attention narrows to villains and blame. It can fix on corrupt officials, apathetic neighbours, ‘elites’ or ‘the media’. In one country, it centres on police violence or election fraud; in another, on inequality or culture wars. It often shows up as indignation at bias, apathy or the endless loop of shouting heads who look like they are debating but are mostly performing disbelief, showing they still care enough to be furious. Algorithms love this, which is why anger is the grief stage most compatible with modern technology. We mistake outrage for engagement, and forget that noise and signal are not the same. Yet anger has a purpose. It is the immune response of conscience. The task is to keep it from turning autoimmune, and to let it fuel stewardship instead of scorched earth.

The next stage of civic grief is bargaining. It sets in once the adrenaline cools. This is the ‘if-then’ logic of the optimist feeling despair. If we educate the next generation better, if more people vote, if we just talk across the aisle, things will get better. Bargaining is democracy’s prayer: let us return to normalcy, and we promise to behave better this time. It is noble but delusional, for it assumes the old ‘normal’ can be restored. Still, bargaining reveals something precious: the refusal to give up. Even naive hope has moral worth. Bargaining may not save democracy, but it prevents cynicism from claiming the soul entirely.

The fourth stage of civic grief is depression, the weight of disillusionment. The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality. This is the stage of numbness: when people withdraw from the public sphere not out of apathy, but out of emotional self-preservation. The ballot box feels like theatre. Debate feels like déjà vu. Facts feel negotiable. Philosophically, this is a dangerous moment, when the demos, the people, cease to believe their will matters. This is a kind of soft despotism from long ago: not tyranny of chains, but of indifference. Depression acknowledges that idealism has limits. Here is when people often ask, what if the system is functioning exactly as designed? What if the system is no longer democratic?

Accepting the stages of our civic grief is important and does not mean surrender. It means we can move on to seeing more clearly. It is where citizens begin to understand that democracy was never an inheritance, but an ongoing responsibility and an act of stewardship and creation. Acceptance is where we stop waiting for ‘the adults in the room’ to fix things and recognise that we are the adults. The work of democracy, it turns out, is not glamorous: it’s reading city budgets, attending community meetings, and listening to people who annoy us. It also requires humility. The idea that one political side or ideology can ‘save’ democracy misunderstands it. Democracy, by nature, is a tense structure built to hold disagreement without collapse. The goal was never unanimity, but coexistence. Democracy was never meant to eliminate conflict. It was meant to civilise it, to keep disagreement from becoming dehumanisation, and to turn competing claims into conditions where dignity, security, opportunity, collective wellbeing and belonging remain possible.

Coming through to the other side of civic grief means no more nostalgia for the previous order. Instead, it brings us to reinvention and action. This kind of hope insists that, even when institutions falter, individuals must act to represent democracy and can still support democratic values of curiosity, empathy, courage, restraint. Hope becomes real when it stops being a feeling and becomes a discipline. It means choosing one part of the common life and tending it close to the ground: a school, a library, a neighbourhood association, a local campaign, a food pantry, a veterans’ organisation, an environmental group. Democracy is rebuilt there, through habits that may outlast us: transparency where suspicion could take root, listening where contempt would be easier, and enough restraint to remember that opponents are still people, not symbols arranged for our convenience.

Emotions are not irrational storms; they are intelligence about what we value. Civic grief says that fairness, dignity and shared obligation were precious enough that their loss hurts. In the body, it feels like heaviness or fatigue. In the mind, it becomes questions: who are we if what we were told to trust keeps failing us? What does it mean to be a ‘good citizen’ when the rules feel soft for some and razor sharp for others? How do you keep caring about an ‘us’ that no longer feels shared?

It can be unsettling to realise that the person who seems to live on the other side of every issue may be grieving a different story about what was lost, but they still felt something crack where they thought ‘we’ lived. Calling this civic grief does not erase our differences; it gives us a shared language for the ache and a first step toward something more useful than fighting or shutting down.

items.title: Why astrophysics needs to abandon the ‘Big Questions’ | Aeon Essays
items.description: In the story of cosmic history, one of the most important supporting characters is dust. As clouds of interstellar gas cooled and condensed in the early Universe, dust grains absorbed and re-emitted radiation, eventually forming stars. Later, dust provided the
items.author: Dylan Jow
paragraphs: In the story of cosmic history, one of the most important supporting characters is dust. As clouds of interstellar gas cooled and condensed in the early Universe, dust grains absorbed and re-emitted radiation, eventually forming stars. Later, dust provided the raw material from which planets could form and grow. Dust grains may even have been the surfaces on which the first complex organic molecules formed. Yet, if you ask most cosmologists, they’ll tell you that dust is a sheer nuisance.

In astrophysics, ‘nuisance’ is a quasi-technical term. Astrophysicists call any phenomenon that gets in the way of the thing they actually want to study a ‘nuisance’. Dust grains emit polarised light that can mimic subtle signals from the afterglow of the Big Bang (the cosmic microwave background) that cosmologists have spent decades and billions of dollars trying to detect. A cosmologist studies dust not to uncover its role in shaping the cosmos, but to subtract it – the term ‘sweeping under the rug’ couldn’t be more apt.

This dichotomy between ‘signal’ and ‘nuisance’ is found across many sub-fields in astronomy. Astronomers who study a phenomenon called ‘weak lensing’ use the subtle distortions of light caused by gravity to map invisible dark matter. For them, the ordinary matter that makes up everything we can see is a nuisance. Pulsar timing astronomers use rapidly spinning neutron stars called pulsars as extraordinarily precise clocks to detect the passage of gravitational waves through the galaxy. For them, the nuisance is ionised interstellar gas, which scatters and disperses the light from pulsars.

Yet one astronomer’s nuisance is another’s treasure. Just as a laser beam reveals the intricate swirls of smoke in a dark room, pulsars illuminate the fine structure of the interstellar medium, the unlit space between galaxies. If you want to study the interstellar medium and its role in shaping our galaxy’s evolution, the light-scattering gas is an invaluable resource.

Whether a phenomenon is a nuisance or something worth studying in its own right clearly depends on the investigator and their interests. But in a discipline as collaborative as astronomy, shared priorities must be developed. Gone are the days of Galileo and other lone scientists in the tower, pointing telescopes built by their own hands wherever curiosity dictates. Modern astronomy is a highly specialised discipline, marked by large collaborations. The tools of the trade – telescopes – are designed, built and maintained by hundreds of scientists and engineers across many institutions. But you can’t just stroll in and ask to use one. Investigators must fiercely compete for time with these advanced instruments. To guide how that access is allocated, the research community has developed a set of shared priorities. Some questions are elevated to the status of ‘Big Questions’ to which all others inevitably become subordinate.

But are these Big Questions necessarily the right ones? Who decides where to draw the boundaries between signal and nuisance, or big and small? Fields of enquiry are defined by the questions they seek to answer. If we want to understand modern astrophysics, it is not enough to understand the scientific and mathematical content of its theories. We also need to understand the human forces that shape the questions themselves and cause some questions to be prioritised, and other questions to be viewed as irrelevant or merely means to those bigger ends.

To identify the Big Questions that dominate the field, you need look no further than the flagship projects set to shape the discipline for decades. These include the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, the James Webb Space Telescope, the Vera C Rubin Observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna. Each of these projects will cost several billion dollars over its lifetime.

When we look at the stated science goals of these projects, consistent themes emerge. For example, the Square Kilometre Array Observatory at Jodrell Bank in the UK is a massive radio array that will define the field of radio astronomy for the foreseeable future. Its website contains a list of science goals. On that list, the early Universe, gravitational waves, dark energy and cosmology are all listed before stars, the interstellar medium and the origins of life. The official page for the much-covered James Webb Space Telescope similarly lists the early Universe – the ‘cosmic dawn’ – before more prosaic matters such as stars, planets and dust. Such priorities are often reflected in media coverage of these projects, which further shape perceptions among young researchers, politicians, funders and the general public about which questions matter most.

The boundaries between the big and small questions often fall along the lines between ‘fundamental’ physics and ‘messy’ astrophysics. This is reflected in the language of many cosmologists who study dark matter, for example. For decades, the study of dark matter has focused on the largest physical scales – giant clusters of galaxies – where the gravitational effects of dark matter can be directly inferred. On small scales, within and around galaxies, dark matter’s effects become entangled with the complex dynamics of interstellar gas. To use the terminology that is widely adopted by cosmologists: the physics of dark matter on small scales is obscured by the astrophysics of interstellar gas. Implicit in this framing is the idea that astrophysics is messy and complicated, and, ultimately, subordinate to clean, fundamental physics.
When the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated

Young researchers encounter this supposed predominance of physics over astrophysics long before they set foot in a laboratory. Growing up, I loved space, as many children do. My parents bought me an amateur telescope, and I spent many nights in the backyard becoming familiar with the winter night sky (the summer sky was more elusive because it appeared after my bedtime). But, by the time I entered graduate school, I had largely forgotten about my early childhood passion for the heavens. Like many of my peers at the time, I wanted to study theoretical particle physics.

Particle physics enjoys a kind of mythical status in popular culture as the apex of the natural sciences. After all, the purported goal of particle physicists is not just a theory of particles, but a theory of everything. Of course, such a theory would be a theory of ‘everything’ only in the limited sense that it would describe how all matter behaves on a fundamental (microscopic) level – never mind the fact that such a description would be functionally useless to describe even basic chemical reactions due to the mathematical complexity. But when the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated.

In the end, I did not study theoretical particle physics as a graduate student. The competition was intense – almost all of my classmates were vying for the few positions available. So, I rekindled my love of astronomy and decided to study astrophysics. But the truth is, at the time, I viewed astrophysics as something of a consolation prize.

This hierarchy, which ranks fundamental physics above all else, is a historical contingency. Over the course of the second half of the 20th century, astronomy transformed from a distinct discipline into a sub-discipline of physics. Historically, astronomy was a science of mapping, cataloguing and observation. But the successes of mid-century nuclear physics, the rise of physical cosmology and the discovery of dark matter and dark energy began a process that fused the two disciplines.

The discovery of general relativity, which describes gravity as a warping of the fabric of space and time, provided a new framework that enabled the quantitative study of the dynamics of the Universe as a whole. Cosmology, which had previously been the domain of philosophers, became the domain of physicists. In the closing decades of the 20th century, this framework enabled the dual discovery of dark matter and dark energy – both mysterious substances unaccounted for by the standard model of particle physics. Crucially, these gaps in the standard model would have gone completely undetected without the observations of astronomers.

The heavens, then, transformed from an object of study in its own right to a new laboratory for testing fundamental physics. This shift is preserved in our vocabulary: the term ‘astronomy’ was demoted in favour of the more prestigious term ‘astrophysics’.
I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything

The rise of astrophysics was, in part, fuelled by the geopolitics of the Cold War, which saw an unprecedented surge in funding for physics, in addition to a rise in the cultural prestige of physics in the public imagination. Governments invested large sums of money in physics mega-projects, cementing a culture of large collaborations dedicated to the study of fundamental, high-energy physics. This was the era of the particle accelerator, in which subatomic particles are accelerated to extremely high energies to test theories of physics that manifest only at those energy scales. But then the Cold War ended, and the cash flow stopped. In 1993, the US Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider project in Texas, after billions had already been spent.

Suddenly, a generation of particle physicists found themselves without the experimental tools to test their theories on Earth. Astronomy, however, provided an attractive alternative. The Universe revealed itself to be the ultimate, free particle accelerator: full of violent events, such as supernovae, colliding black holes and the Big Bang, reaching energy scales that no terrestrial collider ever could. If only the complications of real astrophysical environments could be modelled and accounted for, then the heavens would be the perfect new laboratory for physics.

It was precisely this logic that sold me on astrophysics as a new graduate student. At the time, I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything. I was interested in the messy complications of astronomy only insofar as understanding them would enable us to disregard them.

Today, this ‘physicisation’ of astronomy has left a deep imprint on the cultural norms of the discipline. Modern astrophysics is characterised by massive, hyper-centralised international collaborations, and an often tacit belief that ‘fundamental’ physics sits at the top of the scientific pyramid, while the questions of real ‘astrophysics’ are mere nuisances.

This ideological elevation of the fundamental over the particular is evident in the architecture of modern big-data astronomy. The past few decades have been characterised by experiments yielding massive volumes of data. Yet, these pipelines are not neutral data-gathering machines; indeed, their very design reflects and reinforces the institutional bias towards astrophysics as a barrier to fundamental truth. The logic is that, with enough data, the rich and diverse astrophysical phenomena that manifest in particular cosmic environments can be statistically modelled and averaged away, leaving only what is fundamental.
AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate

Consider, for example, the phenomenon of weak gravitational lensing, where astronomers measure how gravity distorts the shapes of distant galaxies. They can use this to build a map of the dark matter in the Universe, which is otherwise invisible. However, weak gravitational lensing is equally sensitive to the gravitational effects of all matter in the Universe – the dark matter and the ‘ordinary’ matter. The physical interactions that govern ordinary matter complicate inferences of the underlying dark matter distribution. Data analysis pipelines for modern weak lensing surveys flatten the complex physics of astrophysical environments to a set of ‘nuisance parameters’, which, with enough data, can be averaged away. Rich astrophysical phenomena are, from the very outset and in the survey design itself, framed as statistical obstacles to fundamental truths.

This paradigm is further reinforced by the turn towards artificial intelligence (AI). A natural symbiosis exists between the petabytes of data generated by modern observatories and the massive datasets needed to train deep learning architectures. Driven by the hype, if a project promises to use AI, it helps attract funding and allocation of computational resources, even when its capacity for genuine discovery remains unclear.

Foundation AI models are heralded as the best way to digest datasets too massive for detailed human analysis, promising to automatically infer complex astrophysics from raw images of the sky. But there is a fundamental disconnect between the statistical patterns these technologies learn and the underlying physical mechanisms that generate the observations. Whereas you might train an AI to learn what a cat looks like with a set of images of known cats and non-cats, there is no set of galaxy images where all the relevant astrophysics is known. Instead, models need to be trained with synthetic data drawn from astrophysical simulations. However, computational limitations force these simulations to rely on simplified approximations of the very physics in question. As a result, AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate.

This is not a problem if your goal is simply to account for complex astrophysics in massive data sets to infer the underlying fundamental physics. These models are, after all, exceptional at identifying and correcting for subtle correlations in the data. But if your goal is to understand the complex physics of the astrophysical phenomena themselves, the benefit is less obvious.

Thus, modern astrophysics appears to be oriented towards a paradigm of modelling massive data sets to uncover fundamental constants. This paradigm is mutually reinforced by the questions that are institutionally prioritised and the tools used to answer them. However, this loop of reinforcement can create an illusion of field-wide consensus around what the most important questions are, which obscures the daily realities of many working astronomers.

This is nowhere more visible than in the discourse surrounding the ‘Hubble tension’ – the fact that different methods of measuring the Universe’s expansion rate (the Hubble constant) yield contradictory results. Across white papers and popular science articles, the Hubble tension is touted as a profound crisis in physics. If the discrepancy is real (as opposed to a statistical fluke), then it could be an important hint about the nature of dark energy, which drives the expansion.

And yet, in the trenches of astrophysics research, attitudes are markedly different. At nearly every talk I have attended on the Hubble tension, the reaction from working astrophysicists is surprisingly muted. If this discrepancy is the great white whale of modern cosmology, why do so many researchers respond with a shrug?

The reality is that most scientists are passionate and obsessive creatures, devoting many years of their lives to extremely niche topics that others might struggle to care about. Such people naturally find their work intrinsically interesting, not just as a step towards some bigger question. Of course, scientists have complex motivations that are shaped by their institutional environments and that shape the long-term trajectory of their careers. But, on a day-to-day basis, many astronomers really do just care a lot about dust, or gas dynamics, or cosmic magnetic fields.

For myself, the further away I got from physics proper, the more I rediscovered my love of astronomy for its own sake. Whether or not astronomy unearths new fundamental laws of physics, it has much to tell us about our place in the Universe and what it means to be human. Since Copernicus, astronomy has gradually demoted humanity’s position in the cosmos, from occupying the literal centre of everything, to merely occupying an unremarkable planet, orbiting an unremarkable star, in an unremarkable galaxy in a potentially infinite Universe. At the same time, as the bounds of the known Universe expand, we have increasingly understood the rarity and fragility of life in the cosmos. Astronomy, therefore, plays a critical role in the story of the human species. While I remain hopeful that astronomy can lead us to new fundamental physics, that hope is no longer the driving force of my interest in the heavens. I suspect this is the case for many of my fellow astronomers.

Despite this, investigators are required to play a rhetorical game, justifying their deeply specific research within the context of the predetermined Big Questions. When you apply for academic jobs, the advice is: Always, always, always link your work to the Big Questions. Since hiring or grant committees typically comprise faculty with a diverse range of expertise, an applicant cannot rely on the committee sharing an intrinsic interest in their niche topic. Justifying your science in relation to the Big Questions is more likely to lead to a successful application, even if individually none of the members of the committee are particularly passionate about those questions.

Scientific journals reinforce this rhetorical game. The most prestigious journals demand that their articles represent significant advancements in the field. In other words, they require that the research they publish make progress on the pre-defined Big Questions. Investigators are incentivised to frame their papers in this context. I have personally written papers that motivate the work as a step towards resolving the Hubble tension. While technically true, this framing misrepresents the reasons I embarked upon that research and the real reasons I find it interesting.
If you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose?

This is not to suggest that having shared priorities across a research community is somehow wrong – indeed, it is inevitable. But it is important to recognise that these priorities are historically contingent and, to some degree, arbitrary. When investigators play the rhetorical game of justifying their research, the game ends when they link their work to a fundamental question in physics. But why stop there? Why is the search for dark energy or dark matter inherently more justified than the lifecycle of interstellar dust? The ‘fundamental’ questions are no more or less intrinsically justified than the nuisances that get in their way. Rather, we choose which questions are ends in themselves and which require further justification.

Many commentators have made a great deal of the crisis that faces high-energy physics today. Terrestrial collider experiments have failed to reveal any signs of the new physics they were built to find, and we may well be reaching the limit of what astrophysics can tell us about fundamental physics. Even if the Hubble tension is confirmed, we may never settle on the correct physical theory of dark energy. Even as we better characterise the gravitational behaviour of dark matter, its particle nature may remain a mystery forever. The Big Questions are beginning to lose their lustre, and some are beginning to ask whether the billions of dollars spent on mega-projects are diminishing in their returns. But if this is a crisis for high-energy physics, there is no crisis for astronomy. Astronomers will continue to investigate all the weird and wonderful things the Universe has to offer.

If you’re an astronomer reading this – or anyone who would like to play along – I invite you to consider the following hypothetical. If, tomorrow, you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose? Both would guarantee a Nobel, but which one actually feels like the bigger, more meaningful discovery? Although I can speak only for myself, I suspect many astronomers – even bona fide astrophysicists – would choose the latter.

Astronomy has a unique place among the natural sciences. Its immediate practical benefits are limited – especially the further away from Earth you go. It’s hard to imagine a detailed understanding of galaxy evolution directly leading to some technological benefit in any foreseeable timeline. Yet astronomy excites the public imagination like no other science. It’s not because astronomy has the potential to uncover new physics at high energy scales. It’s because we, as a species, have always looked up to try to understand our place in the Universe.

Peering through my backyard telescope as a child, I had no concept of fundamental physics. But looking at the fuzzy haze of the Orion Nebula and realising that I was watching the birth of stars – well, there are no words to describe the sense of wonder I felt. If astronomy must justify itself according to some Big Questions, let them be these: where did we come from, and what is our place in the cosmos?

Ultimately, the priorities of a field are not immutable facts but a choice. Shifting priorities need not be seen as a crisis, but as an opportunity to ask ourselves why we study what we study in the first place – an opportunity to make different choices that better align with those reasons. Astronomers, then, have an opportunity to reorient the priorities of the field away from a reductionist view of physics, and to reclaim the value of the nuisance.

items.title: Damien Jalet: “I’m Not Just Making Steps. I’m Trying to Create Worlds”
items.description: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:
items.author: Barry Pierce
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:

What, exactly, is a body for? Ask a doctor and they may tell you that, on paper at least, it houses the organs that work together to keep us alive. For Damien Jalet, the body means much more than this, and is the vessel by which to explore and interrogate the mysteries of life. Jalet, who just turned 50, is more aware of his body today than ever. As we chat on one of his rare days off, he is feeling good about his half-century milestone. “I arrive at 50 with an incredible amount of experiences, of dreams being realised. I feel like it’s a great vantage point,” he tells me from his hotel room in Guadalajara, Mexico.

Jalet is in rehearsals for a restaging of Omphalos, a work that first premiered in Mexico City in 2018. On a darkened stage, a huge satellite dish rotates into view. Across its curved surface, dancers weave their bodies glacially, until – suddenly – pausing in unison. The bodies appear less like those of a corps de ballet than a strange collective organism controlled by a single force. Following choreography on a flat stage can be challenging enough, but on a curved surface, pitched and rotating? It’s precisely these limitations that excite Jalet.

“Something that I’m always trying to remind you in the work I do is that you are made of the world that surrounds you,” he tells me. There is a sense, when talking to Jalet, especially about the body, that he has spent many years building a personal philosophy around it. Words like “porous” and “organicity” come up again and again. “I often think of the body as being a root – we absorb. We are a moving root, we are wanderers,” he says.

Much of Jalet’s central philosophy, and his spiritualism, stems from his interest in animism. Rooted in the traditions of many Indigenous cultures, animism is the doctrine that the natural world is imbued with spirit or agency, and that humans exist in relationship with the animals, landscapes and forces that surround them. He describes the ritualistic volcanic dances of Indonesia, and how the Tenggerese people gather on Mount Bromo to appease the spirits. He believes that this relationship with dance, and a wider relationship with our bodies, has been lost in Western culture, partly due to the influence of religion and its dogma around the body as something to distrust. “I have a very intimate conviction that we would not be in the situation we are now if we had kept a more animist point of view, or more of a spiritual connection with nature,” Jalet, who studied anthropology and ethnomusicology, says.

Jalet is quick to acknowledge that some could misinterpret his beliefs as New Age. “I’m not hugging trees and giving them offerings,” he laughs. “I’m a very contemporary person. I’m not just there to say, ‘Oh, let’s go back to our roots, let’s leave everything we know.’” There are other more modern concerns flooding Jalet’s day-to-day thoughts, too. The rapidly expanding field of artificial intelligence could be seen as the greatest existential threat to dance since Achilles tendinitis, he says. “In the world of AI, where the body disappears, where there’s no more feelings, everything just becomes information. I think it’s incredibly important to go back to the body before we lose nature for good.”

Initially thinking he’d become a theatre director, Jalet studied at INSAS, Brussels’ National Institute of the Performing Arts. The 1990s in Brussels were, according to him, a time when disciplines collided and contrasted. Choreographers were branching out into theatre, visual art, music and design. Jalet, meanwhile, was finding himself in the city’s gay clubs. “I love the physical collective energy of gay clubs. They are such a space of freedom. They connected me to my body.”

The collective energy Jalet describes is not so far removed from the principles that would come to define his choreographic practice. In it, the human form is porous, responsive and shaped by the bodies it interacts with. Perhaps that is why, years later, Madonna would make Jalet a close collaborator and the lead interpreter of her music through dance. But before there was Madonna, there was Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui.

“We met in 2000, in a ballroom, where we were teaching contemporary [dance].” The occasion was Bal Moderne, a Belgian festival where choreographers teach short dances to the public. By this point, Jalet had abandoned his ambitions to become a theatre director. After a stint in New York, he joined Les Ballets C. de la B., a renowned Belgian dance theatre company. Meanwhile, Cherkaoui was making a name for himself as a young choreographer to watch. Their friendship was immediate. “I felt that we already had so much in common: same age, same double nationality, same feeling of being a bit uncomfortable with the way of things.”

Quickly, they became more than just choreographer and dancer, but close collaborators and artistic partners. Their first major work together, D’Avant, came in 2002. Mention the work to Jalet now and he lets out a little giggle. Meaning “from before”, D’Avant saw Jalet and Cherkaoui, alongside Luc Dunberry and Juan Kruz Díaz de Garaio Esnaola, work as both choreographers and dancers. It was a physically demanding piece, a slapstick epic in which its creators embodied medieval serfs, football hooligans, cross-dressing brides and contorting body illusionists. At one point, they play football with Jalet’s head while singing along to 12th-century polyphonic music. “It was probably the most challenging piece as a performer,” Jalet recalls. “Because not only were we dancing and acting, we were also singing maybe 16 songs that were incredibly technical and that were all about finding harmony.”

A few years ago, Jalet posted a clip from D’Avant on his Instagram. It went massively viral and currently sits at around half a million likes. The reaction totally blindsided him. “The recording looks like it’s from 1973 or something. But it became this phenomenon, this work from literally 20 years ago.” Of the 80-minute show, that short clip is really all that exists of D’Avant now. It’s a problem you run into a lot when looking back over the careers of choreographers: a painter produces a canvas, a filmmaker releases a film, but a choreographer, by contrast, makes something that can only be experienced to its fullest in the moment. Dance is an ephemeral art form – something Jalet thinks about a lot. “Nobody talks about the level of energy that goes into a dance show,” he tells me. “If you feel sick and you have to perform... I can tell you, there is nothing worse. This is why I think of dancers as spiritual people, because they’re doing it for the art, for the act of it. You’re putting all of your life into something that only exists in the moment you do it.”

In 2016, Jalet was contacted by Luca Guadagnino after the director had fallen out with his original choreographer on a forthcoming remake of Suspiria. “It allowed some of my work to survive, to be shared and experienced first-hand,” Jalet says of his first foray into cinema.

On a night out on the Rue de Charonne in Paris in autumn 2015, Jalet was standing near a young man who, moments later, pulled out a gun and started shooting. He ran for his life. Jalet had found himself at the epicentre of the coordinated terrorist attacks that ended in the deaths of 130 people. He describes it as an incredibly traumatic event, saying that his career and work can be divided into two: before and after the night of Friday November 13th. His pieces Thr(o)ugh (2016) and Skid (2017) are direct responses to that night.

Skid, which has become one of his most enduring works, was performed on a flat surface tilted at 34 degrees towards an orchestra pit below. Throughout, the dancers perch precariously on the acutely angled surface. At other times, they appear at the top and slide down into the abyss below. “It’s a piece about vanishing, about being there and disappearing the next second. It’s been an acceleration of things since 2015,” he says. “That was such a near death experience it kind of brought me even closer to my intuition. All the choices I’m making now are still related to this.”

The work Jalet has produced over the last ten years could fill the CVs of several choreographers across entire career spans. There have been major stage works including Vessel (2016), Brise-lames (2020) and Chiroptera (2023), alongside collaborations with Paul Thomas Anderson and Thom Yorke on Anima (2019), Palme d’Or winner Jacques Audiard on Emilia Pérez (2024), and Madonna, for her Madame X tour and a musical short film for her 2026 album Confessions II.

But to talk to Damien Jalet in 2026 means bringing up “Storm”, his viral video for the Swedish rapper Yung Lean. Working with the acclaimed director Romain Gavras, Jalet’s clip for the song is, at the time of writing, nominated for a VMA for Music Video of the Year, a category in which he is competing against himself, with his video for Confessions II in the running too. In “Storm”, Yung Lean stands motionless at the centre of a group of identically dressed schoolboys, who swarm around him in tightly choreographed formations, their movements becoming increasingly frenetic and febrile as the sequence builds. It is unmistakably Jalet, turning simple choreography into something closer to a ritual.

When Gavras described his initial concept to Jalet, all he could see were the myriad ways it could go wrong. “He sent me some references to dances done by groups that obviously spent the whole year rehearsing to get to that level of synchronicity,” he divulges. In the economy of the modern music video, Jalet knew he would have mere days to pull off Gavras’s vision. “I was sent hundreds of videos of people dancing in front of the Christmas tree, because we had planned it over Christmas,” he laughs. From there, he had two days to create the dance and another two to rehearse it. Upon its release, Jalet’s work on “Storm” was instantly hailed as a career landmark. “I had no idea that it was going to be so crazy,” Jalet admits. “I didn’t see it coming.”

Jalet is at a point, now, where everyone wants a piece of him. “I only [collaborate] with people who I’m really truly fascinated with, that I love what they do,” he says, defiantly. Consequently, he has spent the last few months turning down the kind of offers that could easily make him enough money to retire tomorrow. “I say no to so many things because I need to feel a deep connection.”

Jalet cannot help but be amused by this new surge of interest. “I think people have suddenly seen the power of choreography. I’ve never seen the word ‘choreography’ written as much as when ‘Storm’ came out. It felt like, ‘Oh, finally, we have a bit of respect.’ I don’t want to look like the Joan of Arc of dance, but I have experienced how much dance is reduced by the commercial world, how it is tamed.” He wants filmmakers to move beyond using choreography as a lazy way of injecting energy into a scene, and for their contributions to be properly recognised. “Emilia Pérez got 13 Oscar nominations and I was completely expelled from the campaign because I could not get them any awards as a choreographer,” he says.

He recalls the very beginning of our nearly two-hour chat. “What do I have a body for? Is it just to consume? Is it just to be productive? Or is it a tool to sense, to understand more the balance of the world and how we are connected?” At the peak of his powers, Jalet seems ready to share his philosophy more widely. “I’m not just making steps,” he says. “I’m trying to convey ideas, to create worlds.”

Photography JORDAN HEMINGWAY. Styling ELLIE GRACE CUMMING. Hair TASOS CONSTANTINOU at Streeters. Make-up CHARLIE MURRAY using ELEMIS and YSL BEAUTY. Set design SAMUEL OVERS at New School Represents. Photographic assistants MADISON BLAIR, JAMIE SINCLAIR and CHESTER LEWIS. Styling assistants CHARLIE EDWARDS and SAM THAPA. Set design assistants HENRY HAWKSWORTH and FELIX VILLERS. Production ROWAN MACKINTOSH KING. Studio director TARA COMPTON. Studio assistant CAEL DEVERS. Studio intern ALEX BEARDSWORTH. Post-production PURPLE MARTIN
This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man, which is on sale from 5 November 2026

items.title: Parker Posey and Steve Buscemi on Wild Horse Nine
items.description: Two luminaries of US indie cinema sit down to discuss their roles in Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy caper, democracy in peril and weeping openly at mass on a south Pacific island
items.author: Miriam Balanescu
paragraphs: Two luminaries of US indie cinema sit down to discuss their roles in Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy caper, democracy in peril and weeping openly at mass on a south Pacific island

At the centre of the gunslinging black comedy Wild Horse Nine is an old married couple according to director Martin McDonagh: CIA operatives Lee (Sam Rockwell) and Chris (John Malkovich). Trying to tear them apart is Lee’s actual wife, Marge (a needling Parker Posey), and the pair’s control-freak boss, bureau chief MJ (Steve Buscemi). On the cusp of the 1973 Chilean coup, the two agents take a trip to Easter Island – where old-timer Chris has requested that he live out his final days, if Venice doesn’t work out.

It’s a happy coincidence, then, that the film screened in competition at Venice Film Festival, where Buscemi and McDonagh also first discussed a potential collaboration in 2022. “I had met him a couple of times, but I got to know him when he was here with Banshees [of Inisherin],” says Buscemi, when I speak with him and Posey before the premiere in the resplendent gothic Hotel Danieli. “When I read that in the script I was like, ‘Do you know this film is going to come to Venice?’”

Aside from its central bromance, Wild Horse Nine is primarily about reckoning with guilt. With the spiritual backdrop of Easter Island’s ancient moai, Chris, a lapsed Catholic, is forced to reflect on a career of bloodshed, presidential assassinations and American meddling with foreign democracies, not least the currently unfolding crisis in Chile. There are flavours of McDonagh’s previous films: the masculine brooding of In Bruges and Banshees, and the propulsive shoot-outs of Seven Psychopaths.

A Catholic upbringing is one thing that unites McDonagh, Buscemi and Posey. “I went to Catholic school first, second and third grade, but it marked me for life,” claims Buscemi, explaining that the theme wasn’t what drew him to the role. “It’s always the relationships, how they’re drawn, how people relate to each other, what’s going on underneath.”

“I did get to go to mass on the final Sunday at Easter Island,” Posey interjects, describing the service as a combination of indigenous and Catholic traditions. “Venus was in the sky. [It’s a] really bright star at that time of the year [...] The way they were singing brought me to tears because it was so from the gut, and I just started crying. Did you want to hear how it sounded? People are going to start running. Now I’m embarrassed to do it, but I’m going to do it” – at which point Posey cries out an indescribable sound. “If [only] I could go back to my child self who wanted an adventurous life and then go like, ‘Oh my God, I actually got to see something like this.’”

Most of McDonagh’s characters have a reason to want Chris dead. Acting out most of their scenes on the other end of the phone line (shot in real time), Buscemi and Posey vie for Lee’s attention. Playing Lee’s unfaithful wife reminded Posey of her shoot on Ari Aster’s Beau is Afraid, where she was also holding the phone receiver. As in theatre waiting backstage, her job was to “fill in all the colours, get as much information as [one] can to slide in there and hit the right notes.” Her and Rockwell acted as sparring partners: “Couples become one kind of entity of humour [...] It was a lot [of] smoking and screaming.”

“[McDonagh is] Americana, but he’s also Irish,” she continues, recalling how McDonagh would push her to “twist the knife”. “Irish people are, like, really tough. I feel there’s this toughness that [Martin] likes to write.” But beneath all the characters is an unexpected, undeniable softness. As Buscemi observes, “You can’t be hurt by someone that you don’t love.”

Meanwhile, Buscemi was reuniting with his villainous co-star from Con Air for the first time in nearly 30 years. “In this movie, [Malkovich] won’t even give me the time of day,” he chuckles. “He has such disdain for me, but in Con Air, one of my favourite moments is [when I] take off my Hannibal Lecter mask and John says to me, as his character talking to mine, ‘I love your work.’” He jokes wishfully: “No, that’s John saying that to Steve. So this relationship was quite different.”

Both Rockwell and Malkovich have been tipped as major contenders in the Oscars race. Malkovich as Chris is a revelation, cold-blooded and nihilistic on the outside but warm, fuzzy and hopeful within. “I thought this character was so different [...] from a lot of the stuff that he’s done and yet it’s so him,” says Buscemi. “You go, ‘Wow, this is the performance we’ve been waiting for’ from him, even though he’s done so many amazing things.”

McDonagh’s film is timely, arriving in the wake of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro’s abduction by the US. On the Trump administration, Buscemi says, “I don’t even want to get into it because it’s just so frustrating […] And to see that this stuff has happened before, and it can happen, and it’s happening now. And if we don’t learn from it, it will keep happening. And democracy is fragile. And we shouldn’t take anything for granted.”
Finally, I ask, what’s the meaning behind Wild Horse Nine’s title? “I can't help you there,” says Buscemi earnestly. “I’m still trying to figure out what Reservoir Dogs means.”
Wild Horse Nine is out now in UK cinemas

items.title: Bring your magnifying glass: This exhibition contains teeny books only
items.description: Just over a year since its launch at London bookshop Tenderbooks, Veronica Ditting’s exhibition ‘Small Print’ is making its way Stateside, to Marta gallery in Los Angeles.
items.author: Ali Morris
paragraphs: Just over a year since its launch at London bookshop Tenderbooks, Veronica Ditting’s exhibition ‘Small Print’ is making its way Stateside, to Marta gallery in Los Angeles.

Originally comprising 100 miniature books from Ditting’s personal collection, 'Small Print' has more than doubled in size. Its second iteration, opening on Saturday 7 November, features 258 tiny tomes.

New additions include Yoshū Mame Tengoku (translated as Foreign Liquor Heaven or Western Liquor Heaven), a series of 36 books published in the 1960s for Japanese whisky producer Suntory. Exquisitely designed and printed, these little books cover subjects ranging from gardening and glassware to erotica.

Previously, a 5 × 5 mm leather-bound edition of the Lord’s Prayer held the title of smallest book in the collection. It has now been usurped by Das Kleinste Buch der Welt by German artist Josua Reichert. Measuring a mere 2.4 × 2.9 mm, this minute leather-bound book is printed using a specialist technique and legible only with a magnifying glass.

Other highlights include a rare miniature Webster dictionary housed in a custom Tiffany & Co sterling silver case bearing the brand’s hallmark; conceptual art books by Dieter Roth; Robert Filliou’s playful concertina Filliou Standard-Book (c. 1970–75); and a selection of original 'Hanuman Books', the pocket-sized series founded by Francesco Clemente and Raymond Foye.

Moving from an intimate bookshop to an art gallery, the second exhibition offers a new context for Ditting’s collection. She hopes to give Marta’s design-savvy audience fresh perspectives on bookmaking and the possibilities of printed matter.

An accompanying audio tour invites visitors to dial a dedicated number on their mobile phones to hear the stories behind selected books. Narrators also share their own relationships with printed matter. They include Fernando Augusto Pacheco, senior correspondent at Monocle Radio and host of its weekly print-media show The Stack; Ditting’s studio colleagues Harry McArthur and Laura Russell; and Ditting herself.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Ditting’s fascination with miniature books began during her childhood in Germany, with the pocket-sized dictionaries her parents would take on holiday. She credits these practical, everyday resources – now almost obsolete – with shaping her interest in scale and tactility. From there, her obsession took flight.

‘These ‘one-hand’, miniature or thumb books are intimate objects that force us to pay attention to the tiniest of details: the bend of a page; the width of a line; the heft of a spine,’ says Ditting, whose eponymous studio designs campaigns, branding, magazines and exhibitions for clients including Hermès, The Row, Louis Vuitton, Pirelli, Somerset House and Het Nieuwe Instituut. ‘They tell us the printed object is defined by tactility and technicalities. With eccentric proportions, these miniature books revive why we read.’
'Small Print' opens at Marta Los Angeles on Saturday 7 November and runs until 19 December 2026.

Ali Morris is a UK-based editor, writer and creative consultant specialising in design, interiors and architecture. In her 16 years as a design writer, Ali has travelled the world, crafting articles about creative projects, products, places and people for titles such as Dezeen, Wallpaper* and Kinfolk.

items.title: The cars of GTA6 just hit the streets of Miami
items.description: In Martin Amis’ satirical paean to 80s excess, Money, his antihero John Self drives a large, self-regarding, and overbearing purple car. Its name? The Fiasco, ‘a vintage-style coupe with oodles of dash and heft and twang.’ Along the way, Self encounters variou
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: In Martin Amis’ satirical paean to 80s excess, Money, his antihero John Self drives a large, self-regarding, and overbearing purple car. Its name? The Fiasco, ‘a vintage-style coupe with oodles of dash and heft and twang.’ Along the way, Self encounters various other car brands – Farragos, Tomahawks, Boomerangs and Autocrats.

They’re exactly the kind of names that would tickle the creatives at Rockstar Games, who have long populated their Grand Theft Auto series with a variety of outlandish – but not entirely improbably named – vehicles for players to steal, race, collect and cruise around a vast game world.
The cars parked in front of Hilario Candela's 1963 Miami Marine Stadium...
... and rendered virtually in the same spot

GTA 6 is no different. So much so, that Rockstar has allowed the virtual to spill over into the real world, with six fully driveable versions of their digital counterparts seeded on the streets of Miami, Florida, as the ultimate stealthy promo for the game (due out November 2019).

In GTA, vehicles are similar but not lawsuit-adjacent to real-world cars, satirical take-offs of the kind of machines favoured by those on adjacent, outside, above and beyond the law. The unlicensable kind, in other words.
The Grotti Cheetah as created by West Coast Customs...
The Grotti Cheetah as created by West Coast Customs
The Grotti Cheetah in the flesh

For example, there’s the low-slung elegance of the Grotti Cheetah, a dead-ringer for the 80s-era Ferrari Testarossa (as driven by James ‘Sonny’ Crockett in Michael Mann’s Miami Vice, one of the foundational jumping off points for GTA’s sojourns in the city). Or you could choose the Invetero Coquette, a car with more than a passing resemblance to the current generation Corvette.
Invetero Coquette, Rockstar's Corvette equivalent for real
Invetero Coquette, rendered

For a more vernacular feel, there’s the Albany Manana, seen here running the kind of Hi-Riser wheel set-up favoured by the area’s custom culture and based in part on the eighth-generation Cadillac Eldorado (1967 to 1970) – the purest, boxiest era of American car design.
The Albany Manana in the flesh
The Albany Manana in the game
The Albany Manana in the flesh
The Albany Manana in the game

It’s joined by another ‘Albany’ model, the Buccaneer, a mash-up of the 70s Buick Riviera and the seventh-generation Ford Fairlane, albeit with tiny wheels and a menacing grille, both inspired by custom buildings.
