items.title: Meet the Rising Stars Competing for Best New Artist at the Latin Grammys
items.description: One of the most anticipated categories at the Latin Grammys is Best New Artist. In the past, the once-in-a-lifetime award has gone to people who have gone on to become major stars: Puerto Rican disruptors Calle 13, Colombian superstar Karol G, and Mexican sing
items.author: Lucas Villa
paragraphs: One of the most anticipated categories at the Latin Grammys is Best New Artist. In the past, the once-in-a-lifetime award has gone to people who have gone on to become major stars: Puerto Rican disruptors Calle 13, Colombian superstar Karol G, and Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada. Recent winners include Venezuelan prodigy Joaquina, Bogotá-based pop girl Ela Taubert, and Mexico City’s alt-star Paloma Morphy. For the 2026 ceremony, which takes place on Nov. 12 in Las Vegas, 11 upstarts from Latin America, the U.S., and Spain are hoping to take the honor next.

With 11 nominees this year instead of the usual 10, Rolling Stone caught up with four of the promising nominees ahead of the biggest night in Latin music. We spoke to Aria Vega, who is bringing the sound of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to the mainstream; rising Mexican-American singer Delilah, who has been blending genres with ease; Fabian, the son of Peruvian icon Gian Marco, who is blazing his own trail; and Mexican-Swedish maverick Sofia Monroy.
What does the nomination for Best New Artist mean to you?

It means a lot because it represents more than just me. It represents my family, my people, my team, Barranquilla, and everybody who’s believed in me along the way. It also feels like an invitation to bring my world to a bigger audience. I’m still at the beginning of my journey, and having this kind of recognition gives me even more motivation to keep creating, experimenting, and showing people what I’m capable of. I’ve worked so hard to get here, and to have the music and everything we’ve been building recognized in this way is incredibly special. I’m grateful, excited and honestly just hungry for everything that’s still ahead.

How do you feel about representing Barranquilla and the culture of Colombia’s Caribbean coast?It’s a huge responsibility, but also something I do very naturally because it’s who I am. I don’t have to pretend to be from the coast or try to represent it in a certain way. It’s already in my accent, my humor, my music, my personality, and the way I see the world. I love showing people a different perspective of Barranquilla and the Caribbean coast. There’s so much creativity, beauty, character, and culture there. I want people to see us beyond the stereotypes and experience the coast through my eyes. If I can make somebody curious about where I’m from, or make someone from back home feel proud to see themselves reflected in what I do, that means everything to me.
You recently met Shakira during her residency in Madrid.

Meeting Shakira was incredibly special. She’s someone who has represented Colombia and Latin culture on a global level for so many years, so being able to share that moment with her was surreal. She’s opened doors for so many Colombian artists and I have so much respect for what she’s built. Of course I’d love to work with her one day! Imagine two Barranquilleras in the studio together. That would be something very special. I think we’d have a lot of fun!
What can we expect from your debut album that you’re working on?

My album Costeñita Core is my baby. It’s a project where I’m putting together all the different pieces of who I am and the world I’ve been building. It’s very personal, but it’s also playful, colorful, feminine, a little chaotic, and full of personality. Musically, I want people to discover different sides of me. I’m exploring sounds, emotions, and ideas while staying connected to my Caribbean roots. Visually, I’m also putting a lot of myself into the project. I want people to feel like they’re stepping into my world when they listen to it. It’s my universe, my perspective, and my way of showing people what “Costeñita Core” really means. I’m so excited for everyone to finally experience it.
How do you feel about being nominated for Best New Artist?

It’s honestly a dream come true. It’s one of those things you hope and dream about as an artist, but you never really know if or when it’s going to happen. To be recognized by my peers, fellow musicians, and members of the Latin Recording Academy is such a huge honor. It means that the music I’m putting out into the world is being heard, and that means everything to me. It’s also a reminder of how far I’ve come and all the people who have believed in me and supported me along the way. I know there is still so much I want to do and so much I want to explore as an artist. This nomination makes me even more excited to keep creating, growing, and sharing my music with the world.
What does it mean for you to represent women in música mexicana in this category?

It’s a huge honor and something I take very seriously. I want to do the category justice and make sure my voice and my sound are heard and heard well. I want to represent my music, my fans, and everyone who has supported me in a way that makes them proud. Música mexicana has such a rich history. I feel incredibly lucky to be part of a generation that gets to bring new ideas and sounds into the genre while still honoring its roots. I hope I can contribute something meaningful to that. This is especially meaningful to me as a young woman, but also as a big sister. I take that responsibility seriously because I know how important it is for young girls to see women being themselves, having a voice, and making their own choices. I hope I can show other young women that they don’t have to fit into a certain mold to belong in this industry. They can be themselves and do things their own way.
How would you say that being both Mexican and American influences the way that you make music?

It influences my music in so many ways, sometimes in ways I don’t even think about consciously. Growing up in a bilingual household, both cultures have always been part of my everyday life. You can hear it in the way I mix English and Spanish, in different touches throughout my songs, and even in the way I express myself. My background, the music I grew up listening to, and the different influences around me are all incorporated into what I create. I don’t feel like I have to separate those parts of myself. They’re both who I am and I think that combination is a big part of my sound.
What was the experience like opening for Natanael Cano’s concerts at the Estadio GNP Seguros in Mexico City?

It has been an incredible experience both times. Mexico City has such an amazing energy, and being able to perform there and share my music with those audiences, especially opening for an artist like Natanael Cano, is something I’ll always remember and those experiences hold a really special place in my heart. It’s also meaningful to be the only woman to have had that opportunity. I feel proud to represent women in that space and show that I can be myself and do things my own way. I don’t feel like I have to change who I am or fit into a certain expectation to belong on that stage. Being able to connect with those audiences while staying true to myself has made both experiences even more meaningful.
What does it mean for you to be nominated for Best New Artist?

It still feels pretty surreal. I think it’ll really hit me once I get to Vegas. It’s something I’ve dreamt about for a long time, especially because it’s one of those things you only get to experience once in your career. I’m mostly excited about the opportunity to represent Peru and show people just how much talent and how many new, interesting proposals are coming out of our country. I feel really proud to be part of that.
Your sister Nicole was previously nominated for Best New Artist in 2022. How do you feel about following in your family’s legacy?

My family was incredibly excited [about the nomination]. They’ve seen all the work and love that’s gone into this since day one. Nicole actually cried when I called her, which was really sweet. I can only imagine what it’s like to see your little brother experience something you’ve experienced yourself. I’m especially excited that my first Grammy experience is something I get to share with her, especially since she’s also nominated twice this year. It’ll definitely make the whole thing even more special. I’ve always thought that sharing music with my family is one of the biggest blessings. It’s pretty much all we’ve ever known at home. Growing up, I was always taught to approach this career with a lot of respect, love, and appreciation for what it means to make music. I think those values have stuck with me from the beginning. At the same time, I want to find my own way of doing things and build something that feels very much like me.
How are you carving out your own space in Latin pop music?

When I moved from Lima to Los Angeles at nine, I was suddenly exposed to so many different kinds of music. I would go to festivals, discover new artists every week, and find myself getting really excited about all these new sounds and proposals. A lot of what I was hearing resonated with me, but when I tried to find something with a similar approach in Spanish, I couldn’t really find it. I think that’s where the idea for my project started. I wanted to bring some of those Anglo-inspired sounds into Spanish-language music, without losing the way I naturally write and express myself. I guess I’m trying to create the kind of music I wish I had more of when I was growing up.
What can we expect from you next?

I’m currently wrapping up everything for my debut album, which is coming out next year. It’s been an insane process. I started writing the first demos back in July 2025, so the fact that I’m now finishing everything in November 2026 feels pretty crazy. I’ve always been an album person. I think there’s something really special about creating a complete project, and I hope we never lose that culture of making albums.
How do you feel about being nominated for Best New Artist?

It means a lot, especially because it feels like recognition of a journey that hasn’t necessarily been linear. I’ve spent years figuring out who I am as an artist, experimenting, making mistakes, and finding my own voice. I think being nominated is a beautiful reminder that there’s space for different perspectives and ways of making music. But more than anything, I see it as a confirmation that you should always trust your intuition and follow your own path, even when it doesn’t necessarily make sense to anyone else at the time. Sometimes you just have to trust that little voice in your head.
Would you say that being both Mexican and Swedish influences the way that you make music?

I think growing up between two cultures has shaped almost everything about the way I see the world, and naturally, that translates into my music. I’ve always felt like I exist somewhere in between, never entirely one thing or the other. But I’ve also come to realize that I don’t necessarily have to choose. I think I’m a walking contradiction in many ways. I’m made up of two cultures, two languages, two very different ways of seeing the world, and sometimes those things coexist beautifully, and sometimes they clash. I think that’s something that has become a big part of my artistic identity. I’ve stopped trying to make all those different parts of myself fit together into one coherent picture. They’re all equally me.
You’re nominated for your Best New Artist for your album Morena. What do you want people to take away from that album?

I want people to feel something. Morena was born out of a personal search, an attempt to make sense of a lot of things I was experiencing at the time: identity, belonging, grief, love, my roots, and my relationship with life and death. It was also a way for me to reconnect with my father, who passed away when I was young. I think Morena exists somewhere in between all these things. She’s a reflection of different parts of me, but also something that exists beyond me. I guess the album became a way of navigating all these different versions of myself and understanding where I come from. There’s a quote I really like about how we’re not just one thing, but little pieces of everyone and everything we’ve encountered. I think that’s very much what Morena is about: accepting that you can be many things at once, that you don’t necessarily have to choose, and that all these seemingly contradictory parts can coexist within you.
What do you want to achieve with your music?

I want to build a world that people can enter and feel connected to. I want to make music that challenges me creatively, that allows me to experiment and evolve, and that doesn’t necessarily sound or look the same from one project to another. Of course, I have ambitions. I want to reach more people internationally, perform on bigger stages, collaborate with artists I admire, and continue growing my career. But I think one of the most beautiful things about making music is being able to connect with people through emotions. To share something so personal and have someone on the other side of the world recognize a piece of themselves in it. I think that’s quite extraordinary.

items.title: Zohran Mamdani and Puerto Rican Band Chuwi Discuss Gentrification, Music, and Making Change
items.description: The Puerto Rican band Chuwi, made up of siblings Lorén, Willy, and Wester and their best friend Adrián, has spent the last couple years achieving international fame through a major collab with Bad Bunny, also ending up as his opening act on tour. But they’ve a
items.author: Juan J Arroyo
paragraphs: The Puerto Rican band Chuwi, made up of siblings Lorén, Willy, and Wester and their best friend Adrián, has spent the last couple years achieving international fame through a major collab with Bad Bunny, also ending up as his opening act on tour. But they’ve also used their platform to speak out about Puerto Rico — their debut album, Libertad, from last month, tackles government corruption, the economic and social effects of colonialist policies, and more — and on Friday, they joined Mayor Zohran Mamdani in San Juan for a conversation about issues central to the islands’ future.

As part of a visit engaging local organizations and community leaders, Mamdani sat down with the musicians to hear more about their perspective. “I look forward to listening to Puerto Ricans to hear about what the struggles are that they’re facing and how New York City can be a partner in fighting for working people wherever they may call home,” the mayor told Rolling Stone.

The meeting was part of the annual Somos Conference, where New York State lawmakers meet with Latino advocates over four days in Puerto Rico. The conference’s goal is to create a space where attendees can speak directly with those in positions of power about what’s most important to their communities.

This year marks the 40th anniversary of the event, and it is customary for the mayor of New York City to attend. Last year, Mamdani flew down just days after he was elected. This year, he returned, 10 months into his first term, and seemed clear-eyed about what he wanted to talk about during his 72 hours in town. His central focus is bridging the gap between the archipelago and the nearly 600,000 Puerto Ricans who call New York City home, with Mayor Mamdani targeting issues that matter to both.

“What I’ve heard from Puerto Rican New Yorkers is a concern about displacement and gentrification, not only in the neighborhoods that they’ve helped to build in New York City, but also right here in Puerto Rico,” he says.

The mayor met with various coalitions and activist groups, such as Defend Cabo Rojo, FURIA, La Tejedora, and PR No Se Vende (“Puerto Rico Is Not for Sale”) that have dedicated themselves to combatting those challenges. But before those meetings, he scheduled an equally important sit-down with Chuwi, given their mission to spread the word about Puerto Rico’s struggles through their music.

Chuwi became a household name after they collaborated on the song “WELTiTA” off Bad Bunny’s Grammy-winning DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS. They went on to be the opening act of his 59-date world tour. On Libertad, the band went back to their protest music roots and leaned more than ever into the politics. They’ve addressed some of these themes on the album since their earliest EPs, but never as directly as the LP.

Lorén initiated the conversation with Mamdani by describing how she was in New York City the week before the 2025 election. She told him she was impressed by the enthusiasm she saw for his campaign, saying that she found it very inspiring as a Puerto Rican. “What you guys are doing is inspiring,” Mamdani said, complimenting how they use their music to spread important messages without compromising the artistic side.

“When you’re not at a desk, it’s easier to tell the truth,” he said. He noted that as artists, they have the unique privilege of being able to speak out and that their music is a connection to home for many fans. Indeed, even Bad Bunny himself said last year that listening to Chuwi during his time living in Los Angeles pre-DtMF made him homesick.
Willy took the opportunity to ask Mayor Mamdani about how he’s been able to achieve so much in his term so far: “Why is it you can do these policies that other mayors couldn’t?”

“When you get elected you get disconnected,” Mamdani said. He explained that leaders can become cut off from the people they serve, and that the environment can turn into tinted SUVs and private hotel rooms. He gave examples of things he does “intentionally” to stay connected, like biking around the city. “Institutions change slower than people,” and too much patience sometimes inadvertently leads to complacency. “The more you stay with the people the more you stay impatient. You have to keep [them] around you,” he says.

Chuwi pointed out how skeptical many citizens are about politicians, and how cynicism has become the prevalent feeling, especially in a Puerto Rico that has been suffering economically for almost two decades, even before Hurricane María dealt a blow to its infrastructure in 2017.

Mamdani acknowledged that feeling, and said Puerto Ricans might be skeptical because “they know about history.” He said he’s aware of the gap between what politicians promise and what citizens actually expect them to deliver on. “How do you collapse that separation?” he said, sharing that he feels “inspiration” is a stronger force than “disillusionment” and that he tries to wake up every day “ready to fight” and to “use pressure in a productive way.”

Aware of how heated things can get in politics, and having been on the receiving end of a fair share of criticism, Willy asked how the mayor deals with mud-slinging and negative rhetoric in politics. Mamdani said that treating people who disagree with him harshly or with judgment leads to both sides feeling like there has to be a winner or loser in the debate. He stressed the importance of speaking to people who aren’t just “those who feel comfortable with you.”

Mamdani then pivoted to asking Chuwi about their future plans. The band said that they’ll be returning to cities they visited over the summer, hinting at a big tour of their own. Mamdani playfully reminded them he used to be an artist as well — as an indie rapper going by the alias Mr. Cardamom — and reminisced about how rough it was the first few years. “I was the opener to the opener to the opener,” he joked. “I once performed at 5 p.m. for a band that was playing at 9 p.m. I was singing to the seat savers.”
He said he was delighted by the possibility of Chuwi going to different countries with their music, because as he put it, “through that, others will hear and see their own struggles.”

Lorén thanked the mayor for meeting with them, sharing that their grandparents were one of the families that moved to New York City during the post-WWII migration wave, and in fact got married in the city. Mamdani stressed the importance of Puerto Ricans in the history of New York, especially in organized labor movements. Lorén shared that her grandfather worked at a textile factory in the city.

Willy capped off the meeting by thanking Mayor Mamdani for meeting with the organizations working on the ground in P.R. He stressed how important their goals were when it came to pushing for the abolition of Puerto Rico’s tax haven status, protecting the coastal maritime-terrestrial zone, and trying to stop large developments that threaten Puerto Rico’s habitats like Esencia in Cabo Rojo and Moncayo in Fajardo, among other causes. “Politicians [in Puerto Rico] won’t meet with them unless it’s in a court room or public hearings,” he said.

Afterwards, Chuwi told Rolling Stone they felt inspired by the mayor’s words. “Being that he’s the mayor of New York, and New York has significant importance in Puerto Rico, it was super important to be able to discuss these matters with him,” says Wester.

They also pushed back on critics who might accuse Mayor Mamdani of wading into issues outside his jurisdiction. “My counterargument is that we’re a colony of the United States, and New York is — and has always been — extremely important in Puerto Rico. We’re linked,” says Wester. “The rest of the world is watching what’s happening here on the island, yet our own politicians aren’t addressing it. I think it’s fair game.”

“It’s important to understand that this isn’t like the Financial Oversight Board. Just because people from outside — rather than locals — are addressing these issues, it doesn’t mean they’re coming here to exert control or anything like that,” Adrián says. “People hear ‘the United States is coming here to do things in Puerto Rico’ and immediately think, ‘Oh, Junta de Control Fiscal.’ No, it’s not [necessarily] that. It’s about creating a dialogue between the two sides.”

As the meeting wrapped up and Chuwi said their goodbyes, the mayor snuck in one last question: are they doing a show in New York in the near future? Chuwi let Mayor Mamdani know they’ll be seeing each other again soon.

items.title: Deep Purple's Ian Gillan Undergoes 'Successful' Surgery After Medical Emergency
items.description: Deep Purple singer Ian Gillan offered a health update Saturday, a week after a “medical emergency” forced the band to postpone their European tour.
items.author: Daniel Kreps
paragraphs: Deep Purple singer Ian Gillan offered a health update Saturday, a week after a “medical emergency” forced the band to postpone their European tour.
Gillan returned to social media Saturday to tell fans that he recently underwent surgery, which would be followed by a period of rest and recovery.

“I had a procedure yesterday which was successful,” Gillan wrote. “I now have to rest, in order to make a complete recovery and ensure that I’m as fit as can be before getting back to work, thanks everybody for your patience and understanding. I really do appreciate it and apologize for all the inconvenience.”
The group postponed a pair of Germany shows last weekend — and subsequently nixed the remainder of their tour — after announcing that Gillan was hospitalized with an unspecified health issue.

A few days later, Gillan updated fans, saying he “had a medical problem whilst in Leipzig which required urgent attention at the hospital.” However, “I was hoping that I would get the all clear to hang on until the end of the tour, but there are very serious risks involved in me doing so.”

Deep Purple’s postponed European tour was scheduled to run through November 25. As of now, the band’s Latin America tour — scheduled to begin December 5 in Sao Paulo, Brazil and conclude December 19 in Mexico City — is still on the schedule.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: The Great Poisoning
items.description: While we continue to suffer from a lost 18 minutes, this episode was a fun one. The players got one Traitor, and they are celebrating at a candlelit dinner. Everyone got fancy, which normally means some insane wardrobe choices from our D-list celebrity cast, b
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: While we continue to suffer from a lost 18 minutes, this episode was a fun one. The players got one Traitor, and they are celebrating at a candlelit dinner. Everyone got fancy, which normally means some insane wardrobe choices from our D-list celebrity cast, but since these are low-key normie influencers, everyone just looks nice. There is Scottish food! It includes Scotch eggs, which are surprisingly good. Joe tells everyone he threw up a Scotch egg in Vegas, ruining the food for all. I’ve never been to Vegas, but it doesn’t give me Scotch-egg vibes. Is that a Vegas restaurant staple? Was there a mass Vegas Scottish migration? Is there a surplus of Presbyterian churches in Las Vegas?

Joe is in a slightly elevated Hawaiian shirt and a blazer. Almost everyone else is in tartan, so I want to know more about his decision-making process when packing. People start sharing what they’re proud of so far and what the money would mean to them. Abbey B, who must have traveled outside the timeline and read my critiques of her from last week, really shows up this episode. She talks about being home most of the time because she takes care of her daughter, and how it’s very isolating. Abbey did the show to do something for herself, which Kriste fully supports. The enormous jump from medically complex caretaker to “What if I went to Scotland to do a game show?” is funny, but I do also support you, Abbey B. Most parents, when they talk about doing something for themselves for once, go get a massage.

Morgan is proud of herself for helping to get a Traitor. Morgan, I love you and all the videos you post, but you really did not want to vote for Tomica. Shane talks about wanting to help his family financially after the death of his sister. Aghhh. I don’t know what the fix is for this show, because when it’s D-list people, they don’t really care about the money and don’t try enough in the challenges. When it’s your average person who has a great need for the money because our economy and social system are broken, it’s a bummer. It feels more like The Hunger Games when it’s like, “Will Shane continue to constantly fear not being able to provide for his family? Or will he win this game show that is a mix of luck and skill?” Someone (the government) give Shane and his family enough money that they’re not living in fear! Maybe by taking some money from the people who have enough money for thousands of lifetimes but will only be able to use it in one!

Okay, anyway, so yeah, this bums me out. The Traitors are feeling bad for betraying all their new friends. Can we make this game more gamelike and have it wreak less emotional devastation? Or is the devastation part of the allure? Alan hears my plea and emerges from the shadows to invite the players to a nightcap and a deadly game with the Traitors.

We learn that Joe and Katie were given a task two hours earlier. They need to poison another player’s chalice. The players will be able to trade, so it is indeed a “Wallace Shawn in The Princess Bride” moment, and my reference to that in a previous recap was made too early. This is much more one-to-one. Joe wants to poison Victor’s cup, but Katie thinks Victor would try to trade. That’s for sure correct. I think they should poison Wyatt since he’s part of the Victor voting bloc, but no one listens to me.

At the Great Poisoning, Alan tells the players the rules, which include that a Traitor cannot be murdered, so if they drink, there will be no murder. Ben and Victor are suspicious of Kriste for immediately grabbing her chalice. Why? Victor tries to switch with Joe, Katie, and Abbey, but no one will switch with him. Even if Joe and Katie weren’t Traitors, they could fairly assume that Victor would be poisoned. At the last moment, Shane asks Joe to swap, which he does. We will learn who was poisoned at tomorrow’s breakfast.

The next morning, we find that the hilarious Morgan (look, if you haven’t seen her vids, you just have to trust me) is no more. Morgan, I will miss you, but you brought nothing to the table other than your kind and attentive demeanor. To do a quick cast check-in, those remaining are Abbey, Ben, Clyde, Jay, Joe, Katie, Kriste, Shane, Victor, Wyatt. Is that three women and seven men? Yeah. Did we start 50/50? Also yeah. Hm. Interesting.

The mission that day is at the insect cabin. Do you remember the insect cabin? Beetles and mealworms everywhere. Well, it’s back, and now it’s haunted. Alan informs the players that the cabin is haunted by spirits in search of the treasured items they left behind. Once the players are inside, the spirits will call (on the phone) and tell them about the item. They have to find the correct item and hand it to the spirit outside the door within the allotted time. If they fail, the player handing over the item will be dragged from the cabin and removed from the mission. There is also a shield at stake.

Everyone comes in wearing safety goggles. The first spirit asks for a spicy home brew under the floorboards. This is where the game is more fun than I expected (much like the chalice challenge!), because when they pull up the floor, there are so many bottles. Everyone starts tasting the varied, apparently disgusting, bottles. “Not spicy,” says Abbey B. “EVERYONE’S GOING TO HAVE DIFFERENT PERCEPTIONS OF SPICY,” Katie shouts. They finally find the correct one, and Shane hands it over to the spirit. They get $9,000 in exchange.

Clue two is about a wedding outfit. We get the classic beetles and mealworm drop from the ceiling. There are so many white outfits, most of which at the outset look like wedding dresses. Jay hands one over and gets taken by the spirit. The third call is about the shield, which is inside one of the teddy bears in the toybox. VICTOR finds it (boooooooooo) and hides it. The third call is for an amethyst necklace that got flushed down a toilet. Now it’s Abbey’s time to shine. For once, someone’s career is actually paying off. Abbey is a nurse. Abbey does not give one fuck about diving headfirst into a disgusting, filthy toilet and wading through a thick brown liquid to find a necklace for a pretend ghost. She finds it, and they bank another $9,000. No one kill Abbey after this.

At the castle, we don’t have enough time for a roundtable, but we get pre-roundtable chatter. People are suspicious about no one finding a shield. Victor looks squirrelly. Kriste thinks Wyatt is a Traitor and Victor is trying to get people onto Joe. Other people think it’s Kriste. Victor is frustrated that more people are not on his side despite him being right. That is fair, Victor, but in their defense, you are super annoying.

Who would I vote for on Traitors? It’s hard to judge what one would do without having the insider knowledge, because who knows the full context of what’s happening in that castle, but based on what’s presented, here are my picks:

No Insider Knowledge: Ooo, this week is more fun since we don’t know which way they’re going to vote. With the knowledge currently presented, I think I would vote for Kriste, leaving two women in the castle. Internalized misogyny is a thing.

Yes Insider Knowledge: If not Victor, then Wyatt. I’m glad someone is targeting Wyatt now, but do the Traitors even have a strategy here? Or is the strategy “Don’t get found out”? That’s not a strategy, guys!

items.title: Indonesian Horror Hit ‘Pabrik Gula’ Gets 2028 Sequel
items.description: Indonesian studio giant MD Entertainment will release a sequel to its 2025 horror smash “Pabrik Gula” in early 2028 and has Imax films planned for 2027, Astrid Wienardi, the company’s head of content licensing and global business, said Sunday at Taiwan Creativ
items.author: Naman Ramachandran
paragraphs: Indonesian studio giant MD Entertainment will release a sequel to its 2025 horror smash “Pabrik Gula” in early 2028 and has Imax films planned for 2027, Astrid Wienardi, the company’s head of content licensing and global business, said Sunday at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.

Wienardi delivered a presentation on how MD ties its film and series library to broadcast and streaming. The company took control of free-to-air channel NET TV in a deal worth up to $105 million and has brought in investment from Korea’s SBS.

“Pabrik Gula” sold more than 5 million tickets in Indonesia before traveling to Vietnam, Cambodia, Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei, the U.S. and Europe. Its hooks and popularity persuaded MD to commit to a second installment.

The Imax relationship started with “Badarawuhi,” the prequel to “KKN di Desa Penari” and the first Southeast Asian film shot for the format. One of the upcoming Imax titles will draw on “Dhot Design,” a YouTube animated series about four friends that pulls between 8 million and 10 million views an episode. Lionsgate and CJ are also among MD’s strategic partners.

Active for more than two decades across film, series, animation, music publishing and talent management, MD has more than 200 features to its name and plans 12 to 13 releases in 2027, led by horror alongside comedy and drama. “KKN di Desa Penari” sold 10.7 million tickets at home, an Indonesian record at the time.
“Ivanna 2” is due early next year. The original is a spinoff from MD’s “Danur” horror universe about a headless Dutch woman.
“‘Ivanna’ was moderately accepted in Indonesia market, but it did fascinatingly well in Vietnam,” Wienardi said. “It actually broke records in the theatrical Vietnamese market.”

Feedback from platform partners, along with fan comments on social media, decides whether MD extends a series, spins off a title or grows a franchise. Netflix drama “Ipar Adalah Maut,” which Wienardi translated as “Brother-in-Law Is Death,” topped the streamer’s trending list in its first week and stayed in the top 10 for seven straight weeks. A second season is in the works and could launch on Netflix next year.

MD has eight titles on Netflix and three on WeTV, where seven of the platform’s top 20 titles were MD productions, including “Layangan Putus,” which trended in 25 countries. On Prime Video, mother-daughter series “Induk Gajah” (“Mother Elephant”) earned a Season 2 order soon after its 2023 debut and helped pull in new subscribers. A deal with iQIYI, unveiled in mid-October, will see two titles roll out by December and a third in the first quarter of 2027.

Music is part of the playbook too. Netflix series “Suara Hati,” whose two lead actresses are dangdut singers, generated 100,000 first-week downloads across Spotify and YouTube Music, while “Bakti,” a song from “Danyang: Mahar Tukar Nyawa,” which opened Nov. 5, has passed 200,000 downloads on Spotify.

“The golden rule for us is that the universal appeal should never mean stripping away local identity,” Wienardi said. “Local identity is very important for MD. Without local identity, we lose the soul of the story.”
She added that CEO Manoj Punjabi demands that soul at every greenlight meeting, and that MD wants folklore-rooted horror rather than “watered-down thrillers or any Hollywood-like thrillers.”

When an audience member asked how Indonesian films command around 65% of local moviegoing while Taiwanese films account for just 10%-12% at home, Wienardi cited Indonesia’s population of roughly 280 million and a deep well of haunting folklore that parents pass to their children.
“We are surrounded by a lot of mountainous areas where the spiritual taboos are actually discussed on family dinners,” she said.

Horror, MD’s specialty for more than 20 years, is the genre that crosses borders most easily, according to Wienardi, who said it has at times reached the U.S. and European markets. “When it comes to drama, it’s a bit different because then, you know, there’s a lot of sayings in Indonesia that probably are not translated or culturally translated well,” she said.

The traffic runs both ways. MD released adaptations of Thai and Korean properties this year, partnered with Korea’s Barunson on “Sorop” and has fielded co-production inquiries from U.S. and European producers. Wienardi said the studio sees strong potential in bringing Taiwanese and East Asian IP to Indonesia, and wants pitches that arrive with proof of concept, a clear fit for Indonesian viewers and a track record in their home market.

“When we’re talking about NET TV, data is number one,” Wienardi said. Free-to-air and pay-TV ratings land daily at 10 a.m. and determine whether a program is extended or changed, while MD series simulcast on the channel help widen its reach. The channel’s goal is a place in Indonesia’s top five.
Wienardi said she hopes MD will one day work with Taiwanese directors and producers and “share probably a common ground of storytelling.”

items.title: Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominates With $14.5 Million on Friday as ‘Cat in the Hat’ Follows With $6 Million
items.description: Sorry, Dr. Seuss — “The Cat in the Hat” was no match for “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which thrashed its way to the top of the box office on Friday.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub
paragraphs: Sorry, Dr. Seuss — “The Cat in the Hat” was no match for “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which thrashed its way to the top of the box office on Friday.

“Godzilla Minus Zero,” the highly anticipated sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” generated $14.5 million from 3,254 North American theaters on Friday, easily taking the No. 1 spot. It’s a strong start for the Kaiju film, which looks to pull in $32 million by Sunday.

Directed by Takashi Yamazaki, the movie takes place two years after the prior installment as Godzilla regenerates and resurfaces to combat a new monster that’s tormenting postwar Japan. The film has enjoyed glowing word-of-mouth and reviews thus far, with Variety’s Owen Gleiberman writing that the film is “destined to connect with a huge international audience.” “It’s already clear that this won’t be the last of Yamazaki’s kaiju epics,” he continued. “That’s because the movie proves that when you do it right, what seemed old can become timeless.” The sci-fi epic is produced by Japan’s Toho and distributed in the U.S. by GKids.

Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat” landed in second place on Friday, grossing $6 million from 4,003 North American theaters. The new release is expected to gross $18.7 million by Sunday, slightly under early projections of a $20 to $25 million opening weekend.

Bill Hader voices the titular character in this cartooned version, directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja. This iteration of the beloved children’s book revolves around the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous hat-wearing cat arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a new town. This version of “The Cat in the Hat” is the second adaptation of the Seuss classic following 2003’s live-action Mike Myers-led flick, which opened to $38 million.
Angel Studios’ “Drummer Boy” took the No. 3 spot with $3.39 million from 2,850 North American theaters. The patriotic, Christian musical is eyeing $7.9 million by its first Sunday in theaters.

Directed by brothers Ben and Joel David Smallbone, the film stars the latter and third Smallbone brother, Luke, who comprise the Christian music act For King + Country. According to the film’s official description, “Drummer Boy” follows a young drummer boy, an enslaved woman and a divided family as they search for freedom during America’s fight for independence. Variety’s review wrote that the film “provides a confident, mostly pleasing throwback to original screen musicals of yore.”

A24’s “You Can See Everything” held strong with $2.55 million on its fourth Friday from 2,473 North American theaters, good enough for a fourth-place finish just over Searchlight’s dark buddy comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” and should earn $8 million by Sunday, per rival estimates. That’s on top of the cumulative $73.49 million the buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc already pulled in across North America since it opened in theaters on Oct. 16.

“Wild Horse Nine” followed in fifth place with $2.47 million from 1,100 locations per rival estimates, which expect the Martin McDonagh-directed film to bring in $5.5 million by Sunday. “Wild Horse Nine” follows two CIA officers (John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) who are dispatched from Santiago to Easter Island shortly before a Chilean military coup.

Trailing behind was the Indian epic “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” which made $2.4 million on Friday from 1,433 locations and is projected to earn $7.3 million over the traditional three-day weekend and $10.806 million over the four-day Thursday-through-Sunday frame.

items.title: James Bond Shocker: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Late Contenders for 007 After Auditioning for Denis Villeneuve
items.description: As James Bond casting rumors heat up, a couple more A-list actors have entered the mix: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were among the stars who screen-tested to play the new 007.
items.author: Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: As James Bond casting rumors heat up, a couple more A-list actors have entered the mix: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were among the stars who screen-tested to play the new 007.

Both British actors certainly have the acting pedigree to play the suave spy, taking up the mantle after Daniel Craig’s 15-year run. They also have a keen awareness of what it takes to work in major franchise fare: Pattinson stars as Batman for DC Studios and is an alum of both the “Twilight” and “Harry Potter” franchises; meanwhile, Hoult plays Lex Luthor in DC’s Superman movies and starred in the 2010s “X-Men” prequel trilogy. He next stars in the Amazon MGM Studios movie “How to Rob a Bank,” in theaters on Nov. 13. Pattinson also has the Denis Villeneuve factor on his side, after starring in the filmmaker’s upcoming epic “Dune: Part Three.”

Last year, Amazon MGM Studios tapped Villeneuve as the franchise’s next director, with “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight hired to write the script. Getting Bond 26 off the ground has been a top priority for the property’s new stewards, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.

Since then, nearly every 30-something British actor’s name has been bandied about in the U.K. and U.S. press, with rumored top contenders including Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. Variety has learned that Harry Styles has had discussions about the part, and Theo James, 41, also hasn’t been ruled out.

Pierce Brosnan, the Bond of the ’90s, recently gave his stamp of approval to Turner, while Gary Oldman threw his weight behind Lowden, his “Slow Horses” co-star. (Oldman also claimed that the next James Bond has already been picked, but no official casting announcement has been made.)
Amazon declined to comment on the casting rumors.

items.title: Natalia Dyer, Elijah Wood to Join John Cusack and Samuel L. Jackson in ‘1408’ Sequel From Director Mikael Håfström (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Natalia Dyer and Elijah Wood are set to join original cast members Samuel L. Jackson and John Cusack, who are currently negotiating the terms of their return, in a sequel to the 2007 supernatural horror film “1408,” Variety can reveal exclusively. Mikael Håfst
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: Natalia Dyer and Elijah Wood are set to join original cast members Samuel L. Jackson and John Cusack, who are currently negotiating the terms of their return, in a sequel to the 2007 supernatural horror film “1408,” Variety can reveal exclusively. Mikael Håfström, who directed the first film, returns to helm the sequel, which he co-wrote with Mark Verheiden.

While Jackson and Cusack will reprise their original roles, they will be secondary characters in the sequel, according to a source familiar with the project. Dyer will star in the film, and Wood will play a supporting role. Details about their characters remain under wraps.

Lorenzo di Bonaventura, Bluestone Entertainment’s Richard Saperstein, Spyglass Media Group and Frank Mayor serve as producers. Bluestone Entertainment and FilmNation Entertainment are co-financing, with FilmNation representing the international distribution rights, co-representing domestic rights with WME Independent and introducing it to buyers at AFM next week. John Papsidera (“The Odyssey”) serves as casting director. Production is currently slated to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

Based on Stephen King’s 1999 short story of the same name, “1408” follows author Michael Enslin, played by Cusack, who, as part of his new book on haunted hotels, investigates legends of mysterious and violent deaths behind door 1408 at the Dolphin Hotel in New York City. Jackson co-stars as Gerald Olin, the Dolphin Hotel’s manager. Plot details for the sequel have not been disclosed.

“1408,” released by MGM, was a cult hit in 2007, grossing $132 million worldwide against a slim budget of just $25 million. Cusack has gone on record saying it would be the only film he’d ever do a sequel for, telling People in 2025, “I was lucky that I never had the desire, or no one asked me to do any sequels. There’s one that I think would be interesting to do, which would be ‘1408.’ Just because … I think today, you know, most movies suck.”

Dyer rose to global recognition through her breakout role as Nancy Wheeler in Netflix’s marquee series “Stranger Things.” She is currently in production on HBO’s true-crime limited series, “The Trial of Louise Woodward.” She also has Oran Zegman’s rom-com “Goodbye Girl,” starring Kiernan Shipka and Cole Sprouse, on the horizon. Her previous credits include the coming-of-age comedy film, “Yes, God, Yes,” from writer-director Karen Maine.

“Lord of the Rings” icon Wood has become a horror genre regular, recently appearing in “Ready or Not 2: Here I Come,” “The Toxic Avenger” and Osgood Perkins’ “The Monkey.” It was recently revealed that Wood will return to Middle-earth as Frodo Baggins in Andy Serkis’ “LOTR” sequel “The Hunt for Gollum.” Wood is also joining the cast of Netflix’s “The Gentlemen” for Season 3.

Cusack, best known for roles in “Say Anything,” “High Fidelity” and “Being John Malkovich,” was a staple leading man throughout the ‘90s and early 2000s, but has mostly stayed out of the spotlight in recent years. His last big-screen credits were for the 2025 thriller “Fog of War” and a pair of foreign films: “Detective Chinatown 1900” and “Decoded.”

Jackson, the star of “Pulp Fiction,” “Avengers” and “The Hateful Eight,” likewise rose to stardom in the ’90s and has been all over the big screen lately. His most recent film roles were “The Beast,” which hit theaters on Oct. 9, and “Just Play Dead.” His upcoming projects include J.J. Abrams’s “The Great Beyond,” “The Incredibles 3” and “Avengers: Secret Wars.”

Dyer is represented by Circle Management + Production, CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman. Wood is represented by Linden Entertainment, Gersh and Meyer & Downs. Cusack is represented by Link Entertainment, Wolf Kasteler Public Relations and Ziffren Brittenham. Jackson is represented by Anonymous Content, CAA and Jackoway Austen Tyerman Wertheimer Mandelbaum Morris Bernstein Trattner Auerbach Hynick Jaime LeVine Sample & Klein.

items.title: ‘Stranger Things’ Prequel Spinoff ‘Other Worlds’ Ordered to Series at Netflix
items.description: The long-gestating “Stranger Things” spinoff has officially been ordered to series at Netflix, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: The long-gestating “Stranger Things” spinoff has officially been ordered to series at Netflix, Variety has learned.

The show is titled “Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure” and is set to debut in 2028. The announcement comes as part of “Stranger Things” Day, the annual celebration to mark the day Will Byers disappeared in the original show — Nov. 6, 1983.

This is now the fourth project set in the “Stranger Things” universe. In addition to the wildly popular mothership show, which ended its run at the end of 2025, there is also the animated series “Stranger Things: Tales from ’85” and the stage show “Stranger Things: First Shadow,” the latter of which delves more into the backstory of Henry Creel, aka Vecna. The spinoff was first reported to be in the works in 2022.

Plot details are scarce for “Other Worlds,” aside from the fact it will be a prequel set in the 1950’s prior to the events of “Stranger Things” and the “The First Shadow.” In an interview tied to the series finale, Matt and Ross Duffer teased that the spinoff would focus on the events prior to Henry Creel being exposed to the otherworldly substance that gave him his powers in “Stranger Things.”
A teaser asset for “Other Worlds” confirmed that, with the video (see below) revealing that the series will take place in 1955 in Marion, Nevada.

“Other Worlds” is co-created by the Duffer brothers and Kate Trefry, a writer on “Stranger Things” and the writer of “The First Shadow.” Trefry will also serve as showrunner and executive producer on the series. Joe Wright will direct the first three episodes and executive produce, with Shawn Levy of 21 Laps, Paul Dichter, Shelley Meals, Andrea Sperling, and Pavlina Hatoupis also executive producing. The series will film in New Mexico.

“We’ve been dreaming of ‘Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure’ for many years now, and to see it become a reality is surreal and exhilarating,” the Duffers said. “We’re so grateful to our incredible team of collaborators: our showrunner Kate Trefry, who has been in the trenches with us since Season 2 and wrote ‘Stranger Things: The First Shadow;’ and our director, Joe Wright, a brilliant artist whose work we’ve long admired. We can’t wait for you to see what they’re cooking up. It’s Stranger Things, but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting. In the meantime — watch the skies, nerds!”

The Duffers are executive producing under their Upside Down Pictures banner, with “Other Worlds” serving as a carve out of their current overall deal at Paramount. The Duffers were previously under an overall deal at Netflix, but it was announced in 2025 that they would be moving to Paramount for a deal that covered movies, television and streaming once their Netflix overall expired in April 2026.

“The Duffer Brothers gave me my first paying job in Hollywood, and it has been a joy and a fever dream ever since,” Trefry said. “Now, it is my insane honor and privilege to be bringing this new chapter of ‘Stranger Things’ to life alongside them and our incredible director Joe Wright. With the support of Netflix and 21Laps, we have had the time of our lives returning to all the horror, wonder and mystery of the flagship, while also telling a wholly new story, one we hope will blow your minds and break your hearts all over again. There are so many more mysteries to explore. Welcome to ‘Other Worlds.’”

“’Stranger Things’ has always belonged to the fans, and their passion made it a worldwide phenomenon,” said Jinny Howe, Netflix Head of Scripted Series, US & Canada. “Today, on ‘Stranger Things’ Day, we’re honored to partner again with Matt and Ross Duffer and Kate Trefry to give fans a new dimension of this universe to step into. ‘Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure’ takes us to the 1950s with new heroes and all the heart, mystery, and spectacle of the original series. We’re proud to keep building this world with the Duffers, Kate, Shawn Levy, and Joe Wright, and we can’t wait for fans to see what’s next.”

“All of us at 21Laps are thrilled and privileged to be continuing the storytelling legacy of ‘Stranger Things,” Levy added. “With ‘Other Worlds,’ the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry craft a new ensemble and adventure that is imbued with the DNA of our flagship series while exploring a new era, setting and all-new characters, themes and mythology — the seeds of which may have been planted in Hawkins, but now venture into other worlds of spectacle, action and emotion.”

items.title: James Talarico Crashes ‘SNL’ Cold Open, Apologizes for Texting Us So Much
items.description: James Austin Johnson was born for this moment — Donald Trump spinning as he is roundly defeated by Democrats — and he rose to meet in Saturday Night Live’s cold open.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: James Austin Johnson was born for this moment — Donald Trump spinning as he is roundly defeated by Democrats — and he rose to meet in Saturday Night Live’s cold open.
But it was a Democratic politician who stole the show from Trump’s 2026 defeatism tour, as Texas senator-elect James Talarico made a surprise appearance as himself at the end of the sketch.

“I’m James Talarico, the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for five dollars,” the popular Texas politician said as he came out on stage to gasps and cheers from the audience, with Trump mumbly meta-jibing behind him, “In this economy, who can blame you?”
Talarico a moment later invoked the iconic “Live from New York” with Johnson.

Talarico drubbed his Republican opponent Ken Paxton by 12 points in the most expensive race in the history of the United States Senate, in part on the back of the grassroots fundraising campaign he was self-mocking on SNL. The result turned a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time in over 30 years.
Before Talarico showed up in Studio 8H, Johnson had been reveling in his presidential character’s anti-moment.

“I didn’t even say it was rigged,” Trump said of the election tallies. “I accepted the results, which is even scarier in a way. It’s like, ‘What the hell is he planning?'” He then said he only cared about his newly redesigned White House ballroom, before allowing under his breath, “Oh my God, I hate my life.”

Talarico’s cold-open surprise cameo echoed moments like Kamala Harris’ 2024 turn-up, in which she played opposite her celebrity impersonator Maya Rudolph ahead of the election, while Hillary Clinton and Sarah Palin also made unexpected appearances as White House candidates more than a decade ago. A senator or senator-elect, however, is rarer, and the moment both reflected and reinforced the emergent media celebrity of the new class of Congressional Democrats, many of them in their 30s or early 40s.
Johnson’s Trump, at least, is not a fan.

“The next few years are going to be horrible,” he said, pausing a comic beat. “It’s not that they’re Democrats; it’s that they’re Millennials.” He then lamented the return of generational staples like “adorkable” and the show New Girl.

The president and the Republican party were handed several heaping platters of whoopings in the midterms, as Democrats gained at least 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate. Voters rejected both Trump’s policies and personality as they voted for a wide range of change, especially on the economy.

Johnson — who told The Hollywood Reporter last year that “I don’t want to call what I’m doing Shakespeare, but I am trying to find the deeper forms of Trump, who is a rich text” — went full Hamlet Saturday with a digression about when New Girl started finding good storylines (it involved Winston and the cat).

Johnson has been been appearing (or crashing) the cold open as the president seemingly every week since Trump’s return to office, and writers gave Talarico one of the best lines of the sketch in letting him…question that choice.

“People want something new; they want something different,” Talarico said, appearing to be talking about electoral politics, before the comic pivot. “I’m talking about SNL’s cold opens,” he said turning to Trump to ask him how long he will continue doing this shtick. “Infinity,” Johnson’s Trump said. They don’t want to talk about it, but we have to talk about it.

Johnson’s Trump also engaged in what might be a bon voyage to Colin Jost’s Pete Hegseth; with the defense secretary rumored to be leaving the administration, it could end Jost’s well-regarded impression run too.

“Do I look like a person who gets less crazy when backed into a corner?” Jost asked as he walked onto the sketch, adding, “I live a YOLO life: you only lose often.” He then sashayed off, backside first, playing to the new Trumpian rumpian obsession.
The sketch began with Sarah Sherman’s Chuck Schumer and Kenan Thompson’s Hakeem Jeffries taking credit for victories that were only partly their doing and then describing their post-midterm plan.

“As our first order of business we are going to march right up to Donald Trump, look him right in the eye and say, ‘Knock it off buster,'” Thompson’s Jeffries said, mocking a perceived ineffectuality of current Congressional Democratic leadership.
As they rhetorically asked who was responsible for pulling off all the wins, Johnson’s Trump appeared and took upside-down credit: “Me,” he boasted.

Talarico’s appearance on SNL provides a bookend — and a bit of sweet revenge — for the Texas politician after broader threats by FCC chair Brendan Carr led ABC and Jimmy Kimmel in September to move an appearance of Talarico’s on Jimmy Kimmel Live! off broadcast television to YouTube, a decision both Kimmel and the candidate condemned. The ostensible reason that Carr would take issue was because Talarico was a candidate, triggering an equal-time provision, even though both Republican and Democratic candidates have long appeared on late-night shows. With Talarico officially a senator-elect, all of that is moot.
Druski hosted the Nov. 7 episode.

items.title: The Other Midterms Flip: Broadcast Networks, Led by NBC, Dominated Election Night Coverage
items.description: In addition to changing the composition of Congress and a number of statehouses, the midterm elections brought another kind of disruption to the status quo: For the first time in 6 election cycles, more people watched the returns come in on network TV than on
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: In addition to changing the composition of Congress and a number of statehouses, the midterm elections brought another kind of disruption to the status quo: For the first time in 6 election cycles, more people watched the returns come in on network TV than on cable.

Per Nielsen ratings, 31.21 million people watched primetime election coverage on 13 broadcast and cable outlets Tuesday, significantly more than the 25.43 million viewers for the 2022 midterms. Of that audience, 57 percent (17.79 million) watched on broadcast outlets (NBC, ABC, CBS, Univision, Telemundo and PBS), and just 43 percent (13.42 million) on cable channels. That’s exactly the inverse of four years ago, when 57 percent of viewers went to cable for midterm coverage.

It’s been 14 years since broadcast networks drew a clear majority of election night viewers (there was a roughly 50-50 split in 2016). That was also the last election a broadcaster led all comers on — and in both 2012 and this year, NBC finished first.

The network had 6.74 million viewers in primetime Tuesday, more than doubling its 2022 average. ABC also improved considerably, growing by 57 percent from four years ago to 5.19 million viewers. CBS was off the pace some at 2.76 million, but it also improved by 8 percent from 2022. Univision (1.54 million), Telemundo (1.06 million) and PBS (about 500,000) made up the rest of the broadcast total.

CNN and MS NOW also improved their numbers from 2022, but Fox News tumbled by almost 3.5 million viewers (though it still narrowly led its cable counterparts). The big three broadcasters, however, collectively gained more viewers than Fox News lost, so the off night for Fox doesn’t fully explain the shift in balance from cable to broadcast.

So what does? For one, cable as a whole has also suffered across-the-board declines in the past four years. Homes with multi-channel providers (cable, satellite or digital services like YouTube TV or Hulu + Live TV) only represent 42.5 percent of TV homes now, down from 52.3 percent four years ago. That represents a loss of more than 10 million households.

Some of it might also be ideological: Fox News leans right, and a night when Republicans took bruising losses might have helped drive ratings down there. MS NOW’s gains could similarly be put down to a blue wave helping the left-leaning channel.

Tuesday’s viewer leaders, ABC and NBC, work to project big-tent inclusiveness, which seems to have paid off some. Marc Greenstein, executive vp creative production and field operations for NBC News, pointed to reporting initiatives on the NBC Nightly News and Meet the Press that try go beyond the “left-right food fight,” as he put it, and explore substantive issues and points of commonality.

NBC also scored a multi-platform win Tuesday, as its dedicated “Kornacki Cam” live stream of analyst Steve Kornacki throughout the night was the most watched live stream of election coverage. NBC News as a whole led election night streams with 4.39 million hours of viewing on its YouTube channels, according to analytics firm Streams Charts (Twitch streamer Hasan Piker was second with 1.75 million hours).

The Kornacki Cam was also something of a tech breakthrough for NBC News, Greenstein said. Kornacki was stationed about 15 feet away from the network’s main desk, but both the TV broadcast and the live stream were able to run simultaneously without interfering with one another. NBC used software from a company called Waves that filters audio, allowing for clean sound on both despite their proximity.

“I talked to our engineering team maybe a week and a half before the elections, and it just so happened that [Saturday Night Live] had just started using it not too long before,” Greenstein said. “We were literally in the midst of rehearsals when we turned this thing on, and we decided to take the risk and put it out there because we thought it was much more important to really integrate Steve into the [TV] broadcast.”

The live stream and on-air telecast ended up being mutually reinforcing, Greenstein said, possibly helping draw viewers in. NBC’s decision desk was also among the fastest to call some key races and the first to project Democratic control of the U.S. Senate.
That said, Greeenstein didn’t know ahead of Tuesday night that NBC would end up at the top of the ratings.

“We like to think we put in really good groundwork and incredible preparation going into the night, so we always hope that the audience will pay us back for that work,” Greenstein told The Hollywood Reporter. “One thing I will say is that I think NBC, maybe more than others, we just do big events well as a network. You look at the Super Bowl, the Olympics, election night — we just have a bigness and a gravitas. I think that matters on these type of nights, and I think that is an advantage we have.”

items.title: RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd
items.description: Elon Musk, in a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
items.author: Jeremy White
paragraphs: Elon Musk, in a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Produced for less than four years, the polarizing pickup is seemingly dying as it lived, with the news being greeted in a flurry of replies in praise of the EV as well as deriding it. James Star, claiming to be a Tesla employee, posted that it was “the saddest news! Cybertruck (was) the best car Tesla sold,” right next to a user called Captain Ford who simply replied to Musk with “Fuck that shitbox.”

Tesla has not responded to WIRED’s request for comment and clarification that the Cybertruck will no longer be made at all. The Cybertruck is exclusively made at Gigafactory Texas, as this is apparently the only Tesla facility equipped with the machinery required to manufacture the truck’s unique stainless steel body, which supposedly started to rust in some cases.

Despite whipping up a fevered number of reservations—allegedly more than a million according to Musk, who at the end of 2023 crowed that demand was “off the charts!”—the truck failed to sell, shifting less than 50,000 units in total by March last year.

EVWire cites Kelley Blue Book data suggesting that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first three quarters of this year in the US, down 28 percent year-over-year, adding that Musk’s announcement post came about 80 minutes after Tesla raised US Cybertruck prices and paused new orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD version.

The Cybertruck proved not only to be wildly unpopular, it was also beset by troubles before it even reached customers. In 2023, WIRED covered a leaked Tesla report dated January 25, 2022, that showed the Cybertruck had basic design flaws, and that the preproduction “alpha” version was struggling with problems with its suspension, body sealing, noise levels, handling, and braking.

In November 2019, when Musk stepped onto a stage in California to launch his new cyberpunk-styled electric pickup, he decided to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass windows by hurling a steel ball at them. In what has now entered into public relations folklore, the demo truck’s windows smashed not once, but twice. Musk swore, then joked: “There’s room for improvement.”

There most certainly was. In April 2024, a recall was issued for the Cybertruck because its accelerator pedal pad could come loose and get trapped by interior trim, which had the frightening potential of pushing the car to full speed.

In March last year, Tesla had to recall nearly all the Cybertrucks it had then produced because a stainless steel trim panel could become detached from the vehicle while driving, blaming the problem on the wrong type of glue, which then had to be replaced with a new adhesive “not prone to environmental embrittlement.”

Back in May this year, Cybertrucks were struck down by the wrong type of grease, which meant that their wheels could potentially fall off. In what was then the EV’s 11th recall, it was declared that the Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) Cybertruck Long Range model might have faulty brake rotors. In a notice posted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla stated that “brake rotor stud holes may crack and allow the stud to separate from the wheel hub.” Such a situation might have seen some RWD Cybertruck owners merrily driving along only to then be disconcertingly overtaken by their own wheels.

Musk even tried to get President Donald Trump to buy one of his Cybertrucks, creating an impromptu Tesla showroom on the White House South Lawn, no less. But, sadly, even President Trump must have smelt something was off about the truck as instead he shunned the pickup and opted for a 200-mph Model S Plaid in ultra red, clearly impressed with the interior, remarking that “Everything’s computer!”

At the end of 2024, Karl Brauer, executive analyst at car ranking service iSeeCars, told WIRED that he’d calculated that the Cybertruck’s six recalls to date at the time made the EV “worse than 91 percent” of all other 2024 vehicles.

Yet, despite supposedly being so unreliable, the Cybertruck did find a small but loyal audience. WIRED profiled a number of owners last year, all fervently in love with their vehicles, but who were periodically forced to endure insults and taunts that they were Nazis, perhaps referring to an on-stage gesture Musk made at the start of 2025.

However, despite evidence seemingly to the contrary, Musk claims he is killing the Cybertruck, not because of its unreliability and staggering unpopularity, but because he wishes to focus instead on Cybercab, an autonomous EV that is central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions but itself has had a rocky start.

Currently operating in Austin only, with a fleet supposedly numbered only in the hundreds, Musk apparently wants to ramp up production dramatically since he confirmed on an earnings call the first cab came off the line in February.

Musk sees Cybercab as very much the vision of Tesla’s future. The CEO has even said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. “Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

items.title: Refreshed Freetown Memorial is a ‘message of hope’ as well as remembrance
items.description: Sierra Leone's Freetown Memorial, a monument to First World War fallen soldiers created by Sir Edwin Lutyens in 1931, has been refreshed. Oshinówò Studio is the architect behind the project, which features an extension to the original structure in the shape of
items.author: Ellie Stathaki
paragraphs: Sierra Leone's Freetown Memorial, a monument to First World War fallen soldiers created by Sir Edwin Lutyens in 1931, has been refreshed. Oshinówò Studio is the architect behind the project, which features an extension to the original structure in the shape of a prism in structural glass, boldly illuminated in a nod of respect and honour to the local Carrier Corps.
Explore the new Freetown Memorial by Oshinówò Studio

Oshinówò Studio's founder, Tosin Oshinówò, worked on integrating the geometric structure and its mesmerising lighting design with the etching of the names of more than 900 fallen Sierra Leone Carrier Corps members – individually commemorated within the memorial for the first time.

This type of project was a first for Oshinowo too, who was attracted to take part in the competition by the challenge of a new typology, as much as by its importance. 'It has been an absolute privilege to design this monument. That said, I have always been drawn to new challenges, and it was precisely the unfamiliarity of this commission that attracted me. At the time, I was also exploring the relationship between public space and memory as part of an academic enquiry, and I became increasingly aware of these spaces' cultural and historical significance. I brought that curiosity and personal interest into the project, allowing it to inform my approach to the design,' she said.

The structure reaches 8.4m in height, its four glass 'fins' (weighing a total of 4,000 kg) emitting a colourful glow that culminates in a pillar of light projecting upwards and visible from a 5km radius across Freetown. This was the result of the design team's ambition for their scheme to expand its impact and conceptually resonate beyond its physical space.

'Through our engagement with the site and its context, we recognised that the monument, located within the forecourt of the Ministry of Finance, now sits within a controlled-access area. We wanted to create a memorial that could transcend the limitations of its physical location and extend its presence into the wider city. Light became a natural medium through which to achieve this,' Oshinowo explains.

'While the monument serves as a memorial to the fallen, we also saw an opportunity to create a broader space for collective remembrance, acknowledging some of the other tragedies that have shaped Sierra Leone's history. The beam of light will be illuminated on significant days throughout the year, allowing the memorial to extend beyond its immediate commemorative purpose. In doing so, it becomes a contemporary monument that speaks to the people of Sierra Leone today while carrying its message of remembrance and hope to future generations.'

Oshinówò worked with an expert international team to realise this technically complex and important commission. Engineers, glass designers, laser consultants and construction partners from Nigeria, the Netherlands, Spain, Sierra Leone and the UK worked on the project. Meanwhile, stonemasons and bronze specialists worked on the existing memorial, restoring it to its former glory to accompany the new elements' public reveal this weekend.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

This didn't come without its challenges, Oshinowo recalls: 'Conceptually, the project came together quite naturally; the real challenge lay in its technical delivery. It has been an incredibly rewarding experience, but one that presented a number of significant technical and logistical challenges.

'Our first obstacle was that Sir Edward Lutyens’ existing structure had not been designed to carry the additional weight of the new monument. We therefore developed a reinforcement strategy, which I have fondly called a root canal, to accommodate the new structure without compromising or damaging the existing masonry.'
An epitaph from poets Nii Ayikwei Parkes and Julianknxx, written in Krio and English, and inscribed on the pavilion, reads: 'From today you will be carried, you are borne, now and ever.'

'This memorial is part of one of the most significant projects we have undertaken since the Second World War. It is about righting a historic wrong and renewing a promise we made a century ago: that everybody who died for the Commonwealth in the First World War, no matter where, no matter how, no matter who they were, would be commemorated equally,' says Claire Horton CBE, director general at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.

'We were looking for a response that was ambitious yet accurate, one that would allow us, for the first time, to honour by name the servicemen of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps. We wanted to commission a memorial that would transform historical research and knowledge into meaningful action, helping people in Sierra Leone and around the world to have a fuller, international understanding of the global scale of the World Wars and the diverse individuals whose service helped shape our shared history.'

Ellie Stathaki is the Architecture & Environment Director at Wallpaper*. She trained as an architect at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and studied architectural history at the Bartlett in London. Now an established journalist, she has been a member of the Wallpaper* team since 2006, visiting buildings across the globe and interviewing leading architects such as Tadao Ando and Rem Koolhaas. Ellie has also taken part in judging panels, moderated events, curated shows and contributed in books, such as The Contemporary House (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Glenn Sestig Architecture Diary (2020) and House London (2022).
