Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Copping can relate to the desire to create across mediums. He started his own homeware line La Carlière, with his French husband Rambert Rigaud, in 2020, named after the pair’s 15th-century manor house in Normandy and comprising cushions made from rare or antique fabrics constructed using the techniques typically used to create haute couture clothing. The home, which Copping dedicated his time to restoring after his exit from Oscar de la Renta in 2016, would become a place of solace away from fashion (he took a break of around five years before starting at Balenciaga).

‘After Oscar de la Renta, I wanted to take a little time off. But sometimes taking a break can go on a little longer than planned,’ he says. ‘So it was really exciting to go on to work with Demna [at Balenciaga]. It was amazing to be at that house at that time. My job was to get his vision made: bringing in Lésage for the embroidery, or collaborating with [Savile Row tailor] Huntsman, or introducing Philip Treacy to work on the hats. These weren’t the sort of people that Demna had worked with before that.’

Now, at Lanvin, he is orchestrating his own vision once again, with his A/W 2026 womenswear collection marking his strongest yet. Inspired by the 100th anniversary of menswear at the house, Copping explored fabrics more traditionally associated with men’s clothing, like heritage flannels and Prince of Wales checks, as well as the tailoring silhouette. Several of the looks came with dramatic sou’wester-style hats in fabrics that matched the garments, seeing Copping reference a photograph of model Guinevere van Seenus on the October 1999 cover of i-D wearing a similar style he’d designed while at Louis Vuitton. Folded darts on the back of jackets gave a more hourglass line, while a sense of ‘feminine volume’ came in the asymmetric cut of skirts and dresses. Evening wear was inspired by the 1920s, though less ‘up and down’ for a more flattering silhouette, but embellishment remained central – from trailing streamers of shimmering paillettes to intricate beading and tassels. ‘The 1920s was such a strong period for design,’ says Copping. ‘People were looking for something [new] after the First World War. You were seeing decoration reappear everywhere.’

While the numbers – for various reasons, including company-wide restructuring and the closure of bricks-and-mortar stores – are yet to show enormous change, Copping is confident that Lanvin is moving forward (the shows are certainly the strongest, and most cohesive, since Elbaz, and the Lanvin Group reports ‘improving momentum’ in sales). The red carpet is bearing that out (Cate Blanchett, Kate Hudson and Katie Holmes have all recently worn Lanvin's designs), while Copping believes a steadily growing group of clients is turning to him for the kind of craft-rich garments that only a handful of people will own. ‘There’s definitely a clientele looking for something more niche, pieces that are considered and special, that you won’t go to a party and find three other people wearing,’ he notes.

‘Fashion is something that you don’t want to stand still,’ says Copping. ‘It should constantly evolve.’ And for now, at Lanvin, that means taking it back to the clothes themselves. ‘There’s so much scope with Lanvin, it could become a lifestyle brand, but we are a small house and have to pick our timings. I want everything to be special and considered. It’s about the process.’

A version of this article appears in the December 2026 issue of Wallpaper*, available from 5 November in print on newsstands, on the Wallpaper* app on Apple iOS, and to subscribers of Apple News +. Subscribe to Wallpaper* today

Jack Moss is the Fashion & Beauty Features Director at Wallpaper*, having joined the team in 2022 as Fashion Features Editor. Previously the digital features editor at AnOther and digital editor at 10 Magazine, he has also contributed to numerous international publications and featured in ‘Dazed: 32 Years Confused: The Covers’, published by Rizzoli. He is particularly interested in the moments when fashion intersects with other creative disciplines – notably art and design – as well as championing a new generation of international talent and reporting from international fashion weeks. Across his career, he has interviewed the fashion industry’s leading figures, including Rick Owens, Pieter Mulier, Jonathan Anderson, Grace Wales Bonner, Christian Lacroix, Kate Moss and Manolo Blahnik.

paragraphs: Film mandiri Kylo Ren, yang dikembangkan bersama Steven Soderbergh, gagal mendapatkan persetujuan dari para petinggi Disney.
Dibangun selama 14 tahun, destinasi di Korea Selatan ini memetakan filosofi Barat dan sejarah modern Korea di atas padang rumput yang dihiasi 25.000 tanaman.
Koleksi ini meminjam elemen grafis dari desain festival dan korporat lawas.
Jahitan menggantikan setiap lapisan overlay, sementara material kulit perforasi mendominasi bagian eyestay dan tumit.
Siluet low-top ini memadukan overlay suede biru pucat, cutout mesh berbentuk segitiga, dan sol luar berwarna gum.
Simbol-simbol coretan tangan menghiasi bagian belakang jaket penerbang berwarna hijau sage, yang pertama kali dirilis untuk para pilot pada tahun 1972.
Pusat seni eksperiensial asal Miami ini melebarkan sayapnya ke Jepang melalui pameran berskala masif yang menyoroti cahaya dan persepsi manusia.
Motif tartan klasik Barbour menghiasi bagian kerah jaket hingga bagian dalam sepatu.
Aldehida yang cerah dan eukaliptus memberi jalan bagi immortelle yang manis seperti madu dan ambar yang bercahaya dalam aroma transparan pertama rumah mode tersebut.
Tetap ikuti perkembangan tren terbaru di industri mode.

items.title: Пять человек погибли при стрельбе в центре Кракова
items.description: Пять человек погибли при стрельбе в центре Кракова
items.author: Иван Адоньев
paragraphs: Пять человек погибли при стрельбе в центре Кракова
В Кракове 7 ноября мужчина открыл стрельбу на Главной рыночной площади, погибли пять человек, более десяти получили ранения. Об этом со ссылкой на полицию сообщает Associated Press.

Нападение произошло вскоре после 15:00 по местному времени — 17:00 мск. По данным представителя пожарной службы Малопольского воеводства Хуберта Цеплы, мужчина стрелял по случайным прохожим из автомобиля, который двигался к площади со стороны улицы Славковской.
У машины не было регистрационных номеров, передаёт RMF24. Полицейские ранили нападавшего и задержали его, после чего мужчину доставили в больницу.
На место прибыли экстренные службы. Для помощи пострадавшим на площади приземлился вертолёт санитарной авиации. Среди раненых — два сотрудника полиции.

Премьер-министр Польши Дональд Туск заявил, что получает оперативную информацию от министра внутренних дел. Полиция устанавливает обстоятельства и мотивы нападения. Глава МВД Марчин Кервиньский направился в Краков для совещания с представителями служб.

items.title: Что читать, если боишься ошибиться: 5 книг для нового поколения
items.description: Что читать, если боишься ошибиться: 5 книг для нового поколения
items.author: Автор Дарья Терехова
paragraphs: Что читать, если боишься ошибиться: 5 книг для нового поколения

Представители нового поколения нередко боятся ошибиться и сомневаются в правильности своих поступков. Это показало исследование 2025 года: опрашиваемые в среднем отмечали у себя высокий уровень беспокойства из-за возможных промахов. Особенно это заметно среди девушек: они чаще юношей перепроверяют свои действия и сомневаются в результате. Авторы объясняют это тем, что у девушек неуверенность связана с внутренней оценкой работы, а у парней — с ожиданиями окружающих. Страх перед неудачами мешает спокойно принимать решения, подрывает самооценку и усиливает тревогу перед учебой или будущей карьерой.
Обращаться за поддержкой можно в том числе к литературе — конечно, произведения не всегда предлагают готовое решение, но показывают, чего иногда стоит стремление избежать любой ошибки.
Сабахаттин Али, «Мадонна в меховом манто»
Издательская серия «Магистраль. Главный тренд», «Эксмо»
Что почитать, если боитесь быть отвергнутым: «Мадонна в меховом манто», Сабахаттин Али

Прочитала эту книгу буквально неделю назад и делюсь впечатлениями по горячим следам. Роман рассказывает о молодости застенчивого и замкнутого Раифа Эфенди, который отправляется в Берлин и знакомится там с художницей Марией Пудер. Эта встреча оборачивается для него первой настоящей любовью, однако привычка подавлять свои порывы и страх все испортить мешают герою открыто говорить о переживаниях и принимать важные решения.

Сабахаттин Али показывает, как неуверенность в себе и страх быть отвергнутым могут повлиять на всю дальнейшую жизнь. Роман особенно откликнется тем, кто привык ставить чужие желания выше собственных и боится проявлять инициативу. Эта история напоминает, почему важно вовремя решиться сделать шаг навстречу своему счастью.
Фрэнсис Скотт Фицджеральд, «Прекрасные и проклятые»
Что почитать, если слишком стремитесь соответствовать всеобщим представлениям об успехе: «Прекрасные и проклятые», Фрэнсис Скотт Фицджеральд

Без сомнений, это мой любимый роман у Фицджеральда. В центре сюжета — Энтони Пэтч и его жена Глория, молодая пара, привыкшая к светским развлечениям и праздной роскоши. Они уверены, что впереди их ждет блестящее будущее, но вместо того, чтобы самостоятельно обустраивать свой быт, герои полагаются на ожидаемое наследство и продолжают поддерживать образ беззаботного благополучия, даже когда их положение становится все более шатким.

На примере Энтони и Глории Фицджеральд показывает, как стремление соответствовать представлениям об успехе может мешать человеку понять истинные желания. Но главное, что я вынесла из этого романа: бездействие тоже имеет последствия, а попытка избежать принятия решения иногда обходится дороже самой ошибки.
Иван Тургенев, «Вешние воды»
Издательская серия «Магистраль. Главный тренд», Эксмо
Что почитать, если боитесь упустить перспективы или не можете довериться сердцу: «Вешние воды», Иван Тургенев

Порой в попытке избежать ошибки мы начинаем подвергать сомнению даже то, что действительно важно для нас. Главный герой, Дмитрий Санин, во время путешествия по Европе знакомится с молодой итальянкой Джеммой и влюбляется в нее. Кажется, молодой человек уже знает, чего хочет, однако обстоятельства заставляют его столкнуться с соблазном и принять решение, от которого зависит его будущее. Тургенев мастерски показывает, как легко потерять уверенность в собственных эмоциях, если рядом возникает альтернатива.

Эта история для тех, кто постоянно ищет более удачный вариант и боится закрыть перед собой остальные двери. Тургенев напоминает, что невозможно заранее просчитать все последствия своих поступков и получить гарантию правильного выбора. Но страх упустить другие перспективы (тот самый FOMO) и неспособность довериться сердцу порой приводят к большим сожалениям.
Фридрих Ницше, «По ту сторону добра и зла»
Серия «Мыслители эпох. Классика», АСТ
Что почитать тем, кто часто колеблется при выборе и зависит от одобрения окружающих: «По ту сторону добра и зла», Фридрих Ницше

Иногда сложно решиться на что-то не потому, что мы не знаем, чего хотим, а из-за сомнений в правильности личных убеждений и оглядки на чужое мнение. Для тех, кому хочется обратиться не только к художественным историям, но и к философии, я добавила в подборку Ницше. В этой книге он подвергает сомнению привычные моральные нормы и общепринятые ценности, которым мы следуем автоматически, даже не задумываясь об их истоках. Его глубокие, порой провокационные размышления заставляют по-новому взглянуть на обыденные вещи и найти свои ответы.

Вся книга пронизана призывом к свободе мышления и смелости оставаться собой, даже вопреки мнению большинства. Труд стоит прочесть всем, кто часто колеблется при выборе и зависит от одобрения окружающих. Ведь прежде чем бояться ошибиться, стоит задуматься: действительно ли наши представления о добре и зле принадлежат нам самим?
Пегги Гуггенхайм, «На пике века. Исповедь одержимой искусством»
Издательство музея «Гараж»
Что почитать, если вам не хватает решимости и хочется поступать по-своему: «На пике века. Исповедь одержимой искусством», Пегги Гуггенхайм

История Пегги Гуггенхайм наглядно доказывает: можно жить по собственным правилам, даже если окружающие уже расписали твое будущее. Рожденная в богатой американской семье, она не пожелала оставаться просто светской наследницей — Пегги посвятила себя авангарду и стала одной из самых влиятельных галеристок XX века.

Парижская богема, знакомства с художниками и писателями, экстравагантные вечеринки, открытие выставок в Лондоне и Нью-Йорке — ее будни походили на роман. Но за этим ярким фасадом скрывается судьба женщины, которая не боялась идти наперекор обществу и безоговорочно доверяла своему вкусу. Эта книга способна подарить ту самую недостающую решимость тем, кто хочет поступать по-своему, не оглядываясь на чужие ожидания.

items.title: TEEKS Is Done Being a Sad Boy
items.description: photography HOLLY SARAH BURGESS
items.author: Alex Kessler
paragraphs: photography HOLLY SARAH BURGESS

With a baritone that could make just about anyone weak at the knees, TEEKS has spent much of his career singing about love, usually the painful kind. But five years after releasing his platinum-selling debut album, Something To Feel, the New Zealand singer has made peace with heartbreak and is ready to have some fun. “I decided going into this project that I wasn’t going to write sad songs,” he says. “By that point I just wanted to enjoy life and have fun.”
On Lovers Comet, his new album, the Māori musician is feeling himself: “Leaning into my sexuality and drawing from it as a source of power,” he says.

But there’s more to it than sex. The album finds TEEKS reconsidering masculinity, embracing his queer identity, and figuring out what he actually wants from love. Not that he’s got it all worked out. He admits to once flying halfway across the world on Valentine’s Day to win someone back. “Is it poetic or pathetic? I’m not sure.”
Below, TEEKS talks romantic red flags, what makes him feel sexy, and the art of flirting through intense eye contact.
ALEX KESSLER: What’s changed most about you since your debut album?

TEEKS: I’ve done a lot of living and learning within these five years. I’ve experienced some pain and discomfort, but those hardships have been a catalyst for growth. I’ve also had the time and opportunity for self-discovery. I’m at a point now where I feel more sure of myself than ever before.
Tell me about Lovers Comet. Where did it all begin?

To me,Lovers Comet is a meditation on desire. It explores love not as fantasy but as a cosmic phenomenon. The beauty and the destruction. The purity and the shadow. It actually began with a poem I wrote about someone, using the comet as a metaphor to describe the impact they had on me.
What’s the story behind “My Boy”?

I wrote “My Boy” after doing back-to-back writing sessions, meeting and working with new people every day. I was frustrated with myself because people would assume my sexuality, and I never corrected them. I came home and did a session with good friends and longtime collaborators Josh Fountain and M Basa. I felt empowered to write something more direct that left no unanswered questions.
Were you nervous about being so open on this album?

My writing up to this point had always had a level of mystery and obscurity, so there were some nerves around how honest and audacious I was being. But I’m at a point in my life where I couldn’t care less about other people’s opinions, in the best possible way.
How has your relationship with masculinity evolved?

My belief is that masculinity and femininity are two sides of the same coin. Healthy masculinity, in my opinion, is embracing the feminine and vice versa. It’s required a lot of unlearning, but also a reclamation of culture and tradition. Being a man can look and feel like so many different things.
How has your Māori heritage shaped your music?

My people are orators and storytellers, and music and dance play an integral role in the retention and transfer of knowledge. Because of my relationship with music in a cultural context, I’m able to approach my work with a sense of spirituality, tradition, and ceremony.
Who are your musical heroes?

Bob Marley was a constant in my household growing up. My father indoctrinated his children. Lauryn Hill and Stevie Wonder also come to mind. Eventually, I discovered D’Angelo and Frank Ocean, who altered my brain chemistry. Sade is and always will be my northern star.
What makes you feel your sexiest?
I feel my hottest when I’ve been consistent enough at the gym and you can see the pump through the clothes.
Are you a hopeless romantic or a heartbreaker?
It depends on the situation, but I’d say hopeless romantic for sure.
What’s your biggest red flag?
I have an addictive personality.
How do you approach… flirting?
Maybe roasting the person and cracking jokes mixed in with some intense eye contact.

items.title: Instagram Rings’ 2026 Picks Are Pure Gold
items.description: If you’ve woken up this morning to a shiny, gold ring around your Instagram profile picture: congratulations! And if you haven’t, don’t worry, there’s always next year! Today, IG announced the 2026 winners of Instagram Rings, its annual awards celebrating the
items.author: I-D Staff
paragraphs: If you’ve woken up this morning to a shiny, gold ring around your Instagram profile picture: congratulations! And if you haven’t, don’t worry, there’s always next year! Today, IG announced the 2026 winners of Instagram Rings, its annual awards celebrating the courageous creatives that use the platform, and awarding them with both a virtual gold halo and a real ring, designed by slow-fashion maverick Emily Adams Bode Auijla. So who bagged one, then?

This year’s Rings luminaries span every corner of creativity. The beauty scene got its flowers: Demna’s ride-or-die Sam Visser, viral blush pioneer Ngozi Edeme, LISA’s nail artist Juan Alvear and “wavy brow” aesthete Me Love Me A Lot have all been recognised.

Across fashion, there’s groundbreaking Chanel muse Bhavitha Mandava, “Portuguese girl aesthetic” neologiser Vic Montanari, Brooklyn-based it-girl Skylar Marshai, buzzy sneaker designer Salehe Bembury, and LaWatch Party thrower Lyas.

But that’s not even half of it. Behind the lens, lo-fi music video director Medet Shayakhmetov, ICE magazine founder Renell Medrano and otherworldly style photographer Szilveszter Makó all got kudos. Move-makers Damien Jalet—the choreographer who worked with Yung Lean on that video—and Sabrina Carpenter’s right-hand-woman, Jasmine Badie, also feature. And in the world of music, wrap your ears around Mexican trio LATINMAFIA, rapper-actor Little Simz, and Latin Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter Joyce Alane.

Comedy’s hot right now on Instagram, so it’s great to see Club Kid writer and director Jordan Firstman, Brooklyn Coffee Shop skit creator Pooja Tripathi, and Subway Takes Kareem Rahma all get a showing. For foodies, Alexis Nikole Nelson AKA Black Forager and culinary creator Steven Moto both got nods. And for bookworms, the Under The Cover book series. Completing the dream guestlist, two ballers: freestyler Muhammed Riswan and the raccoon-toting, goal-scoring GOAT himself: Erling Haaland.
Rings winners don’t just get an accolade—they’re also being co-signed by a panel of genuine icons.

This year’s judges included the no-introduction-needed Chloé Zhao, Isamaya Ffrench Donatella Versace, who i-D readers recently got the chance to DM. Joining them were hitmakerFINNEAS, street artists OSGEMEOS, alpine skier Mikaela Shiffrin, Emmy-winning choreographer Charm La’Donna, editor Will Welch, rapper A$AP Rocky, Indian celebrity chef Vikas Khanna and resident internet librarian Jack Edwards.
The lineup was finished with Instagram’s CEO Adam Mosseri and head of fashion partnerships Eva Chen, plus this year’s Rings designer Emily Adams Bode Auijla.

What were the judges looking for? (This is where you take notes for next year.) “I’m always looking for people with a unique voice and a point of view that is distinct and instantly recognizable as their own. Especially if they are able to build a whole cinematic universe,” Welch tellsi-D. He gravitated to the people whose Stories and Reels he never misses, the accounts he’s always keen to see more of. “If I already follow you and I think of your account as appointment viewing, I nominated you.”

When voting on other judges’ nominations, it was about instant originality. “If I landed on a profile and immediately felt vision and work that just kind of radiates electric newness, I cast a vote.” Instagram, he says, is a portal to experience this next gen of visionaries. “Radical newness comes from subcultures, and through Instagram we get instant access to all these niche areas of global interest and expression.”

In the words of Subway Takes’ Kareem: “100% agree.” Rings’s Class of 2026 provides the ideal inspo for zhuzhing-up your Instagram presence. These gold-gilded profiles are the circles you want to be moving in—so start sending those DMs, you never know. But remember, it’s about creativity, not clout.

As FINNEAS puts it, “My advice is not to wait, to keep writing, working, creating, sharing and putting your art out there. You might just reach someone and change their life, it could even change your life. You just never know what might happen and who you might reach.”

Case in point—when he sent a message to Lizzy McAlpine, resulting in a collab. Don’t be afraid of shooting your shot. “I’m usually the one asking creators I admire to collaborate on a project. When they say yes, it’s a good day.”

items.title: Macklemore Says Nine U.S. Venues Turned Down 'Free Palestine' Tour: 'They Got Me F-cked Up'
items.description: Last month, Macklemore launched his Free Palestine tour in response to his removal from Ed Sheeran’s tour at the behest of stadium owners who opposed his vocal support of Palestinians in Gaza. It proved to be a success, with three sold-out shows in Paris, Dubl
items.author: Larisha Paul
paragraphs: Last month, Macklemore launched his Free Palestine tour in response to his removal from Ed Sheeran’s tour at the behest of stadium owners who opposed his vocal support of Palestinians in Gaza. It proved to be a success, with three sold-out shows in Paris, Dublin, and London. Confident fans would show up in support and solidarity, he made plans to bring the tour stateside — but he claims nine different U.S. venues turned him down.

“In over twenty years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” Macklemore wrote on Instagram. The outreach process began weeks ago, he claims, and “by mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year. But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table. The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”

The named locations include Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center, and UBS Arena in New York; Prudential Center in New Jersey; Intuit Dome, Kia Forum, and Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles; Chase Center in San Francisco; and Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle, the rapper’s hometown.

Following publication of this article, an MSG Entertainment spokesperson tells Rolling Stone, “We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena-level act.” (Representatives for the other venues did not immediately return Rolling Stone‘s request for comment.)

“The trouble with buying power is believing you’ve bought the people too. The billionaires depend on our silence and complicity. They forget that we buy their tickets. We fill their arenas. We build their empires. And we have the power to bring them down,” the rapper added. “The people have spoken. We want an end to the genocide and we want a Free Palestine. The arenas have made their decision. Now we’ll make ours. If they think the threat of never playing another arena in America will make me retreat into silence, they got me fucked up.”

In September, the promoter of the U.S. leg of Sheeran’s Loop Tour said venues booked for the tour notified them “that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup.” Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium just outside of Boston, confirmed as much, saying the location is committed to “providing a welcoming environment for all guests and ensuring that all events held at our venue do not provide a platform for hate speech.”

“I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life,” Macklemore said. “We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending. Today it’s Palestine. What will it be tomorrow? To these owners, the words Free Palestine represent a threat. Not because they endanger anyone, but because those words challenge the systems of power they have built their fortunes on.”

Sheeran argued that the decision to remove Macklemore as an opener, backed by the venues and promoters, came down to not wanting to disappoint fans or impact the other people working on the tour by cancelling. The explanation weakened as the rest of his opening acts withdrew in solidarity, as well as his backing band, Beoga, who joined Macklemore during the Dublin concert on the Free Palestine tour. A wave of artists spoke out in defense of free speech and artistic expression; and when it came time to back Macklemore’s tour, acts like Hozier and Kneecap joined eagerly.

“To the artists who are afraid of what those two words [“Free Palestine”] might cost them, I understand that fear. I felt it myself, especially when I was still wrestling with whether to speak out. But I believe that fear begins to lose its power the moment we realize we’re not standing alone,” Macklemore said. “I dream of a world where saying Free Palestine is not controversial. It is expected. Where artists value their freedom of speech and collective liberation more than their brand deals.”

He added, “Look at what just happened in Europe. Three sold-out arenas. Tens of thousands of people from different backgrounds, religions and walks of life standing together. More than forty artists and speakers putting their names and platforms behind Palestinian liberation. For all the attempts to paint this movement as one rooted in hatred, what filled those rooms was love.”

Proceeds from the Free Palestine Tour benefitted a collection of organizations supporting Palestinians in Gaza, including Medical Aid for Palestinians, Palestinian Youth Movement, Heal Palestine, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Jewish Voices for Peace, and the UNRWA USA National Committee.

In his statement, Macklemore emphasized that the support of this movement extends far beyond music. He mentioned Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who “won his Senate race on a platform that included ending the genocide in Gaza and stopping U.S. arms sales to Israel.” (Humanitarian groups and a United Nations commission have said Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute a genocide. Israel and its allies, including the United States, have denied this.)

A ceasefire agreement approved by Israel took effect on Oct. 10, 2025. The Associated Press reports over 1,400 have been killed in Gaza since then, with the total Palestinian death toll since October 2023 rising to more than 74,000. Millions of others have been displaced due to the destruction of the landscape.

Macklemore is committed to continuing to raise funds and stand in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza through both speech and performance, even if he doesn’t yet know where those will be allowed to happen. “We’ll keep working with other artists and organizers, continuing where we left off in Europe. We’ll probably just take that shit outside where it belonged in the first place,” he said. “There comes a point when the world changes, not because those in power give us permission, but because the people stop asking for it. We will build our own stages. They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will.”
This article has been updated on Friday, Nov. 6 at 3:20 p.m. EST to include a statement from MSG Entertainment.

items.description: Macklemore is accusing some of America’s most iconic arenas of shutting his “Free Palestine” tour out.
items.author: William Earl
paragraphs: Macklemore is accusing some of America’s most iconic arenas of shutting his “Free Palestine” tour out.

The rapper, who recently had dates in Dublin, Paris and London at the end of October, took to Instagram on Nov. 6 to say that he has been turned down by American venues, including New York City’s Madison Square Garden, New Jersey’s Prudential Center, Brooklyn’s Barclays Center, Long Island’s UBS Arena, L.A.’s Intuit Dome, Kia Forum and Crypto.com Arena, San Francisco’s Chase Center and Seattle’s Climate Pledge Arena.

“By mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year,” he said in the Instagram post. “But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table. The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”

“In over 20 years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” he also wrote. “I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life.”

“We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending,” he later wrote. “Today it’s Palestine. What will it be tomorrow?”
Macklemore ended his post with, “They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will. FREE PALESTINE!”

A spokesperson for MSG Entertainment responded to Macklemore’s claims in a statement to Variety: “We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena level act.”

In September, Macklemore was fired from Ed Sheeran’s “Loop” tour over pro-Palestine comments he made during his opening set at MetLife Stadium. All of the tour’s other openers and Sheeran’s own backing band ended up quitting the tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.
Variety has reached out to the nine arenas Macklemore mentioned for comment.

items.title: Why Does Amazon Want a TV Show Starring Melania Trump?
items.description: Amazon, it seems, cannot get enough “Melania.” And at this moment, they feel like the only entity for whom that’s true.
items.author: Daniel D'Addario
paragraphs: Amazon, it seems, cannot get enough “Melania.” And at this moment, they feel like the only entity for whom that’s true.

The company has announced its plan to release a two-part documentary series about First Lady Melania Trump on Nov. 20; this follows on the stilettoed heels of their feature film documentary, “Melania,” released in theaters in January. Back then, director Brett Ratner’s film — while failing to recoup the astonishing $75 million Amazon spent on rights and marketing — did well for a documentary, earning some $16.6 million. But that film came amidst the seeming height of a cultural shift toward forever-Trumpism that began in November 2024 — one that has now been decisively ended. In the wake of the midterms offering a stunning nationwide repudiation of her husband, what’s left to say about Melania?

There’s reason beyond the shock Democratic Party victories from Kansas to South Carolina to suspect “Melania,” the series — which, Amazon promises, will be split into episodes following Melania’s experience of the 2024 presidential transition and then the immediate aftermath of Donald Trump’s second inauguration — will meet an indifferent public. “Melania,” the film, covered the same territory with astounding vacuity. This viewer went in not expecting my opinions of Melania’s husband to shift but curious about the by-every-indication extraordinary life Melania herself has led. And I grew numb at the umpteenth shot of her walking into and out of rooms, random stylists and decorators burbling away in her wake.

Even by this family’s low standard, it seemed shameless: Melania Trump was willing to accept a staggeringly large check but seemed not to feel even the slightest twinge that would have prompted her to offer something, anything, to earn the fee. But the film was a document of an aesthetic, and a movement, that was ascendant.

The day after the 2024 election, a perception began spreading that the surprising nature of Trump’s popular-vote victory meant that not merely was Trump more popular than ever before but that our society had fundamentally changed. In Trump’s first term and through the Joe Biden presidency, corporations took tones between studied neutrality and resistance. Now, though, corporate America flocked to Trump, with Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his soon-to-be-wife Lauren Sánchez among the guests of honor at Trump’s inauguration. As such, a film about how Melania prepared for said inauguration had a grim civic-duty feel. Want to see America? This was it — an oligarch’s wife flatly bragging to camera that she’s always had an intuitive feel for design, and charging you for the privilege of being in her company.

Something’s shifted! Trump is still the president (and Melania still the first lady), but we’ve just been issued as striking notice as possible that whatever change Trump has lost control of the national conversation. (Notable, perhaps: “Melania” came out in theaters before the launch of the disastrous war in Iran, a turning point for the president’s popularity.) This ought to have been predictable: Beyond the fact that Trump’s own tendencies seemed likely to doom his popularity sooner or later, no moment in time lasts forever, and electoral victories are just that, not restructures of society at every level.

This may be a hard pill to swallow for Bezos in particular, whose gut-renovation of his public image seemed designed to earn himself and his wife permanent seats at Mar-a-Lago. (Bezos’ tasteless June 2025 wedding, commandeering seemingly the entire city of Venice, was a stunning let-them-eat-cake moment from the onetime nerdy Seattle bookseller.) Amazon has, reportedly, discussed rebooting Trump’s old reality franchise “The Apprentice” with Donald Trump Jr. as its lead. Now that making the president happy seems like a less urgent concern — and that the negative optics of currying favor with him seem clear — one wonders how committed Bezos is to the new values he discovered in 2024.

An “Apprentice” reboot wouldn’t just be politically toxic at this moment, it’d never work: Everyone knows the only Trump who’s any good on TV is Donald. Just look at “Melania” — its subject seems to be gritting her teeth in order to get through a film designed to show her in an exclusively flattering light. But Amazon already spent the money they spent on it, and recutting it into a TV series will give Trump something to talk about. Increasingly distracted, the President spent the run-up to the election discussing men’s physiques and the day after his electoral thumping touring his under-construction ballroom; being able to spin a story about his wife now having the highest-rated TV series on streaming, or whatever, will at least give him something to do, while the rest of the country tunes out.

But the project is symbolic of a series of bets corporate America made that Trump’s opposition would never win again. Oops! At Skydance, for instance, opinion journalist Bari Weiss, in charge of CBS News, has radically revamped the division into something that suited the moment for, well, a moment, and now couldn’t seem less like what viewers crave. And, more consequentially, the new Democratic Senate majority is signaling that they will, after taking over in January 2027, subpoena tech companies — including Amazon — over their donations to Trump’s ballroom project. The donations made, somewhat like the $75 million spent on a documentary that’s now a time capsule, are the kind companies make when thinking only in the present tense. And, this past week, they collided with a future in which buying off the powerful may not work as well. At least Amazon will always have footage of Melania Trump singing “Billie Jean” to Brett Ratner, for whatever that’s worth.

items.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Barrels Toward Historic $32M Box Office Launch With ‘Cat in the Hat’ at No. 2
items.description: Godzilla Minus Zero is king of the box office in its opening weekend as the sequel feature looks to dominate the frame that also sees the debuts of The Cat in the Hat, Ramayana, Wild Horse Nine and Club Kid.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: Godzilla Minus Zero is king of the box office in its opening weekend as the sequel feature looks to dominate the frame that also sees the debuts of The Cat in the Hat, Ramayana, Wild Horse Nine and Club Kid.

Hitting 3,254 North American theaters from GKids and Toho, Godzilla Minus Zero conquered $14.5 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, as it heads toward an estimated $32 million for the weekend. This is being touted as the highest-grossing live-action foreign-language opening at the box office since 2004’s Hero launched with $17.8 million. (It’s behind the debut of last year’s animated Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle with $70.6 million, while 2004’s The Passion of the Christ and its massive $83.8 million opening is not included in the category as an American-produced project). Filmmaker Takashi Yamazaki‘s sequel to 2023’s Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One earned an A CinemaScore from audiences and is performing far above the distributor’s projected opening in the mid-$20 millions.

Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe and Min Tanaka star in the new movie that carries a reported budget in the mid-teens. It centers on postwar Japan dealing with attacks from the three-headed Ghidorah and the possibility of Godzilla’s return. Godzilla Minus Zero holds an impressive 90 percent critics approval on Rotten Tomatoes, with The Hollywood Reporter chief film critic David Rooney calling it a “thrilling jolt of marauding monster action.”

The sequel is making an even bigger footprint than Godzilla Minus One, which opened in December 2023 with $11.4 million domestically and reached $57.1 million for the run, adding $56.9 million internationally. The film rode its massive breakout success to become Japan’s first feature to win the best visual effects Oscar.

Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat grossed $6 million domestically from 4,003 North American locations on Friday, including Thursday previews, and it is set to pounce on around $18 million for its opening frame. The studio had projected that the $92 million-budgeted film, which earned an A CinemaScore, would open with $20 million and hopes for word of mouth to help it play through the Thanksgiving holiday and into December.

Directors Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni’s animated adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ classic 1957 children’s book centers on the titular feline being given a final chance to prove his worth by helping a pair of siblings. Bill Hader leads the voice cast that also includes Matt Berry, Quinta Brunson and Xochitl Gomez. The movie marks Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s first title since Bill Damaschke took over as president and chief creative officer in 2023.

Critics have been a bit aloof on the film, as it holds a 45 percent Rotten Tomatoes score from reviewers, with THR critic Frank Scheck calling it “more taxing than enjoyable.” It’s certainly getting better notices than Universal’s 2003 live-action The Cat in the Hat starring Mike Myers, which holds an 11 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes. That movie opened to $38.3 million domestically en route to a North American cume of $101 million against a $109 million budget.

Sony Pictures releases Prime Focus Studios’ Ramayana: Rise of a Legend in 1,433 North American locations, with the film grossing $2.4 million Friday and headed to a sum of roughly $7.3 million for the weekend and $10.8 million for the four days. Boasting the widest domestic launch ever for an Indian movie, director Nitesh Tiwari’s religious epic focuses on the life of Prince Rama, with the two-film project’s budget reported at $420 million and beyond. It holds a 76 score from critics on Rotten Tomatoes, along with an 89 from audiences.

Also likely debuting in the top five is Angel Studios’ Drummer Boy, with directors Ben and Joel David Smallbone’s historical drama grossing $3.5 million Friday from 2,850 North American locations for a weekend opening around $7.9 million. Earning an A CinemaScore, the faith-based movie focuses on an unlikely bond during the American Revolution and stars Joel David Smallbone in the title role. On Rotten Tomatoes, it has a 50 critics score and a 93 from audiences.

Academy Awards hopeful Wild Horse Nine opened in 1,100 North American theaters with around $2.4 million Friday for an estimated frame of $5.5 million. John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell and Steve Buscemi lead writer-director Martin McDonagh’s comedic thriller about two CIA operatives who travel from Santiago, Chile, to Easter Island in 1973. The Searchlight Pictures release holds a 94 critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, with Rooney’s review describing it as “uniquely affecting.”

Looking to squeak into the top 10 is Burns & Co and Fathom Entertainment’s Jimmy, with the Jimmy Stewart biopic collecting $832,000 Friday from 1,470 North American theaters for a likely $2 million frame. Scheck’s review calls star KJ Apa “top-notch” but deems director Aaron Burns’ film “heartfelt to a fault.”

Another Oscar hopeful launched in platform release as A24 debuted Club Kid on six screens, with the Cannes standout grossing $175,398 on Friday. Making his feature directorial debut, Jordan Firstman also stars as a party promoter who learns he has a 10-year-old son. Set to expand into Thanksgiving, it boasts a sterling 100 score from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes, with THR critic Richard Lawson heralding it as “winning and clever.”

Amazon MGM Studios releases I Play Rocky in seven locations, and it grossed around $160,000 on Friday. Anthony Ippolito stars as Sylvester Stallone in director Peter Farrelly’s making-of story for the 1976 classic Rocky. In his review, Rooney wrote that the movie — which holds an 88 Rotten Tomatoes score from critics — creates “a wave of warm nostalgia.”

Among holdovers, A24’s much-discussed Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything looks to pull in around $8 million for the weekend as it competes with Ramayana and Drummer Boy for third place. The domestic cume for directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s feature stands at $73.4 million through Friday.
Next weekend brings the Johnny Depp studio comeback vehicle Ebenezer, along with How to Rob a Bank and Paper Tiger.

items.title: Bill Skarsgard Says He’s “Spent” Playing Bad Guys but Would Still Play a James Bond Villain
items.description: Bill Skarsgard is feeling “spent” when it comes to playing villains.
items.author: Lexi Carson
paragraphs: Bill Skarsgard is feeling “spent” when it comes to playing villains.

The 36-year-old actor is known for taking on dark characters, including Pennywise in the It movies, Count Orlok in Nosferatu, Eric Draven in The Crow and Marquis Vincent Bisset de Gramont in John Wick: Chapter 4. But during a recent episode of Josh Horowitz’s Happy Sad Confused podcast, Skarsgard explained that he’s becoming more selective about taking on villain roles.

“For a villain, it would have to be something that felt original to me, that was something that I hadn’t done before,” Skarsgard said. “I feel, kind of, spent with those things. But there’s villains [that] could be really fun in different ways and if it’s the right kind.”
Horowitz then brought up Skarsgard’s longtime interest in playing a villain in the James Bond franchise.

“Yeah! Well, because they didn’t call me about James Bond. I don’t know what that was about,” Skarsgard quipped. “Maybe they were like, ‘We can’t do a Swede for this guy.’ I wasn’t even thrown into the mix.”

The Dead Man’s Wire actor agreed with Horowitz that he wouldn’t necessarily want to commit to leading the James Bond franchise for 10 or 15 years. Instead, he said he’d be interested in taking on a one-off villain role, citing Mads Mikkelsen and Javier Bardem as examples.

Skarsgard’s comments come as the search for the next actor to play 007 continues ahead of Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming film. The Hollywood Reporter previously reported that Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor had screen tested for the part. However, on Friday, THR reported that Robert Pattinson had also screen tested, while Nicholas Hoult’s name has emerged as another potential contender.
As for Skarsgard, he stars in Peter Berg’s war film The Mosquito Bowl, which is currently playing in theaters and set to release on Netflix Nov. 25.

items.title: ‘Jimmy’ Review: KJ Apa Tries, in Vain, to Save Ploddingly Dutiful James Stewart Biopic
items.description: Reflecting its subject himself, an aura of decency permeates the new drama depicting the wartime years of actor Jimmy Stewart’s life. That Stewart’s daughter serves as executive producer provides a clue that Jimmy will be a loving tribute rather than a warts-a
items.author: Frank Scheck
paragraphs: Reflecting its subject himself, an aura of decency permeates the new drama depicting the wartime years of actor Jimmy Stewart’s life. That Stewart’s daughter serves as executive producer provides a clue that Jimmy will be a loving tribute rather than a warts-and-all biopic. And since the previous credits of director Aaron Burns and screenwriter Justin Strawhand include the faith-based drama Birthright Outlaw, it’s not surprising that the film places strong emphases on faith and military patriotism.

But those aspects are not the real problems with the film, which simply doesn’t prove compelling despite a top-notch performance from KJ Apa (Riverdale, I Still Believe) as Stewart and a moving depiction of the post-traumatic stress the actor suffered after wartime experiences that fueled his agonized performance in It’s a Wonderful Life. Feeling much longer than its two hours, it has a plodding, episodic quality that makes it play as more dutiful than inspired.
Cast: KJ Apa, Max Casella, Kara Killmer, Julian Works, Sarah Drew, Rob Riggle, Christopher McDonald, Jen Lilley, Jemma Donovan, Karolyn Grimes, Neal McDonough, Jason Alexander
Screenwriter: Justin Strawhand
Rated PG-13, 2 hour 0 minutes

Bookended by scenes involving that 1946 Frank Capra classic, the story essentially begins in 1941 with Stewart at the top of his Hollywood game after winning the Oscar for the previous year’s The Philadelphia Story and enjoying romances with such stars as Ginger Rogers (Jemma Donovan).

His life changes drastically when he gets drafted for the military. Although eager to serve and follow in the footsteps of his military veteran father (Neal McDonough), he lets himself be convinced by MGM boss Louis B. Mayer (Jason Alexander) to let the studio get him out of it. When he’s described as cowardly in print by the ever-hovering gossip columnist Hedda Hopper (Sarah Drew, Grey’s Anatomy), Stewart follows his instincts and enlists. The military mainly wants him for propaganda purposes, but Stewart, an experienced pilot, is determined to serve and, after being sent to England, manages to convince Col. Terrill (a nicely underplaying Rob Riggle) to let him fly B-24 bombers. During his distinguished deployment he flew 20 combat missions, received numerous decorations, and rose to the rank of colonel.

But his wartime service comes at an emotional price as Stewart becomes tormented by the loss of many of the men under his command and must tackle the duty of writing condolence letters to their families. For solace, he turns to the British Lady Julia (Kara Killmer), a character who serves as a composite for the various women with whom Stewart had romantic relationships before his marriage. (And if reports are to be believed about the actor known as “The Great American Bachelor,” any composite has a lot to live up to.)

Hampered by the low budget, the film’s war sequences don’t prove arresting. Jimmy becomes much more interesting when Stewart returns home after the war and is offered the role of George Bailey by frequent collaborator and fellow military veteran Frank Capra (an excellent Max Casella). He’s initially consumed by insecurity and doubts about his ability to play the role, but encouraged by the director and co-star Lionel Barrymore (Christopher McDonald), he eventually manages to channel his trauma into his now-iconic performance.

The best aspect of the film is the lead performance by Apa, who doesn’t resemble Stewart all that much but conveys his essence and aw-shucks appeal with body language and perfect vocal imitation. Never lapsing into mere mimicry, he delivers a soulful turn that fully draws us into the character — although he can’t compete with the five minutes of real-life footage of Stewart that accompanies the end credits, vividly reminding us of his enduring appeal.
Distributor: Fathom Events
Cast: KJ Apa, Max Casella, Kara Killmer, Julian Works, Sarah Drew, Rob Riggle, Christopher McDonald, Jen Lilley, Jemma Donovan, Karolyn Grimes, Neal McDonough, Jason Alexander
Screenwriter: Justin Strawhand
Producers: Aaron Burns, Angela Galgani Sullivan, David Cook, John Norton, Jack McClintock
Executive producer: Kelly Stewart-Harcourt
Director of photography: James Mather
Production designer: Paki Smith
Costume designer: Emma O’Loughlin
Casting: Angela Galgani Sullivan
Rated PG-13, 2 hour 0 minutes

items.title: David Sims Looks Back at the Images That Defined a Generation
items.description: “I’ve always had a resistance to looking in my own archive,” says the photographer David Sims. “It’s a very dark and forgotten place. And seeing it en masse, it just became clear that this person”—i.e., himself—“was in a state of mild psychosis.” In fact, stud
items.author: Alex Needham
paragraphs: “I’ve always had a resistance to looking in my own archive,” says the photographer David Sims. “It’s a very dark and forgotten place. And seeing it en masse, it just became clear that this person”—i.e., himself—“was in a state of mild psychosis.” In fact, studying the torrent of photographs he has taken since the late ’80s felt so unnerving to the 59-year-old that he decided to give the exhibition it has yielded the title “The Hamster Becomes the Problem.” “If you’ve ever owned a hamster, you’ll know that they keep chewing on the cage bars and running on the wheel,” Sims says. “Eventually this delightful, cute, furry animal becomes a torment.”

Sims might have found looking at his old work tormenting, but few of the visitors to the Marta Ortega Pérez Foundation, in A Coruña, Spain, are likely to. “The Hamster Becomes the Problem” seems set to reveal to a wider public what insiders have always known: that Sims is one of the best fashion photographers of all time. “He doesn’t just define a style—he builds a character,” says Fabien Baron, the creative director who gave Sims an exclusive contract at Harper’s Bazaar when the photographer was just 26. “He’s learned the craft so well that he can do anything. In his use of light, he’s the most impressive photographer—and I’ve worked with them all.”

Many of Sims’s photographs convey a feeling that we know the person being depicted, or someone very much like them, perhaps from school or from the fuzzy depths of a long-ago late night. “He created characters and stories that were immediately identifiable to lots of people growing up in the 1990s and 2000s,” says Charlotte Cotton, the exhibition’s curator. “In 1997, he said to me, ‘I want to create the visuals of our time.’ And he’s done that.”

Given the consistently high quality of his work, it seems strange that Sims hasn’t had a full solo exhibition or monograph before. In 2000, he published Isolated Heroes, a book of extraordinary portraits of models taken backstage at a Raf Simons show, which commands huge prices on the resale market today; and in 2013, a touching exhibition named “Bowievirus,” in which a group of skinny male models embodied the Thin White Duke, was shown at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London. But Sims has disseminated most of his work specifically through magazines. Before the Internet existed, that was how he could reach people in places that weren’t cultural hot spots like London or New York—people like his younger self.

Sims grew up in Sheffield, in the north of England, though his family’s roots are in Liverpool. His father sold contraceptive pills to pharmacies (“I always used to say that he was a drug dealer”), and his mother was a secretary. His extended family were musical—he remembers them singing together on Sundays in the pub—while Sims was an avid reader of music magazines about cult figures such as Iggy Pop, his hero. For the photographer, music is still essential on a shoot to conjure up the character and image in his mind; for years, he even employed his own DJ for that purpose. “There has to be a moment when the right song comes on,” he says.

Sims, who admits that he was “opinionated and frustrated” as a teenager, was hugely unpopular with his teachers. The head of his high school art department wrote to a college to which Sims was applying, warning them that Sims was the worst student he’d come across in 30 years. “When I tell that story, it’s like I’m taking pleasure in it,” Sims says. “But it was devastating.” Things clicked when he was offered a job in a photographic darkroom in his hometown. “I thought almost immediately, I’ve got this. I know what I’m doing. It was the first thing I’d been asked to do that fell into place, and I ran with it.”

Entirely self-taught, Sims learned photographic and developing techniques—“trying to produce the perfect negative”—and immersed himself in the medium’s history, studying masters such as Irving Penn, Richard Avedon, Robert Mapplethorpe, and the great war photographer Don McCullin. He moved to London, started working as an assistant to more experienced photographers, and quickly fell in with a fashionable crowd. “We were friendly with a few pop stars, so life was quite exciting,” Sims says. “I remember being ushered into clubs just because we were with Boy George.”

Yet, by the late ’80s, Sims was getting antsy. While he initially enjoyed the acid house scene, “that rave high suddenly felt way too chicken feed to me.” He thought that London’s excitement “had dipped a little bit—there was a resurgence of a more conventional middle-class influence in magazines. I thought, God, we’ve got to take back our ground here.” He found allies and collaborators in two like-minded stylists, Melanie Ward and Anna Cockburn, who had a similar iconoclastic urge to bring a new sense of realism to fashion imagery.

Baron remembers first seeing Sims’s early work when he was judging a photography competition in Monaco: “a bunch of pictures of guys and girls against a white background. Avedon-esque, but the spirit was more youth-based, punkish. There was an English flavor. They were in your face, but they had soul.” Magazines such as i-D and The Face started giving Sims work. “I had an Australian girlfriend, so I went to Australia for a month, which seemed an eternity at the time,” he says. “And when I came back, some pictures had come out and people were suddenly very interested.”

Sims was whisked to New York, where Baron and Harper’s Bazaar editor Liz Tilberis signed him, despite what Baron remembers as his grungy “yellow hair.” He started photographing supermodels and shooting major ad campaigns—“sucking on the corporate tit,” as Sims puts it today. “The thing that New York had that London didn’t was mounds of money. It was my first experience with that resource and what comes with it.”

It’s a mark of Sims’s independence that his work for big brands and big magazines was just as idiosyncratic as the pictures he’d made for himself. Pushed by Baron to photograph Linda Evangelista for Bazaar, Sims came back with a magnificently weird shot of her wolf-whistling. “He showed how you could maintain your integrity through these tiny little gestures,” says Cotton. More editorial and commercial work followed, with clients including Jil Sander and Helmut Lang—an image from a 1997 campaign for the latter brand, of a husky, topless young man wearing a cape, subverted both masculinity and fashion advertising conventions, and is now in the collection of the Victoria and Albert Museum, in London.

Nonetheless, Sims was burning out. “I’d driven my friendships too hard and exhausted them,” he says. When Jil Sander didn’t renew his contract, he decided to take a break, which lasted roughly three years—some of that period spent traveling with the barman of a pub in Devon, England, that Sims had visited while camping on a nearby beach. When he returned, fashion photography had moved from film to digital, and Sims was forced to follow suit. “I was horrified when it first happened,” he says. “I felt completely disoriented by it.” But he decided to experiment with the new medium, “to see the things that lay deep within it, and that’s when the psychedelic thing kicked in.”

As “The Hamster Becomes the Problem” will show, Sims’s 21st-century work often has a narcotic, dreamlike quality. Jagi is a 2019 image of someone standing at the top of what looks like the steps of a playground slide in a dramatically hued field, against a sky full of Turner-esque clouds. There will be an installation that focuses on his cousin Lee Armitage, a Liverpool-based painter with whom Sims has “a degree of fascination…we’ve led these sort of quantum parallel lives.” In one image, Armitage is topless, with closed eyes and an open mouth, which is colored bright pink, denoting some kind of ecstatic experience. Another room, Rave, contains hundreds of pictures and, Cotton says, is like “a fever dream.”

Sims’s work often digs into his memories of his childhood in the postindustrial north of England—barbed-wire fences, tower blocks, violently patterned wallpaper in council flats, people smoking dope while listening to Pink Floyd. He is still creating characters, but now he’s using his impeccable photographic techniques to venture deep into their inner spaces. “He’s not dialing it in, in any way,” Cotton says. “Helmut Newton, or any of those libidinously driven photographers, they go back to the same place every time they take a picture, like they’re pressing repeat. David doesn’t. It’s like you’re following a journey of a life.”

Sims says that his ultimate inspiration is his unconscious, and he hopes that his symbolism, though intensely personal, might nevertheless resonate with viewers. “I was looking at the archive and wondering, What the hell was I even thinking?” Sims says. “It’s a chimera—something you’ll never quite get to. You’re building a structure that will hold the illusion of your fantasy. Really, this show could have been called ‘Castles in the Air.’ ”
All images courtesy of David Sims.

items.title: Every Must-See Look from the 2026 CFDA Awards Red Carpet
items.description: On Monday, November 2, fashion heavy hitters and stylish stalwarts gathered at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City for the 2026 CFDA Awards. Now in its 45th year, the annual ceremony—often dubbed the Oscars of fashion—celebrates the brands,
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: On Monday, November 2, fashion heavy hitters and stylish stalwarts gathered at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City for the 2026 CFDA Awards. Now in its 45th year, the annual ceremony—often dubbed the Oscars of fashion—celebrates the brands, designers, and talent shaping the industry in America and abroad.

Hosted by Keke Palmer, the 2026 CFDA Awards promise to be as electric as ever. Tory Burch is this year’s Positive Change Award recipient for her philanthropic efforts through the Tory Burch Foundation as well as a nominee for American Womenswear Designer of the Year. Famed architect Peter Marino, who has designed flagships for brands like Chanel, Dior, and Louis Vuitton, is this year’s Fashion Icon honoree. Notably, Anthony Vaccarello is to be named International Designer of the Year, honoring his influential tenure at Saint Laurent. After a decade at the helm of the French brand and a final gold-dipped spring 2027 show in Paris, the designer officially left his role as creative director last month.

Along with a star-studded audience, select A-listers will also grace the stage to present. Lupita Nyong’o will announce the American Womenswear Designer of the Year, Matt Damon will present the American Menswear Designer of the Year, and Naomi Osaka will give out the American Accessory Designer of the Year. As has become tradition, before any awards are announced, the 2026 nominees and honorees will hit the red carpet with a handful of their friends and muses. For Vaccarello, that means likely appearances from his pals and house ambassadors Hailey Bieber, Zoë Kravitz, and Rosé. You can expect VIPs wearing custom looks from everyone from Khaite, Diotima, The Row, Luar, Colleen Allen, Michael Kors and more.
