Charli XCX was in the same headspace when she released Brat and It’s Completely Different but Also Still Brat in 2024. “There’s still so many different versions of that song that could be made using a tiny element of the production from the original, or a tiny reference to a lyrical concept, or a literal lyric,” she said at the time. “It can all be deconstructed and put back together again. Why not? Why just be like, ‘It’s the album, and it’s done?’”

The possibilities are endless, especially when it comes down to locking down features. For Girl’s Trip, Larsson reached out to potential collaborators via DMs, shifting her approach depending on whether she already had an existing relationship with them. Sometimes MNEK made the connection. Margo can’t quite remember which route led to Shakira featuring on “Eurosummer,” but does recall the craziness of that particular yes. “We gotta figure this out,” she thought. “We gotta make this a bop.” It wasn’t the only version they made. There’s a “Eurosummer” remix with Romanian dance-pop stars Alexandra Stan and Inna sitting on a computer somewhere. “I know that has been very wanted by the internet, and there were a lot of rumors going around about it,” Margo says. “It does exist. That’s all I can say.”

Robinson’s process was far more free-flowing in comparison. He primarily reached out to friends and people he thought would be cool to spotlight, like the indie-pop singer EJEAN who he found through a twist of fate (read: Instagram Reels, in an incredibly rare instance, he says). “I would love to hear your version of ‘Year of the Cup’ because I think you would make the most heartwrenching version of this,” Robinson said in a message to EJEAN.

“Year of the Cup” is not really the kind of song you can flip. The original ballad samples a Lil Wayne interview from 2009 in a way that is both disjointed and completely enchanting. “It’s almost impossible to make a dance remix of it,” Robinson says. EJEAN covered it instead. Their stripped back acoustic version is the standout moment on Smile! : D Plus+.

It struck Robinson to process someone else singing words that hold so much weight to him. “When I heard them say ‘something’s in the air like vanilla,’ or these experiences where I know specifically where my two feet were in the world when those moments happened in my real life,” he says, “it gave me this twisted up feeling inside. It was like, ‘I wonder what that means to them.’” Even beyond lyrics, the sheer tone of a voice can communicate emotion so differently. Turnstile showed as much with Never Enough: Versions, a 22-track cover project with a host of guests including Hayley Williams, Elton John, and A. G. Cook. “You put everything into making an album,” Robinson says. “Anything that you can do to refresh it and remind people of its importance and remind people of what it means to you, and extend its lifespan culturally — I think there’s good reasons to do that.”

There’s a certain trust and vulnerability required to let another artist reconfigure songs born from such specific experiences and perspectives. Sometimes, doubt gets in the way. Robinson considered reaching out to Jane Remover to participate in Smile! : D Plus+ through the rapper-producer’s EDM side project, Leroy. There were threads of influence and connection there, but they hadn’t properly met before, so he decided against it. “I was too shy to ask,” he says. “I should have just asked.” He would have also loved to hear something from Smile! : D reimagined by a K-pop artist, like KiiiKiii or Aespa, similar to how PinkPantheress recruited Seventeen for “Illegal.”

These crossovers are as exciting for the artists as they are for the audience. They offer something new without completely compromising the original listeners fell for, while also potentially expanding their palette. “It’s a non-algorithmic, non-AI way of finding new things you like, and you’ll never find the end of things that you like,” says Angel. The special moments created on these projects — whether something as explosive as “Stateside,” or Lorde and Charli XCX working it out on the “Girl, So Confusing” remix, or Robinson pouring back into a lineage of his own influence — are the product of true connection.
“It’s so amazing for me to be able to hold hands with those people and the respect is so mutual,” Robinson says. “And doing it as a way of celebrating the album, it’s a win-win for everybody.”

items.title: Adam Driver Won’t Return for ‘Girls’: ‘I Wish Them the Best of Luck’
items.description: Adam Driver had a major breakout thanks to his role on “Girls,” but the actor shut down the idea of returning for the reboot of the iconic series in a recent interview.
items.author: Pat Saperstein
paragraphs: Adam Driver had a major breakout thanks to his role on “Girls,” but the actor shut down the idea of returning for the reboot of the iconic series in a recent interview.

While talking about his role in James Gray’s new movie “Paper Tiger,” Driver was asked by Cinema Blend if he will be returning for the revival. “No, but I wish them the best of luck,” he told the outlet.

News of the new “Girls” series broke in mid-October, with creator and star Lena Dunham set to return as Hannah Horvath alongside co-stars Allison Williams as Marnie Michaels, Jemima Kirke as Jessa Johansson and Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna Shapiro. Andrew Rannells also returns to the role of Elijah Krantz.
The series will have a limited five-episode run on HBO with production starting in 2027.

Driver’s career took off after his run as Hannah’s boyfriend on “Girls.” In addition to his role as Kylo Ren in three “Star Wars” movies, he starred in “Marriage Story” and “The Meyerowitz Stories” for Noah Baumbach; “The Last Duel” and “House of Gucci” for Ridley Scott; “Ferrari” for Michael Mann and this year’s “Misty Green.” He’s also worked with director Jim Jarmusch on “Paterson,” “The Dead Don’t Die” and “Father Mother Sister Brother.”

In her recent memoir “Famesick,” Dunham described her tumultuous relationship with Driver, saying, “He could be short-tempered and verbally aggressive, condescending and physically imposing. He could also be protective, loving even,” Dunham writes. After the last episode of “Girls” wrapped, Dunham says Driver told her, “I hope you know I’ll always love you” before he said goodbye.

items.title: James Bond Surprise: Robert Pattinson Screen Tested to Play 007
items.description: In a surprise few saw coming, Robert Pattinson has emerged as a contender for 007. The actor, 40, is among those who have screen tested for the role of James Bond, multiple sources tell The Hollywood Reporter, joining hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jo
items.author: Borys Kit; Aaron Couch
paragraphs: In a surprise few saw coming, Robert Pattinson has emerged as a contender for 007. The actor, 40, is among those who have screen tested for the role of James Bond, multiple sources tell The Hollywood Reporter, joining hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor.

Conventional wisdom has been that the next man to get the license to kill would not be a globally recognized star like Pattinson, one of the biggest actors of his age cohort, and already the face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise. The screen tests are said to have occurred the weekend of Oct. 24. THR previously reported that four, possibly five actors were in the mix but only three names surfaced at the time.
Another name now surfacing as one of the Bond mystery men is Nicholas Hoult, a runnerup to Pattinson for Batman years ago.

Pattinson is a favorite of auteurs from Robert Eggers and the Safdie brothers to Christopher Nolan, whose 2020 spy movie Tenet might feel like a Bond audition in hindsight. And more importantly, he worked with Bond director Denis Villeneuve on the upcoming Dune: Part 3, which bows Dec. 18 and is said to have gone well for the two men.

The actor is in the midst of the biggest year of his career, with a key role in Nolan’s The Odyssey and as the co-lead of A24 hit The Drama and anchoring the well-reguarded movie Primetime, also from A24. He’s currently filming The Batman Part II in London, where screen tests have been taking place.
Amazon had no comment on the testing.

While conventional wisdom goes against a world famous Bond, these are unprecedented times in the franchise. It is the first Bond movie made under the control of Amazon, which bought out the creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025. And producing are Spider-Man‘s Amy Pascal and David Heyman, producer of the Harry Potter movies. A young Pattinson broke out with a tragic role in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, before gaining global fame a few years later in Twilight.

The Bond casting search comes 21 years after Daniel Craig was set as the next James Bond back in October 2005. He retired from the role after five films with 2021’s No Time to Die, his tenure including the franchise’s first and only $1 billion hit, the 2012 feature Skyfall.

items.title: ‘The Bachelor’ Returns, ‘The Rookie’ Moves as ABC Sets Midseason Schedule
items.description: ABC had previously announced premiere dates for The Rookie and its spinoff, The Rookie: North. Both shows are set for Wednesday, Jan. 6 — a move from The Rookie’s Tuesday home of the past few seasons.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: ABC had previously announced premiere dates for The Rookie and its spinoff, The Rookie: North. Both shows are set for Wednesday, Jan. 6 — a move from The Rookie’s Tuesday home of the past few seasons.

The network has now released it full midseason lineup, and the move for The Rookie is not a temporary one: It and The Rookie: North will form a two-hour block on Wednesday nights, giving the veteran show an earlier time (9 p.m. instead of 10 p.m.) and the new spinoff a well-established — and presumably very compatible — lead-in as support.

Season three of Shifting Gears will join the two Rookie shows on Wednesdays. The comedy starring Tim Allen and Kat Dennings will premiere with two episodes on Jan. 6; Abbott Elementary will rejoin the lineup the following week.

Will Trent and High Potential are set to return in their usual Tuesday spots on Jan. 5. An ABC News Studios-produced unscripted show called Surviving a Scandal will fill the 10 p.m. hour. High Potential is also getting the post-Super Bowl showcase on Feb. 14.

At the far end of ABC’s midseason slate is the return of The Bachelor franchise to the network on March 21. With behind-the-scenes upheaval and last season’s scrapped Bachelorette season starring Taylor Frankie Paul, the Bachelor-verse has been absent from ABC since the November 2025 finale of The Golden Bachelor’s second season. The Bachelor last aired in March 2025.
American Idol is set to begin its 25th season (and 10th on ABC) on Feb. 8. The network has also set a retrospective special about the show for Feb. 1.
One other note: ABC has pushed the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff it ordered in the spring to the 2027-28 season. That’s not a surprise, considering the show hasn’t been cast yet.
ABC’s midseason dates, including those for the Grammys and Oscars, are below. All times are ET/PT unless noted.
10 p.m.: Surviving a Scandal
10 p.m.: The Rookie: North
8 p.m.: Celebrity Jeopardy!
8 p.m.: American Idol at 25 (working title)
7 p.m. ET/4 p.m. PT: Grammy Awards
10 p.m.: Shark Tank (new night)
6:30 p.m. ET/3:30 p.m. PT: Super Bowl LXI
7 p.m. ET/4 p.m. PT: The Oscars
10 p.m.: What Would You Do?

items.title: 22 Killer Watches I Saw at One of New York’s Most Exclusive Collector Hangs
items.description: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.
items.author: Cam Wolf
paragraphs: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

I knew the watch collector meetup I was going to was legit when its organizer sent this text to the group: “We’ve engaged an off-duty NYPD detective to work security for our dinner. So, now really no reason not to bring your best!”

Last Wednesday night, at a fancy steakhouse in Midtown Manhattan, I was reminded why I love these enthusiast-organized events. This one was relatively small in comparison to blowouts like Rolliefest, but the idea was the same: A dozen or so collectors brought along their most prized timepieces and plunked them down on the table unattended (besides the off-duty NYPD detective, of course). When I asked one attendee if I could take his Breguet—similar to one heading to auction this weekend with a $73,000 estimate—across the room to take a photograph, he reacted like I’d asked if I could breathe oxygen: Of course! What a silly question. Events like these genuinely reflect the best of the hobby: deeply passionate collectors who really just want to share their watches with like-minded obsessives.

Between bites of miniature beef wellingtons and medium-rare steak, the guests passed around and ogled the dozens of grails on display. There were new classics on the table—including Vacheron Constantin’s Ultra-Thin, a leading contender for watch of the year—alongside plenty of old ones, including every flavor of vintage Rolex, from GMT-Masters to Daytonas to Explorer IIs. I was standing with one collector as he examined a pretty vintage Rolex GMT-Master. He stopped and looked around. So-and-so must be here, he muttered aloud. How did he know? Because he recognized the shade of the patina on the dial.

This particular group started getting together a couple of years ago, after the collectors @HorologicallyMinded, @s_h_lemon, @null_islands, and @jmsfisk (everyone at the event asked to remain anonymous) met at another watch-related retreat. @HorologicallyMinded, or HM, says that collecting was at one point something he did in solitude. “People generally judge when they learn how much watches cost,” HM tells me. “You paid how much for that!?” But he and the other three founders began meeting up for monthly dinners before eventually taking turns to organize these larger events. “This group has been the most rewarding part of this hobby,” HM says. “It’s been so great to have a group of people that have a common interest, but it’s not work-related and no one judges.”

Although the group has grown, the core four are still instrumental in making sure the functions go off without a hitch, with just the right spread of watches on the tables. “It is very deliberate and the four of us generally coordinate on it,” HM says. “We specifically make sure there is something for everyone.” That means ensuring there are at least a handful of watches worth less than $10,000—this time, that included several Rolex Datejusts, a Vulcain Cricket, and a gold Breitling from the 1940s. “We knew we were having some relative newbies and different people have different budgets, and we want everyone to be comfortable.” On the other end of the spectrum, some grail-level pieces were special requests from other members of the group.

All the watches wound up getting plenty of TLC. “I love the fact that we’re a group that can, and did, totally geek out about a vintage Longines Legend Diver, while a Doré dial Patek is on the same table,” HM says.
Below are some of the very best pieces I saw that night.
A Patek Philippe ref. 3970, part of the house’s historic lineage of pieces that combine a perpetual calendar with a chronograph. The dial on this one is so tasty.
A skeletonized Breguet Ref. 3355PT00PA0—maybe the watch of the night for me—on a show-stopping platinum bracelet.

A few years ago, MB&F started making more approachable versions of its sci-fi-ready watches and allocating them through a lottery system. This is the M.A.D2, with an outer ring on the dial that spins around very quickly. It’s really fun.
The aforementioned Rolex GMT-Master is a ref. 16760, a model produced during the ’80s that’s nicknamed the “Sophia Loren” thanks to its curvaceous profile.
Omega has incredible stuff in its archives. This is a chronograph from the ’30s that’s controlled entirely through that single button at 2 o’clock.

A couple of real bangers here. The Vacheron on the left is known as the “Cioccolatone,” because it resembles a square of chocolate. At the center is the Patek Philippe ref. 3417, an antimagnetic watch with just about the prettiest typography you’ll ever see on a watch. Zohran Mamdani should adopt that cursive for signs in the city, because it can make just about anything look nice: Warning: Rats. Or maybe, No Dumping Here.
A cloisonné dial from—of all brands—IWC! I am such a sucker for a cloisonné, which refers to the intricate images carefully fashioned from wire and colorful baked enamel.

A beautiful example of one of the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch from the ’50s through the ’70s, back when the latter was still a rugged outdoor outfitter. The shades of orange, yellow, and blue are dreamy.
A monochromatic take on the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar, which was produced in the ’80s and ’90s but looks incredibly modern.

Universal Genève finally relaunched last year after decades on the shelf, but it’s hard to beat the originals. This Polerouter comes on an extremely cool “wave” bracelet, which basically uses a repeating chevron pattern to make the slinky bit of metal appear to be in motion.

During World War II, a dozen watch manufacturers came together to make models following a strict set of specifications for the British Ministry of Defence. One of those brands was Longines, which produced this strapping piece.
You didn’t think we’d wrap this list up without a gorgeous yellow-gold Daytona, did you?
The ultimate fusion of sport and luxury watches. Heuer supplied this ’70s-era Carrera to Ferrari’s racing team, including legendary drivers like Jacky Ickx, Niki Lauda, and Clay Regazzoni.
This Patek is cool, but the bracelet is insane.

This isn’t your average Patek Philippe Nautilus. PP began producing this reference 3800 in 1981 as a smaller counterpart to the original. The few times I’ve gotten to try one on, I’m always struck by how perfect the proportions are. It’s nice and thin and looks just right on the wrist.
The United States Merchant Marines’ logo really punches up this Day-Date.
The ref. 6541 is the most beloved version of the Rolex Milgauss. It was produced in the ’50s and features a signature honeycomb dial. One sold for $2.5 million at auction in 2023.
Is there a better way to time your yacht race than with this Heuer Skipper? Probably not.

items.title: ‘I’m 100 Percent at War With Trump’: MAGA Revolts After Midterms Wipeout
items.description: Many MAGAworld figures are already pointing the finger of blame for their midterm losses squarely at President Donald Trump and his policies.
items.author: David Gilbert
paragraphs: Many MAGAworld figures are already pointing the finger of blame for their midterm losses squarely at President Donald Trump and his policies.
Trump spent Tuesday evening lashing out at Fox News for platforming the Democrats who swept aside their GOP opponents in deep red states and took control of the House and Senate.

“[Fox] bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” the president wrote on Truth Social. Later in the night, he called in to Fox News, where he congratulated the Democrats on their results.

Trump made clear that he doesn’t think the historic blowout was a reflection of his popularity, writing, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” He then posted a picture of a red baseball hat with the word VETO embossed on the front.
But in the hours that followed, MAGA revolted.

Matt Walsh, a right-wing podcaster, called the results “a political catastrophe of historic proportions” and Trump “an 80-year-old lame-duck president.” Walsh blamed Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran and his focus on trivial matters like attempting to rename artificial intelligence super intelligence and the White House ballroom.
For right-wing commentator Mike Cernovich, it was Trump’s decision to ostracize libertarian voters that was partly to blame.

Mike Flynn, the disgraced former national security adviser who was among the most prominent voices pushing bogus conspiracies about the 2020 election being stolen, also blamed Trump, writing on X, “Someone needs to look in a mirror.” Flynn also blamed Christians for not showing up to vote.
But noted conspiracy theorist Alex Jones had another take on why Trump was to blame.

“I think he’s a Democrat. I’m gonna just say it right now,” Jones said on his show Tuesday night. “I’ve tried to salvage Trump. I’ve not been sure. I’ve invested so much—maybe I was blind to it—I think he’s the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell, and he works for them. I’m 100 percent at war with Trump.”
Other MAGA figures like right-wing commentators Jack Posobiec and Nick Sortor both blamed Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran for the losses but didn’t directly name Trump in their posts.

Unsurprisingly, Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former congresswoman who broke decisively with Trump earlier this year, also blamed the president. “Tonight was a total referendum on Trump. He told people to vote like he was on the ballot and they did,” Greene wrote on X.
One notable aspect of MAGAworld’s response to Tuesday’s GOP wipeout was the relative silence coming from some of Trump’s biggest supporters.

Elon Musk, who poured hundreds of millions of dollars into supporting losing Republican candidates, has not said who was to blame for the results. He did post a joke saying his “election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time” and commented that it was “interesting” that an exit poll showed the Iran war was a “massive losing issue.”

Rogan O’Handley, a vocal MAGA influencer known as DC Draino who posts incessantly on X about politics, has also not reacted publicly to the results. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, who was reelected on Tuesday night, said the results were “not what we’d hoped and fought for” but failed to say what or who was to blame.

White House deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser Stephen Miller has also not commented publicly on the results, but his wife, Katie Miller, who boosted election conspiracy theories earlier on Tuesday, laid the blame on the media, which she called “a propaganda arm of the woke left.”

There were, however, a few right-wing figures who continued to publicly support Trump despite the losses, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who wrote, “President Trump is a hero for stopping Iran from having a nuclear weapon, and now he should finish the job.” Instead of blaming Trump, Loomer spent Tuesday evening lamenting the end of America and the rise of communism.

Another right-wing figure continuing to back Trump was the former Fox News host turned conspiracy theorist Lara Logan, who blamed an anonymous group of Republicans who conspired to bring about the defeat so they could “get rid of the MAGA movement and the establishment would retake the party.”
Chaya Raichik, who runs the hugely popular LibsofTikTok accounts, blamed the losses on a years-long Democrat plot to import “millions of foreigners.”

Kari Lake, Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Jamaica, also refused to lay the blame at the president’s feet and was one of the few election deniers who continued to boost claims of a stolen election. “America, do you think that our elections are honest? Do you have complete confidence that only legal votes were counted?” Lake wrote in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

Others, like Harrison Smith, a host on Steve Bannon’s War Room show, turned their ire on their fellow right-wing influencers. He blamed Loomer, Ben Shapiro, Mark Levin, Will Chamberlain, and AIPAC, the prominent lobbying organization, for the losses.

But at least one former Trumpworld figure did take the blame on themselves. Former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem posted on X that the massive losses happened because “we were too successful in the first year of the Trump administration.”

items.title: Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist
items.description: For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphone
items.author: Matt Burgess
paragraphs: For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.

Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.

Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.

“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”

Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.

Binance says activity linked to the hack can first be traced back to June this year. At the time, its update says, an engineer the company refers to as Engineer A downloaded a “tampered Homebrew installation” they found searching online. While the company says this was detected and dealt with, information about the employee was later “exposed to the hacker.”

At the start of September, Binance says another software engineer, identified only as Engineer B, was contacted on “a legitimate job-hunting platform” and then attended a video interview where the fake recruiter shared legitimate-looking social media accounts and personal photos to make them seem real. The Binance engineer progressed, unsurprisingly, to a second-round interview that was conducted using an online chat. “Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” Binance’s report says.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” the company writes. It adds that hackers took steps to hide their activity, a common practice.

Toward the end of October, a little more than a week before the hack, Binance says, the attackers used their access to the engineer’s machine to “gain control” over the wallet of Engineer A, who had been compromised months earlier, and “another Wallet Software Engineer C.” Then on October 29, Binance says, the attackers logged in to the computer of another staff member, Software Engineer C, and used stolen login details before launching the attack. On the evening of the theft, according to Binance, the attack unfolded quickly. “The attacker exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process,” the company writes.

Sophos’s Pilling says TraderTraitor “excels” in its attacks through detailed planning and being able to understand how the services of those it hacks operate. “The initial compromise is just a foothold,” he says. “The real attack is carefully engineered around how the victim actually moves money.”

While Binance says its findings are only the initial step of its investigation, security and crypto tracing experts say that the hackers are undertaking efforts to launder and cash out the stolen cryptocurrency. Since the start of 2017, according to analysis by TRM Labs, North Korean–linked hackers have stolen around $12 billion in cryptocurrency—with more than half of that coming from heists this year.

Despite the astronomical sums, it is unclear how much of this money makes it back to North Korea. As in the Binance case, some cryptocurrencies can be frozen and made inaccessible, while other transactions can be blocked by some cryptocurrency exchanges. Crypto tracing company Elliptic has said the laundering from the Binance attack has been “highly complex” and likely to be automated. “In its first three and a half days it used about 12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains, roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, and more than 40,000 transactions,” Elliptic cofounder and chief scientist Tom Robinson wrote in a blog post.

If the money can be laundered successfully, there is a chance it will be converted to cash and used to bolster the development of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program and ballistic missile systems, according to a report published last year from the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which includes experts from the United States, South Korea, and nine other countries. “They are highly reliant on Chinese underground banking and China-based facilitators, though they sometimes rely upon facilitators in other countries.”

items.title: Anti-Oligarchy Activists Plan to Dox Elon Musk and Hundreds of Billionaire-Linked Homes
items.description: An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s boar
items.author: Dell Cameron
paragraphs: An underground activist group says it plans to start openly doxing billionaires as part of a phased campaign against what it calls the American oligarchy—beginning this month with a release that maps the homes of Elon Musk, his brother Kimbal, and Tesla’s board, alongside investors and suppliers that keep the corporation afloat.

Two of its members, interviewed by WIRED on the condition of anonymity, say they spent the past year constructing dossiers on billionaires—and one trillionaire—and the people they consider their top lieutenants, using nearly every method available to a private investigator, and some that are not.

The pair say the group is international and includes grassroots activists, researchers, journalists, and artists, including some who received top honors in print, television, and digital media in their former careers. For security, many work in “silos” and do not know each other’s names. Through its connections, the group says it has raised more than $1.2 million from “a heartening number of wealthy class traitors” who share in the view that concentrations of extreme wealth and political power pose an “existential threat.”

In a press release Monday, the group says it intends to publish in coming releases more than 150 home addresses, most of them previously unreported. It also promises more than 3,500 records on people with a combined wealth of about $1.4 trillion, plus reporting on what the group alleges are “criminal exploits and security lapses.”
Members of the organization call themselves Capytistas, a play on Zapatistas, the Indigenous insurgents of southern Mexico.

The capybara, a placid rodent famous for getting along with almost any other animal, became the group’s avatar during the early days of Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency, as a secret rival to the Shiba Inu—the Doge meme Musk used to brand the agency. (The meme has since been reclaimed by pro-Ukranian activists who post as cartoon dogs to mock Russian propaganda and raise money for the war.)

Americans have long used the term “oligarch” to refer almost exclusively to Russian tycoons who carved up state industries after the Soviet collapse. But it entered mainstream American politics decisively in January 2025, when President Joe Biden used his farewell address to warn that an “oligarchy is taking shape in America.” No one typifies the “extreme wealth, power, and influence” Biden described more than the trillionaire Musk, who held an unpaid job as a special government employee for much of 2025 and has thrown more than $700 million into federal elections since 2023; the equivalent of roughly 15 million typical donations online.

Doxing—the Capytistas’ chosen tactic—has meanwhile become a favored weapon of political guerrillas and self-appointed state informants: In March 2025, as protesters gathered outside Tesla dealerships, an anonymous site called DOGEQuest posted what it claims were the addresses of Tesla owners and DOGE staff. Months later, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement official testified that his unit drew more than three-quarters of its deportation referrals from Canary Mission—a site with similarly nebulous funding but radically different goals: building dossiers on pro-Palestinian students and professors.

Few have done more to expand doxing than the Department of Homeland Security itself, which simply broadened the term to include, effectively, any “videotaping” of law enforcement. Its aggressive stance on keeping officers’ faces hidden, and its refusal to identify those credibly accused of crimes, has all but ensured public campaigns to unmask its employees. Last week, hackers published the names and work contacts of more than 40,000 DHS employees and contractors, citing its practice of collecting data on the public while hiding who its officers are.

Pressed on whether its strategy amounted to doxing, the Capytistas members agree that it does, saying they have no qualms with describing their efforts that way. The group has even taken as its creed an adapted quote from the late folk singer and labor organizer Utah Phillips: “Democracy is not dying, it’s being killed,” they say, “and those who are killing it have names and addresses.”

Most of the Capytistas’ work involves digging up property records, court filings, and the LLCs and trusts that wealthy people use to buy real estate. The activists say they turn occasionally, but far less often, to physical surveillance, human infiltration, and advertising intelligence, the location and profile data bought and sold through online ad markets.

To remain profitable, one of the Capytistas argued, the businesses billionaires operate need to continuously collect people’s personal information, often nonconsensually, even as their owners and executives enjoy relatively private lives—entire fortunes built around “doxmaxxing.”

A copy of the Musk dossier seen by WIRED sorts its subjects into tiers and contains 32 home addresses tied to Musk and his executives. Musk is the “primary target.” Tesla’s board members and top executives—among them board chair Robyn Denholm and Kimbal Musk—are “secondary targets.” Each profile pairs a critical biography, drawn from court rulings, labor board decisions, and securities filings, with a home address. Investors such as Vanguard and BlackRock and nearly 40 suppliers are considered “tertiary targets,” listed only by corporate office, factory, or mine.
Tesla’s press office and investor relations team did not respond to requests for comment.

The Capytistas see Musk as effectively a gateway for normies who have yet to join its class war. Its file on him is among the smallest it has prepared, and he ranks among its “least important” targets, members say. But he was chosen first because no other person draws as much public anger, and the group hopes to harness that and release it upon others whose fortunes rely on forever wars, omnipresent surveillance, and carceral expansion.

Law enforcement records obtained by WIRED show how quickly that anger spread across the country last year. Within months of Musk’s arrival in Washington, attacks on Tesla vehicles and dealerships had hit at least nine states, according to a joint FBI-DHS bulletin released under public records law. Other documents show intelligence analysts warning cops across the country that calls to boycott Tesla and protest Musk were multiplying alongside the attacks. Hundreds of demonstrations were planned barely two months after Trump took office for the second time.

In Nevada, analysts were forced to issue formal first responder guides to fighting electric-vehicle battery fires, which they said can take up to 8,000 gallons of water to extinguish. “As a high-profile tech company tied to immense wealth and business culture, Tesla can potentially represent those grievances,” one bulletin said of vandals who had “expressed anti-corporate or anti-capitalist views.” Musk’s role at DOGE in particular, a Northern California agency wrote, had made Tesla dealerships “symbolically larger targets.”

The Capytistas say doxing gives them one thing above all: a sense among those targeted that someone is watching. Some, they hope, will simply fold under the sheer weight of that attention. For the rest, the group wants the public to make its displeasure well known, hoping for protests outside homes and on golf courses—confrontations with those who buy their way into government in the very places they go to escape all the outrage.

Privacy is the one thing that the group believes billionaires, and now trillionaires, value that activists can take away. “The Capytistas intend to level the playing field,” it says, “by giving oligarchs a taste of the invasions of privacy they commit, and monetize, every day.”

Tech executives’ homes have already become targets. In April, San Francisco police arrested a 20-year-old man they say threw an incendiary device at the home of OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, setting fire to an exterior gate. The man returned less than an hour later to threaten to burn down the company’s headquarters. No one was hurt.

In the interview with WIRED ahead of the release, one member pointed to the killing of UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson in December 2024, arguing that what the group is doing is trying to prevent such bloodshed—a sentiment echoed in a statement released by the Capytistas on Monday: “While Elon Musk and the other individuals we target will undoubtedly try to frame our work as extreme and stochastic, what we’re doing is using radical accountability to build an off-ramp that might prevent the inevitable violent and tragic outcomes the oligarch class has been steering us toward.”
“In the end,” they said, “we may be doing them a favor.”

items.title: Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
items.description: At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed
items.author: Matt Burgess
paragraphs: At first glance, the self-proclaimed “pet portrait” app Viefur appears to be just another AI slop generator. Using digital coins sold in the app—around $4 will buy 130 coins—pet photos can be turned into an “anthropomorphic portrait,” with the critter dressed in “human clothing” and inserted into bizarre scenes. Think a hamster wearing beach shorts, sunglasses, and lounging in a swimming pool or a Hawaiian shirt-wearing cat, drinking from a coconut.
All of this is cover for what appears to be the app’s true purpose: creating sexually abusive deepfake images.

A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps that, like Viefur, often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

The network was discovered hiding in plain sight, by multiple researchers, after they investigated links from thousands of video ads containing explicit deepfake content that were published on Meta’s Facebook and Instagram. As WIRED has reported in recent months, hundreds of these ads contained AI generated child sexual abuse material, including images of real children and a member of a European royal family. The ads reached tens of thousands of people and have prompted investigations from regulators around the world.

In each case, the ads linked out to the deceptive apps in Apple and Google’s app stores—allowing people to generate explicit images and make payments using Apple and Google Pay. The network behind the nudify apps appears to have been publishing them for around a year, at times publishing dozens per week. This is despite Google, Apple, and Meta saying they enforce their policies that do not allow harmful deepfake content on their platforms.

The apps and domains investigated by WIRED appear to be run by Chinese developers and a Hong Kong registered entity called KeLing Technology Limited, according to a review of web domains and how the services operate. Email addresses linked to the entity, apps, and related services, did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED, but after being contacted, they appeared to erase public connections between KeLing Technology Limited and the deepfake tools.

“This is an organized, commercially run operation: One operator behind hundreds of disposable apps and domains, cloaked to pass App Store review and pushed through tens of thousands of Meta ads under fake payer names,” says Paul Bouchaud, a lead researcher at the nonprofit AI Forensics, who investigated the network. “They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.”

Download one of the apps in the deepfake network and you may see exactly what was advertised—such as an app to create AI pet pictures. But behind the scenes, researchers found, the apps are quietly making determinations about whether to show the benign content or load a web interface showing explicit deepfakes.

“Each time the application is downloaded, there is a call to the server with some information, such as where the user is coming from, the language, some unique identifier, and then the server replies whether or not to show the explicit or the non-explicit version of it,” explains Bouchaud, who reverse engineered the apps’ and associated websites’ code. They say there’s no clear list of reasons why one user may be shown the explicit version of an app, but one trigger appears to be downloading it after clicking an associated ad on Meta’s platforms.

Websites linked to the apps have revealed the network’s secrets and the scale that it operates on. Opening one of the apps’ websites will likely show an entirely black screen and no content. The only noticeable change is that the URL updates to include the word “risk.” But the websites host the hidden explicit deepfake layer that can be loaded in each app.

This web interface contains dozens of pornography deepfake video and image templates—with users able to upload images of people to be added to the sexual scenes. The interface allows the purchase of “diamonds” to generate images and links to other social media accounts where users can contact the developers with questions or complaints.

Also hidden in the websites’ code are details about the entire network. A JavaScript bundle that can easily be unpicked, researchers say, contains a list of all the domains and apps that have been created by the developers—including app package details, encryption keys, Facebook advertising trackers, and more.

“They contained this giant configuration list of other domains with different encryption keys,” says Maël Le Touz, a staff threat researcher at security firm Infoblox, who identified almost 500 linked domains. “They run the same code and they all reference one another.”

Bouchard’s analysis of when domains were registered found that the apps started to appear toward the end of 2025, with a spike during the spring of this year. At one point, around 30 nudify apps-websites were being registered each week, the researcher says, with 27 live on Google’s Play Store in September. These apps had been downloaded more than 350,000 times collectively and many were rated suitable for all age groups, Bouchard’s research says.

One of the most popular apps, called DiffAI, was created in December 2025 and has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store. A user review on Google’s Play Store stated: “This app contains templates for creating CSAM and other types of pornographic material. It performs no age verification.”

DiffAI was removed from the Play Store shortly before WIRED contacted Google about the network. Google did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, though it had removed the majority of the apps ahead of being contacted. (Portions of the deepfake network were reported on by Danish journalists in September.)

Similarly, Apple removed 19 apps from its App Store, including pet photo app Viefur, after WIRED asked the company about the activity and shared associated domains. “We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for our users, and nudification apps and other pornographic content are strictly prohibited,” says Apple spokesperson Adam Dema.

“We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them,” Dema says. “After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.” The company says it has suspended tens of thousands of apps for using these “bait-and-switch” tactics over the last year and recently updated its app store rules to further restrict “nudify” tools.

Central to the “nudify” network appears to be a host of Chinese developers whose identities seem to have been intentionally hidden. “It’s using exclusive Chinese hosting, the code is written in Chinese and has a lot of comments in Chinese,” Le Touz says, noting explicit videos in ads posted to Meta’s platforms promoting the apps contained watermarks from Chinese-language video editing software.

The apps and domains across the network have often used generic privacy policies, free email addresses from Gmail or Outlook, and obscure developer names as part of their alleged efforts to hide their connections. Ads for the apps posted on Meta’s platforms have also used apparently false names—such as Draftmondcreldbro Duhustepre and Swaldmungsha Glasirdcroldshold—and pages with no followers. Since the start of this year, Bouchaud’s research has found tens of thousands of explicit deepfake ads linked to the network—often using similar language in their advertising copy—on Meta’s platforms.

“These ads violate not just one, but several of Meta’s policies,” says Katie Paul, the director of the Tech Transparency Project, who first uncovered the ads showing deepfake explicit depictions of minors. “There is no question about what you are seeing, what the app is advertising,” she says. Paul says tech companies need to answer questions about where money generated from the apps goes and how those behind the nudification apps and services constantly seem to bypass their content moderation and safety systems.

KeLing Technology Limited appears to be a significant part of the operation. While the company’s website is little more than a shell, its name was listed as the contact details of the first website registered in the network. This website’s brand name also appeared as part of the contact details within the explicit deepfake template that was used in the apps. Bouchaud also identified an administration login page linked to the explicit deepfake interface that mentions “Keling.” And email addresses using the company’s domain appeared on at least one app that have been removed from app stores.

Towards the end of September, a notification sent to users of the explicit deepfake interface announced that a new AI model could be used—the model was called Veyra, with a tagline in the apps of “More real. More natural. More wild.” The homepage of a website called Veyra AI listed its contact email as a KeLing Technology address.

When WIRED contacted KeLing email addresses, plus some of those listed in apps privacy policies, we received no response. However, after WIRED reached out, someone renamed some of the associated online social media channels, removed KeLing email addresses from the AI Veyra website, and removed the KeLing Technology Limited address from the first registered website.

Meta says it banned KeLing Technology Limited from advertising in 2025 after it failed to “comply with a cease and desist letter.” (Meta declined to share the letter with WIRED citing legal reasons.) “We have strict rules against promoting nudify apps and work aggressively to keep this material off our services,” a Meta spokesperson says. Meta says that while KeLing Technology Limited has continued to try and advertise through other ways, it takes action against the ads when it becomes aware of them.

After WIRED shared the 400-plus domains with Meta, the spokesperson said they had shared more than 3,000 associated ads linked to them, two-thirds of which it had already removed from its systems. Meta later told WIRED it has taken action against 11,600 ad accounts, more than 4,700 business pages, 5,200 users, and 15,000 pages linked to the domains, blocking 209 apps from advertising on its platforms.

“The criminals behind them take increasingly deceptive steps to evade detection—hiding behind fake names and identities, running ads that look benign, and sometimes linking to Google's and Apple's app stores, with the ads' true intent revealed only after a click,” the spokesperson says.
As WIRED finished reporting this story, similar ads and apps continued to be published on the tech platforms.

items.title: The American Dream Wasn’t Built for Climate Change
items.description: This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
items.author: Kate Yoder
paragraphs: This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

To Sierra Isley, the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.”

Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville.

It was a blessing in disguise. One month later, while Sierra and Jamie were still unpacking boxes and building furniture, the remnants of Hurricane Helene turned Asheville into a disaster zone. The basement of their apartment flooded, but they were luckier than some of their neighbors, whose homes had been destroyed.

Owning a home has long been seen as a cornerstone of the American Dream—a way to build wealth that you could use one day to pay for your children’s education and fund your retirement. That arrangement was always more precarious than it was made out to be. But as fires and floods damage homes and drive up insurance rates, pouring your life savings into a house has become riskier than ever. In a report called “Property Prices in Peril,” the firm First Street projected last year that climate risks could knock nearly $1.5 trillion off the value of American homes by 2055. For some people, the sociologist Rebecca Elliott wrote, “the American dream of homeownership may become a nightmare.”

Americans are beginning to grasp the threat that climate change poses to their aspirations. According to exclusive polling for Grist from the think tank Data for Progress, 58 percent of likely U.S. voters believe that climate change will hinder their ability to achieve the American Dream over the next 20 years, including 42 percent of Republicans. The survey suggests that people are worried that climate change will increase the cost of living, and such widespread concern very likely played a role in the major gains for Democrats last Tuesday.

The irony is that fossil fuels have long been promoted as necessary ingredients for the American “way of life.” Starting a century ago, oil and gas companies led extensive campaigns to tie their products to comfort and prosperity, a narrative that has been repeatedly deployed by politicians and oil industry executives to thwart climate action. President Donald Trump’s administration has often said that efforts to rein in fossil fuels threaten the American Dream. Earlier this year, when the administration scrapped Biden-era rules to cut emissions from cars, along with the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority to regulate climate change, it touted the effort as “restoring the American Dream.”

But the fossil-fueled American Dream is in the process of destroying itself. Greenhouse gas emissions from burning coal, oil, and gas have ushered in a new period of precarity, undermining the promise that each generation can expect a better life than the last. Scientific reports warn that climate change “imperil[s] the quality of life” for communities in the United States, disrupting livelihoods and cultural traditions.
Either Americans decide to reimagine what makes up the American Dream and abandon that oil-soaked version of prosperity, or climate change will dismantle it for them.

The memories of living through Hurricane Helene are still fresh in Isley’s mind. Hauling water from their flooded basement up to the toilet to flush it when the water ran out. Driving to Jamie’s parents’ house in Atlanta, holed up in a room with both of their cats until they couldn’t take it anymore. Coming back to Asheville and cooking meals in the Crock-Pot with disposable liners because even when the water was running again, it wasn’t safe to wash dishes with.

Two years later, Isley browses Zillow for fun, but she looks at homes through a post-disaster lens. “Now I have that fear in the back of my mind—anywhere near a river, or even a stream, if there’s a little bit of water on the map, I’m like, ‘Oh, no,’” she said. Jamie is trans, and after Trump was elected in 2024, the two of them briefly entertained the idea of moving somewhere with more protective policies, like California. But Isley’s mind immediately went to wildfires. Out of the question.

Isley had fled from hurricanes before, when she lived in Florida during college. She thought she’d be safe from them tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville was supposed to be a “climate haven,” somewhere that would fare better than the rest of the country as the world warmed. Those promises were shattered when almost 14 inches of rain fell on Asheville over three days in September 2024. The French Broad River overflowed its banks, flooding homes and destroying parts of the town’s River Arts District. In western North Carolina, more than 74,000 homes were damaged and only about 4 percent had flood insurance, resulting in $9.5 billion in uninsured residential property losses.

Home values in western North Carolina have declined since the storm, especially in the hardest-hit counties. Asheville’s average home price shrunk 5 percent over the past year, while the national average increased 1.2 percent.

To some degree, housing markets are already pricing in the risk of increased environmental hazards. Homes within FEMA’s high-risk flood zones sell for 2.8 percent less, on average, than what they would otherwise sell for, according to a 2023 study published in the journal Nature Climate Change. The researchers found that homes exposed to flood risk were still overvalued by between $121 billion and $237 billion, though—and they identified Appalachia as a hot spot of overvaluation, one year before Helene hit. The devaluation of homes in high-risk zones is unfolding unevenly and causing “tremendous social harm,” said Elliott, a sociology professor at The London School of Economics and Political Science.

Homes are billed as a way for people to build wealth, but they can turn into a trap. After Superstorm Sandy devastated New York City and the New Jersey coast in 2012, many homeowners couldn’t sell their houses for enough money to buy a new place, leaving them stranded. Even homes that haven’t seen any kind of devastation are at risk of losing value as more people become wary of living in floodplains, coastal places exposed to storms, and wildfire-prone areas. “Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable,” Elliott wrote in a study about property values and climate change.

Insurance is meant to offer a measure of safety when taking on a huge debt for a mortgage on a house. Douglas Heller, the director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, called it “the safety net for the American Dream.” But insurance rates are part of what’s making homeownership unaffordable for so many. Since 2020, property insurance costs have ballooned almost 80 percent, with the average single-family mortgage holder now paying $209 per month. Homeowners in the riskiest areas are paying substantially more, and many in California have been dropped by their insurers. Home insurance rates are rising faster in the Midwest than any other region, driven by the costs of severe storms.

“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace,” Heller said. The more extreme weather we’re seeing is only part of the story: He argues that the insurance industry has become a “climate opportunist,” using climate change as an excuse to justify excessive rate increases.

People relying on Social Security benefits who own condos around Lake Tahoe are particularly vulnerable to rising rates, said Andrew Engler, the founder and CEO of Rock Rose Risk, who helps people in California protect their homes against wildfire and get their insurance premiums down. They’re facing ballooning homeowners association payments, to share the cost of insurance in a risky wildfire area, on a limited paycheck. If they try to move, their properties are worth significantly less because of the huge HOA bills, Engler said. Economists estimate that rising insurance costs linked to disaster risk have reduced the growth of home prices by more than $40,000 in the most hurricane- and wildfire-prone ZIP codes.

Renting might make you more nimble, but it doesn’t insulate you from these costs. One reason rents are going up is because landlords’ property insurance rates are increasing. “Whether you are a homeowner or a renter, we’re all paying for living under the increased risks of climate change,” said Caroline Nagy, the associate director of housing policy at Americans for Financial Reform. That makes it harder for people to save for a home—if that’s even a good idea anymore.
When Sierra Isley walks around her neighborhood these days, she sees the evidence of Helene all around her—in the form of banners with the slogan “Asheville Strong” and shirts that say “WNC Strong.”

One of the most surprising things about disasters might be the way that people who live through them rise to the occasion and come together. In the aftermath of the Helene, with the power and cell service knocked out, Sierra and Jamie walked all around town, talking to their neighbors to try to learn what had happened. People started congregating at the fire station where there was fresh water.

“It’s hard to put into words what that experience was like, but I’ve never felt more of a community, and really having to lean on my neighbors and feeling like my neighbors were leaning on me,” Isley said.

While the American Dream is usually all about independence and personal freedom, living through a disaster has a way of revealing how people depend on each other. The experience can prompt people to hold tightly to what they have, doubling down on protecting their communities, said Nick Tinoco, a sociology researcher in a doctoral program at the University of California, Los Angeles, who interviewed survivors of the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Los Angeles County. Some of the residents he talked to have taken things into their own hands and organized volunteer fire brigades and plan to stay behind to defend their neighborhoods during future fires.

As supposedly safe “climate havens” like Asheville experience more disasters, the idea that people can simply move out of harm’s way is losing its grip. “I think we have to just reckon with the fact that we’re going to have to make people secure in the places that they live,” Elliott said.

She thinks it’s time to rethink the bargain of the American Dream—the expectation that so much of a person’s economic future depends on the fate of a single structure. Many young people have begun to define success differently. A poll from Ipsos last year showed that 46 percent of baby boomers associate homeownership with the American Dream but only 13 percent of Gen Zers do, suggesting that there’s room for its defining features to change.

Sierra and Jamie couldn’t help but wonder what happened to the house they’d almost bought, and they drove over to check it out soon after Hurricane Helene hit. It was still standing, but they couldn’t see if there was any damage hidden inside. “Who knows if it flooded or anything like that, what kind of storm damage it took, and that would have immediately been our problem,” Isley said.

Living through Hurricane Helene didn’t just make Isley relieved she hadn’t bought a house in Asheville. It has shaped what she wants for her life, helping her discover a passion for public health and pushing her to want to work in emergency preparedness. Now she’s applying to schools to pursue a master’s degree in public health.

“I think I owe it to people like me, people in other rural communities who are going to face the same kind of climate change emergencies, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters,” Isley said. “I just feel such a calling.”

items.title: Mormon Wives Star Jen Affleck Has Filed for Divorce
items.description: The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Jen Affleck, 27, has reportedly filed for divorce from her husband, Zac Affleck, 30. On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Jen filed a petition for divorce on Tuesday in Utah as well as a proposed parenting plan. The couple shar
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Jen Affleck, 27, has reportedly filed for divorce from her husband, Zac Affleck, 30. On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Jen filed a petition for divorce on Tuesday in Utah as well as a proposed parenting plan. The couple shares three children, and Jen is currently pregnant with their fourth.
Shortly after news of the divorce filing broke, a source told People that Zac is “doing okay.” “He and Jen are staying focused on preparing for the baby and supporting their kids,” the source added.

In a statement to People on Thursday, Zac said that he will “always be Jen’s supporter.” “Hope she is happy in this next phase of life,” he told the outlet. “Just focusing on my kids and figuring out what’s next for me.”

Later on Thursday, Zac posted a five-minute TikTok detailing the split. He said that he found out about Jen filing for divorce from a “TMZ reporter” but that it was “something we’ve been talking about for a long time.”

“Jen came to me about a year ago after Dancing With the Stars and told me she was unhappy and wanted a divorce,” Zac said. “And I basically begged her to stay, told her [I would] work on things, fix things, become whoever she needed me to be, and ultimately just we couldn’t make it work.”

Zac said that his top priority was his children and that he fears that he “failed them.” “I’m worried that I’m going to cause them damage,” he said. “And I just hope that we can still give them a normal childhood. But as far as that goes, Jen and I are definitely on the same page of wanting to give them the best life we can, the best childhood we can and be teammates and work together and do that.” He also added that he would continue to “support” Jen and “be her biggest fan.”

Jen posted a TikTok of her own on Thursday, suggesting things were not so harmonious. It was an old video of her attempting to film her daily routine, with Zac offering his own commentary off-camera. “I hope you’re not making a TikTok looking like that,” he said, referring to Jen wearing a bathrobe. “Your boobs are literally like — your tits are sagging all over. You don’t want to post that, baby, I can tell you that right now.” The SLOMW star captioned the post “he was never my biggest supporter.”

The Afflecks — who may or may not be related to Ben — met in 2018 through a Mormon dating app. They got married in 2019 and had their first child, Nora, in 2021. They then had Lucas in 2023 and Penelope in 2025. In June, Jen announced she was pregnant again, calling it “Chapter Four” on Instagram. The couple’s oldest just turned 5, which means they narrowly missed having four under 4.

In July, Jen shared that she was suffering from prenatal depression, calling it “painful, confusing, and exhausting.” She later told People that she was “deathly ill” during her first trimester and that Zac had to step up. “There’s a lot that we’ve been navigating behind closed doors,” she said, “but I do have to say, I wouldn’t have survived the first trimester without him.”

Jen and Zac’s relationship struggles have been a central plot point on SLOMW over the years. Following the first season’s premiere, Jen said that the show found them “in a rocky place.” “Since filming, we’ve done therapy nonstop,” she told Vulture in September 2024. “If we continue in our relationship, there are changes that need to be made. If they’re not made, we might have to … look at other options.” The couple briefly separated after that first season but ultimately reconciled and announced their third pregnancy in February 2025.

The divorce comes at a particularly busy time for Jen. In addition to being pregnant, she’s helming the SLOMW spinoff The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, which premieres next week. If you have questions about the end of Jen and Zac’s relationship, I assume many of them will get answered when the new series drops.
This post has been updated.

items.title: Thomas Markle Was Arrested by the FBI
items.description: Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle’s father, was arrested by federal agents in Florida on a charge connected to child sexual-abuse material. In a press release, the FBI stated that Thomas was taken into custody and charged with one count of possession of child porno
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle’s father, was arrested by federal agents in Florida on a charge connected to child sexual-abuse material. In a press release, the FBI stated that Thomas was taken into custody and charged with one count of possession of child pornography. He was arrested in Lakeland, Florida, where he had reportedly been staying at a rehabilitation facility following leg-amputation surgery last year.

Following a tip about a storage unit in Los Angeles, the FBI said they searched two storage units owned by Thomas in L.A. In the storage unit, officers say they found sexually explicit images of Thomas with prepubescent girls. First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli promised to “prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

Last month, Thomas Markle Jr. told the Sun that he had reported his father to local police and the FBI after discovering “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual-abuse images in Thomas Sr.’s Phillippines home. Thomas Sr. denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail, “I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

Meghan addressed the allegations against her father in a statement last month, saying she was “deeply distressed” by the news. She said that, in 2018, the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection shared a letter with her containing “troubling and disturbing allegations against my father” and told her they would be investigated. Meghan added she had distanced herself from her father in order to “protect” her children, who have never had any contact with him.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan said.

items.title: Don't Stress! We Found 23 Self-Care Gifts For Every Budget
items.description: Don’t Stress! We Found The Best Self-Care Gifts For Every Budget
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: Don’t Stress! We Found The Best Self-Care Gifts For Every Budget

At Refinery29, we’re here to help you navigate this overwhelming world of stuff. All of our market picks are independently selected and curated by the editorial team. All product details reflect the price and availability at the time of publication. If you buy or click on something we link to on our site, Refinery29 may earn commission.

For me, self-care isn't just about indulging in little luxuries — it's also about being more present. And that often means putting my phone down. I recently got a Brick, a clever little device that helps curb mindless scrolling by physically locking distracting apps until you tap your phone against it to unlock them. It's been a game-changer for holding myself accountable to screen-free time, and it's the kind of genuinely life-upgrading gift that's perfect for anyone hoping to be a little more mindful in 2027.
Being Frenshe Wind Down Ritual Set

Ashley Tisdale French's lifestyle brand, Being Frenshe, made its Ulta debut earlier this year, and this dreamy, lavender-scented gift set has quickly landed at the top of our wish lists. Inside, you'll find everything you need to enjoy a blissful night in: a room and linen mist, nourishing lip balm, soothing eye patches, and a pair of cozy socks. Consider it a little self-care starter pack for anyone who could use some extra R&R.
Blissy Signature Adjustable Pillow

Quality sleep is the ultimate form of self-care, and this luxuriously plush pillow makes getting your beauty rest feel like you're in a five-star hotel. Its adjustable fill lets you customize the height to your liking, offering cloud-like comfort and plenty of neck support whether you're a back, side, or stomach sleeper. (Of course, we'd expect nothing less from the brand behind some of our favorite silk pillowcases.)
Nodpod Mineralized Silk Weighted Sleep Mask

The Nodpod isn't your typical sleep mask — for starters, there's no elastic band in sight. But that's part of its genius design: The gently weighted mask drapes comfortably over your eyes, blocking out light without the tight, restrictive feel of a traditional mask. Whether you're a back or side sleeper, the silky-soft, cool-to-the-touch fabric adds an extra layer of luxury to your bedtime routine. As someone who falls asleep within minutes of putting mine on, I can confidently say it's a gift that keeps on giving.
Gap VintageSoft Baggy Wide-Leg Sweatpants

Few things bring me more comfort than slipping into a soft pair of sweatpants. I recently picked up a matching set featuring this wide-leg style from Gap, and they've quickly become a staple in my cozy-day rotation. The relaxed, baggy silhouette feels a little more elevated and effortlessly chic than your average joggers, making them equally perfect for lounging at home or venturing out for a coffee run. (Plus, they come in petite, tall, and regular lengths, so everyone can find their perfect fit.)
Lola Blankets Faux Fur Original Blanket

If you haven't noticed, ridiculously soft things are a recurring theme in my approach to self-care. Case in point: I'm now the proud owner of not one, but two Lola Blankets (after reviewing my first, I wasted no time adding another to my collection). Yes, they're pricey — probably more than you'd ever imagine spending on what is essentially a giant piece of fabric — but nothing else I've tried comes close to the deliciously plush, substantial feel of these faux-fur blankets, which strike that perfect balance between sumptuous softness and cozy comfort.
I Am Everything Affirmation Card Deck

This affordable affirmation deck makes it easy to start each morning on an uplifting note. Featuring 30 different affirmations, consider this a thoughtful stocking stuffer for anyone who could use a daily dose of good vibes.
Gardenuity Succulent Terrarium Desktop Garden

A little greenery can work wonders for brightening up a space, especially a desk or home office that could use some extra TLC. This kit comes with everything you need to create a gorgeous succulent terrarium, complete with a beautiful glass planter. Even better, it includes on-call plant care support for anyone (me) who somehow manages to kill even the supposedly indestructible varieties.
Snow Fox Large Gua Sha Brush

Part scalp massager, part hairbrush, Snow Fox's handmade gua sha brush turns an everyday hair-care ritual into a meaningful moment of self-care. Its gold-plated bristles gently stimulate the scalp, helping boost circulation and melt away tension around the temples and other pressure points. Regular scalp massage may even help support healthier-looking hair over time.

items.title: JORDAN FIRSTMAN - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut
paragraphs: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut

Jordan Firstman (American, 35 years old, completely fabulous) might be familiar to readers from his brassy internet memes, or his brilliant leading role in ‘Rotting in the Sun’, 2023’s crime thriller set in sexy Mexico. Or from the news that his debut as a director ‘Club Kid’ (which he also wrote and plays the lead in) was heralded with a seven-minute standing ovation at Cannes earlier this year and triggered a fierce bidding war between the biggest studios in Hollywood. A star was born.

Because he does so much, Jordan often struggles with knowing what to call himself. Luckily, help is at hand from Luca Guadagnino, Jordan’s friend of close to ten years and the director of ‘I Am Love’, ‘Call Me by Your Name’, ‘Queer’, ‘Challengers’ and so many other cinema highs. Here, Jordan gets some handy life advice from his fellow multi-tasking director, who also photographed and interviewed him for this story. The following Q&A has been edited for maximum readability and pleasure. Ready?
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Text and photography by LUCA GUADAGNINO
JORDAN — Did I get too sunburnt?

L — A little bit. You’re a bit red, like a lobster. One second, baby, that’s not the beginning of the interview. It should start this way: Okay, Jordan Firstman has always been at the forefront of the most up-to-date things: the most up-to-date behaviour, the most up-to-date public persona. You have been directly and indirectly commenting on the state of the world and making fun of it and finding a way to showcase your personality and individuality. Eventually this has allowed you to be perceived as who you actually are. Not many people succeed in that. How do you see that in the face of the way the world works right now, the way in which authority expresses itself, the way in which parts of the world are in flames but not for the right reason?

J — Well, thank you. That’s a compliment, I think. I’ve always just tried to go from the inside out, and I’ve always known I’ve had a problem with saying everything that was on my mind, and I think it took, from high school, about a decade to figure out how to say that in a way that worked for me and didn’t hinder me. I remember my high school theatre teacher told me that I had special powers, and he said, “But you have to use your powers for good and not evil,” because I think he saw me. He saw that I was capable of both.
L — What kind of evil were you capable of at that stage in your life?

J — I’m able and have since I was a kid been able to see through things and speak honestly about them. He saw that I’ve always felt a strong sense of justice, and when people weren’t treating me or my peers right, I would be outlandish.
L — Is this something that comes out when you deal with power, or people in positions of power?

J — Until very recently this is how I have felt with a lot of people, where I think there is something hidden in their actions. Maybe they feel like I’m going to corrupt the system they have made, so they want to take my voice or my thing away from me, and I often respond very strongly to that.

L — I don’t know anyone, or at least haven’t met anyone in the last ten years, who has been able to express themselves through so many different mediums and through so many different types of performance in the way that you do.
