items.title: Kathy Hochul Is Sort of Crushing It
items.description: This year’s midterms marked a new era for Democrats across the nation, with the party securing stunning wins in Texas and multiple other states, as well as flipping control of both chambers of Congress. Tuesday also sent a signal of a different kind in New Yor
items.author: Nia Prater
paragraphs: This year’s midterms marked a new era for Democrats across the nation, with the party securing stunning wins in Texas and multiple other states, as well as flipping control of both chambers of Congress. Tuesday also sent a signal of a different kind in New York, where Governor Kathy Hochul cemented her second full term in office with a demonstrative win over Trump-friendly Nassau County executive Bruce Blakeman — officially silencing the doubters of her political might.

In 2022, Hochul put a big scare into state Democrats when her GOP challenger, Lee Zeldin, came within six points of defeating her — the narrowest margin in a state gubernatorial race in decades. Four years later, it’s not even close. With approximately 95 percent of the votes in, Hochul is leading Blakeman with 60 percent to his 39.8 percent, receiving over a million more votes than the Long Island leader.
“That’s a nuke. She crushed him.” analyst and political strategist Michael Lange told me. “I don’t know of another way to describe it.”

Lange pointed out that the governor appears poised to outperform Blakeman in the Hudson Valley as well as the red firewall of Long Island, where she leads in both Suffolk County as well as Nassau County, his home territory. “Hochul ran a really good race, miles better than four years ago,” he said.

Christina Greer, an associate professor of political science at Fordham University, agreed that Blakeman did not appear to be as strong a candidate as Zeldin was four years ago but noted “we’re in a very different political universe” compared to that time. “In 2022 versus 2026, we didn’t have $9 gas. We weren’t in a war with Iran. We weren’t as polarized when it comes to Middle East strategies. We weren’t in a second term of Trump, where he is off the rails and has a personal vendetta against not just partisan politics, but, it seems like, a large percentage of the American people,” she said.

There have been some bumps. Early on, Hochul was forced to find a new lieutenant governor after her first pick, Brian Benjamin, resigned after being indicted on wire-fraud and bribery charges. (They were later dropped.) His replacement, Antonio Delgado would ultimately fall out with Hochul and briefly launch a primary challenge against her. She was at the helm as the state was engulfed by a messy and protracted redistricting fight that went all the way to the state’s Court of Appeals.

But Hochul is now one of the most popular politicians in the state. She had a 51 percent favorability rating statewide in a late October Siena University poll — a few points higher than New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who received 47 percent. A similar Siena survey from September showed Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — whom many speculate is mulling a future statewide or even presidential bid — at 43 percent across the state.

Shawn Donahue, a professor of political science at the University at Buffalo, noted that when Hochul first ran for a full term, most of her public exposure had been in the far less visible role of lieutenant governor and during her brief stint in the U.S. House of Representatives. “Since then, she has been able to come more into her own as governor,” he said.

Hochul has also developed a fruitful working relationship with Mamdani, the pair backing each other’s political campaigns and working together on shared policy goals including the expansion of universal child care statewide and joint support for a pied-à-terre tax, the closest the governor has come to supporting Mamdani’s aspirations to tax the rich. In the waning days of the election cycle, Hochul campaigned alongside Mamdani across New York City, and they even met up with Ocasio-Cortez to watch the governor’s hometown Buffalo Bills at a bar in Queens.

In her acceptance speech on Tuesday, Hochul paid tribute to the mayor, who had spoken earlier at the state Democratic Party’s Election Night event, telling Mamdani, “Thank you for standing with me and bringing a whole new energy to New York City.”

Greer predicts that their dynamic will inevitably shift now that the governor has won another term. “Mamdani is up for reelection before Kathy Hochul. He will go to Albany with his tin can, as all mayors do, to ask for money,” Greer explained, but she thinks Hochul still recognizes how popular he is and that “she needs to stay within the relative good graces of Mamdani and his coalition because they are quite active, especially in primaries.”

Hochul has also racked up a number of accomplishments on her own, including implementing, after a little bit of drama, a congestion-pricing program for New York City. When President Trump subsequently tried to revoke federal approval for the program and referred to himself as a “king” who had “saved” New York, Hochul embraced the fight like it was an in-kind contribution. And while the governor has sought to maintain a cordial line of communication to Trump, she’s remained a strong critic of the president, ripping the economic impacts of his trade war and antagonism of neighboring Canada while playing up Blakeman’s strong fealty to Trump. During their lone debate, Hochul quipped that he was the head of Trump’s “fan club.”

Trump’s unpopularity undoubtedly helped Hochul at the polls. “Remember this: Just a few weeks ago, Donald Trump came to New York and told voters to pretend that he was on the ballot,” she told the crowd on Tuesday night, referring to a rally Trump appeared at with Blakeman. “Well, Mr. President, you got your wish.”

To Lange, there’s been a clear evolution. “I think early-days Kathy Hochul was relatively cautious and risk-averse because her position as governor — it felt quite tentative. She steps into the Cuomo vacuum, Democrats want to challenge her, and Lee Zeldin mounts a very close bid,” he said. “But I think now, her standing as the leader of the statewide Democratic Party in New York is very secure. It’s her and Mamdani who lead New York. It’s not Chuck Schumer. It’s not Hakeem Jeffries. Letitia James is popular, but Kathy Hochul — it’s her state.”

He continued, “So I think that bodes very well for folks who want more progressive measures passed through Albany, and I think Hochul is going to be as unencumbered as she’s ever been, which is going to be really interesting.”

Hochul has also left the door open to collaboration on the right, if done in the interest of her constituents. When her mention of Blakeman calling to concede sparked boos throughout the room, Hochul was quick to shut them down. “Nope, not here, not here,” she said, adding that she would always partner with Blakeman for the people of Nassau County.
The governor also said she would be willing to work with Trump to lower costs for New Yorkers or help keep communities safe, but not if he threatens or acts against the state.

“I think that she’s really kind of found her footing, credit to her. Feel like she’s really found her voice and I think that she knows what she wants to do coming into this next legislative session,” Lange said. “I think folks have a lot of reasons to be optimistic.”

items.title: Cinco experiencias de bienestar sonoro en hoteles que necesitas conocer
items.description: Quedan menos de tres semanas para el solsticio de verano, lo que significa que es momento de empezar a bajar el ritmo y disfrutar de un merecido descanso.
items.author: Ricardo Diaz
paragraphs: Quedan menos de tres semanas para el solsticio de verano, lo que significa que es momento de empezar a bajar el ritmo y disfrutar de un merecido descanso.

En la última década, los espacios dedicados al bienestar han ganado protagonismo gracias a sus innovadores spas y a los aromas distintivos que reciben a los huéspedes desde el vestíbulo. Ahora, una nueva dimensión sensorial está cobrando fuerza: el sonido. Los hoteles de lujo están apostando por experiencias de bienestar sonoro con salas de escucha, sesiones en vinilo y presentaciones analógicas en vivo que invitan a desconectarse del ruido cotidiano y sumergirse en un estado de calma.

Más que una simple tendencia, estas experiencias están diseñadas para fomentar la creatividad y crear conexiones entre quienes comparten el espacio. En lugar de quedarse en la habitación con servicio a la habitación, los huéspedes son invitados a formar parte de una comunidad donde la música se convierte en el hilo conductor de recuerdos, conversaciones y nuevas experiencias.
Si este verano buscas una escapada donde el descanso vaya acompañado de una gran selección musical, estos hoteles merecen un lugar en tu lista.

Lo que alguna vez fue un estudio de grabación en un sótano hoy es uno de los hoteles más singulares de Los Cabos, con una misión clara: impulsar la creatividad y la expresión artística. Las jam sessions, los estudios de grabación y los conciertos íntimos con huéspedes como audiencia han convertido a El Ganzo en un destino donde la música es parte esencial de la experiencia.

"Ofrecemos a los artistas un espacio para compartir su música original y expresar su identidad, algo que muchos músicos talentosos rara vez tienen la oportunidad de hacer, ya que suelen interpretar versiones en bares y recintos locales", explicó Paco Rosas, director musical de Hotel El Ganzo, en un comunicado. "Lo que hace único este proyecto es que los huéspedes no solo asisten a las presentaciones, sino que crean vínculos genuinos con los artistas y con la diversa comunidad creativa que ha encontrado aquí un hogar."
Si te hospedas en Hotel Volga, en Ciudad de México, hay un lugar que deberías visitar antes que cualquier otro: el Minos Sound Room.

Este anfiteatro subterráneo funciona como escenario para conciertos en vivo, sesiones de DJ, fiestas para ver eventos deportivos y encuentros culturales en un espacio de diseño contemporáneo. El resultado es una experiencia inmersiva donde la arquitectura y la música se complementan para crear uno de los puntos de encuentro más interesantes de la ciudad.

Dentro de Gale Miami Hotel & Residences se encuentra el recién inaugurado 400 Vinyl Room, un espacio concebido para disfrutar de la música con total atención. Con capacidad para solo 50 personas, iluminación tenue y un sistema de sonido pensado para una escucha envolvente, esta sala pone el foco exclusivamente en la experiencia auditiva.
Su cuidada selección de vinilos incluye funk, soul, disco y clásicos de la música latina de los años 80, convirtiéndola en una parada obligada para melómanos y coleccionistas.
Listening Room, Julie Soefer

En Hotel Saint Augustine, en Houston, los huéspedes pueden redescubrir el placer de escuchar música de manera analógica en el recién inaugurado Listening Room. Equipado con un tocadiscos y una extensa colección de vinilos, este espacio invita a practicar una escucha más pausada y consciente, recuperando el ritual de disfrutar un álbum de principio a fin.

Al cruzar las puertas de Locke at East Side Gallery, en Berlín, es difícil no sentirse atraído por su espacio social, cuyo protagonista es ANIMA, un elegante listening bar dedicado al vinilo. Diseñado por el estudio neoyorquino Grzywinski+Pons, el lugar se encuentra junto al tramo más extenso que aún se conserva del Muro de Berlín, hoy convertido en la icónica East Side Gallery, donde la historia convive con el arte contemporáneo y la cultura musical.

items.title: 'Avalancha' at 30: The LP That Recharged Cafe Tacvba After the Burnout of 'Re'
items.description: Thirty years ago, the members of Café Tacvba found themselves physically and emotionally wiped out. The Mexico City quartet had completed an extensive tour promoting its sophomore effort, Re, which since then has been routinely hailed as one of the best albums
items.author: Ernesto Lechner
paragraphs: Thirty years ago, the members of Café Tacvba found themselves physically and emotionally wiped out. The Mexico City quartet had completed an extensive tour promoting its sophomore effort, Re, which since then has been routinely hailed as one of the best albums in the history of Latin rock.
To make matters worse, Tacvba’s label expected a new record, and the demos that the band had been taping between tours were far from ready to become a cohesive whole. Things got a bit tense.

“We played the Viña del Mar festival in Chile, and our longtime producer Gustavo Santaolalla happened to be there,” remembers Tacvba keyboardist Meme del Real. “He saw what was happening to us. ‘You’re always playing covers of songs by other artists,’ he said. ‘Why don’t you make an EP of covers? That would get you back in the studio and working on a different frequency.’ He had the right perspective, and pointed us to a path of healing.”

The result was Avalancha de Éxitos, a mini-album of radically reimagined songs that, experienced as a whole, sounds significantly more epic than the sum of its parts. Released on Nov. 5, 1996, it was not only commercially successful — five of its eight songs were released as singles — but it also made Tacvba stars in countries like Argentina, which had never embraced Mexican rock before.

A brisk, exuberant record, it is also subtly conceptual, depicting Latin American culture as a chaotic, dissonant tapestry where beauty and depth can be found in a musty bolero from decades ago (“No Me Comprendes”), a melancholy pop ballad (Leo Dan’s wide-eyed “Cómo Te Extraño Mi Amor”), or a tropical anthem of hope transformed into son huasteco (Juan Luis Guerra’s socially alert “Ojalá Que Llueva Café.”)

Tacvba’s sense of humor, playful and subversive, injected an adrenaline rush into provocative Mexican rock songs like opening stomper “Chilanga Banda,” with its indolent groove, and the industrial corrosion of “Alármala De Tos,” originally by Eighties troublemakers Botellita de Jerez. David Byrne guests on “No Controles,” an aggro inversion of the 1985 techno-pop hit by Mexican female group Flans (itself, a cover of Spanish band Olé Olé).

“I remember that record with so much affection,” says singer Rubén Albarrán from his home in Mexico City. “We were so inspired by the process of stepping out into the streets of the cities that we visited and discovering the spirit of Latin America. We were coming face to face with the realities that have become more obvious since then: the intervention of foreign countries; the genocide of our people. Our resistance was formulated by selecting ingredients from the blend of cultures and histories, and coming up with something new. We were deeply moved by discovering who we really were.”
The same irreverence that Tacvba had exhibited on original songs like “La Ingrata” seeped into the Avalancha sessions.

“We had the impudence not to give a damn about what the composers of the original songs may think,” laughs Albarrán, who fittingly chose the moniker of Anónimo for the project. “Perhaps they would even be offended.”

“It’s so much easier to quote and unquote destroy a song if the author is not present,” adds del Real. “That was a big part of the fun — the element of adventure involved in every single arrangement. And it wasn’t like the songs were required to suffer a profound transformation. It was more like, ‘What would happen if we grab these songs and push them to the limit? What if we choke them so that they are forced to breathe again in a completely different context?’ We were really pushing the envelope.”

“I think the fact they had created a work as imposing and sonically diverse as Re left them in a complicated position in terms of the follow-up album,” says Enrique Blanc, a Mexico-based music journalist and author of the book Café Tacvba — Bailando por nuestra cuenta. “Making Avalancha was like going into recess for them; a fun project echoing their beginnings as a band that played covers.”

Originally, the group planned to record Duran Duran’s debut single “Planet Earth” (according to del Real, a demo still languishes in the vaults.) But Albarrán felt awkward singing the English lyrics, and the song selection remained Latin American throughout — a powerful statement in itself.

“We have a different cultural context than Pink Floyd or Radiohead,” explains Albarrán. “We need to talk about other things that are more important to us and the people we share our lives with. Something happened with Avalancha, where the pristine sound quality achieved by Santaolalla and [co-producer] Aníbal Kerpel merged with our conscious decision not to copy anything from the Anglo mainstream. We have our own emotional world. It’s just as valuable as anyone else’s.”

Interestingly, one of the album’s most haunting moments arrives during an obscure track: “No Me Comprendes,” a cabaret miniature by Cuban eccentric Bola de Nieve. Like most of Avalancha, it conjures up a stately, fetishistic atmosphere by combining psychedelic guitar with hand percussion and a musical saw. Toward the end, the tropical bolero suddenly morphs into a lilting bossa nova segment — almost as if the record itself chose to embrace the power of beauty over chaos and satire.

“That’s one of my favorite Tacvba songs,” says Albarrán. “It’s such a gorgeous moment when that bossa bit blooms — it nourishes my heart and soul. The mocking undertone in my voice mirrors Bola de Nieve’s original interpretation. He was such a strange and uncomfortable character, and the song itself is difficult to pin down. The saw and the bossa segment — it’s like the sound of fairies, or the song of sirens.”

“I remember putting on the headphones and recording my part on a grand piano,” adds del Real. He is in a hotel room in Querétaro, a few hours before stepping onstage for a concert presenting La Montaña Encendida, his debut solo album. “It felt like dining at an expensive restaurant in Paris — the kind of establishment you only get to visit once or twice in your life. I was having such a wonderful time playing, and I think my enjoyment can be heard on the final product.”

It was the album’s closing track, “Cómo Te Extraño Mi Amor,” that became its biggest hit — a quintessential Tacvba moment. Whereas the Leo Dan original is fragile and wounded, Tacvba’s bouncy cover bursts out of the speakers with the shuffle of a ska beat and youthful Beatlesque confidence.

“That’s Gustavo’s [Santaolalla] magic,” says Albarrán. “He captured that fleeting impression, how happy and young we were. We were experiencing success doing what we loved. It was just thrilling, and on this song you can hear the lightness in our step. It wasn’t only the music that we tackled with that kind of energy: so much laughter, and attitude, and desmadre. It was life itself.”

Avalancha’s brilliance was acknowledged by both critics and the band’s fans the moment it was released. It was the record that everyone talked about as 1996 came to a close, and it generated another massive tour. Eventually, Tacvba returned to the demos of original material that had been pushed aside, and in 1999 released the stunning double album Revés/Yosoy.
Still, Avalancha may well be the finest Latin covers album ever made.

“I’m so proud of it,” says del Real. “Avalancha helped us realize how vulnerable we could be as a band. It defined our identity while helping us to recover from a few maladies we had picked up along their way. Once again, music and the creative process gave us the chance to rediscover why we remained together. Our group psychotherapy was commanded by a sense of adventure.”

“It wasn’t just us,” Albarrán emphasizes. “We were part of a movement that was taking over Mexico and many other countries. There was Maldita Vecindad and Santa Sabina. We were all reformulating our roots with different results. Music was our medicine and refuge; the one place where we could find an answer for everything.”

items.title: Russell Brand Found Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault in London Trial; Taken Into Custody
items.description: Russell Brand, the former actor and comedian, was convicted Thursday on three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape in his London criminal trial. He was found not guilty of two other rape charges and a count of attempted indecent assault.
items.author: K J Yossman; Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Russell Brand, the former actor and comedian, was convicted Thursday on three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape in his London criminal trial. He was found not guilty of two other rape charges and a count of attempted indecent assault.
The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, informed Brand that “obviously a custodial sentence of some length will result” and said it was unlikely he would extend the former comedian’s bail any further.

“You’ve been convicted of a number of offenses, including one of rape,” he said. “My current view is that I therefore have to remand you in custody not least because the temptation to avoid coming back to court to receive that sentence will be overwhelming.”

He allowed both Brand’s legal team and the Crown Prosecution Service a break of 20 minutes before returning to make submissions as to whether bail should be extended. Ultimately, however, the judge denied the application to extend bail and remanded him into custody until Monday, when he will return to receive his sentence. As Brand was taken to the cells, he mouthed “I’m OK” and “I’m good” to his lawyers and gave a thumbs-up sign, according to Sky News.

In the U.K., a rape conviction can result in up to 19 years in prison and potentially even a life sentence, depending on the seriousness of the offense. The maximum sentence for sexual assault is 10 years.
Sky News reported that the Met Police are now investigating further allegations of rape made by two women.
Brand did not visibly react when the verdicts were read out. His wife, Laura Gallacher, rushed out of the courtroom when Brand was taken to the cells to wait before his bail application.

Brand was accused of raping three women at various locations between 1999 and 2009. One of the alleged victims also accused him of sexual assault in addition to oral rape. He was also accused of one count of attempted indecent assault at MTV’s U.K. offices in 2001 and one count of sexual assault in 2009.
The jury was on its third day of deliberations when it reached the verdict, following a three-week trial.

Brand got his start as a comedian on MTV in the U.K. before rising through the ranks of British media to host shows such as “Big Brother” spin-off ” Big Brother’s Big Mouth” on Channel 4 network E4 and his own radio show, “The Russell Brand Show” on BBC Radio 6.

He then broke through in Hollywood after appearing in the 2007 comedy “St Trinian’s” starring Talulah Riley, Juno Temple and Colin Firth, set in a girls’ boarding school. Roles in “Forgetting Sarah Marshall,” “Get Him to the Greek” and “Rock of Ages.” He also voiced a recurring character in the “Despicable Me” franchise, Dr Nefario.
He eventually launched his own podcast and moved into influencing and politics via his YouTube channel.

However his media empire came crashing down in 2023 when The Sunday Times of London and Channel 4 documentary series “Dispatches” published/broadcast a joint investigation into Brand’s allegedly predatory behaviour, in which five women accused Brand of sexual assault and misconduct.

items.title: ‘Rockford Files’ Reboot Sets NBC Release Date, Launches Jim Rockford Hotline
items.description: NBC has set the premiere date for “The Rockford Files” reboot starring David Boreanaz.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: NBC has set the premiere date for “The Rockford Files” reboot starring David Boreanaz.

The new take on the classic series will air its premiere episode on Saturday, Jan. 2 at 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT immediately following the night’s NFL telecast. It will then be available to stream the next day on Peacock. The show will then move to its regular timeslot on Thursday, Jan. 7 at 8 p.m. ET/PT.

And in keeping with the iconic answering machine message at the beginning of the original show, NBC has launched a Jim Rockford hotline that fans can actually call. You can call (760) JIM-ROCK to hear a message from Boreanaz and sign up for text message updates from the show.
Check out an ad for the hotline below.

The logline for the new “Rockford Files” states, “Newly paroled after doing time for a crime he didn’t commit, James Rockford returns to his life as a private investigator using his charm and wit to solve cases around Los Angeles. It doesn’t take long for his quest for legitimacy to land him squarely in the crosshairs of both local police and organized crime.”

Along with Boreanaz, the cast includes Michaela McManus, Ilfenesh Hadera and Jacki Weaver. Mike Daniels serves as writer and executive producer, with Carl Beverly, Sarah Timberman, and David Hudgins also executive producing. Universal Television is the studio.

The original “Rockford Files,” created by Roy Huggins and Stephen J. Cannell, aired on NBC from 1974-1980 with James Garner in the lead role. The show ultimately aired for over 120 episodes, while Garner reprised the role of Rockford in eight TV movies at CBS between 1994 and 1999.

items.title: Nithya Raman Wins L.A. Mayor’s Race as Karen Bass Concedes
items.description: Nithya Raman will be the next mayor of Los Angeles, as incumbent Karen Bass conceded defeat after a hard-fought campaign.
items.author: Payton Turkeltaub; Gene Maddaus
paragraphs: Nithya Raman will be the next mayor of Los Angeles, as incumbent Karen Bass conceded defeat after a hard-fought campaign.

In a video, Raman thanked Bass for her service and vowed to provide a city government that is “actually capable of delivering on its promises.” She cited priorities such as affordable housing, parks and public transit.
“I love this city, and I love its people, and I cannot wait to get started on building a better future together with all of you,” Raman said. “Thank you so much, Los Angeles.”
Bass conceded on Thursday morning as Raman’s lead continued to grow.

“While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said in a statement. “I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”

Raman surprised the City Hall establishment by entering the race at the last minute in February, and appeared likely to finish third behind reality star Spencer Pratt through much of the primary. But she was able to rally enough voters fed up with Bass and open to a Democratic alternative.

Early tallies on election night saw Bass with a slender lead over Raman — but not nearly enough of a margin to account for Raman’s strength with late-arriving ballots, which skew toward young voters and renters. Raman took the lead late on election night and the margin has continued to grow.
As of the update on Thursday morning, Raman held a 4.2% lead over Bass — with many thousands of ballots still to count.

Bass sought to focus on public safety, warning that Raman had opposed police funding and was against anti-camping zones. Raman, meanwhile, argued that the city needed fresh leadership that was not captive to relationships at City Hall.
Raman’s husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, is a veteran TV writer and producer, and many Hollywood writers and comedians contributed to her campaign.

“Nithya reached out to me and many other writers months ago, in an attempt to better understand the challenges with local TV and film production,” said Mike Schur, creator of “Dig.” “She is committed to finding ways we can keep Hollywood in L.A. where it belongs. I’m thrilled we have elected someone who thinks big and has real ideas for helping the industry.”
Raman led in several polls taken during the fall. But a Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll on Oct. 28 showed the two candidates tied, with both earning 40% of voters’ support.
On Tuesday night, shortly after 11 p.m., Raman addressed her supporters at her election-night event in the plaza of L.A.’s Greek Theatre. “I’m very hopeful,” she told the crowd.

Raman first joined the Los Angeles City Council in 2020, becoming the first Asian-American woman and the first South Asian ever to serve. She was re-elected for a second term in 2024. Raman holds degrees from Harvard and MIT, and worked as an urban planner before turning her focus to politics. She also served as the co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council Homelessness Committee and co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition.
Raman other Hollywood supporters included Tina Fey, Adam Scott, Mindy Kaling, Colin Jost, Nicholas Stoller, Cord Jefferson and David Mandel.

Bass, who has served as Los Angeles’ mayor since 2022, faced considerable challenges in winning back voters who were upset about homelessness, civic disorder and her handling of the 2025 Palisades fire.
Michael Schneider contributed to this story.

items.title: Letterboxd in Negotiations to Be Acquired by New York Times Company
items.description: The New York Times Company is in exclusive negotiations to acquire the online movie buff community Letterboxd, the Times reported Thursday.
items.author: Pat Saperstein
paragraphs: The New York Times Company is in exclusive negotiations to acquire the online movie buff community Letterboxd, the Times reported Thursday.

The price is reported to be about $330 million, which amounts to more than 20 times Letterboxd’s projected earnings for 2026 of about $15 million. The New York Times said that the deal was not yet final.

Variety reported in September that the New York Times and A24 were among the bidders for the company, with Netflix, Sony Pictures Entertainment, Skydance, private-equity giant TPG and Reddit co-creator Alexis Ohanian also expressing interest.
Co-founders Matthew Buchanan and Karl von Randow are expected to remain in charge, reporting to a N.Y. Times executive, the report said.

A24 had promised independence in operating the site, but dropped out when the price rose, according to the report. Letterboxd numbers some 30 million film-obsessed users who use the site to keep track of what they have watched and rate the titles with a star system. Last year, Letterboxd also launched an online film-rental platform that is available in 23 countries.

Though Letterboxd’s core features are free to users, the app offers a paid Pro tier for $19 a year that removes ads and provides more personalization features. The $49 Patron tier ads customized posters and backdrops and access to some beta features.

New Zealand-based Letterboxd was founded in 2011 and has been shopping itself to interested parties in recent months. Canadian holding company Tiny acquired a 60% stake in Letterboxd in 2023 at a valuation of $50 million-$60 million, while Buchanan and von Randow own the remaining 40% share.

The purchase would be a natural continuation of subscription-based companies the New York Times has acquired to increase reader engagement including sports site The Athletic, product review service Wirecutter and the popular game Wordle.
The New York Times had no comment.

items.title: Rosamund Pike Set to Star in and Produce ‘Feed,’ Body Horror Movie From Leslye Headland
items.description: Rosamund Pike will star in and produce “Feed,” a new body horror movie from “The Acolyte” director Leslye Headland and screenwriter Daniella Isaacs.
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: Rosamund Pike will star in and produce “Feed,” a new body horror movie from “The Acolyte” director Leslye Headland and screenwriter Daniella Isaacs.

Inspired by the 2022 Finnish horror movie “Hatching,” the official logline for “Feed” reads: “When a desperate mother discovers an obscure collagen supplement that promises to make her tween gymnast daughter an influencer star, the fame and success they crave come fast. But as her daughter goes viral, she begins a monstrous transformation.”

“Long have I wanted to make a film that plays anarchically with our obsession with social media and self-improvement, our desire for fame without notable admirable skill and, let’s put it out there, the monstrosity of modern motherhood,” Pike said. “‘Feed’ deals with all these things.”

Pike will produce through her Primitive Streak banner. Other producers include Shelley Browning for Magnolia Entertainment, Steven Schneider for Spooky Pictures, Ara Keshishian and Petr Jakl for ZQ Entertainment and Sam Ritzenberg for Agile Films. ZQ Entertainment financed development on the project. The Veterans will represent the international sales rights, with CAA Media Finance handling the United States. Sales will commence at the American Film Market next week.

“Daniella’s script is audacious, disturbing and deeply human and Rosamund is among the boldest actors working today,” Headland added. “I couldn’t ask for better partners to take on the darker corners of this story and I feel incredibly lucky to be making this film with two women whose work I admire so much.”

Pike, best known for her roles in “Gone Girl,” “Pride & Prejduice” and “Die Another Day,” was last seen in Guy Ritchie’s action comedy “In the Grey” alongside Henry Cavill and Jake Gyllenhaal. Her other recent film credits include “Ladies First,” “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t” and “Hallow Road.” In 2027, she will reunite with Ritchie for “Wife and Dog,” which also stars Anthony Hopkins and Benedict Cumberbatch.

Headland has been out of the director’s chair ever since helming the short-lived Disney+ series “The Acolyte.” Before that, she directed series such as “Single Drunk Female,” “Almost Family” and “Black Monday.” Her last feature directorial credit was in 2015 with “Sleeping with Other People.” Coming up, she has “Cult of Love,” a Christmas family dramedy currently in pre-production.
Pike is repped by CAA, United Agents and Magnolia Entertainment; Headland is repped by CAA and Sugar23; Isaacs is repped by Curtis Brown Group.

items.title: Hollywood Quietly Banning Prediction Market Betting on Movie News, Release Dates (Exclusive)
items.description: If you’re an industry insider tempted to drop a few thousand on Kalshi predicting who will be cast as the next James Bond, think again.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: If you’re an industry insider tempted to drop a few thousand on Kalshi predicting who will be cast as the next James Bond, think again.
The Hollywood Reporter has learned studios and production companies have been quietly issuing new guidelines to employees warning them not to engage in prediction market betting.

The warnings prohibit employees from placing bets on news events like studio earnings, casting, or even release dates. Passing information along to friends and family for them to place bets is likewise forbidden. At least one company set up a hotline where staffers can anonymously report on their fellow employees suspected of placing bets.

In a way, such updates are an expansion on longstanding rules which forbid employees from insider trading in the stock market. And many instances of prediction market profiteering using insider corporate information might violate federal law already. But with prediction markets allowing betting on everything from who will be cast as the next Wonder Woman to who will be eliminated on Dancing with the Stars, the opportunities for stealthily cashing in on insider knowledge has dramatically increased.

“You now have, essentially, an explosion in the number of employers who have to think about insider trading rules from an ethical standpoint,” says Joshua Mitts, a law professor at Columbia University who has extensively studied the legalities and trends surrounding prediction market betting. “And totally apart from the question of criminal prosecution, is just the compliance problem — educating your employees on what’s allowed.”

THR’s parent company, PMC, which also owns Dick Clark Productions and other publications such as Variety and Deadline, has likewise updated its employee handbook to ban prediction market betting in recent weeks. Among other things, the company forbids betting on “award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates.”

Some improper betting among entertainment industry insiders has already made headlines, yet the reported cases almost certainly represent just the tip of the iceberg in terms of betting behind the scenes.

In February, Kalshi disclosed that a video editor working for MrBeast’s company made $5,000 by improperly using confidential information to place bets about MrBeast content. The employee was fired and slapped with a $20,000 penalty.
While in April, a Puck column revealed someone who worked on a CBS competition show and had been making money through prediction markets.

One TV network source lamented that even though their company’s insider trading policy prohibits betting on prediction markets related to their work, the opportunity for insider bets remain rampant. For example, there are markets on what a guest will say on the Tonight Show, Saturday Night Live or other talk shows, many of which are pretaped or have dress rehearsals. Some of those shows have audiences made up of the public, and those people could bet without fear of breaking any rules.

Interestingly, one major betting site, BetOnline, temporarily pulled its page allowing people to wager on the who will be cast as the next James Bond this week after the final auditions were expected to have taken place. The reason, according to a representative: “Sharp money” suddenly came down hard in favor of Callum Turner, surging him to the top of the odds chart above longtime favorite Jack Lowden, causing internal concern that the bets might be the result of a credible leak.

In March, a study by Mitts and University of Haifa’s Moran Ofir estimated $143 million in anomalous profit being made across Polymarket during a two-year period, a figure that’s certainly ramped up dramatically since given the number of betting categories that have increased.

While some prediction market betting has been argued to have societal value — for instance, a company hedging against a costly change in government policy — Mitts notes betting on entertainment industry news isn’t really one of them.

“There’s a high degree of asymmetric information [in terms of a handful of studio insiders knowing certain upcoming announcements], and a high degree of secret information, but there’s very little social utility to having this priced correctly,” says Mitts. “With a straight face, can you really say society is making better decisions because we know the probability of who’s going to win a reality TV show, or the probability of a movie sequel?”

That said, while a couple of insiders have been caught betting on entertainment news, studios will have a very tough time stopping employees from betting. Prediction market bets can be difficult for employers to trace to individual employees, particularly on blockchain-based platforms. “With blockchain-based trading, it can be basically impossible [to catch a better] if you know how to use a mixer correctly and know how to hide your identity behind multiple layers of intermediation,” Mitts says. “So it’s quite hard for employers to suss it out through an open source investigation.”
Perhaps most famously (and worrisomely), in February six newly created Polymarket wallets earned $1.2 million by accurately betting on U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Nobody has been caught.

Over the summer the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the U.S., put out an open call for the industry to weigh in on what should be legal to trade on, and what shouldn’t. The CFTC declared that betting on award shows like the Oscars and Emmys should be allowed “because the award turns on evaluative judgments, not on measurable occurrences dependent on the participants’ skill or athletic ability in the activity itself, it is a contest, not gaming.”
However, it was less certain about other forms of entertainment:

“For example, should game shows, reality show competitions, pageants and similar events be considered to be ’gaming’?” the CFTC wrote. “The Commission notes that game shows are typically subject to varying standards intended to promote impartiality and fair competition. Other competitions may allow departure from such standards to enhance their entertainment value. Music and talent competitions often have similarities to elections. How, if at all, should the Commission consider these characteristics in the context of event contracts involving these activities?”
A number of comments to the CFTC complained about bets made on the last season of Survivor, where the winner appears to have been tagged early, thanks to aggressive bets on prediction markets.

In a quirk of financial history, there are only two types of prediction market bets explicitly outlawed by Congress in the Onion Futures Act of 1958: Onion futures contract, and motion picture box office receipts. In other words, it is illegal to offer bets on how much revenue a film will see at the box office, despite all the myriad other bets available that touch on the entertainment business.

If regulators decide to crack down on prediction market betting, Mitts notes that the entertainment industry might be a prime candidate for increased regulatory scrutiny given the high potential for insider trading and “low social benefit” of the bets. “If you’re going to prioritize an investigation or strict policies, it would seem that these kinds of entertainment markets might be good candidates for that.”
Alex Weprin contributed to this report.

items.title: ‘Gilmore Girls‘ Star Kelly Bishop to Release First Novel
items.description: Gilmore Girls star Kelly Bishop is making her literary debut.
items.author: Lexy Perez
paragraphs: Gilmore Girls star Kelly Bishop is making her literary debut.
The actress will make her fiction debut to be published by William Morrow in Fall 2027 written with New York Times bestselling author Ali Rosen, it was announced Thursday.

The actress, also known for her acclaimed roles in Dirty Dancing, The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel and originating the role of Sheila in A Chorus Line (for which she won a Tony), will write a novel that “blends the friendship and humor of The Golden Girls with the banter of Sex and the City.“

The novel, titled Broad Appeal, will center on four women in their 70s who unexpectedly become roommates in a Manhattan apartment and discover that life’s greatest adventures can happen long after retirement.

At the center of the novel is “Roz, a 78-year-old retired divorcée whose comfortable Upper West Side life is upended when rising housing costs threaten her ability to keep the apartment she loves. Forced to take on roommates, she finds herself sharing her home with an eccentric entomologist sister-in-law, a former trophy wife rebuilding after financial disaster and a spirited dance teacher she met while protesting gentrification in Spanish Harlem. What begins as a practical arrangement soon becomes an unexpected family, until long-buried secrets, financial pressures and unresolved heartbreaks test the bonds they’ve built.“

“Filled with sharp wit, unforgettable characters and keen insights into the complexities of human relationships, the novel marks an exciting new chapter in Bishop’s celebrated storytelling career,“ William Morrow said of Bishop‘s novel.

“I’m so excited to share Broad Appeal with readers,” Bishop said in a statement. “This story is about friendship, resilience, second chances and the surprising ways our lives can change when we least expect it. I’ve always believed that growing older doesn’t mean growing smaller. If anything, it means there are still stories worth telling and lives worth reinventing. I’ve had so much fun with Ali Rosen bringing this novel to life.”

“With this novel, Kelly Bishop has created a cast of characters readers will immediately invest in, delivering a story that is both entertaining and deeply resonant,” Jennifer Hart, senior vp and deputy publisher, William Morrow, said in a statement. “As a devoted Gilmore Girls fan, I know firsthand the power of Kelly’s storytelling, and this novel showcases that gift in an entirely new way.”

William Morrow vice president and executive editor Liz Stein added, “Kelly has charmed audiences for decades with her intelligence, warmth and unmistakable voice. Those qualities shine brilliantly on the page in Broad Appeal. It’s funny, wise and deeply moving, with unforgettable characters readers will want to spend time with long after the final page.”
Bishop released her New York Times bestselling memoir, The Third Gilmore Girl, in 2024.

items.title: ‘La Bola Negra’ Ups Planned Theater Count Heading Into Netflix Film’s Widest Weekend Yet (Exclusive)
items.description: Netflix‘s La Bola Negra is adding theaters for its widest frame to date.
items.author: Ryan Gajewski
paragraphs: Netflix‘s La Bola Negra is adding theaters for its widest frame to date.

The acclaimed drama feature will expand to 465 domestic theaters this weekend after Netflix previously had projected that the film would hit between 200 and 300 locations, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. Directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film stars Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau as it explores queer identity over three timelines.

La Bola Negra grossed $418,000 last weekend from 38 North American theaters and has now surpassed $1.3 million domestically for the run that heads into its fourth frame. During its debut weekend, its $69,375 per-screen average from four theaters was the second-highest ever for a non-English language release, behind only 2019’s Parasite. For its debut frame, 50 percent of the U.S. audience was under age 35.

This week, La Bola Negra hit No. 3 on Spain‘s all-time box office chart for a Spanish film. The feature, which counts Elastica Films as its distributor in Spain, is also among the top 10 highest-grossing titles ever in that country. Penélope Cruz, Glenn Close, Carlos González, Milo Quifes and Lola Dueñas round out the cast.

La Bola Negra premiered earlier this year at Cannes, where Calvo and Ambrossi won best director. It recently took the audience award at the London Film Festival, joining such previous accolades as the TIFF people’s choice award and the San Sebastián International Film Festival audience award. It is expected to be a major Academy Award contender and was Spain’s entry for the best international feature Oscar.

Madonna is among La Bola Negra’s famous fans, as the music superstar took to Instagram to encourage her followers to seek the movie out. “Go and see this film!!!” she captioned her post over the weekend. “A transformational experience.”

La Bola Negra holds an 86 critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, along with a 97 percent audience rating. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter, critic Richard Lawson praised it as “vivid and transporting.” After opening in theaters Oct. 16, the film hits Netflix on Dec. 2, making its 47-day theatrical window the longest yet for the streaming service.

items.title: Bob Dylan Dressed Like Timothée Chalamet to Meet the Pope
items.description: Today, millions of Americans awoke to social media feeds awash with images of and commentary about a landmark event that seemed nigh-impossible a mere 24 hours earlier. I speak, of course, of this image:
items.author: Ian Grant
paragraphs: Today, millions of Americans awoke to social media feeds awash with images of and commentary about a landmark event that seemed nigh-impossible a mere 24 hours earlier. I speak, of course, of this image:

As the nation began to digest the results of a historic election that seemed to herald the arrival of a new America, two of our very best Americans met for a private audience on the other side of the Atlantic: Bob Dylan, the Great American artist, and Pope Leo XIV, the first American Pope. Dylan is in the midst of yet another lengthy European tour—his strongest in some number of years, judging by recent bootleg tapes. On November 2, he played a show at Milan’s Unipol Dome, then jetted over to Rome ahead of a November 5 performance at the Palazzo dello Sport. What better way to kill an off-day than a quick chat with the Vicar of Christ?

It wasn’t the first time Bob met a Pope, as some pointed out. In 1997, he performed for John Paul II at the World Eucharistic Congress in Bologna, donning a dapper Western suit and a fine Stetson for the occasion. He and JP2 made for a bit of an odd couple, the mysterious American gunslinger and the seemingly-nonplussed Polish holy man.

Dylan has somewhat more in common with Pope Leo, a.k.a Robert Francis Prevost, a fellow Midwesterner. But even if the two men hail from similar geography, the sight of them together under the bright fluorescent lights of an anonymous Vatican office looked like the product of a well-crafted AI prompt, if not an outright fever dream. The images were so unexpected, so uncanny, I would’ve been convinced they were fake had they not been published by an official press organ of the Vatican.
Much of the whiplash stemmed from the two men’s appearances. Angel and devil. Spy versus spy. The man in the long black coat and the man in the short white mozzetta. The one liners wrote themselves.

On Wednesday, the Pope wore a clean white cassock and a tidy little zucchetto, with an iron cross hanging down around his neck. In short, he looked like the Pope. I suppose I would say the same about Bob: that he looked like himself. As any good Dylan fan knows, however, the meaning of that phrase has changed radically over the years. Bob’s shifting appearance is almost as notorious as his shifting artistic sensibility. Dust bowl refugee, sharp-suited mod, bohemian poltergeist, whatever this is—the man has worn many hats.

Sometime in the early 1990s, Dylan took a liking to the humble hoodie, a stylistic evolution that intersected neatly with his booze-fueled artistic nadir. The hoodie allowed him to hide in plain sight, even as he continued to take the stage around the world on his Never Ending Tour. It was practical, yes, but it was also a defense mechanism, a way to synthesize his compulsion to perform and his aversion to being seen. That it often looked hard as hell did not hurt. (It should come as little surprise that Timothée Chalamet, who may as well have been born wearing a hoodie, seemed to riff on this era when he was channeling Bob all those months ago.)

In the 21st century, Bob came unstuck from time. On landmark records like “Love And Theft” and Modern Times, Dylan burrowed into an imaginary musical past situated somewhere between the Civil War and the Great Depression. His style shifted to match. In the early aughts, he adopted a full country-western guise, complete with a Lee Van Cleef mustache. In the years that followed, his sartorial inspirations shifted east: a little less cowboy, a little more riverboat gambler, often performing in wide-brimmed hats, long frock coats, and string ties. “Rock and roll Mark Twain” wouldn’t have been an inaccurate descriptor.

Which brings us back to today’s meeting with Pope Leo. On first glance, Dylan’s ensemble is bonkers: western black blouson with contrast stitching along the chest and collar; beneath that, a heavyweight black hoodie zipped to the chest; beneath that, a white collared shirt with several buttons undone, collar loosely drawn together with a polka-dot cravat. The hood is decidedly up, stationed atop a black flat brim cap. In some shots, Bob can even be seen sporting leather gloves and an old-fashioned umbrella, which seems to double as a cane.

Part “Man in Black” sobriety, part rock star debauchery, with a dash of the hypebeast flavor from Timmy’s A Complete Unknown press tour—the man got a damn fit off in Vatican City. There’s no other way to describe it. (It’s a shame Pope Leo left his Rhude jacket back at the Papal Palace.)

Still, it’s a look with roots in Bob’s past, or pasts: the hoodies of the ’90s, the Westernwear of the 2000s, even the polka dots of 1965. No one but Bob would ever dare to pair all these disparate elements, particularly for a private audience with the Bishop of Rome. No one but Bob could.
Someone should come up with a word for that.

items.title: Montana’s Newest Congressman Dresses Like a Ralph Lauren Model
items.description: You couldn’t ask for a better embodiment of the blue wave than Sam Forstag, the 32-year-old rookie Montana Democrat who defeated his Republican rival in yesterday’s midterms to flip an important House seat. While unaffordability was a key issue in the midterms
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: You couldn’t ask for a better embodiment of the blue wave than Sam Forstag, the 32-year-old rookie Montana Democrat who defeated his Republican rival in yesterday’s midterms to flip an important House seat. While unaffordability was a key issue in the midterms across the country, it’s especially noticeable in Montana, where an influx of billionaires and tech companies has sent the cost of living soaring. Like many of his compatriots, Forstag campaigned on promises of affordable housing, better healthcare, and getting money out of politics. Unlike his fellow Democratic challengers, however, he did it in a wardrobe that looked straight off a rack at the RRL store.

Last night, in front of a crowd of supporters in Missoula, Forstag delivered his victory speech dressed in a hickory-striped work shirt, jeans, a big western belt buckle, and a pair of weathered brown forestry boots. Forstag’s fit stands in contrast to the standard election night business-casual look favored by political hopefuls on both sides of the aisle, but he’s far from the first candidate to lean into the dress codes of blue-collar Americans. From Tim Walz’s camo hats and Filson Mackinaw jackets to John Fetterman’s Carhartt hoodie, workwear remains a potent symbol of working-class solidarity. In this case, however, it’s not just blue-collar cosplay.

Straight out of college and looking to pay off his student loans, Forstag joined the US Forest Service as a wildland firefighter and spent the next eight years battling blazes around the country, including four years as a smokejumper parachuting into fire zones. As a result, he comes by his love of Levi’s and sturdy, Goodyear-welted footwear honestly, and—Montana being a place where jeans and work shirts are considered business-casual for many—didn’t need to change his look for the campaign.

As authentic as Forstag’s election-night outfit was, he also appears to be a guy who understands the power of styling. While his shirt likely didn’t have Ralph Lauren’s initials on the tag (wildland firefighters only make $20 an hour), the way he wore it—half unbuttoned, layered over a red thermal henley, and tucked into his jeans—owes a debt to the romantic take on Western style Lauren has been trafficking in since the ’70s. Or, equally likely, the Montana cowboys who the designer borrowed it from. Either way, Forstag’s look, like the progressive politics he and his Democratic colleagues campaigned on, will be a welcome disruption to business as usual on Capitol Hill.

items.title: This New G-Shock Looks a Lot Like One of the Most Iconic Watches Ever Made
items.description: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: If we were playing matchmaker for some of our favorite watch brands, we wouldn’t have thought of pairing a Casio G-Shock with Patek Philippe’s iconic Nautilus. However, the Japanese watchmaker’s new GMC-2500 proves that opposites do attract.

The 2500 Series is a new collection that “reimagines the design DNA of the watch that started it all,” according to Casio. The brand is nodding towards the original G-Shock ref. DW-5000C from 1983, a watch designed to be tough enough to keep ticking even when dropped. The team famously tested prototypes by hurling them out of the third-floor men’s bathroom of the Casio offices. The new 2500 series is a close descendant of the shock-absorbent watch's original design.

The first G-Shock featured an octagonal digital display, four buttons on the case flanks, and an integrated rubber strap. The 2500 Series incorporates most of those features—but this time, the display is analog rather than digital, and a pair of case “ears” makes the model look a lot like Patek Philippe’s famous flagship luxury sports watch.

Designed by Gérald Genta and released in 1976, the Nautilus is based on a porthole—hence the “ears,” which mirror the hinges/securing mechanism used to open and close a ship’s window against the elements. You may also recall that this isn't the first time that Casio has taken inspiration from a famous Genta watch: the GA-2100 Series (aka ‘CasiOak’), with its octagonal bezel design, bears a remarkable similarity to the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak.

The watch community has been waiting impatiently for the announcement of the 2500 series since Casio’s Japanese website accidentally listed these pieces back in September. In the months since, collectors have already given the watch the “CasioNaut” nickname. (What good is a watch without a clever nickname, after all?) The wait isn’t over just yet, though. The line will officially go on sale through Casio’s website on November 6th.

The 2500 Series is much more than a quartz-powered Nautilus copy. At the center of the design is the Multi-Mission Date function that operates through a three-cell display at 3 o’clock. Besides indicating the date, it can also display the watch’s current mode, elapsed stopwatch minutes, and setting information. Meanwhile, a small-seconds display at 9 o’clock shows passing seconds, but can also be paused and restarted as necessary. (Pausing the function can extend the battery life up to five years.)

The timepiece's tech uses G-SHOCK’s familiar four-button arrangement and comes packed with all the features we've come to expect from the Japanese brand. For starters, the watch automatically keeps rigorous time through 2099 after you input the year, month, and date. LED illumination ensures everything is legible even in low light, while a magnetic system steadies the watch’s hands even if dropped, bumped, or roughed up. Water-resistant to 200m, the 2500 Series is just as capable as you’d expect from a hard-wearing G-SHOCK. Available in simple resin cases with matching rubber bracelets for $145; with metal accents and rubber bracelets for $280-$300; and with full-metal bracelets for $350, the handful of launch references come in a variety of versatile colors and weigh between 47 grams (resin) and 160-180 grams (metal).

Though Casio releases oodles of fresh colorways in existing G-SHOCK families each year, it’s not every day that the world gets an entirely new model family. Fun, streamlined, and much more affordable than the watch it's nicknamed after, the 2500 Series is certainly on its way to becoming a hit.

items.title: Pierpaolo Piccioli Steps Down As Creative Director of Balenciaga
items.description: Pierpaolo Piccioli is leaving Balenciaga after less than two years. The news was confirmed on Thursday by Gianfranco Gianangeli, the lable’s president and CEO.
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: Pierpaolo Piccioli is leaving Balenciaga after less than two years. The news was confirmed on Thursday by Gianfranco Gianangeli, the lable’s president and CEO.

“We are deeply grateful for Pierpaolo’s contribution to Balenciaga,” Gianangeli said. “Through his vision, he reaffirmed the couture origins of the house, bringing his considered approach to craftsmanship, construction and creativity. I would like to sincerely thank him for his dedication, generosity and collaboration.”

The Italian designer originally took on the role in May 2025 following both his predecessor Demna’s departure for Gucci and his own exit form Valentino in 2024. Though the romantic, colorful aesthetic he etablished at Valentino varied drastically from Demna’s streetware-savvy and often subversive work, expectations were originally high. Piccioli proved had proved his immense couture abilities, and it was assumed those talents would transfer over to the Balenciaga couturier. Many predicted a return to the classic innovative form of Cristóbal Balenciaga’s original collections.

But Piccioli struggled in the position, thanks in part to his predecessor. Demna, though controversial, brought a very specific vision to his Balenciaga, which proved to be successful. “I didn’t want to come here to find the same people with the same experiences,” Piccioli told W of his goals when starting at Balenciaga. “I wanted to face something new.” Unfortunately, it seems like the brand’s parent company, Kering, had other ideas. Reports suggest that Kering wanted to continue pushing an edgier and youthful look for Balenciaga, but that has never been Piccioli’s forte.

Piccioli showed his first collection for the brand in October 2025 as part of the spring 2026 season. As expected, he dove into the Balenciaga archives, presenting a collection of color-blocked looks with voluminous proportions that riffed on Balenciaga’s 1957 sack dress with oversized sunglasses to match. For fall/winter 2026, he presented darker offerings—including a collaboration with the HBO show Euphoria—which received lukewarm reviews. Notably, sales of menswear, a source of growth under Demna, have taken a dip since Piccioli’s appointment.

According to Vogue Business, Balenciaga’s parent company, Kering, said that in Q2 of 2026, “Balenciaga faced a more challenging quarter.” The third quarter, meanwhile, was also “challenging” for the brand.

You can’t say Piccioli didn’t try, though. A pre-fall collection alluded to the world of sports and was followed up by a collaboration with the NBA, perhaps Piccioli’s attempt to court streetwear fans. He maintained relationships with famous faces, dressing Demi Moore for the Vanity Fair Oscar Party and Cannes red carpet this year and recently adorning many stars, including Mikey Madison and Tracee Ellis Ross, for the Academy Museum Gala. But not all of his celebrity placements worked. Hudson William’s was ridiculed for his baby blue matador-adjacent Balenciaga suit at the 2026 Met Gala, and the look Shailene Woodley wore to the Emmys in September was meme’d to death online.

While Piccioli’s future is unclear, we have a bit more insight into Balenciaga’s succession plan. Kering has said that the brand’s new creative director will be announced shortly. Of course, rumors are already floating around, and it is believed that Martine Rose will step into the position. It will mark a homecoming for the British-Jamaican designer who acted as a menswear advisor for Demna’s Balenciaga. This choice would prove that Kering is looking to focus on Balenciaga’s menswear, as that is Rose’s bread and butter. Her eponymous label, which she founded in 2007, has been a cult favorite for years, but a 2021 acquisition by the brand accelerator Tomorrow left Martine Rose floundering. The Balenciaga appointment is an exciting prospect. Not only would Rose be the first woman to design for the brand, but the job would also provide Rose with a larger budget than she’s ever had control over, and who knows what creative genius could come from that.

items.title: What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections?
items.description: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramat
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.

While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.

Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans. Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second.

Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.

There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.

The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.

With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.

Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout.

Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.

And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.

We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

items.title: Is This What Hope Feels Like?
items.description: The air began to feel electric around 9 p.m. on Election Night. Polling locations in most states had closed, and early results were making the electoral map look quite blue already. My group chats started lighting up, cautiously weighing how much excitement we
items.author: Andrea González-Ramírez
paragraphs: The air began to feel electric around 9 p.m. on Election Night. Polling locations in most states had closed, and early results were making the electoral map look quite blue already. My group chats started lighting up, cautiously weighing how much excitement we should feel. But it was too early to read into the vote count — plenty of time for everything to still go to hell yet again.

By 10:15 p.m., I was full-on libbing out. “I feel insane,” we texted each other back and forth, alongside clips of NBC News projections and memes of the Blue Man Group. Georgia had elected Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, making her the first Black woman to become governor in U.S. history. Democrats were projected to retake the House in what was looking like their biggest victory in years. And Democrat Annie Andrews had pulled a stunning upset, flipping the Senate seat in ruby-red South Carolina. The blue wave was actually here; now it was just waiting to see how big it would be. “Is this what hope feels like????” a friend wrote.

By 11 p.m., Democrats had gained enough seats to retake the Senate; Texas had gone blue for the first time this century, electing a Democratic governor and senator; and even Mississippi seemed like it could be in play. Wave? More like an actual tsunami — in coastal cities, in the prairie lands, in the Midwest, in the Deep South.

In some ways, no one should be shocked: The polls were consistently projecting a Democratic sweep. But the polls have also been horrifically wrong before, and given President Donald Trump’s election-interference attempts, skepticism felt like the safer bet. We’ve become so accustomed to feeling disappointment and heartbreak that it’s like our nervous systems have forgotten how to process optimism and joy. But despite the $474 million broligarch Elon Musk poured into GOP candidates this cycle — more than any other donor in history — he had embarrassingly nothing to show in return. And the Republicans’ blatant attempt at rigging the electoral map via last-minute gerrymandering failed as their decades-long control of certain House districts, Senate seats, and governor mansions evaporated before our eyes.

Every demographic in the country shifted toward Democrats, even in states that Trump carried in the 2024 presidential election, by double digits. Trump’s gains with young men, Latinos, and Black voters were wiped away — the “realignment” of his 2024 coalition was a mirage. Even white working-class workers, who have been a reliable Republican voting bloc for the past decade, had swung about 15 percentage points left as of last night’s estimates. It’s the kind of generational shift I doubted I’d ever see.

A few months ago, I wrote about how some of the people who were most politically active in the Trump 1.0 days now seemed to be numbing out, paralyzed by the constant stream of horrors and opting to disengage. It concerned me that there was a sense that the fast slide into fascism was inevitable — that there was no way to stop the Trump administration’s madness, just slightly mitigate its effects. This, of course, serves the authoritarian playbook: Moving fast and breaking things overwhelms people to the point they can’t even keep track of what new nightmare the administration is cooking up. Someone who feels terrified, helpless, and like nothing will change as a result is unlikely to rise up against a regime. Would people even show up to the polls if they felt like it’d be pointless? Thankfully, voters chose another path. Numbing out is easy, but they did the hard thing instead, stepping up to the plate when the time called for it.

Trump repeatedly told Americans to vote like he was on the ballot, so that’s exactly what they did. For 21 months, communities have seen up close MAGA’s brand fascism and everything that comes with it: the unnecessary wars, the tariffs and cuts worsening our financial future, the campaign of terror against immigrants, the corrupt self-dealing, the carte blanche being given to billionaires, the gleeful cruelty. On Election Day, they decisively rebuked all of it.

Democrats’ wins nationwide open a world of possibilities. By ending two years of one-party rule in Washington, they’ll now be able to keep Trump in check. They have a long wish list of things to accomplish: undoing some of his most harmful policies, aggressively investigating wrongdoing in his administration, finding creative ways to address the crises that voters have tasked them with tackling. Even Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito’s decision not to retire may come back to haunt him, as the Democratic majority in the Senate will now have the power to reject Trump’s judicial nominees. Downballot wins in governor and state legislature races will have an even more immediate impact on voters’ daily lives, from addressing the affordability crisis to restoring reproductive rights. These state-level victories will also create yet another firewall against Trump’s federal overreach, as they can take him to court to challenge his policies.

But the Democratic Party, which so often snatches defeat away from the jaws of victory, would do well to remember that voters are a fickle thing. A seismic change like this is not set in stone — for the next two years, they need to rise up to the occasion and deliver on the promises they made. This is not the time to fall back into the old way of doing politics; nationwide, the desire for change is bigger and deeper than that. Anything less than being brave is unacceptable. After all, voters delivered a clear message: This imperfect, heartbreaking, remarkable country is worth fighting for. Time to get to work.

items.title: Are Your Parents Hiding Their Money From You?
