items.title: I'm 37, I Have A $352K Joint Income & I Love My Stanley (Pry It Out Of My Cold, Dead, Hydrated Hands, Haters)
items.description: A Week In Dallas, TX On A $352,000 Joint Income
items.author: R
paragraphs: A Week In Dallas, TX On A $352,000 Joint Income
This week: A client relations advisor working in finance who makes $122,000 per year and spends some of it on shoelaces.

If you'd like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we're not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.
Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We'd love to hear your thoughts here.
Joint Income/Financial Setup: My husband makes $230,000, so in total, we make $352,000. We share all money, and I manage our finances.
Investment account: $76,000
Retirement accounts: $310,000
Paycheck Amount (biweekly): $18,850
Housing Costs: $4,137 (we own our home).
Loan Payments: $657 (my husband's car payment).
Savings (split between various accounts): $225, plus whatever is left over at the end of the month.
Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?

It was always a given that I would go to college. I was the first person on my mom's side to earn a college degree (my mom dropped out to marry my dad when they were 20), but my dad has always been very forward-thinking and education-focused. I finished my BA in 3.5 years, took a break for an internship, then finished my Master's degree in 1.5 years. My options in the summer were to do summer school full time or else come home and work. I chose summer school almost every year. My parents paid for my BA outright. My dad always made it known he was saving for our college and it was important that we appreciate it and do our best in school. I took out loans for my Master's, but my dad paid them all off once I finished the degree and got a job. I realize how lucky I am, and I only become more appreciative as I get older. I know I am only “ahead” of many of my peers because I was able to enter adulthood with no student loans and no car payment, as well as help with a home down payment (mentioned below).
Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?

I think it's important to note that my parents have basically achieved the American Dream. They both grew up at the lower end of the income spectrum (my dad was extremely poor as a child). He worked full-time through college while taking a full load of classes. He is brilliant, as well as having a high EQ and knowing how to manage people well, so he moved up the ladder faster than his peers. He also had my mom at home taking care of the household and my brother and me, which is a huge and valuable contribution. As I got older, my dad made more money. In high school, I basically got everything I needed and everything I really REALLY wanted, but nothing over the top. After I finished high school, my dad's star really started to rise, and now they are very well off. It helps that both he and my mom are very modest. They have no desire for fancy clothes or status symbols, even now that they can afford basically anything within reason. Their biggest splurges are probably family travel and new cars more often than is strictly necessary. My dad discussed budgeting with us often. When I was 12, he bought me a calculator and taught me how to budget based on different incomes and different needs/wants. He also taught me how to calculate car payments and house payments based on interest rates and down payments. As a pre-teen, I was so bored, but looking back, I'm very grateful for the common sense lessons. Even though he taught us to be money conscious, he was never open about exactly how much money he made or what we had. He worried a lot, but by the time I was old enough to realize what was going on, I think his worry was more a product of his childhood than any real financial danger. He always told us he didn't want us to have to work in college like he did, and he's very frugal, so he and my mom really maximized planning for our future as a family over short-term rewards.
What was your first job and why did you get it?

The summer after my freshman year of college, I worked for the company my dad works for. I was a glorified runner — taking meeting minutes, picking up visiting employees from the airport, delivering documents to the city, etc. I made $12.50/hr (my dad thought my boss offered me way too much) and I felt RICH.
Did you worry about money growing up?

I didn't worry about having enough money for food or housing, but I knew we didn't have infinite money. Most vacations were road trips in the summer, or ski trips to New Mexico, staying in a small cabin owned by relatives. I remember when all the girls were getting CHI hair straighteners ($100) in junior high, and I begged for one for months, and my parents finally surprised me with one for Christmas. That was a BIG deal, if that gives insight into how I grew up.
Do you worry about money now?

I go back and forth. Up until recently, I didn't really worry past making sure we weren't overspending and ending up with more outflow than inflow at the end of the month. My husband's mother died of cancer when she was just 42, so we try to balance saving with also living for today and not waiting until retirement to travel or do things we really want to do. But we have decided recently that I should try to leave my job to focus more on our son. He's entering a tough age, and we know academics are going to require a lot of time, plus he has extra medical concerns and extra emotional concerns due to his differences becoming more obvious to his peers. We just want to do the best we can for him. A few months ago, I went through all our spending and cut out extras (including Amazon Prime…Jeff doesn't need my money), and I've been trying to be cognizant and intentional about what I'm buying. While I worry about day-to-day life, I'm lucky I don't really have to worry about retirement or college expenses for my son. We have a 529 we contribute to, but my parents have a much larger account for him, and I know when they pass away I will receive an eight-figure inheritance. But they are young and vibrant, and I hope they live to be 110.
At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?

I worked through my Master's degree and paid for my rent and living expenses, but when I got married right before I finished my Master's, my dad removed me from everything else (phone plan, car insurance, health insurance, etc.). My husband and I were 23 then. However, I know my parents would be a safety net if we ever needed it. Our goal is to never ask them for money and not accept money every time it's offered. For example, we had a major leak and needed a new AC a few years ago and instead of taking the $15K in cash my dad offered, we took it out of our investment account. There have been times we accepted it, though. We were so broke when my son was born; he had insane medical expenses (born with a rare disability) and I had to take unpaid FMLA to stay home longer than the standard six weeks due to my son having surgery and other major medical events. I ended up owing money when I went back to work due to health insurance premiums. My husband and I were also completely traumatized by everything going on in his infancy, so even just making sure our bills were paid was a herculean effort. We would not have made it through that time without my parents financial and emotional support.
Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.

I received $5,000 in cash when one of my grandfathers died in my early 20s. My parents owned a small farm. Once they sold it they gave my brother and I each 25% of the proceeds (about $90K). We used almost half of it to put down on a house, and the rest to start our investment account. Oh, and I bought my first-ever designer bag with $2,000 of it (sadly, I didn't inherit my mom's disinterest in designer clothing and accessories).

Besides the symphony tickets, I think this is a pretty fair reflection of our regular expenses. Thinking of what I was going to write in this diary did make me consider whether or not I NEEDED to purchase things, so maybe internally writing a Money Diary every day would help me save on little treats and unnecessary things.
The first step to getting your financial life in order is tracking what you spend — to try on your own, check out our guide to managing your money every day. For more Money Diaries, click here.
Do you have a Money Diary you'd like to share? Submit it with us here.
Have questions about how to submit or our publishing process? Read our Money Diaries FAQ doc here or email us here.

items.title: The psychology of separating church and state | Aeon Essays
items.description: The idea of separating church and state – now entrenched in many modern liberal democracies – is in some ways strange. After all, governments must keep themselves informed and inform their citizens. That’s why they turn to the science of meteorology to predict
items.author: Neil Van Leeuwen; Jacob Eisler
paragraphs: The idea of separating church and state – now entrenched in many modern liberal democracies – is in some ways strange. After all, governments must keep themselves informed and inform their citizens. That’s why they turn to the science of meteorology to predict weather patterns, to economics to understand patterns of growth and decline, and to the medical sciences to improve public health. So why wouldn’t governments also keep close alliances with religious institutions to know what’s going on with God?

Separating church and state appears strange from other perspectives as well. In the historical sweep of large-scale human societies, it’s a relative newcomer, often associated with the United States’ founding father Thomas Jefferson. In 1802, Jefferson asserted the principle of separation in a letter to the Danbury Baptist Association in Connecticut:

Believing with you that religion is a matter which lies solely between man and his God … that the legitimate powers of government reach actions only, and not opinions, I contemplate with sovereign reverence that act of the whole American people which declared that their legislature would ‘make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof,’ thus building a wall of separation between Church and State.

We’re fans of Jefferson’s principle, one of us (Neil Van Leeuwen) being a philosophy professor who grew up in the Christian Reformed Church, and the other (Jacob Eisler) being a law professor who regularly attends synagogue. But Jefferson’s letter makes putting the principle into practice sound simpler than it is – as though governments could be entirely hands-off when it comes to people’s beliefs, or ‘opinions’. That, however, can’t be right: engaging with and shaping political, social and other kinds of beliefs is actually a core function of government. Public education guides what people believe about everything from mathematics to history to astronomy. Governments also shape beliefs for policy reasons. If fire department officials learn that people believe a building is safe when it isn’t, they will try to change what people believe about the building’s safety. Belief is also a category of legal interest. If a psychotherapist, for example, believes a patient is a danger to himself or others, the therapist is obligated by law to report that belief.

All this means that Jefferson’s ‘wall of separation’ can’t sensibly prohibit governments from intervening on beliefs of any type whatsoever. Rather, Jefferson – along with advocates of the principle who came after him – must have presupposed that there is something distinctive about religious beliefs that makes it reasonable to give them a different legal status.

But what is this distinctive thing? Is it that religious beliefs concern God? No, because Buddhism is a religion with its own beliefs, yet Buddhism has no supreme deity. Is it that religious beliefs concern the supernatural generally? No, because many superstitions that aren’t part of a religion concern the supernatural too. Is it that religious beliefs concern morality, as the biologist Stephen Jay Gould once suggested? No, because many religious beliefs aren’t about morality, and many moral beliefs aren’t religious. In any case, any system of government must presuppose some moral beliefs – eg, that murder is wrong – to be a government at all. These considerations might make one despair of articulating the psychological distinction of interest – what’s different about religious ‘belief’? – that’s needed to make sense of separating church and state in the first place.

Such attempts at characterising religious belief fail, we think, because they focus on belief contents, or what the believing is about. But since any given idea can be believed in a religious way or not, that won’t work. Our suggestion, then, is that religiously believing is a different attitude from ordinary matter-of-fact believing – a different way of relating to ideas – and that this is what’s distinctive about religious belief. In other words, sacralising an idea is different from just taking it to describe how things are. Furthermore, empirical research in cognitive science and anthropology of religion, along with accompanying philosophical analysis, can help reveal characteristic features of the difference in attitude we’re after. To have specific terms, we call that the difference between religious credence and factual belief. Understanding this difference, we’ll see, helps make sense of Jefferson’s wall of separation, and supports the rationale for separating church and state in liberal democracies more generally.

Whatever they are, ‘beliefs’ come in different varieties. The word ‘belief’ is polysemous – meaning it can refer to a range of different-but-related things – and it subsumes a motley crew: from humdrum factual beliefs (say, about where the ice-cream store is) to superstitions (like those found in astrology), and from moral beliefs about murder to philosophical beliefs about how ‘all is one’. As mentioned earlier, beliefs can also be categorised by their contents (what is the belief about? Is it about politics? Or maybe about a probable scientific theory?) Or by the attitude they embody (how does a person relate to given ideas or contents?) Here, however, we focus on the differences between matter-of-fact believing and religious credence as distinct ways in which people process ideas. There are, of course, more varieties of belief-like attitudes. But we home in on factual belief and religious credence since the differences in those attitudes matter most to the psychology of separating church and state.

Ethnographies of religion, like the anthropologist Tanya Luhrmann’s When God Talks Back (2012), feature the devout talking of their ‘beliefs’ as a matter of choice. One of the congregants from the Vineyard Church whom Luhrmann interviewed told her: ‘There is always a choice to believe what it is.’ And a common theme in the Vineyard is choosing Jesus, which means choosing to believe in Jesus. Nor is choosing ‘belief’ unique to Christianity. People around the world switch religions for reasons of romance or for other social incentives, which means voluntarily choosing what religious credence to have.

But suppose someone offered you $1 million to believe, in a matter-of-fact way, that lions are vegetarians. Could you do it? We doubt it, even if you wanted the money. You could voluntarily imagine that lions are vegetarians, or you might pretend to believe it. But if you know that lions eat meat, you can’t just choose to believe the contrary. This is one illustration of how factual belief is not under voluntary control. Or, as one of us (Neil) has put it in Religion as Make-Believe (2023): if you factually believe it, you can’t help believing it. Try for a moment to factually believe that New York City is in Quebec, that Iceland is in the Southern Hemisphere, or that Justin Bieber speaks Swahili as his mother tongue.
This gives us our first processing difference between religious credence and matter-of-fact belief:
Difference number 1: religious credence is voluntary, while factual belief is involuntary.

But if matter-of-fact belief isn’t voluntary, or responsive to the will, what does it respond to? Numerous psychological pressures come into play, including distortions like biases and misremembering. But that shouldn’t obscure the main driver of factual belief: evidence. Examples are so simple they’re easy to overlook. If you think, in a matter-of-fact way, that you started the washing machine and then, an hour later, see that the clothes you loaded are dry and still dirty, the evidence of your eyes extinguishes your prior factual belief. If you think the supermarket is open and then arrive to find its lights are all out, that evidence changes your factual belief.
Noah was an exemplar of faith for building an enormous boat when there was no evidence of an impending flood

Empirical research reveals such evidence-responsiveness already in children and even infants. According to The Scientist in the Crib (1999) by the developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik and colleagues, young children and even babies learn about the world by forming mini-theories in different domains, and testing them – much like scientists do. According to the research of the developmentalists Paul Harris and Melissa Koenig, children are also evidentially discriminating in how they learn from other people. Among other things, children are more likely to believe sources that have been accurate in the past than sources that have been inaccurate.
Is religious credence similarly responsive to evidence?

Consider faith. In Hebrews 11:1, we read: ‘Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.’ If that’s right, then religious credence doesn’t depend on evidence in the way factual belief does. In the Gospel of John, for example, we read about Doubting Thomas, who demands evidence that the man before him is Jesus resurrected; he consequently is an exemplar of what faith is not. In the Old Testament, Noah was an exemplar of faith for building an enormous boat when there was no visible evidence of an impending flood. Examples can be multiplied. If faith is to stand strong, religious credence must endure the slings and arrows of absent, or even contrary, evidence.

Contemporary cognitive science of religion bears out this point. In a series of cross-cultural studies, researchers have found that, from a young age, people, even in religious societies like Iran and the US, report lower levels of confidence in the invisible religious entities they profess, like God and angels, than in invisible scientific entities, like germs and oxygen. That difference in confidence is presumably due to the felt poverty of evidence for the invisible religious entities. Yet people in some sense nonetheless ‘believe’ (read: religious credence) in the invisible religious entities. The psychologists Emily Liquin, S Emlen Metz and Tania Lombrozo conducted studies finding that participants indicated a lower need for explanation when it came to religious beliefs as opposed to scientific beliefs, while at the same time having a higher mystery acceptance for religious beliefs. So people are often fine treating their religious credences as inexplicable and mysterious.
That gives us our second difference between religious credence and matter-of-fact belief:
Difference number 2: factual belief is highly vulnerable to evidence, while religious credence is not vulnerable to evidence.

There are, of course, complications here. Religious apologists, for example, claim evidence for the stories and doctrines they profess. But claiming evidence is not the same as having one’s credences be vulnerable to it, and apologists are outliers anyway against the broad background of faithful who don’t usually pretend to treat their religious credence in an evidence-based way.

Those differences, voluntary choice versus evidence-responsiveness, are differences in how religious credence versus factual belief arise in the first place. But what about downstream differences, like how they bring about action and behaviour?

This brings us to the third difference. Have you ever heard the expression ‘once-a-week Christian’? The phrase describes people who act as though their Christian ‘beliefs’ are true one day a week – and then largely leave them dormant otherwise. Having grown up and participated in different religious traditions ourselves, we can say from personal experience that more people fit this compartmentalised model than would like to admit. Even those who practise devotion daily may act as if God is real specifically in sacred or ritual times and places, but then not really act this way otherwise. If one asks religious people whether God is ever-present in their lives, they might say yes. But such probes might be like opening the refrigerator to see whether the light is always on. In Breaking the Spell: Religion as a Natural Phenomenon (2006), the philosopher Daniel Dennett highlights this behavioural pattern in even blunter terms. He points out that people do things with God watching that they wouldn’t do with their own mothers watching, and then asks pointedly: ‘Do you really believe God is watching you? Perhaps not.’ We would say that people who profess to religious credence do typically have religious credence in a watchful deity – but, to Dennett’s point, not factual belief.

Empirical studies and ethnographic observations further exemplify the compartmentalisation of religious credence. According to one study, people in the Bible Belt start subscriptions to pornography sites at the same rate as in less conservative regions of the US – though not on Sundays, when the rate is significantly lower. According to another study, charitable giving among the religious is not significantly different from among the secular – except for on Sundays. Turning to a different religious context, the experimental economist Erik Duhaime found that, in an economic game, 100 per cent of Moroccan shopkeepers in the Medina of Marrakesh chose the most charitable option while the call to prayer was audible, dropping to 50 per cent in the 20 minutes following it.
Even if one pretends that a slab of concrete is a soft bed, one still stretches out on it slowly so as not to injure oneself

Another way of putting the point about compartmentalisation would be to say that religious credences tend to guide people’s symbolic actions – prayer, liturgies, rituals or even charity – but not their everyday instrumental actions, like commuting to work or feeding the dog. In those cases, the world is just a world, and supernatural beliefs are largely dormant. And even if a religious tradition says its religious ‘beliefs’ should govern actions all the time, the fact that such norms exist and are hard to follow is actually evidence that such religious credences usually don’t guide action outside of sacred settings. (If they did, why have such a norm?)

Matter-of-fact believing, however, is not compartmentalised in this way. Factual belief, in the sense at work here, is a person’s default cognitive map of the world, and it is always on, whenever we act. Examples of ideas most people factually believe help to illustrate this point. Dried concrete is always hard. Electricity just exists. Wood comes from trees. And so on – at least for people who believe those things in a matter-of-fact way. This lack of compartmentalisation can also be illustrated through a contrasting reference to pretend play: even if one pretends that a slab of concrete is a soft bed, one still stretches out on it slowly so as not to injure oneself, rather than flopping down on it. That’s because the factual belief that concrete is hard still guides action even when one is pretending otherwise. Whenever you perform actions, you act on a mental model of how things just are, and a person’s default mental model of what the world is like is what we are calling factual belief.
This gives us the following:
Difference number 3: religious credence is compartmentalised, while factual belief is uncompartmentalised.

This is all just a snapshot of some of the psychological processing differences between religious credence and factual belief. There are, of course, complications and details to sort out – including hard-to-categorise examples, like conspiracy ‘beliefs’, along with quasi-religious ideological credences – but those shouldn’t obscure the overall picture. Religious people, by and large, have a two-map cognitive structure with factual belief and religious credence playing distinct roles. Factual belief is the evidence-responsive default cognitive map that guides action across settings, and religious credence is a chosen, compartmentalised cognitive map that becomes active in sacralised ritual settings. Those settings may occur as often as several times a day, just one day a week, or even more rarely than that, but compartmentalisation is there in any case.

Before returning to the issue of separating church and state, let’s just address one more question about this overall psychological picture: are lay people (not just people who read and write essays like this one) aware of the psychological difference between factual belief and religious credence?
The answer, the evidence suggests, is yes – at least in a vague way.

To start, people often express their religious credences by saying things like ‘I personally believe…’ But one would not express a matter-of-fact belief, say, that their bicycle is in the garage, by saying: ‘I personally believe my bicycle is in the garage.’ They would rather say: ‘I think my bicycle is in the garage’ or just ‘It’s in the garage.’ The inclination to use ‘personally’ suggests people have an intuitive awareness that the kind of ‘belief’ being expressed is a different attitude, a different way of relating to ideas from matter-of-fact belief. And there is more systematic empirical evidence for this point, as well. One of us (Neil) together with colleagues has conducted experimental studies showing that English speakers tend to use the word ‘believes’ when it comes to describing religious attitudes but just ‘thinks’ when it comes to describing matter-of-fact beliefs.

Furthermore, such linguistic differentiation has parallels in other languages, including Fante (a dialect of the Akan people of Ghana), Thai, Mandarin and Bislama (a creole spoken in Vanuatu). Further studies show that people’s use of the word ‘believes’ correlates with seeing an attitude as being held voluntarily and not for evidential reasons – for example, out of loyalty – and as giving rise to symbolic action, like public pronouncements. People’s use of the word ‘thinks’, on the other hand, correlates with seeing an attitude as being held for evidential reasons and as giving rise to truth-dependent instrumental action (like buying property or making investments). All of that suggests that most people are at some level tracing the differences that the foregoing theory makes explicit – and they’re often using the words ‘believe’ versus ‘think’ to report religious credence versus factual belief.

Let’s return to Jefferson’s idea and to the political realm more generally. How does the psychological difference between factual belief and religious credence support the political principle of separating church and state? We think that understanding the difference – psychological dynamics and all – helps us see two justifications that we couldn’t have articulated clearly otherwise.

First, the fact that religious credences are not vulnerable to evidence helps justify the idea that liberal democracies should not establish state religions, in the sense of compelling people to adhere to them. (This is the part of the ‘wall of separation’ captured in the so-called ‘establishment clause’ of the First Amendment to the US Constitution.) The reasoning here is simple. It starts by recognising that any actions a government takes will, in point of fact, be based on, and justified by, ‘beliefs’ of some sort. For example, quarantining people who return from the Democratic Republic of Congo at the time of an Ebola outbreak is based on officials’ factual belief – justified in this case – that those people risk spreading the disease.

Importantly, if the beliefs in question are vulnerable to evidence, as we argued that factual beliefs are, then they will be susceptible to change through the kind of dialogue-based argument and reasoning that is the deliberative heart of democracy. Basically, factual belief-based reasoning and policy-making allows everyone to participate, since factual beliefs respond to evidence, and evidential reasons are the property of everyone.

But, conversely, if a ‘belief’ is not responsive to evidence, as we argued religious credences are not, then it won’t be movable by falsification-oriented argumentative reasoning. Only people who already have the ‘belief’ will be convinced by decisions based on it. Thus, a policy explicitly religious in nature – imposing religious practice, for example – would lack tractability to the defining practices of democratic decision-making. In short, liberal democracies should exclude religion-establishing policies in order to safeguard the rational communal deliberation that is at their centre.
Private motivation and public justification are different things

This perspective illuminates why policy is justified the way it is in liberal democracies. Even when they happen to be motivated by spiritual convictions, citizens tend to, and legislators must (if they are to be constitutionally respectable), frame the descriptive claims in their arguments in terms of matter-of-fact, universally tractable evidence. Such framing yields public explanations that are better suited to liberal democratic coexistence than the mere direct clash of disparate religious ‘beliefs’. This is apparent in one of the most controversial areas of contemporary policymaking: abortion law. Right now in the US, abortion policy runs from fairly permissive in some states to materially restrictive in others. Yet, while it’s true that many political actors are motivated to take positions on this issue that align with their spiritual beliefs and religious affiliations, they still attempt to justify those positions by appeal to beliefs that can be contested by reason and evidence. As a result, debate over how to respect ideals like sanctity of life can, at least in principle, be a matter of public dialogue that includes everyone.

We’ve focused on the US case here, because it is prominent in the history of separating church and state. But commitment to the kind of separation spelled out in the US with the First Amendment is mirrored across the globe, from Japan to Mexico and from Portugal to Namibia. Even the United Kingdom, which has state religions in the form of the Church of England and the Church of Scotland, places strict limits on what those state religions can and can’t do in the public sphere. Importantly, again, none of this prevents citizens and leaders from being motivated to prefer one policy over another due to their religious commitments. But private motivation and public justification are different things. Our present point is that the psychological difference between factual belief and religious credence helps explain why a principle that teases apart those two things makes sense.

Second, the fact that religious credences are psychologically compartmentalised helps justify the idea that, in a liberal society, ‘free exercise’ of religion is a reasonable ideal. (This is the other side of the ‘wall of separation’, also captured in the First Amendment: government shouldn’t stop people from choosing which religion to follow, if any.)

Here’s how this argument works. The compartmentalisation of religious credence, along with the fact that it operates as a ‘map’ distinct from factual belief, means that people who have religious credences are at least capable of setting them aside when it comes to interacting with people outside their own religion. (For example, people who have religious credence in the existence of demons don’t typically perform exorcisms on strangers in the supermarket.) So, since people are capable of setting their religious credences aside in the public sphere, they should be free to keep and venerate them in private, in light of general considerations of privacy and autonomy. Public deliberation can then proceed on the basis of evidence-responsive factual beliefs, as well as moral beliefs that respond to reasons. In short, the default compartmentalisation to which religious credence is prone makes it possible for people with a plurality of religious ‘beliefs’ to co-exist in a free society without a need for the state to challenge any of those ‘beliefs’ per se.

To put this all together, our argument is this: the deal that separation of church and state offers to the religious – namely, that everyone gets religious freedom in exchange for abiding by a constitution that prevents government from establishing their specific religion – can work only because religious credences are psychologically compartmentalised and operate at a different level from factual belief. But the very fact of that default compartmentalisation is precisely what makes such a deal worth striking. Jefferson, we suspect, intuitively sensed this, when he composed his letter to the Danbury Baptists, quoted at the outset, assuring them that they wouldn’t be oppressed for their religious commitments. And perhaps we hear a foreshadow of the very idea of compartmentalisation in his line: ‘religion is a matter which lies solely between man and his God.’

The possessive pronoun in that phrase (‘man and his God’) bespeaks the personal nature of religious credence. Religious credence, after all, is voluntary. That personal nature makes religious credence inapt for entry into public deliberation, but it also makes it ripe for receiving the freedom from government interference into private lives that characterises liberal societies generally.

items.title: Meryll Rogge: The Books That Made Me
items.description: As she launches her collaboration with Brussels-based Saint Martin Bookshop, Meryll Rogge reflects on the books that shape her creative world
items.author: Pedro Vasconcelos
paragraphs: As she launches her collaboration with Brussels-based Saint Martin Bookshop, Meryll Rogge reflects on the books that shape her creative world

“I don’t have much time to read,” Meryll Rogge tells me on a call as she stands in front of a bookshelf stacked to the brim. The Belgian designer has plenty to keep her occupied. Since founding her eponymous label in 2020, Rogge has developed an eclectic approach to womenswear, interpreting the everyday wardrobe through an offbeat, playful lens. With previous stints at Marc Jacobs and Dries Van Noten, she is now balancing her own label with the role of creative director at Marni, a mantel she took up in 2025. Reading has become something of a luxury, reserved for “less chaotic times”.

Still, to reduce Rogge’s relationship with books to the novels that occupy summer days would be misguided. Her recent collaboration with Brussels bookshop Saint Martin offers a glimpse into that long-standing fascination. The project invites a rotating cast of friends of the house to curate capsule collections of one-of-a-kind books – independent publishing rarities of the kind Saint Martin has become synonymous with – set to accompany Rogge’s seasonal releases. For its first edition, ceramist and collaborator Elise Gettliffe, whose natural-glazed pottery explores the imperfections of traditional craft, takes the lead. “Elise has been a good friend since my Royal Academy days – she’s an artist now – and over the years she’s helped with our show installations,” Rogge explains. Gettliffe brings together 20 books – including Studio Mumbai’s Recollections and Martine Syms’ Boon – that draw on a fascination with everyday life akin to Rogge’s.

“When I began working, the internet existed but books were still law, and I started to understand them as a medium that could inspire me,” she says. In her early career, hours spent photocopying books began to infiltrate her creative vision, finding their way into collections like Autumn/Winter 2025, which was inspired by Gordon Matta-Clark’s Walls Paper. “For my brand, books are an essential way to understand our world,” she explains. Yet their influence reaches far beyond her work, shaping the way she sees and relates to those around her.

Across art, film and literature, Rogge finds herself drawn to the mundane – what she calls “the common thread”. “That’s why I like autobiographies. People who live extraordinary lives are always seen through the big picture, but I find comfort in their daily challenges.” This sensibility carries through to her selection for AnOther, a collection of books she describes as being as “fragmented as life itself”.
The Coats of James Castle: A Plane of Singularity by James Castle, 2026

“My husband has a publishing house called Primitive Books. This is one of its most recent publications. It is around the work of American artist James Castle. Castle was from a rural and isolated area of Idaho and was completely self-taught. His work is so vast but the book focuses on his coats. For many years he used materials from his surroundings to create these sculptures of pieces of clothes. Truly an astonishing and beautiful universe. It’s inspiring because the art came from a need to express or to create. Which makes it so pure. It’s shedding a different light on an everyday object.”
One for All, All for One by Gordon Matta-Clark, 1979

“I discovered Gordon Matta-Clark in my Art History class in Antwerp. It was an introduction to a whole new way of thinking about art. It took me a few years to grasp his work. Later in life, I went deeper into it and found it incredibly raw. I am drawn to work that is conceptually complex but still harmonious. When you see documentaries and interviews with him, you can see the hard labour behind it. He was hand-sculpting these buildings, it was deafening noise but, when you look at the final product, it’s almost light. Another one of his works, Walls Papers, was an inspiration for a past collection.”
Donald Judd Furniture by Judd Foundation, 2024

“Donald Judd is another artist whose life fascinates me just as much as the work. I’ve been to Marfa two or three times. All the houses, the furniture, the office spaces have so many layers, so many stories. There’s a purity in his work. I think about his furniture a lot, I hope to one day own one of his pieces. There’s a rigour in his life mission that I find inspiring. His personal and professional life were not separate, it was all part of one big life.”
Take a closer look at five of Donald Judd’s most enduring designs here
The Catcher in the Rye by J D Salinger, 1951

“I heard about Catcher in the Rye for years before I actually read it. It’s one of those classics. But the first time I opened it I was probably in my mid-twenties living in New York. Sometimes literature can be intimidating. You’re afraid of a certain book because it might be too intense, you’re scared of what will be on the next page. This was the complete opposite – it was a page-turner. I had never experienced this way of writing before, it’s almost energising. There was something really moving about living in New York, where the story takes place, and reading this coming-of-age story. It was such a specific time in my life, and having the book gave me something that I can’t forget.”
A Confederacy of Dunces by John Kennedy Toole, 1980

“There’s this one Anglo-Saxon bookshop in Paris that I went to for research. The wonderful person working there gave me a few books to read. This was one of them – there are, of course, so many more, but you gave me a very hard challenge to narrow this list down to five books – but this guy somehow completely got my taste and what I wanted to read. Confederacy of Dunces is incredible because the author John Kennedy Toole was only published posthumously. After it was released it won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. In a weird way it speaks to my interest in biographies. This was an author who couldn’t get published, who nobody took seriously. Only after his death, that happened by choice, was his talent discovered. It’s horrible – actually, it’s infuriating. The novel’s main character, Ignatius, reminds me of Larry David’s Curb Your Enthusiasm, because it can actually be quite frustrating to read. Sometimes while reading I had to close the book because I was so annoyed and just pick it up the next day. But that to me is a sign of a well-written book. It’s pure chaos.”

items.title: Grandexport, the Label Giving New Life to the No-Longer Needed
items.description: Paulina Münzing and Gent Berbatovci, the designers behind Berlin-based brand Grandexport, make “post heritage luxury products” from disused garments – “each piece becomes a conversation between us,” they say
items.author: Madeleine Rothery
paragraphs: Paulina Münzing and Gent Berbatovci, the designers behind Berlin-based brand Grandexport, make “post heritage luxury products” from disused garments – “each piece becomes a conversation between us,” they say
- Who is it? Grandexport is the label from Berlin-based design duo Paulina Münzing and Gent Berbatovci.
- Why do I want it? For time-slipped pieces made from forgotten fabrics, as clever as they are wearable.
- Where can I find it? Grandexport will soon be available at H Lorenzo, Los Angeles.

Who is it? Four years before they had even an inkling of what the clothes would look like, designers Paulina Münzing and Gent Berbatovci had a name for their label: Grandexport, borrowed from a street near their home in Berlin which is lined with import-export shops that sell “everything from fragrance to car tyres, TVs to children’s playthings.” “We liked it because you don’t know what it is,” says Berbatovci of the cryptic quality the name shares with the shops. It’s a fitting provenance for a brand with a knack for transposition: following a small first drop at the start of 2026, its second, and most recent, collection, Trophies, carries military knitwear, old GDR blankets and secondhand tracksuits a long way from their first lives and into what the pair call “post heritage luxury products.”

Where Münzing trained in fashion design, Berbatovci came into the label almost sideways, via product design and illustration. The latter has given him an understanding of silhouette and body, but product design has taught him to look at making a jacket, as Münzing puts it, “like making a stool.” Each design passes back and forth – “he starts sketching, I start three-dimensional” – until “the pieces become a conversation between us,” she explains. At fittings Berbatovci will ask the model whether she can move her arms, sit down and walk, then turns to Münzing with his second question: “Would you wear it? Yes or no?” And if the answer is no, the piece is cancelled.

For Trophies, the pair enlisted photographer Sharna Osborne, who shot the collection in her signature filmic lo-fi – a canny hedge between then and now, a sort of refrain of the label’s time-slipped designs – alongside stylist Emma Wyman, art directors Carina Frey and Stefanie Barth and casting director Julia Lange. “It’s also nice to start with a team who knows exactly what they’re doing from the start,” Münzing reflects, “because we can go together as we grow.”

Why do I want it? Unlike the shops behind the name, which trade in happy nonsense, Grandexport’s garments are curious yet entirely logical: they barely resemble the materials they began as, though each keeps the charge it was made with. A batch of counterfeit Sergio Tacchini tracksuits, bought from a man whose uncle had been selling them before the Berlin Wall fell, have been picked apart and puzzled into dresses, with a corset inside, a wired-open neckline and the jacket’s ribbed waistband for a hem. Army tent fabric from the GDR, once woven to be strong enough for any terrain, becomes a camouflage mini skirt and top which button together, come apart and recombine with the layers above.

Strip away the salvage and the designs hold up on their own, novel in cut and construction. A leather babydoll dress, made in black and in a dusty rose from GDR stock a dealer was ready to write off, is wired down the front so the leather holds a ripple, the pleated satin cups of a 1950s bullet bra set into its neckline; the same wire runs through a leather pencil skirt, letting it take a new line at the wearer’s hand. A ribbed red jumper zips at both collar and hem, so it can be worn either way up, and a double polo flips to change the shoulder. On first glance, each piece is askew and odd enough to catch the eye, but after closer inspection it comes into itself, making perfect sense.

With past and present so neatly stitched, Grandexport envisages growing the way its clothes are made, by the same lateral logic. Berbatovci, the inveterate hunter of the two, tracks down unworn stock and the pair mixes his finds with deadstock, since his finds alone would yield, they reckon, “like one collection in three years”; even so, the collections stay small and concise. Everything is made in Berlin, between a leather specialist and their own studio, outside the seasonal calendar – the gift is in how they look at what they find. It is, as the pair put it, “like a natural scarcity that we work with, which we like totally.”
Where can I find it? Grandexport will soon be available at H Lorenzo, Los Angeles.

items.title: It’s a visual feast! The Wallpaper* Entertaining Issue is on sale now
items.description: The Wallpaper* Entertaining Issue, on newsstands now in its December 2026 iteration, is a timely reminder that it's never too early – or too late – to dim the lights and dial up a favourite playlist or two, safe in the knowledge that we have left no stone untu
items.author: Bill Prince
paragraphs: The Wallpaper* Entertaining Issue, on newsstands now in its December 2026 iteration, is a timely reminder that it's never too early – or too late – to dim the lights and dial up a favourite playlist or two, safe in the knowledge that we have left no stone unturned in our search for the best and brightest opportunities to celebrate in style.

To this end, we deliver a veritable feast for the senses, inviting us all to consider how a degree of old-school decadence can transform a dining tableau. And, keeping conviviality at the heart of the matter, we take a trip to St Clement, the riverside London hotel co-developed by Mark Wadhwa and Nick Jones, atop which the capital's favourite chef, Florence Knight, has worked with interior design and furniture studio Eagle + Hodges to create Lunette, the city's most in-demand restaurant.

Elsewhere, we run around town with the impresarios re-erecting some of Paris' legendary nightclubs; honour the timeless appeal of the Greek klismos chair, a classic style given a contemporary twist by contributing editor Nick Vinson; and profile the winner of the inaugural Fendi Design Prize.

Further afield, we tour a trio of private homes that put a warm welcome at their heart; discover the bountiful, and beautifully packaged, world of Japanese confectionery; reveal the ‘Ferrari of football tables', as its designer, Jaime Hayon, describes this one-of-a-kind objet featuring ‘players' delightfully fashioned after Hayon's whimsical ‘Chicken'; and consult our resident astrologer on what we can look forward to (and what should join us) as we see in a new year. And if peering into the future fills you with dread, then fear not – for this month's End Paper, our design critic Hugo Macdonald explains why fortune favours those prepared to see what's written in their stars. Thank you for reading, and enjoy the issue.

Wallpaper’s December 2026 Entertaining Issue is available from 5 November, in print on newsstands, on the Wallpaper* app on Apple iOS, and to subscribers of Apple News +. Subscribe to Wallpaper* today
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Bill Prince is a journalist, author, and editor-in-chief of Wallpaper* and The Blend. Prior to taking up these roles, he served for 23 years as the deputy editor of British GQ. In addition to editing, writing and brand curation, Bill is an acknowledged authority on travel, hospitality and men's style. He is the author of two books, Royal Oak: From Iconoclast To Icon – a tribute to the Audemars Piguet watch at 50 – and The Connaught, a history of the legendary Mayfair hotel, both published by Assouline

items.title: Discover Black cowboy culture with photographer Ivan McClellan
items.description: Oregon-based photojournalist Ivan McClellan has spent more than a decade immersing himself in contemporary Black cowboy culture. In 2024, he told Wallpaper* about uniting the results of his years spent travelling with his camera across the United States in the
items.author: Hannah Silver
paragraphs: Oregon-based photojournalist Ivan McClellan has spent more than a decade immersing himself in contemporary Black cowboy culture. In 2024, he told Wallpaper* about uniting the results of his years spent travelling with his camera across the United States in the book Eight Seconds: Black Rodeo Culture. Now, in 2026, he has created a second edition – Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion – with 91 previously unpublished photographs and a new introduction and foreword.

Its title referring to the length of time a cowboy must stay on top of a bull or horse in order to qualify and score, the new Eight Seconds places rodeo in the context of the animals and land. McClellan’s imagery, encompassing the wide skies and open plains of the American West, looks to the future of rodeo, putting a younger generation at its heart.
Discover a selection of McClellan’s photographs below, as described by him.
Ivan McClellan on the story behind the images
Jumpmen kick off a Pony Express relay race in Okmulgee, Oklahoma, 2021. They pull back their horses who are eager to take off until the whistle blows and the let them sprint around the arena.

Dantey Eldridge, a professional bull rider, sits on a bucking barrel at an 8 Seconds bull-riding training camp in Wasco, Oregon. We put on these camps at no cost to the riders to elevate their skill set.
I shot 16-year-old barrel racer, Kortnee Solomon, at her ranch in Hempstead, Texas. As we stood in the pasture talking all of her horses gathered around, curious what we were doing.

Kamal Miller is an urban cowboy in Carson, California. Here he is working out a horse at his stable. The spirited horse was so happy to be out of his stable that his ran around in a circle with Kamal holding the reins for 15 minutes.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Trevonte and Randy riding horses in front of a Ward Chapel Church in Boley, Oklahoma, 2025. I saw these two walking down the street and they stopped for a moment in front of the the church that I happened to be standing in fron of. It was a serendipitous moment.

This is taken at the Roy Leblanc Invitational Rodeo in Okmulgee, OK in 2022. This is my favourite rodeo at golden hour. Everyone is getting ready for the rodeo. Athletes are putting on their rodeo outfits and getting their horses ready for competition. The moment the sun goes down the energy explodes with the Pony Express, a relay race on horseback.
Spectators watch the rodeo on a sweltering hot summer night in 2020 the height of the Covid pandemic. The stadium lights glisten off of sweaty Black skin, not a mask in sight.
Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion, published by Damiani Books, is out now, available from damianibooks.com and bookstores such as waterstones.com as well as amazon

Hannah Silver is Head of Art & Culture at Wallpaper*. A writer, editor and author with over 20 years of experience in journalism, spanning national newspapers and independent magazines, she has overseen offbeat art trends and conducted in-depth profiles for print and digital, as well as writing and commissioning extensively across the worlds of culture and luxury since joining in 2019.

items.title: Yeezy Is Officially Sampling Itself
items.description: It’s Yeezy Season all over again — as in, we’re starting over with Yeezy Season 01. To debut the first-ever Los Angeles Yeezy flagship store and apparently reintroduce Yeezy proper, Ye hosted a guerilla-style runway show late on November 4 titled “Season 01,”
items.author: Maya Kotomori
paragraphs: It’s Yeezy Season all over again — as in, we’re starting over with Yeezy Season 01. To debut the first-ever Los Angeles Yeezy flagship store and apparently reintroduce Yeezy proper, Ye hosted a guerilla-style runway show late on November 4 titled “Season 01,” suggesting a full reset from first principles. And if today is the day when Yeezy is born anew, it’s worth asking: what even is, or was, Yeezy? To understand the brand’s future, you must study its past.

On Wednesday night, instead of a full Yeezy reset, we saw a self-referential carousel of some of Ye’s greatest design hits. The runway was packed with various lengths of his preferred earth-toned catsuits, mock-neck jackets, faded jeans, and cargo pants, with a couple of lingerie bits thrown in for good measure. Shades of the other Yeezy Season 1, Season 2, Season 3…

The fact that the collection demands a visual aid to be fully appreciated speaks to one of Ye’s greatest design strengths: his ability to identify specific products with broad appeal, then make them in a zillion colorways so they still feel new. Ye has always done this in his music. Now, we’re seeing him do the same thing in fashion.

In a 2020 interview with Forbes, Ye declared “Yeezy is for everyone,” a maxim that would serve as his philosophy for YEEZY GAP. And even when YEEZY GAP was “engineered by” Balenciaga, the clothes — whether they were collarless puffer jackets or perfectly boxy hoodies — were priced at or under a comfortable $90.

Over the past half-decade, Yeezy has delivered on that egalitarian aim, even after YEEZY GAP fell apart and the Yeezy website began offering everything from in-house iterations of the ubiquitous adidas YEEZY slides ($40) to relatively anonymous black hoodies ($40) to the “merch” created for Ye and Ty Dolla $ign’s Vultures ($20). Even the oft-viral collaborations with longtime Ye cohort and English designer Mowalola, ranging from the skin-tight WET tanks to “KITTY” intimates that debuted at London Fashion Week, were priced to match ($20-$40).

A lot of the people involved in current-day Yeezy are members of my personal nightmare blunt rotation, such as head of design Gosha Rubchinskiy and manufacturing partner Dov Charney. In the context of public opinion, Ye and some members of his circle are controversial, and for good reason. In the context of the fashion industry, Ye is employing power players who can execute his desired minimalist-hype clothing at his desired prices — Charney with his production résumé and Rubshinskiy with the ability to translate subculture into product. (Footwear designer Mats Rombaut, who helped create new Yeezy shoes including the sheath-like SL-01, SL-02, and SL-03 models, has a comparatively clean track record.)

Ye, I’m happy to have you back doing what I think you do best in fashion: designing clothes to make women feel sexy and men feel tough. Both end up looking really steezy, as in the true definition of the portmanteau of “swag” and “easy.” The footwear, which encompassed tall opaque heels and less-tall military-style boots, accomplished the same goal.

It’s Ye doing Yeezy 2015 in 2026, not a redux so much as it is a sample — a remix. If anything, it’s a reminder of how perennial Ye’s taste is. To quote him, “It’s not that I’m not right, I’m just not right now.”
