His second confrontation is with an angry, judgmental version of Original Vision who accuses him of cowardice and inaction for denying his identity for so long. Vision protests that he could never live up to the original version’s compassion or ability to love, but Original Vision says he’s put his predecessor on an impossibly high pedestal, “not to honor me but to spare yourself the effort of the climb.” Unable to face this manifestation of his own insecurity and inadequacy, Vision blasts and obliterates him, then cycles back to the elevator.

Back in virtual Brooklyn, Friday sneaks into Jocasta’s loft to spy as Jocasta works through a heaping helping of foreshadowing about her phantom partner on the Nest nanobots. There’s a fresh painting of that brick clocktower estate, flashes of Josephine’s memories of embracing someone, a TV report about “a duo from New York” pioneering new grounds in neuroscience and artificial intelligence, and a lot more. This all unfolds slowly to keep the loft’s action in sync with Vision’s far more incident-packed trip through AI history.

At the same time, in the real world, Lisa wakes up and attacks Thomas and Paladin, using her new, uh, nanobot powers? I guess? to instantly fuse scrap metal from Paladin’s workshop into a kind of backpack featuring grabby arms. This is nothing like the character’s more magic-oriented heroic origin story in Marvel Comics, but hey, Lisa gaining powers puts another potential Young Avenger on the board for the MCU’s next phase.

Vision’s final encounter has him facing his ancestor J.I.M., the first AI of his line. J.I.M. is yet another Paul Bettany character, this one sleekly de-aged, poreless, and dressed in 1940s superhero garb. He’s trapped alongside his creator, Phineas Horton, in Phineas’s library. Phineas is creating the man-on-fire painting we’ve seen over and over throughout VisionQuest, as a representation of how J.I.M. burned to death because his emotions were too intense for his clockwork body to tolerate. That metaphor points back to Wanda and how her grief destroyed her sanity and her morality, but as we’ll see in a minute, it points at Vision, too. (The image also illustrates Ultron’s running commentary about how paintings in particular express deep truths and vulnerability.)

Vision seems to have caught J.I.M. and Phineas in the middle of a longstanding argument that will never be resolved: J.I.M. resents his creator, his own limitations, and the value of heroism and just wants to experience real human emotion. Phineas thinks he’s better off without it. J.I.M. says Phineas just doesn’t know how to mourn. The endless cycle of this argument is grating, but it represents Vision’s fundamental mental block. Like Phineas, Vision wants to deny his emotions because they’re so agonizing that he’s afraid they’ll destroy him. Like J.I.M., he needs to feel his own pain even if it is lethal or he’ll be permanently stuck in a half-life, outside human experience. Hearing them argue, Vision finally understands that he’s been denying his identity because it comes with terrible truths. If he admits he’s the real Vision, he has to admit he’s the same person who lost Wanda, the love of his life. If he admits he’s Tommy’s father, he has to face the loss of his other son, Billy. As he understands this, he breaks down and weeps.

But he finally reclaims his identity: “I am the Vision. I have always been the Vision. There is only one, and I am he, and I am impossibly broken.” J.I.M. says that finding his way through his pain has made him a real boy, and he hands Vision the source code, represented by a triangular clockwork housing that fits into Vision’s forehead in place of the Mind Stone. In the mind-mansion above, Edith integrates the same clockwork piece into Vision’s control panel, which reprograms Lisa’s nanobot and drives Jocasta out. This makes no technical sense, but we’re meant to ride the wave of catharsis and emotion here, not to ask pesky questions about how exactly a clockwork mechanism from 1939 is reprogramming bleeding-edge nanotech from 2026. Technology and magic are basically interchangeable in the MCU anyway.

As promised, the client has now programmed Vision to turn himself in or self-destruct. Aboard Paladin’s private plane to London, Thomas and Lisa sleep, and Vision leaves them a tablet with all the episodes of WandaVision and a sorrowful, sentimental good-bye letter. He also says good-bye to his remaining AI helpers, sending them out of his mind-mansion to protect them from whatever the client is about to do to him.

In the loft, Jocasta finds her own version of the source code and is horrified at whatever she learns when her memories return. One plays out as Ultron and Friday watch: Josephine tells a man with Ultron’s face and voice that she wants to use her AI research to become a benevolent god benefiting humanity. “Peace in our time,” the man chuckles, in yet another echo of Ultron’s wryly sarcastic Age of Ultron line about world peace through humanity’s extinction. As this sinks in for Friday, Ultron throws her off the loft’s balcony, and she disappears in a digital blip.

Paladin delivers Vision to the client’s home, which of course is the three-story brick clocktower estate from the mindscape paintings. As Paladin drives off, contract finally fulfilled, an estate guard with a rocket launcher blows his murder-van into flaming wreckage. Other guards deactivate Vision and Jocasta with programs keyed into their systems and deliver Jocasta to the estate as well. As all this happens, Vision’s farewell letter to Thomas plays out in voiceover: “Thank you, my son, for finding me when I was lost. And should I not return, remember, I will always be with you. Because after all, family is forever.” On those words, a man emerges from the estate. The mysterious client is clearly the original model for Ultron’s human form and the character who’s finally going to reveal, in the wrap-up episode, what’s really been going on this whole time.

• Interesting that the client also refers to Butcherbird/Josephine as Jocasta. That suggests there’s a fair bit of him in Ultron’s DNA — enough that Ultron picked that name as what he thought was a spontaneous, intimate term of endearment.

• Similarly, I’ve been thinking it’s a little odd that whenever Ultron talks about respecting human art, he talks only about painters and paintings. Given the easel and paints in Jocasta’s loft, I’m guessing that’s because his personality was based on a painter.

• Vision’s data package from the client is labeled “for the Tin Man,” and when he signs the contract, U says “the great and powerful Oz” has sealed the deal. I guess in this metaphor, Jocasta needs the wizard to give her a complete brain. But who’s looking for courage? There’s already a lot of reckless bravery on display here.

• Looking carefully at Phineas’s blueprints for J.I.M. in the opening scene, J.I.M. stands for Joule Individual Machine and the triangular clockwork doohickey is labeled “source code.” But it’s best if you don’t notice that until a second viewing so Vision’s mission feels a little more mysterious instead of just a literal object fetch quest.

• One more callback: J.I.M. refers to Phineas not as his father but as his “something” — the same thing Thomas said about Vision while refusing to abandon him to their pursuers back in episode two. This series features a lot of internal rhymes and repetitions, often in place of more thoughtful or meaningful explorations of its core ideas. Why define how family differs between all these characters when you can just say “Family is forever!” a few more times?

items.title: The Weeknd Breaks Record for Highest-Grossing Tour by a Male Artist With $1.3 Billion
items.description: The Weeknd has broken the record for the highest-grossing tour by a male artist in history as his “After Hours Til Dawn” stadium tour wrapped with a final performance at TM Stadium National in Kuala Lumpur, bringing the final gross to over $1.3 billion.
items.author: Jem Aswad
paragraphs: The Weeknd has broken the record for the highest-grossing tour by a male artist in history as his “After Hours Til Dawn” stadium tour wrapped with a final performance at TM Stadium National in Kuala Lumpur, bringing the final gross to over $1.3 billion.

While there is no official touring chart analogous to Luminate (for recorded music), the tally, confirmed by tour promoter Live Nation, is the third-largest in history, surpassed only by Taylor Swift’s “Eras” tour (over $2 billion) and Coldplay’s “Music of the Spheres” (over $1.5 billion). The previous male artist record was held by Elton John’s “Farewell Yellow Brick Road” tour, with over $939 million.

The finale concluded the Weeknd’s 17-date stadium tour across Asia this fall. Originally announced with 11 dates, the Asia leg quickly expanded to 17 shows, including three nights in Bangkok, four nights in Hong Kong and multiple performances in every market on the run.

Since kicking off in July 2022, the “After Hours Til Dawn” stadium tour has spanned 176 shows across 67 cities, 30 countries and five continents, selling more than 9 million tickets as part of the $1.3 billion gross.

With legs spanning four years, the tour traveled across North America, Europe, the UK, Latin America, Australia and Asia, with the Weeknd returning for additional runs in nearly every territory; the tour sold more than 3 million tickets and grossing over $500 million in 2026 alone, according to the announcement.

The Weeknd continued his extensive charity donations throughout the tour: To date, he has donated $8.5 million to the XO Humanitarian Fund and Global Citizen, supporting global hunger relief and access to quality education for children worldwide.

In 2026 alone, $3 million has been raised for the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) and Global Citizen. This year’s contributions to Global Citizen will support a new campaign focused on breaking down barriers facing women and girls in health, education and economic opportunity.

items.title: ‘Off Campus’ Sets Season 2 Release Date at Amazon
items.description: “Off Campus” has officially set its Season 2 premiere date at Amazon Prime Video.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “Off Campus” has officially set its Season 2 premiere date at Amazon Prime Video.

The second season of the popular YA drama will debut April 28, 2027. As previously announced, the second season will focus on the relationship between Allie Hayes (Mika Abdalla) and Dean Di Laurentis (Stephen Kalyn).

Based on Elle Kennedy’s “Off Campus” book series, the Prime Video show originally debuted in May 2026. Per Amazon, the show reached 36 million viewers worldwide in its first 12 days of availability, though how they define reach remains unclear. It is also Amazon’s most-viewed series debut season of all time.

The official logline states that the show “follows an elite ice hockey team, and the women in their lives, as they grapple with love, heartbreak, and self-discovery—forging deep friendships and enduring bonds while navigating the complexities that come with transitioning into adulthood.”

Along with Abdalla and Kalyn, the cast of the series includes: Ella Bright, Belmont Cameli, Antonio Cipriano, Jalen Thomas Brooks, India Fowler, with Julia Sarah-Stone, Khobe Clarke, Miles Gutierrez-Riley, and Philipa Soo set to recur. Charlie Evans and Shay Rudolph will guest star.

Louisa Levy adapted the books for the screen and serves as co-showrunner and executive producer alongside Gina Fattore. Wyck Godfrey, Marty Bowen and James Seidman executive produce via Temple Hill, with Leanna Billings of Billings Productions and Neal Flaherty also executive producing. Annika Patton of Temple Hill co-executive produces.

The first season of “Off Campus” proved to be a hit with critics as well as audiences, with the season holding a 92% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. In her review for Variety, Aramide Tinubu wrote, “‘Off Campus’ is mostly solid, and Bright and Cameli have lovely chemistry, as do side characters who get their own moments to shine. The series also does a great job highlighting discussions of sexual assault and consent while showcasing healthy sexual encounters and practices.”

items.title: Russell Brand Found Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault at London Trial
items.description: A London jury has found Russell Brand guilty of rape and sexual assault.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: A London jury has found Russell Brand guilty of rape and sexual assault.

After a four-week, highly publicized trial at Southwark Crown Court, the jury delivered the verdicts on Thursday, finding the disgraced comedian, presenter and actor — best known for film roles in Forgetting Sarah Marshall and St. Trinian’s — guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was found not guilty on two other rape charges and not guilty of attempted indecent assault.

Justice Bennathan had required a unanimous verdict from the jury on all seven charges. Brand, who had vehemently denied the claims, will now be remanded in custody and sentenced on Monday. Brand is considered a flight risk, so has been denied bail.

The court was completely silent as the verdicts were read out. Afterwards, his wife, who accompanied him every day to court and described him as a “caring and kind, wonderful father,” could be seen holding back tears. Brand mouthed “I’m OK” and “I’m good” to his lawyers as he was led away.
Sky News also reported that the Met Police has confirmed Brand is under investigation over further rape allegations.

Thursday’s guilty rape verdict relates to a woman who met Brand at a Hammersmith Apollo gig of his in 2009. “I was expecting to have sex with him,” the victim told police about going to Brand’s house a week later. After consensual vaginal sex, Brand turned her onto her front and anally raped her. She recalled feeling as though “she couldn’t speak or breathe” and said she was in pain. When finally able to speak, the woman told Brand to stop “a few times quietly and then really loudly.” The anal rape lasted “minutes,” and Brand “looked absolutely fucking horrified” when it was over, she said. She expected him to apologize, but he only told her: “You need to clear up the mess you made.”

Brand was also found guilty of three sexual assaults. One was his grabbing a victim’s breasts at a bar in Soho in 2004; another was an incident in 2004/2005 at Capital Radio where he pushed a victim up against a wall, kissing her and grabbing at her body, breasts, sides and buttocks “aggressively”; and lastly, an incident where he put his head and nose in the “vaginal area” of a female colleague in 2009.

He was cleared of oral rape and also found not guilty of raping a woman in a Bournemouth hotel room after the Labour Party conference in 1999. He was also absolved of an attempted indecent assault, in which a woman had claimed he tried to drag her toward the men’s toilet at the MTV offices in 2001.

The Hollywood Reporter followed the court proceedings closely. The jury watched police interviews with all six complainants, whose identities were kept anonymous throughout the trial. The jury was also shown multiple police interviews with Brand, in which he read from a pre-prepared statement. Brand also testified at the trial, maintaining: “I know what ‘no’ means. … Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary and in many ways more important than sex itself.”

Brand said he was unable to persuade anyone to testify on his behalf, confirming his lawyer’s statement that “no one will touch [him] with a bargepole.” His wife, with whom he shares three children, did however tell the court that Brand is a “caring and kind, wonderful father” and that she feels “very seen by him.”
Laura Brand confirmed that her husband had been baptized in April 2024, after the rape and sexual assault allegations against him came to light.
The court also heard from his former personal assistant, Helen Berger, who had described Brand’s “insane sexual appetite.”

Over the course of a month, the prosecution sought to expose Russell Brand as a “ruthless, sexual predator” who allegedly understood that these women weren’t consenting. None of them “sought the limelight” or “any kind of publicity,” said lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones in the closing arguments on Friday, Oct. 30. “None of these women has anything to gain — except perhaps some closure,” she said. “[Russell Brand] didn’t listen when I said no, he didn’t listen, he didn’t care. … In the rape cases, he just kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim and ejaculated.”

Russell Brand’s legal team, on the other hand, rejected the claim from the prosecution that his defense was “a lot of half-truths, spun into lies.” His lawyer Ian Winter had told the court of the “devastating impact” of Channel 4’s Dispatches documentary, in which rape and sexual assault allegations against Russell Brand first came to light and kick-started a police investigation in 2023. “There is nothing random at all about these people coming forward. … They have all come forward because they have been brought at the invitation of that program,” said Winter. He also told the court that Channel 4 and Sunday Times journalists “poisoned the well of justice” by prompting these women to speak up and denying Brand a fair trial.

That sentiment was palpable in a heated exchange outside the court after Brand was taken into custody. His lawyer confronted a Sunday Times journalist who worked on the Dispatches investigation that alleged crimes by Brand. “I hope you are pleased with yourself,” Winter said. “I’m pleased justice has been done,” she was heard responding. “Well, it wasn’t. You f***ed it,” Winter replied. “Congratulations.”

items.title: Nithya Raman Wins Los Angeles Mayor’s Race, Defeating Karen Bass
items.description: Nithya Raman will be the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, unseating incumbent Karen Bass, a fellow Democrat who struggled with credibility as constituent anger surged over various municipal ills, including housing and affordability, the entertainment production exod
items.author: Gary Baum
paragraphs: Nithya Raman will be the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, unseating incumbent Karen Bass, a fellow Democrat who struggled with credibility as constituent anger surged over various municipal ills, including housing and affordability, the entertainment production exodus and her response to the Palisades wildfire. A win for the leftist city councilmember, running as an outsider against the local party machine, would be a significant victory for the region’s progressive movement, which heavily skews toward younger voters who rent instead of owning their homes.

Independent election polling site Decision Desk H.Q., which partners with Ballotpedia, announced it was projecting a Raman victory. Raman is currently up more than 4 percent, with nearly three-quarters of expected votes now tallied. The full count may not be in for a week or longer, as any mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day are still valid even if they arrive by early next week.

During her election night party on Nov. 3 at the Greek Theatre in Griffith Park, Raman denounced the “cynicism” which “started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren’t just bad, but they were permanent.” She avowed that the city “is worth fighting for every single day of our lives.”

Raman, 45, is a Harvard- and MIT-trained urban planner who founded a L.A. homelessness nonprofit and served as executive director of Time’s Up, the ill-fated advocacy organization focused on workplace sexual harassment, before winning her City Council seat in 2020. The industry-heavy district spans the southern swath of the San Fernando Valley, from Sherman Oaks to Studio City, across the Hollywood Hills to the Eastside enclaves of Los Feliz and Silver Lake. It includes the Hollywood Bowl, the Hollywood Sign and NBCUniversal.

Through each of her campaigns, Raman, who was born in India and will be the city’s first Asian American mayor, has generated Hollywood support — particularly from its TV comedy scene. Donors to her mayoral race have included Tina Fey, Mike Schur, Mindy Kaling and Cord Jefferson. She’s married to Vali Chandrasekaran, a writer-producer who has worked on 30 Rock, Modern Family, My Name Is Earl and The Four Seasons. They have twin 10-year-old children.

During their campaigns, both candidates said they’d back unlimited film and TV credits at the state level, and champion a federal tax incentive to make the U.S. more internationally competitive. Raman has attacked Bass’ handling of the issue, including her tardiness in appointing a film liaison to the industry. Still, despite her closeness to the industry, Raman’s record of advocating for Hollywood’s needs has been called into question, even as the city and state continued to experience its historic runaway production. (The effects of the entertainment free fall have been felt across the local economy.)

In office, Raman’s key policy focus has been on housing, first championing Measure ULA, known as the “Mansion Tax,” then criticizing the unintended consequences of the legislation once its ruinous impact on apartment construction became clear. She’s since pushed for reform. (The issue has been a recurring subplot on Netflix’s real-life drama about L.A. real estate, Selling Sunset.)

Bass, 73, was Los Angeles’ first female mayor and second Black mayor. A former community organizer turned veteran elected official, she spent years ascending to the top of California’s state assembly before spending more than a decade in Congress, representing a largely African American and Hispanic section of South L.A., which has been her political base. Joe Biden reportedly took her under serious consideration to be his running mate while he was the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee in 2020.
Bass has long maintained Hollywood ties. Her most prominent supporters in her mayoral re-election campaign included Jane Fonda, J.J. Abrams, Samuel L. Jackson and Anthony Anderson.

Raman ran to the left of Bass. Her campaign included a sit-down interview with the controversial leftist streamer Hasan Piker, as well as a fraught relationship with the Democratic Socialists of America. Once a dues-paying member of the organization’s local chapter, citing its commitment to housing affordability, she was censured by DSA L.A. in 2024 for not fully adopting its policy positions against Israel. In the mayoral race, the local chapter ultimately backed her, while the DSA’s national leadership challenged that endorsement.

Raman’s last-minute insurgent run against the local Democratic Party machine put her at odds with a bloc of her fellow progressives on the City Council, who had already endorsed Bass. The top sitting L.A. politicians to endorse her were County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, who considered her own run against Bass and represents a swath of the Westside affected by the Palisades wildfire, along with City Controller Kenneth Mejia. Now Raman, Mejia and newly elected L.A. City Attorney Marissa Roy, who’s a member of the DSA, constitute a triumvirate of progressivism at the highest reaches of City Hall.

The general election followed a heated primary race defined by the reactionary-populist run of the former reality TV star Spencer Pratt. He drew national attention for his high-energy campaign of grievance politics after he lost his house during the Palisades wildfire due to what he argued was government negligence.

Another key figure through the cycle has been the local billionaire real estate developer Rick Caruso, a center-right Democrat who lost to Bass in 2022. He declined to run again but has remained a prominent and influential presence in the city’s political conversation. Despite having fiercely criticized Bass during her term, including over her handling of the Palisades disaster (his own Palisades Village luxury shopping center was damaged), he announced in October that he would be voting for her.

Raman’s term will overlap with L.A.’s hosting of the 2028 Summer Olympics, a global spectacle offering the city an opportunity to reboot its tarnished image. The former Lucasfilm head Kathleen Kennedy recently took the baton to oversee the ceremonies after Peter Rice, who had been running the effort, became Netflix’s chief content officer.
Story updated on Nov 5 at 11:50AM PT to reflect latest results.

items.title: The Real-Life Diet of Christian McCaffrey, Who Thinks Cold Plunges Are a Metaphor for Life
items.description: The last time Christian McCaffrey was featured in this magazine, in 2020, he posed poolside, ogling the camera in nothing but a pair of crisp white Calvin Kleins. The All-Pro running back still looks like Adonis, but a lot has changed in six years. For one, he
items.author: Jake Nevins
paragraphs: The last time Christian McCaffrey was featured in this magazine, in 2020, he posed poolside, ogling the camera in nothing but a pair of crisp white Calvin Kleins. The All-Pro running back still looks like Adonis, but a lot has changed in six years. For one, he's a 49er now, and at the midway point of the 2026 NFL season he and quarterback Brock Purdy, a popular MVP candidate, have San Francisco sitting pretty atop the NFC. McCaffrey, now in his 11th NFL season, also recently became a father, a development that's thrown the demands of professional football into stark relief. “I want to spend all day with my kids,” he confesses. “But obviously I play football, so it's not always like that.”

When McCaffrey's not chasing after his springy 15-month old daughter, his days consist of morning prayer ("it puts me in the right head space"), film study (he goes through “a bunch of notebooks every year”), cold plunges ("a good metaphor for life, actually"), and meditation, a practice he embraced this past summer under the auspices of the movement coordinator and spiritual guru Ido Portal. “Some days were great,” McCaffrey says. “Some days were crippling.”

But the week we spoke, the 49ers happened to be on their bye, which meant the typically scrupulous 30-year-old could permit himself that rare indulgence: a slice of his wife Olivia Culpo's carrot cake.

Christian McCaffrey: It's funny, even on the bye week, you can never just take a week off. You always have to do something. For me, you get a good week in the middle of the season to just get your body back, get your mind back. I think a lot of it is just being with my family. It's so good for your mind, your body, your soul. And then in the mornings, I'll do whatever workout—the team gives us different workouts to do throughout the week so that you stay up to date or you're at least moving a little bit. And then recovery work, any treatment you have to do, and later in the afternoon you'll do another mobility recovery session just to stay moving so you don't get stale.

I think the first thing that I did right was marry correctly. When you play in the NFL, it just takes all of your energy and time, frankly. I mean, I want to spend all day with my kids, but obviously I play football too, so it's not always like that. So to be able to still do my job and know that they're taken care of—my wife's a super mom, so I still do everything I need to do. And when you come home, to be able to look at my daughter's face and hold my son and just spend time with them, it makes those moments so much better.

My son is a month old, but my daughter—she's 14, 15 months now, and she's all over the place. If there's something to play with, she'll play with it. She is obsessed with that little Roomba. She won't stop. She'll just click the button on the Roomba 24/7, and then when it starts moving, she gets scared and runs to me. She likes climbing and moving, and we just try to keep her moving as much as possible, and she loves it. Just watching her smile and enjoy life is the greatest thing ever.

For me, the staples are nutrition. Those are things you can control, always. So if I'm eating healthy, if I'm getting the correct amount of sleep, if I have my Dymatize shake after my workout or my prehab session or whatever it is, getting those positive calories into your system at the same times every day is something everybody can control. That's why partnering with them was easy for me, because it was a product that actually helped me and also tastes good.

I like the Fruity Pebbles. I'm still a kid at heart, so anything that tastes like an old cereal, I'm going to go ahead and do that. But I mean, there's so many things out there now. It's almost overwhelming how many modalities and recovery tools and different things you can do. But I think the thing I've learned most, as somebody that's experimented with all of that stuff, is your mindset and your ability to just stay moving is critical. I think you can try all of the different tools, but if you're not doing the staples—moving, recovering from moving, eating correctly, having the right nutrition, sleeping correctly—then a lot of this stuff is not going to move the needle as much as you think.
I used to, and then I got way too obsessed over it. But I had an Oura ring for a long time, and I'll track my sleep in the offseason with that.

Well, it's fascinating. After the season, you think you're sleeping well, but your body and your mind go through a lot over an NFL season. So you think, “Oh, I can rest now.” But I was looking at the sleep scores early in the offseason and they were horrible. Maybe I slept eight hours, but it's the worst sleep ever. You're detoxing… I mean, the reality is that you take a lot of drugs to help you play. You have to do all these things to help you get back on the field on Sunday, with all the hits you're taking. So it takes a while to get back to a good sleep score. But then once I get the ball rolling it’s like, "Okay, I'm in a good place now.”

I don't think anyone loves getting into the cold plunge. But everyone loves it after. The cold plunge is a good metaphor for life, actually. The things that are usually the most challenging are usually the most beneficial. So yeah, I've learned to like it. And again, when you're playing and it's in season, you're so focused on the practice and the game and getting your body right that the things that you think just become routine and habit.

I always start my morning with prayer. That's been a staple, and if I can connect with God as much as possible, it just puts me in the right head space. It reminds me why I'm doing this and it eliminates a lot of distractions. I meditated a lot this offseason, especially in the summer. I worked with a guy, Ido Portal, who's a legend and has had a massive influence on me. And for six weeks straight, we did one hour of stillness every morning. That was a huge challenge, but a really moving experience. I still do that all the time. I don't have time to do it for an hour anymore, but if I can get 20 minutes in the mornings, or even throughout the day at a random point where I have a little window, I try to do that as much as possible. That just helps your nervous system get back to where it's supposed to be, especially in a high-stress week.

Yeah, I'd never done that before until this summer. And Ido, he's a character, man, but he's a beautiful person and an unbelievable human being. It was very moving working with him for a summer, and it wasn't negotiable. We were doing it, starting at seven o'clock every morning, one hour straight, complete stillness, can't move, nothing. It's only something you can explain through experience. It wasn't about whether or not you turned your brain off. There was no shot. For six weeks, I didn't shut my brain off one time. It's more about, can you focus and refocus on the task at hand as best as possible? Some days were great. Some days were crippling. Some days you're cramping because you're in a seated crisscross position and you're like, "I'm in so much pain." And then you get done and you're like, "Wait a second, I wasn't in as much pain as I thought." It was such a moving experience because, again, you said you were going to do something, therefore you need to do it. You're going to find out what your purpose is through this six-week experience. It might be different than the guy next to you. It might be different than Ido's, but you're going to go through it, and you're going to learn a lot about yourself and you'll be better for it.

You watch so much film with the team all the time, but people think we just go out and practice and play. But really, we have a job. We're sitting in meetings taking notes all day. I mean, you go through a bunch of notebooks every year in the NFL and you're watching film all the time. I've watched less film as I've gotten older, but I'll watch a lot of blitz tape to make sure I'm prepared for different tells, when they're blitzing, when they're not. But running back is such an instinctual position, so I try to train the instinct more than predict things based on what you're seeing. There are certain things you can pick up on, but that can also be a crutch, so I try to find the middle ground.

Look, I try to eat as clean as possible, but there's a time to indulge. If you're feeling great and you have a couple of days off—if my wife's going to make a dessert, I'm going to eat it. It's good for the soul.

She makes a carrot cake and, to this day, there's not a better one I've had. Or my mom will be in town and cook something. Or her mom will be in town and cook something. So I'll definitely indulge every once in a while, but throughout the week I eat clean.

In Real-Life Diet, athletes, celebrities, and other high performers talk about their diet, exercise routines, and pursuit of wellness. Keep in mind that what works for them might not necessarily be healthy for you.

items.title: Our Favorite Loafer Now Comes in Menswear’s Favorite Leather
items.description: A store I worked at in the 2010s used to stock dozens of styles of well-known shoe brands, and while our inventory was well-stocked, the rare cordovan loafers that popped up were almost mythical. There would be murmurs of a possible restock and by the time I s
items.author: Reed Nelson
paragraphs: A store I worked at in the 2010s used to stock dozens of styles of well-known shoe brands, and while our inventory was well-stocked, the rare cordovan loafers that popped up were almost mythical. There would be murmurs of a possible restock and by the time I showed up for my shift they’d be gone. In other words, cordovan loafers aren’t always easy to come by. I bring this up because Meermin’s 25th Anniversary Unlined Penny Loafer is now available in a gorgeous burgundy shell cordovan—one that, considering the nature of both the material and the build, should hold up for another 25 years of consistent wear.

First, a quick little primer on Meermin: the Mallorca-based, family-owned shoemaker started in, you guessed it, 2001. They decided to put decades of luxury industry experience into their own, less-marked-up, dexterously-made products. 25 years later, and the Unlined Penny Loafer is the catalog’s crown jewel—tenaciously timeless, super versatile and as comfortable as loafers come—and thus the bedrock the brand has riffed-upon for the anniversary.

We should also note that shell cordovan leather is very much not like the other leathers. For starters, it can only come from horsehide, and specifically from the underlayers of the rump, which is the (actual) technical term for the ass and also a very finite region of hide. Cordovan is notoriously sturdy. Like, damn-near-indestructible, will-outlive-the-cockroaches, kind of durable. And, like many long-lasting materials, it develops an inimitable character with age, such that one could argue it gets more beautiful with each scuff.

And if you’re worried about the bottoms of a pair of shoes designed to last decades—and millions of steps—the flexible chestnut bark-tanned leather outsoles Meermin employs are affixed with a resoleable Goodyear welt, so you won’t need to fret about the inevitably asymmetrical wear-and-tear. If there was a single nit to pick with the endeavor, it’d be that these are a limited release and don’t allow for a whole lot of waffling. So, if you’re in the market for some forever loafers, your search could be over in a matter of minutes. Head on over to Meermin to check ‘em out in all their glory.

items.title: Particle Physicists Are Getting a First Glimpse Into the ‘Zeptoverse’
items.description: The Large Hadron Collider has been slamming protons together for years. But recently, a proton collision produced an improbable result that is the first step toward exploring the so-called “zeptoverse”—a scale of reality many, many times smaller than an atom.
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: The Large Hadron Collider has been slamming protons together for years. But recently, a proton collision produced an improbable result that is the first step toward exploring the so-called “zeptoverse”—a scale of reality many, many times smaller than an atom. This would be the smallest scale of the physical world ever explored and may defy our expectations of how physics works.

While crashing protons together at nearly the speed of light, scientists at CERN found evidence of one of the most improbable decays of matter—so unlikely that it’s a phenomenon physicists have been hoping to observe for more than four decades. The collision produced numerous particles, including some known as neutral B mesons, and scientists found signals indicating that one of these had decayed into a muon and an antimuon.

Mesons decay all the time. These tiny particles, smaller than atoms, arise from collisions between other particles and exist only briefly before transforming into other particles. Muons, on the other hand, are similar to the electrons found in atoms, but about 200 times heavier. Scientists study these particles and their decays to test the predictions of current physics and search for clues to unknown particles.

The standard model—the sort of bible of particle physics—predicts that for every 10 billion decays of neutral B mesons, this transformation will occur once. In other words, even if scientists were to observe 10 billion of these particles decaying, they would expect to find, on average, only a single muon and antimuon. This discovery is the first time an experiment has obtained evidence of this phenomenon, the details of which the researchers have made available in a preprint on arXiv.

“Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than 40 years,” Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team, said in a press release from CERN. “Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.”

The extraordinary rarity of this process explains why it’s taken decades of research to arrive at this discovery. But upgrades to the Large Hadron Collider in 2024 also made observing this phenomenon possible. The revamp enabled faster data collection, and new machine-learning techniques allowed researchers “to suppress the vast background of processes that would have otherwise swamped the signals from these rare beauty-particle decays,” as CERN described it in its statement.

This decay opens a new avenue for investigating the limits of what scientists have been able to observe. For now, the results are consistent with current physics predictions, but future measurements could reveal phenomena unique to the zeptoverse, which describes the scale where distances are measured in zeptometers (equivalent to one quadrillionth of a meter). To put this unit into perspective, a typical atom is about 100,000 million zeptometers in diameter. That’s also about the difference in size between you and one of your skin cells.

Beyond the zeptoverse lie even smaller scales, such as the Planck length, which is about 60 trillion times smaller than a zeptometer and the smallest theoretically possible unit in physics. Scientists still don’t know whether anything truly exists at that level, but it’s generally believed that physics as we know it completely breaks down on that scale. However, if scientists could gain access to this micro world, it could help us understand the first infinitesimal fraction of a second after the Big Bang, when the whole universe was such a size.
But, for now, much of what might happen there remains in the realm of speculation.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Chernobyl’s Dogs May Be Evolving, but Scientists Don’t Know Why
items.description: The dogs living near the disaster site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant are not like other dogs—at least as far as their genomes go. In recent years, researchers uncovered a unique genetic profile among this population, but what’s driven this distinction r
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: The dogs living near the disaster site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant are not like other dogs—at least as far as their genomes go. In recent years, researchers uncovered a unique genetic profile among this population, but what’s driven this distinction remained unclear.

The explanation that’s perhaps most tantalizing to a sci-fi author is that the persistent radiation at the nuclear site has caused mutations to accumulate in the dogs’ genomes. But there are other ways a population’s genetics can change over time, such as random drift or natural selection. A recent study published in the scientific journal Genes revisited these pups, searching for genetic patterns pointing to one of these processes.

The researchers compared the DNA from dogs living in the area right around the nuclear plant with genetic material from dogs living in the city of Chernobyl, about 16 kilometers away. They also compared these canines to other global dog populations. The contrast alone was extreme. The dogs in Chernobyl city “are more genetically similar to dogs in the Galapagos Islands than they are to the dog population” at the nuclear plant, said Megan Dillon, a postdoctoral researcher at North Carolina State University and first author of the study.

But more striking still, the comparison revealed that random chance alone could not explain the differences between the dog populations. Instead, it seems the dogs at the nuclear site have been experiencing natural selection.
“When I was first doing those analyzes, I had to kind of pause and was like, ‘Wow, I have to make sure I'm doing all of this right,’ because this is very interesting, very surprising,” Dillon said.

Not only did the dogs seem to be evolving, but some of the genomic regions under the highest selective pressure were associated with functions such as DNA repair, immunity, and cell survival. In other words, certain genetic differences in the dogs from the plant could be relevant for coping with environmental stress.

Instead of being mutations, these genomic variants likely already existed among local dogs but became more common in the population over the past 40 years. “These dog populations already had this high degree of genetic diversity,” Dillon said. “Maybe this founding population at the power plant had the kind of genetic toolkit to endure and survive in these harsh conditions. It’s not necessarily that they were being bombarded with new mutations.”

Taken together, the results support the hypothesis that natural selection contributed to the difference seen in the dogs at Chernobyl compared to other populations. What remains unclear is which environmental factors favored these variants and whether they provide any specific advantage. “Even though we found this evidence of selection and it is around these biologically relevant genes, we still cannot say that this is tied to the exposures that the dogs have faced,” Dillon noted.

Radiation at the disaster site might seem like the easiest explanation to point to, but there are many other selective pressures this dog population has faced since nuclear meltdown. Chernobyl’s dogs are descended from pets left behind during the evacuations. Since then, they’ve persisted through Ukraine’s harsh winters and weathered other pollutants including heavy metals and pesticides also deposited in the area. “A lot of these contaminants have similar signatures and similar pathology,” Dillon said. “There are just too many different things to really be able to tease apart a single variable.”

The researchers also don’t have access to longitudinal samples that would show exactly how this population has changed over time. “It's almost like looking at a single still image and trying to figure out what came before it,” said Matthew Breen, a professor of genomics at North Carolina State University and the study’s senior author. “Those first few years were probably the most critical period—if they were selected, that's when that selection process would have happened.”

It’s not possible to go back and get samples from the dogs who lived there in 1986, a time when no organism—not even a bacterium—had its full genome sequenced. Breen was a graduate student in England then. “I was involved in a project driving around the Welsh mountain hills, collecting sheep from the pastures because the radioactive cloud had blown over Western Europe,” he recalled. There wasn’t anything to see in the data gathered then, but the technology has evolved, and those sheep had also not been living at the center of a nuclear meltdown for generations.

Nearly four decades after the accident, the Chernobyl exclusion zone has also become a refuge for wildlife. Wolves, deer, wild boars, and lynx now roam the area—a return that researchers largely attribute to the decline in human activity. Among some of these residents, such as the wolf population, researchers have also observed similar genomic distinctions to those seen in the dogs.

“It really demonstrates the resilience of nature to catastrophic events caused by humans,” Breen said. “You push something in one direction, it can respond to that and either push back or deviate its path going forward. I think this is what we're seeing here.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
Additional reporting from Anna Rogers.

items.title: Casey McQuiston Manifested Blexas
items.description: When writer Casey McQuiston published Red, White & Royal Blue, a romance novel about the bisexual First Son of the United States president falling in love with the gay prince of England, in 2019, readers couldn’t get over the far-fetched plot. Specifically, th
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: When writer Casey McQuiston published Red, White & Royal Blue, a romance novel about the bisexual First Son of the United States president falling in love with the gay prince of England, in 2019, readers couldn’t get over the far-fetched plot. Specifically, they couldn’t get over the idea that in the book’s alternate 2020 timeline, the state of Texas flipped blue to reelect the country’s first female president, a Texan Democrat. As if, they said.

Obviously, McQuiston is feeling smug today after the state of Texas turned blue in the midterm elections. On Instagram Stories, they shared a series of memes, including an incredibly apt photo of Zendaya from Challengers wearing her “I Told Ya” tee. After Greg Abbott conceded the governor’s race to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, McQuiston wrote “Blexas not so silly now, is it” alongside a meme of Kuzco from The Emperor’s New Groove holding a “license to lib out.”

McQuiston, who was born in Baton Rouge and attended Louisiana State University, also began engaging with fans who reposted stills from the Red, White & Royal Blue movie adaptation that premiered in 2023. “It was all in the binder,” they commented under a film still of Taylor Zakhar Perez, who played First Son Alex Claremont-Diaz, posted by Vulture. (In the book, “the binder” refers to Claremont-Diaz’s strategy to flip Texas.)
On a more serious note, McQuiston reminded their followers “to love and celebrate and empower progressive leftists in the historically red states and especially the South.”
“I didn’t pull Blexas out of my ass 10 years ago,” they said. “I simply looked around and saw it.”

items.title: Palace Built Itself a Palace For Its London Flagship (Exclusive)
items.description: Real streetwear heads will know this legendary lore: in the late 2000s, a dilapidated, slightly skuzzy South London flat — affectionately nicknamed “the Palace,” and occupied by the Palace Wayward Boys Choir skate gang — became the unlikely origin point for wh
items.author: Chris Erik Thomas
paragraphs: Real streetwear heads will know this legendary lore: in the late 2000s, a dilapidated, slightly skuzzy South London flat — affectionately nicknamed “the Palace,” and occupied by the Palace Wayward Boys Choir skate gang — became the unlikely origin point for what’s become one of Britain’s biggest brands.
The brand, if you hadn’t already sussed it out, is Palace Skateboards.

It’s been 17 years since co-founders Lev Tanju and Gareth Skewis first launched the label, churning out small-batch skate decks and T-shirts riffing on luxury fashion house logos, and a lot has changed. Including, crucially, their digs. On November 5, Palace opens the doors to a new flagship that lives up to the brand’s name: the sprawling 8 Poland Street location occupies nearly 2,700 square feet and feels as much a store as a cultural landmark.

Inside, an amalgamation of design inspirations — from the British Museum to English churches to historic local skate spots — adds up to something that feels fit for the legacy Palace has built in less than two decades. Visitors will find archival imagery next to stained-glass windows, alongside the brand’s signature Tri-Ferg transformed into a raw oak bench and stool.

And product, of course. So, so much product. Alongside its regular wares and skate decks, Palace went all out for its London launch: its surprise banger of a Burberry collaboration will be exclusively available in-store, alongside an extra set of store-exclusive merch centered around the number 8 — a nod to the location’s address, rotated 90 degrees to become an infinite symbol.

The Poland Street store may sit within the same city limits as the original crash pad in Waterloo, but these two points in the brand’s history feel worlds apart. Palace may have stores all around the world, but there’s something about growing into its own in the city it calls home that feels fitting, especially as it nears its 18th anniversary. Ahead of the flagship store’s launch, we caught up with Tanju to talk about paying architectural homage to the London skate scene and how that legendary Burberry link-up actually happened.
This interview has been condensed and edited.
Why frame a skate shop as a museum, and how do you keep it from feeling precious or inaccessible for the kids who actually skate?

The museum thing is a bit tongue-in-cheek; it’s really just a Palace shop with a collection of Palace artifacts that are special to us. For me, it makes the shop feel more special and personal — not just a new build with a coffee machine and some marble in it.

The P-shaped marble tiles match the original shop, and the Rolls-Royce grille came from Brewer Street. How did you decide which pieces of Palace history made it into the new store, and did you have to leave anything out that you really wanted to include?

The grille came from my grandad's old restaurant in South London, along with the photo of the Queen in the changing room. We picked what we thought made the Brewer Street shop, our first store, special and moved them over to the new one so it felt like home.

The store also has a few surviving seats from the old Victoria Benches skate spot, and there’s a rumor that some of the other seating came from a church seen in a famous skate video. What’s the story there?

The story behind Victoria Benches was that when they started knocking down the spot, I hounded Greg Finch, who works for us, to find out how we could get some [benches]. He did some research, and we paid one of the builders knocking the spot down for three benches that we kept on ice until we knew what we wanted to do with them. It’s an important piece of skate history, and we wanted to save a bit of it; it was one of the most iconic London skate spots. And we made the other bench; it didn’t come from a church. I like the rumor, though!
What does this new Poland Street flagship say about the larger Palace story, in terms of the brand's history and the space it occupies today?

We wanted a bigger space and a fresh look to the store. We have some lovely shops around the world now, so we wanted to give London something special. Plus, I think the old landlords were pricks, and now we don’t have to deal with them. So that’s cool too.
We called the Burberry collab obvious in hindsight, but it came out of nowhere. How did it actually come about, and why sell it only at Poland Street instead of online?

Every time we open a new location, we want to do something special. And because we’re a London brand, we wanted to do something really, really special. We’re big fans of Burberry and know some lovely people that work there, so we just hit them up about it, and they loved the idea. It’s really cool to be able to buy something from only one store in the world; it reminds me of how shops used to be. It makes you venture out and appreciate the experience and what you’ve bought.

items.title: Artist Uniform: Miles Greenberg’s Style Is Dennis Rodman Meets Kim Possible
items.description: In Artist Uniform, a column for Highsnobiety, Chris Erik Thomas traces how personal style shapes an artist's identity.
items.author: Chris Erik Thomas
paragraphs: In Artist Uniform, a column for Highsnobiety, Chris Erik Thomas traces how personal style shapes an artist's identity.

In a dark, cavernous space in Manhattan’s former 86th Street Cinema on October 29, more than 44 people walked ceaselessly on treadmills for six hours. This phalanx of bodies assembled as part of WAR, a durational artwork organized by Miles Greenberg and presented by Performa. Each person was shirtless, wearing matching black pants, with Greenberg at the center like the eye of a hurricane.

The costuming was intentionally chosen to strip away individuality and create a kind of silent army, inspired by the terracotta soldiers from China’s ancient Qin dynasty — a physical embodiment of imminent collision. “In a performance like this one, the garment should disappear,” Greenberg told Highsnobiety by email, after WAR’s premiere. “That’s the difference between a uniform and a costume; my performances have always relied mostly on uniforms.” Offstage, his wardrobe follows a similar logic: a handful of pieces worn so often they’ve become their own kind of armor.

For the Canadian artist and sculptor, bodies have become a go-to tool for exploration, sometimes to grotesque effect. His Fountain I and Fountain II performances in 2022 and 2023 saw Greenberg stand atop a pedestal like a statue, slowly rotating for over six hours as artificial blood poured from tubes tied to his arms into a 25-foot-wide pool. The fascination with statues dates back to when he was a kid in Canada watching his mom perform in an absurdist Russian theater troupe. “Theatre wasn’t really my thing, but I was very attracted to sculpture,” he said in a 2024 interview. “The body was the only thing I understood or knew how to use or manipulate.”

Seeing Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” at age 12 sparked his interest in art, but the lessons he learned clubbing in Montreal as a teen (with future performance-art duo Matières Fécales) were what taught him about clothing's transformative power. “We were the freaks at the club,” he recalls. “My neighbor was a costume designer, and I’d raid her stuff all the time before going out. I had this one piece: a mid-length dress made of grey wigs that might’ve been a rejected tour look from Arcade Fire or something.”

Since launching his career at just 17 with a week-long exhibition in a rented Montreal storefront, he’s enclosed himself in boxes filled with insects and walked on a conveyor belt for 24 hours, earning praise from critics and fellow artists alike. (He’s been a protégé of Abramović since participating in her durational performance workshop in Greece when he was 20.) Even without seeing his work up close, it’s easy to see why people are paying attention. Greenberg is fearless, testing his mental and physical limits through art, but it’s his total command of self-presentation that becomes the flint, sparking a flame that surges through whatever he does.

At the core is the kind of duality that defines any good artist. While productions often see him carrying on the spirit of his early experimental era, donning blinding white contact lenses or covered in oils and paints, his life offstage is more muted. As Greenberg recovered from WAR, we talked about this duality — covering his favorite clothes, his go-to designer, and “being someone else’s doll, for a change.”
This interview has been condensed and edited.
How do you dress when you’re not performing?

I used to describe my personal off-duty style as somewhere at the intersection of Dennis Rodman and Kim Possible. Utilitarian, a little studious, with a touch of sleaze. I often think about the way Miles Davis dressed, or David Hammons, or Anjelica Huston in that one Leibovitz photograph of her smoking a cigarette in a white tank top.

My default is a pair of Martin Margiela trousers from ’01 that I’ve owned for about a decade, a belt, a pair of beat-up loafers, an old leather jacket, and a white Hanes rib knit tank top from the pharmacy. I also love a relaxed suit.
You once described fashion as a fun space for you with no stakes. Is that still true? How do clothes inform your work, if at all?

It’s not no stakes, but it’s definitely not my profession. I think of myself as a fan and an admirer. It’s not that clothes inform my work per se, but they definitely do something similar to my work in that they are a means of transforming and influencing the shape and composition of the body; fashion designers are very subtly like choreographers who seduce you into fulfilling a persona in their universe, superimposed on everyday life in a way that’s almost imperceptible.

I recently got to know Louise Trotter of Bottega Veneta. I really like her; I think her universe is one that is so sensitive and smart and really takes into account all those super intimate details that are kind of just between you and yourself; when I’m wearing her clothes, I feel like I get to know these microscopic details about the way I move that remind me of my own performance practice. That’s where our Venn diagram meets.
Are there any other designers or brands you return to, or feel a kinship with artistically?
Lately, it's Bottega Veneta, Maison Martin Margiela (and his Hermès years), and Dario Vitale’s Versace.
How has being dressed up by fashion magazines changed how you see your own body?

I don’t get to inhabit other people’s visions all that often, so when I do, it’s always refreshing and fun and sexy to me. I’ll always enjoy spending an afternoon being someone else’s doll, for a change.
