items.author: Rivka Galchen
paragraphs: A mathematician is a machine for turning coffee into theorems. This was a line often invoked by the Hungarian mathematician Paul Erdős, who was fuelled by coffee and amphetamines, slept little, travelled near-constantly, never married or had children, and published almost fifteen hundred papers in his lifetime, in collaboration with hundreds of other mathematicians. But Erdős was, in most ways, not machinelike. He called lecturing in mathematics “preaching,” woke friends at odd hours by asking, “Is your brain open?,” wore only silk underclothing on account of his sensitive skin, and claimed not to have learned how to butter toast until he was twenty-one. He gave away most of his earnings to charitable causes and to young mathematicians in need of funds for their education, and he offered bounties (sometimes ten dollars, sometimes a thousand) for solutions to mathematical problems he’d proposed. Mathematics was his life. Mathematicians were his family. It has been said that, even above his remarkable contributions to the mathematical literature, he helped the discipline most profoundly by turning people who might otherwise have become hedge-fund managers or F.B.I. agents or lost souls into mathematicians. When he died, in 1996, at the age of eighty-three, he left behind about a thousand problems. Solving an Erdős problem is a great honor, as is having a low “Erdős number,” a term that describes how many degrees of separation one is from having published work with him.

Terence Tao was ten years old when Erdős visited his home town of Adelaide, Australia, in 1985. Erdős loved children and called them epsilons. Tao, a mathematics prodigy, had started taking college-level courses at age nine. Erdős posed a problem for him and Tao to work on together. A photograph of their meeting, taken by Tao’s mother (who had been a math teacher before having kids), shows the young mathematician and the old one deep in thought, hands at chins, looking at the notepad before them. “I wish I remembered more about the encounter,” Tao recently said. Erdős later sent the Tao family a note, handwritten on Bell Labs stationery, that, after brief wishes of a good New Year, reiterated the problem they had discussed: “Let 1 ≤ a1 < a2 < . . . atn ≤ n be a sequence of integers . . .”

In May of 2023, the mathematician Thomas Bloom began gathering the known remaining unsolved Erdős problems on a website, erdosproblems.com. Their depth and difficulty vary, deliberately. Erdős described some of them as “marshmallows” and others as “acorns.” In a talk in February of this year, titled “Machine Assistance and the Future of Research Mathematics,” Tao quoted Erdős’s characterization of a marshmallow as “a tasty tidbit supplying a few moments of fleeting enjoyment,” and of an acorn as “requiring deep and subtle new insights from which a mighty oak can develop.”

The role that artificial intelligence will play in research mathematics has been talked about a fair amount in the past five years, and a fearsome, unbounded amount in the past five months. Tao—a professor of mathematics at the University of California, Los Angeles, and a founder, in 2025, of the Foundation for Science and AI Research—has been one of the most prominent voices in this discussion. This is in part because he is a venerated mathematician who won a Fields Medal, the highest honor in the discipline, at age thirty-one; in part because, like Erdős, he is especially collaborative and community-oriented; and in part because he was already thinking seriously and publicly about A.I. when many of his peers still thought, as Tao put it, “Oh, it’s a toy, it makes so many mistakes, it’s never going to be useful.” A.I. labs such as Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic were trying to demonstrate otherwise. From their perspective, math problems are practical benchmarks to measure the capabilities of their products. Mathematical proofs can be digitized and objectively verified, and the field of mathematics is highly respected. Early on, A.I. tools were conspicuously bad at basic math. When OpenAI’s GPT-4 Turbo was asked to count the number of “L”s in “lollapalooza,” it answered “Five.” The tools have since improved dramatically, but even now L.L.M.s find difficult some tasks that we find easy, and vice versa. “The means by which an A.I. solves a problem is just so orthogonal to the way a human solves a problem,” Tao said, in a recent lecture. A.I. proofs often devote pages to what would be obvious to an undergraduate, then offer only a few lines on what to a human mathematician is a large, cloudy move.

In 2024, A.I. tools began performing well at the International Mathematical Olympiad, scoring at the silver-medal level and, in 2025, at the gold level. Only top high-school students and a handful of prodigies participate in the I.M.O. (Tao won a bronze at age ten, a silver at age eleven, and a gold the next year. His longtime friend and mathematical collaborator Allen Knutson recalled how an ex-girlfriend who had been on Mexico’s I.M.O. team told him about an annoying little kid with a stuffed animal who would come out of the exams saying, “Too easy”—it was Tao.) Then, in early 2026, mathematicians and math hobbyists using A.I. tools started solving some of the more marshmallowy Erdős problems. In January, GPT-5.2 Pro appeared to have solved Erdős Problem #728 largely on its own; Tao and others took on the necessary task of verifying the proof. Then more Erdős problems began to fall. Tao explained that some of these problems had remained unsolved on account of “an attention bottleneck,” meaning that no one had given much thought to them; others were problems that had already been solved, but the solutions were not widely known, and the A.I. had effectively retrieved them. But, on May 20th, OpenAI published a proof of Erdős Problem #90, the unit-distance problem, a combinatorics problem that involves arranging points on a plane so that as many pairs as possible are spaced an equal distance apart. This was not a marshmallow. Top-level mathematicians had spent time on it, nudging it forward.

Then, there was the Navier-Stokes existence-and-smoothness problem. The problem has to do with how a set of equations that model the movement of fluids seems to imply solutions with infinite speed, which should be impossible. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, had announced seven Millennium Prize Problems, chosen and formulated by the institute’s Scientific Advisory Board, each with a million-dollar award for solving it. The Millennium Prize Problems are acorn problems, and Navier-Stokes was one of them. On September 8th, OpenAI announced that it had solved it. Much of the mathematical community, which was already distressed, tipped over into existential crisis.

“I have had the strangest week ever in my life,” Tao declared at the start of a talk he gave three days later, at Caltech. Usually, when lecturing, he appears in a collared shirt, tucked in. At this talk, he wore jeans and a black T-shirt. The shirt featured the Edo-era woodblock print “Under the Wave Off Kanagawa,” a famed art work noted for its fractal-like patterning—the wave comprises smaller, similarly shaped waves, which themselves comprise yet smaller ones. “Ordinarily, I would use A.I. and create some fancy version of this,” Tao said, gesturing at the bare-bones graphic on the screen behind him. “I used PowerPoint,” he admitted, to laughter. He then described the current state of the field. Solutions were being published, often with little explanation or detail, relying on the good will and free labor of mathematicians to verify and illuminate them. A.I.-generated submissions were overwhelming mathematics journals and databases, and the field’s genteel ecosystem of people volunteering their time to referee submissions was collapsing under the weight of slop. Sometimes even the person submitting the paper did not understand it. Answers were being found, but, in math, answers are often not very important; the insights and inventions that arise while working toward an answer matter much more. “We have to slow down,” Tao said. “It’s insane, the pace.” During the Q. & A. portion of the talk, an audience member observed that A.I. has thus far been solving problems that already exist. Where did Tao think new problems would come from? New problems, Tao said, emerge from “the slow, deliberative process” of working toward a solution, “and this is what’s being destroyed.”

In another era of mathematics, which is to say, in April, I visited Tao at his office in the Mathematical Sciences Building at U.C.L.A. The building was connected through a mazelike series of corridors and stairs to Boelter Hall, where, in 1969, the first message was sent on ARPANET, the precursor to the internet. One of the hallways had a telephone booth. Tao’s office was spacious and mostly unadorned, with beige carpeting and a beige sofa, six blackboards mounted onto two long walls, and stacks and shelves with hundreds of books bearing titles such as “Advances in Analysis: The Legacy of Elias M. Stein,” “Number Theory Volume I: Tools and Diophantine Equations,” and “The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves.” Near the light switch, there was a drawing of a toothy monster in a black suit and tie, next to a message in code (“LWKIRLCS,” part of it read) written on a sheet of paper. His oldest child had made it for him years ago. “I don’t think I remember how to decode it,” Tao said. None of his many prizes and honors were on display, but there was a wall hanging—made by the Mathematics Genealogy Project, of North Dakota State University—recording generations upon generations of who had studied under whom.

Tao is slim, wears his dark hair boyishly grown out, and has a gentle and calm demeanor. He is fifty-one but looks a decade younger. He rides a bike to work, and he has several tennis racquets in the corner of his office, though he said that he hasn’t really had time to play tennis in years, owing to his proliferating duties. “If you want to profile a mathematician, I’m maybe not a good example,” he told me. “I get to do math on Tuesdays and Thursdays. And sometimes on airplanes.” He lives with his wife, Laura, their two children, four cats, a dog, and three rabbits. The family had intended to give the oldest rabbit, Spumpkin, away to a friend, because Spumpkin was “traumatized by the traffic” outside their house, Tao said. But that didn’t work out, so Spumpkin is still with them, which is O.K.; Spumpkin and the oldest cat are close friends.

Many mathematical geniuses have been as celebrated for their eccentricity as for their work. Erdős is only one of many examples. The eighteenth-century Italian mathematician Maria Agnesi, who wrote an early textbook on calculus, gave away most of her money and abandoned mathematics to devote herself fully to theology. The logician Kurt Gödel, whose incompleteness theorems revealed that no mathematical system could express every mathematical truth, came to believe that doctors had a secret book in which they wrote honestly about medications, that the I.R.S. was after him, and that his friend who had died decades before was still alive in the Soviet Union. John Nash (famous for contributions to game theory), Grigori Perelman (famous for solving the Poincaré conjecture), and Alexander Grothendieck (famous for developing a new foundation for algebraic geometry) all dramatically withdrew from their social spheres. Tao does not fit this tradition. He is very much of the world, which is somewhat surprising, considering that, when he was two years old, he was reportedly found typing out a favorite children’s story on his dad’s typewriter.

As a kid, Tao imagined that what professional mathematicians did was solve problems assigned to them, sort of like homework. By age seventeen, he was a graduate student in the mathematics department at Princeton University, and still somewhat in the dark about what he was meant to do with his mathematical imagination. He played a lot of video games, easily completed his coursework, and almost failed the qualifying exam for his doctorate. Not all child prodigies go on to brilliant careers. Tao, however, went on to become one of the most revered mathematicians alive today, praised for his profound contributions to an astonishing range of subjects, from the study of numbers to the analysis of waves—a polymath of math.

The election of Donald Trump for a second term, in 2024, made Tao even busier. Federal funding for U.C.L.A.’s Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics (IPAM), where he serves as the director of special projects, was frozen, as were National Science Foundation grants that supported his department’s research, including his own. And, as the Trump Administration unrolled various anti-immigration orders, students and postdocs had visa troubles. Tao spent many months fund-raising among private donors to support the stipends and T.A. positions relied upon by his graduate students. Some of these donors were hedge funds and banks that had in the past offered him large sums to work for them. He had always declined, “but those connections were useful in that moment,” he said.

One of the companies that offered funding to IPAM was OpenAI. Earlier this year, Tao was interviewed alongside an OpenAI executive, Mark Chen, in what the company called a fireside chat. In the interview, Tao expressed both hopes and concerns about A.I. in mathematics; OpenAI later used some of his bullish bits in a promotional video, which featured Tao saying that A.I. is “ready for prime time,” and that it will reduce cognitive friction “down to zero.” Tao has collaborated with researchers at Google DeepMind, and one of his projects was sponsored by the A.I. startup Math, Inc. For these reasons, among others, he was for a time portrayed as almost uncritically enthusiastic about the role of A.I. in math; in a June article in Quanta Magazine, he was described as an “evangelist.”

It is true that, for a few years now, Tao has suggested that the chalkboard-dominated field of mathematics might be overdue for change. He has expressed hope that A.I. could help make a “living spreadsheet” of mathematics, which could self-update as new mathematical discoveries are made; he has worked to develop open-source A.I. tools, in addition to helping organize events to encourage a collaborative approach to A.I. In 2024, he started the Equational Theories Project, which involved dozens of professional and amateur mathematicians who, with the assistance of A.I., tried to determine the truth or falsity of about twenty-two million mathematical implications of some forty-five hundred invented mathematical laws. He has spoken about how A.I. could enable even more large-scale collaborations. He would like mathematics to be able to ask questions more in the tradition of biologists’ population studies (“What makes lemur populations rise and fall?”) rather than case studies (“What can we say about this particular lemur and from there gain some insight into lemurs in general?”).

Recently, though, Tao’s muted optimism has given way to alarm. He has begun to speak in praise of cognitive friction, and has described A.I. companies as having “managed to optimize by removing all the humanity out of the process.” In his office, he told me, “We have to actively experiment and figure out what works for us. Because otherwise what’s going to happen is that the tech companies will release these products—you know, ‘Here’s my artificial scientist’—and there’ll be no competing products.” He doesn’t advocate that mathematicians avoid using A.I. But, at his lecture at Caltech, he pointed out that the effect of A.I. on math followed what he called nonlinear dynamics. He went on, “Any kind of monotone, one-dimensional thinking—Oh, a little bit of this is good, therefore a lot of it is going to be a lot better—one of the lessons of math is that most systems don’t work like that.” Human understanding needed to remain central. For example, with a proof written by a human, he noted, “you can talk to that person and say, ‘What was your experience? What was your inspiration?’ You have some insight into the process. They can give talks. And, years later, they’ll still be in the community, and they can pass on their expertise to their students. They contribute to the whole ecosystem of mathematics.”

In his office, Tao had compared the crisis that the mathematical community was facing to the transition that cities underwent when the horse and buggy was replaced with the car. “You need parts of the city that are still for pedestrians and parts that make sense for travelling by car. But you can’t have the whole city designed to be optimal for cars,” he said. “Because no one wants to live in that city.” This was an analogy he used often in talks and interviews. In a more recent talk, he recalled his reliance on the analogy with a slide demarcating lanes for pedestrians and ones for automobiles. “This is where we want to go,” he said. “But, unfortunately, this is sort of where we are now—” He advanced to a slide that depicted people running away in terror from what appeared to be autonomous machines.

Much of the math we learn as kids is mechanical, which may be why mathematics is sometimes misperceived as an unimaginative field. A more accurate understanding might come from recalling that Charles Dodgson, better known as Lewis Carroll, was a professional mathematician. In some ways, the writing of “Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland” resembles mathematical research. Mechanical calculation, in this analogy, is the basics of composition: spelling, subject-verb agreement. But, in order to explore logic and whimsy and wonder and paradox, Carroll invented characters like the White Rabbit, the Cheshire Cat, and the Queen of Hearts, and situations like the Mad Tea Party and the Caucus Race. These characters and scenes are akin to the objects and techniques mathematicians invent as they explore mathematical ideas. When Andrew Wiles proved Fermat’s Last Theorem, more than three hundred and fifty years after its initial postulation, mathematicians were thrilled, but not because of the answer, which wasn’t surprising. (No, there are no positive whole numbers such that an + bn = cn if n > 2.) What was wonderful about Wiles’s proof was the mathematical techniques he’d developed along the way. That was what advanced mathematics.

But coming up with characters and story lines is challenging—which is probably why it’s satisfying. I sat in on a meeting Tao had with his postdoctoral mentee, Iqra Altaf, who was working on a problem in geometric-measure theory. “Mathematically, the news is not good,” Altaf said. She went to the chalkboard and began writing out a counterexample to a conjecture she had thought would prove true. “Math is like a video game, or like ‘Groundhog Day,’ ” Tao said. “Every time you die, you come back.” En route to failure, you learn something that aids you in the next go-around. He quoted the Russian mathematician Vladimir Arnold, who once said, “Mathematics is the part of physics where experiments are cheap.” In another conversation, Tao compared learning mathematics to watching “Emily in Paris,” a show that he and his wife enjoyed. “It’s completely ridiculous fluff, but it’s also fun. You learn the tropes, and you can kind of see how it’s going to go,” he said. “But if you’re just given a synopsis of the plot, like, ‘Here’s the premise, and this is what happens’—that’s not the point.” And, if you want to learn how to write your own show, “then it’s not helpful at all.” Seeing scenes done poorly and done well, watching how plots are resolved even in formulaic shows—that’s how you learn to direct your own series. Among the crises that the arrival of A.I. has brought to mathematics, “the most urgent one is, How are we going to train our graduate students?” Tao said. It is a question that he has been asking for several years. The modest-sized problems that graduate students would once have spent months on—learning to think mathematically in the process—can now sometimes be solved by A.I. tools in hours.

On October 9th, Tao gave a talk (another!) hosted by the American Institute of Mathematics. Three days earlier, OpenAI had released three hundred and seventy-two additional results contributing to or solving open problems in mathematics. (OpenAI’s statement announcing the results briefly mentioned that four thousand problems had been tried, but that detail didn’t get much notice.) Tao started out by explaining that, when he had been invited to give the talk, a year earlier, the title of it had been “Machine Assisted Proof”—that was, in fact, the title on the posters advertising the event—but that “by this point the idea that machines could assist proof was maybe not quite as novel.” So he changed the title to “Math 2.0.”

Math 1.0—“math up to 2025,” Tao said—operated under the basic assumption of “proof scarcity.” Proofs were a sort of currency, central to publishing papers, winning prizes, and getting jobs. The landscape had now changed to one of proof abundance, which Tao compared to food abundance, when “you become a bit pickier about what food gets crammed into your mouth.” We would soon be living in a vast sea of low-quality A.I. proofs, with mathematicians left to fish out what was worthwhile. Math 2.0 would follow from figuring out “how to actually integrate A.I. and humans” to “find a new frontier of tasks,” only some of which would be problems.

During the Q. & A., a first-year graduate student at Caltech asked Tao what advice he would give to her generation. He hesitated. He blinked several times. He closed his eyes. “Get involved,” he said. “In—um—you know, in policy. In general.” He paused and then spoke more fluently: “Don’t try to pretend A.I. doesn’t exist. Actually learn what it can and can’t do.”

The mathematician Geordie Williamson, of the University of Sydney, in Australia, described one A.I.-assisted solution to me as “like this beautiful thing for the whole math community” and another as “like the weed killer Roundup being sprayed on a garden.” Both results were published by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic. The beautiful thing concerned an eighty-seven-year-old problem, the Jacobian conjecture. We can think of the problem as having to do with the possibility of a one-to-one mapping from one shape to another. On July 19th, the day of the Spain-Argentina soccer game, Alpöge posted on X, “hello there the jacobian conjecture is false thanx to my close friend akhil”—a human—“for asking about it and my other close friend fable”—an A.I. model—“for working during the world cup final.” Claude Fable 5 had produced a counterexample to the conjecture, much like how an ostrich is a counterexample to the conjecture that all birds can fly. Williamson said, “Within thirty-six hours, mathematicians had kind of understood where the counterexample comes from and why it’s natural.” A handful of mathematicians, including Tao, explored the proof, came to understand it—a process that I kept hearing mathematicians refer to as proof digestion—and reconstructed the algebraic geometry that underlay it. On July 21st, Tao posted the work on his blog, including the transcript of a conversation he’d had with ChatGPT as he looked into the details. By July 22nd, Semon Rezchikov, of Barnard College, had created a visualization of the counterexample using only high-school-level mathematics. The proof had opened up thinking, not decapitated it.

But then there was Williamson’s Roundup story: On August 12th, Alpöge posted again, though it was not immediately clear what the new disclosure was about. “It was this crazy tweet, just a whole sequence of pluses and minuses. It looked like a secret code,” Williamson told me. He soon recognized that it was the next in a series of what are called Hadamard matrices. The first few Hadamard matrices had been described in 1867, and the matrices have fascinated mathematicians ever since, with breakthroughs and new insights turning up every couple of decades or so, the most recent in 2004. At a talk not long before, Williamson had been encouraging mathematicians to find the next one. Then there it was, on X. “At first, I was, like, Awesome,” Williamson told me. But then he saw that Alpöge had posted more than just the next matrix—“also the one after that, and the one after that, and the one after that,” he said. Typically, someone solving this kind of problem would be transparent about the methods used to get there; for years, mathematicians have been sharing their work freely on the open-access website arxiv.org. Such is not the M.O. of the A.I. companies. Anthropic did not release logs showing how the solutions were reached. Williamson said that he felt as if an entire garden of mathematics had been killed. “It was the nightmare scenario, like, ‘Here’s the answer, it’s forty-two.’ ”

It was less than a month later that OpenAI made its Navier-Stokes announcement. The day before, Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at N.Y.U., posted a statement saying that he and Alpöge, working with the assistance of A.I., had made significant progress toward a solution. OpenAI, which spent millions of dollars’ worth of compute to get there first, said that it had taken less than a week. In Buckmaster’s statement, he voiced concern that OpenAI had accessed his work (he and Alpöge had used OpenAI’s public Codex model, among other L.L.M.s), which the company denied. According to Buckmaster, Sébastien Bubeck, the head of the team at OpenAI that was behind the solution, had offered him authorship of their paper, on the condition that he agree not to include Alpöge. Buckmaster said no. When he threatened to make his interaction with OpenAI public, Bubeck apparently responded by asking, “Why would you ruin your career?”

An initial group of twenty-five Fields medallists, Tao among them, responded with an open letter noting that “solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.” Problem-solving and insight were decoupling, it observed. “The letter was correct to call out bad behavior,” Williamson said. “But my broader sense is that I don’t think mathematicians had been grappling as much as we should have been with the impending reality of A.I., and I think that is somewhat visible in the letter. It’s a letter that reflects what was already a reality six months ago.”

Socrates is said to have worried that writing would ruin our memories—and Socrates’ crowd probably did remember longer stretches of the Odyssey than any of us do. But the Fields letter argued that the use of A.I. was not like merely off-loading the memorization of poems or phone numbers; it was more like off-loading, or bypassing, daydreaming and debating and thinking. It’s not that humans will come to know too much too quickly but that they will understand less and less—eventually less than we understand now. “The most precious resources of our profession are students and ideas, and these we nurture with great care,” the letter said. Mathematics is a living discipline and an oral tradition, not just a written one. The symbol of the working mathematician is a chalkboard, representing knowledge that can be erased after it’s understood because it is now in the mind.

The mathematical community has not reached a consensus on whether OpenAI has actually solved the Navier-Stokes problem, which has not yet been verified by humans. Charlie Fefferman, a professor at Princeton, wrote the description of the Navier-Stokes problem for the Clay Mathematics Institute. “I think it’s probably correct,” Fefferman told me. The A.I. relied on an approach that had been conceived by his former student Diego Córdoba and Córdoba’s former student Luis Martínez-Zoroa. “And so, in addition to whatever other people felt, I felt personal joy at their achievement,” Fefferman said.

Fefferman, like Tao, was a child prodigy, an early winner of the Fields Medal, and a professor of mathematics by his early twenties. He is now seventy-seven. I asked him how he would describe what working on a math problem feels like. He told me that he had sometimes described it to non-mathematicians as playing chess with the Devil, “but you get to take back moves.” The Devil is a much better chess player—“he crushes you again and again.” But then you go back to the beginning. You experiment with different approaches. You’re still crushed and don’t understand why. “But eventually you hit on something,” Fefferman said. “The whole time, there’s this angel whispering in your ear things like ‘No, no, pin his bishop!’ ” Initially, the angel’s voice is too quiet to make out, but it gets louder. “And your ears get better.” Until, finally, you win one match. And then you’re back at the beginning. “That’s something I love about being a mathematician,” Fefferman said. “If you have a thousand dumb ideas and one really good one, you’re a good mathematician. And that’s not true in many walks of life.”

Like everyone I spoke to, Fefferman said that no one knows, really, what will happen to mathematics. He sees both pessimistic and optimistic scenarios, and he suspects that the future will consist of a bit of each. In an optimistic scenario, he can envision A.I. broadening the kinds of questions that can be asked. He explained that sometimes you have a line of thinking that feels like it has only a five-per-cent chance of working out. You might say, “I don’t want to think about this, since it will take me a lifetime to find out.” “That’s different from ‘O.K., it has a five-per-cent chance of working, and it will take me two days to find out,’ ” Fefferman said. “I think people will become more courageous and more imaginative and be freed.” He said that mathematicians used to need both originality and technical power; he had known a very

items.title: The Need to be Needed
items.description: In Jenny Erpenbeck’s novel “Go, Went, Gone,” from 2015, Richard, a newly retired classics professor, finds himself at loose ends. Until recently, he was busy packing up his office and drafting lesson plans for his successor. (“The one departing must arrange hi
items.author: Joshua Rothman
paragraphs: In Jenny Erpenbeck’s novel “Go, Went, Gone,” from 2015, Richard, a newly retired classics professor, finds himself at loose ends. Until recently, he was busy packing up his office and drafting lesson plans for his successor. (“The one departing must arrange his own departure,” he reflects.) But now that he’s relinquished his key and said his goodbyes, how is he supposed to fill his days? Travel, reading—that’s what people say. But can a life be built out of such optional amusements? From a window of his house, Richard can see a lake where, earlier in the summer, a swimmer drowned; apparently, some boaters saw the man waving, but thought he was joking and rowed away. There is bottomless need in the world. And yet there seems to be no need for Richard, in particular.

Psychologists say that “mattering” is a pillar of happiness, along with belonging and self-esteem. We know we matter when other people notice us, when they invest in us—and when they need us. Young people, accordingly, flourish more when they find ways to be relied upon in their families and communities. Older people tend to stay healthier when they don’t just receive care but give it. The sense of being unnecessary is deflating; the belief that you’re a burden can be even worse, can act as a stepping stone to depression and suicidal thought.

Being needed comes naturally in certain lives, and in certain stages of life. Your kids are small, your parents are old, or both; you’re important to your employer, your friends, your town, your church. At such times, you might be needed so much that it’s overwhelming. Yet it’s also possible to feel superfluous amid a busy life. You might have what the anthropologist David Graeber called a “bullshit job,” full of meaningless tasks. Your teen-agers might wish you’d disappear; your band might have broken up. Or maybe society itself, through its values, somehow makes you feel unneeded or redundant. In “The Diary of a Superfluous Man,” from 1850, the Russian novelist Ivan Turgenev depicted a well-off gentleman who’s prevented, by the rules of his social set, from doing anything concretely useful. Fourteen years later, in “Notes from Underground,” Fyodor Dostoyevsky imagined the “underground man,” who feels entirely unnecessary to his society and so strikes back at it out of spite.

Reflecting on the Second World War, Hannah Arendt suggested that totalitarianism takes root in societies where lots of people feel unnecessary or unwanted. After the 2016 election, it was common for the media to report on underemployed people in the Rust Belt who felt that they’d been cast aside. Today, manosphere ideology rages against a society that, allegedly, claims not to need men, and young people wonder whether there’s room for them in an A.I.-saturated workforce. Recently, even world-class mathematicians have felt the sting of redundancy. In a blog post titled “The Mathocalypse,” the mathematician Scott Aaronson recounts what his nine-year-old son told his wife, the computer scientist Dana Moshkovitz: “Mommy . . . I heard that a robot solved the math problem you worked on for your whole career!”

We have a real need to be needed. And yet many forces—thinking machines, aging, economic and social dislocation—appear to be making us feel redundant. Are we building a world in which no one is particularly necessary? Do we already live in such a world?

There are circumstances in which it’s obvious that everyone is needed. In “Tribe: On Homecoming and Belonging,” from 2012, the journalist Sebastian Junger explores the mini-societies formed by soldiers in combat. In a unit at war, everyone lives together, experiences events as one, and contributes toward shared goals; it’s a way of life in which “individuals are assessed simply by what they are willing to do for the group.” It can be difficult, therefore, for soldiers to return to a civilian existence in which “most people work outside the home, children are educated by strangers, families are isolated from wider communities, and personal gain almost completely eclipses collective good.” Junger concludes that “humans don’t mind hardship, in fact they thrive on it; what they mind is not feeling necessary. Modern society has perfected the art of making people not feel necessary.”

We live, by and large, in a fluid, transactional world of relative plenty and freedom. It’s good, in many ways, that there’s a possible substitute for almost every need, and for almost every needed person: redundancy can be a form of luxury, a route to peace of mind. And yet there’s a downside when needs become fungible, and easily recast as preferences. In “The Dignity of Dependence: A Feminist Manifesto,” the Catholic writer Leah Libresco Sargeant describes the care she wants to provide to her young children, and notes that it is “technically possible to delegate.” If someone else can watch the kids, feed them, and put them to bed, then in which ways, exactly, do they still “need” their mother? You’re valued at your job, but another employee might do; your basketball team needs you, but new players arrive every year. Something is lost in every switch, but it takes work to articulate it. The loss might even be impossible to articulate.

Partly as a result, Sargeant argues, we tend to downplay our needs in an almost anticipatory fashion. We too easily adopt “a narrow definition of ‘normal’ life as autonomous,” and comply when we’re “asked to prune the connections that tie us to others.” We might say that capitalism makes us needy people who don’t need people: we’re full of wants for products and services, but not necessarily for the individuals who provide them. (We, in turn, aren’t strictly necessary, even if our services are.) But there are also political and psychological reasons to make autonomy the default. We prize liberty, independence, and self-definition; we’re wary of the emotional costs of depending on others and being depended upon. As a society, we practice what therapists call an “avoidant” attachment style. “I am a rock / I am an island,” Simon & Garfunkel sang. “I have no need of friendship, friendship causes pain / . . . I touch no one and no one touches me.”

In an essay from 2000, published in Wired and titled “Why the Future Doesn’t Need Us,” the computer scientist Bill Joy worried about society’s direction: by 2030, he predicted, we’d be able to build computers “a million times as powerful as the personal computers of today,” making “the prospect of human-level computing power” realistic for the first time. (By some measures, today’s most advanced A.I. chips can be about that fast.) Joy feared that such technology, coupled with genetic engineering and other advancements, might “replace our species”—an anxiety that becomes even more credible when you realize that it’s existed for nearly two centuries. Dostoyevsky’s Underground Man argued that individuals had become “piano keys” that could be played on command, in a composition coördinated by supposedly rational rules. In “Signs of the Times,” from 1829, Thomas Carlyle warned that we were entering a “mechanical age,” in which not just “the external and physical” would be “managed by machinery, but the internal and spiritual also.” Leo Tolstoy, in his 1886 novella “The Death of Ivan Ilyich,” imagined a man who was basically successful but who realized, on his deathbed, that he’d lived on autopilot. These thinkers suggested that we might internalize modernity’s logic of redundancy, finding ways to be unnecessary not just to one another but to ourselves. From this perspective, the development of technologies such as A.I. is just a furtherance of a long-standing trend.

Will A.I. really take our jobs? Will scientific and economic developments actually render the traditional human way of life obsolete? Maybe (hopefully!) not. But even the possibility of such outcomes wounds us. How can we insist upon—and really feel the existence of—our necessity, when so many forces seek to minimize it?

It helps to recognize that, just as there’s a rich discourse of redundancy, so there are many perspectives that clarify how and why we’re needed. In his book “Deep Utopia,” from 2024, the philosopher Nick Bostrom, who studies A.I. and coined the term “superintelligence,” asks how we might find meaning in a “solved world” in which A.I. does everything for us. He imagines people devoting themselves to hobbies, spirituality, the arts, sports, food, conversation, and “other domains which can serve as playgrounds for our souls,” and which will allow us to learn about each other and develop “our virtues and potentialities.” Hobbies, conversation—these seem slight against the steamroller of modernity. Yet my wife sings in a choir on Sundays, and, because there aren’t many altos, she can’t miss a rehearsal without letting the group down. Our participation in communal life really does make us necessary; it conjures, out of nothing, a place we need to be.

In “The Dignity of Dependence,” Sargeant suggests that, by believing in our own autonomy, we create the very conditions that obscure how much we’re needed. In his book “Dependent Rational Animals,” from 1999, the philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre argued that we should do the opposite, by acknowledging that both needing and being needed are fundamental to our existences, from our vulnerable childhoods to our dependency in old age. Across our lives, MacIntyre wrote, “in order to flourish, we need both those virtues that enable us to function as independent and accountable . . . and those virtues that enable us to acknowledge the nature and extent of our dependence on others.” One of the complexities of being a dependent, rational animal, he pointed out, is that we’re not always needed and needful at the same time; in life, there are some periods when we give help, and others when we receive it. If you feel needed today, know that you’ll have needs later; if you feel unnecessary now, the odds are that you’ll be relied on down the road. Apocalyptic thinking tells us that we’re on a one-way journey to obsolescence. Actually, we’re on a wheel.

Our societies can make us atomistic, giving us the impression that we’re increasingly cut loose and wandering free, for better and worse. But, Sargeant proposes, we are also like atoms in that we are “stochastically vulnerable to each other,” always colliding and connecting unpredictably. Often, she writes, “we don’t know for sure when or where the next need is going to emerge.” The question, therefore, becomes one of readiness—of “whether, when that need comes, we will be able to offer a stable bond in response.” We need not just to be needed but to be ready to be needed. We’re waiting, for an uncertain duration, for a call that’s certain to arrive. ♦

items.title: Did Substack Fix the Internet?
items.description: The question of how to survive as a writer is only slightly older than the impulse to be one in the first place. How to express yourself freely but also to be valued for said expression? Historically, strategies for making ends meet have included seeking relig
items.author: Kyle Chayka
paragraphs: The question of how to survive as a writer is only slightly older than the impulse to be one in the first place. How to express yourself freely but also to be valued for said expression? Historically, strategies for making ends meet have included seeking religious or royal patronage; producing printed books; serializing your work in publications; and hustling to sell your own subscriptions, as Alexander Pope did when he funded his eighteenth-century translation of the Iliad. The investigative journalist I. F. Stone had his own printed-and-mailed newsletter I.F. Stone’s Weekly, which cost five dollars a year and ran from 1953 to 1971, reaching some seventy thousand subscribers. In more recent years, the go-to option for an aspiring writer has been starting a newsletter of her own, often on Substack, a digital platform that launched in 2017 to allow writers to charge money for their writing. Hamish McKenzie, Substack’s co-founder, argues in a new book (that venerable format!), “How to Save the Media,” that Substack’s ecosystem of individual authors behind personal paywalls has solved the problem of cutting through the social-media cacophony and fulfilled writers’ quest for a livelihood. In McKenzie’s estimation, Substack represents “a better system design that distributes rather than concentrates both power and responsibility.”

McKenzie is a journalist by trade, who spent much of his career covering tech startups. With “How to Save the Media,” he has published something between a memoir and a manifesto, delivered in the quippy tone of twenty-tens blogging. He breezily recounts his life in the media industry, which began when he escaped his youth in small-town New Zealand to study journalism in Canada. After finding fecund ground in the Hong Kong tech scene, he landed in San Francisco during Silicon Valley boom times. He endured stints at such niche publications as PandoDaily before working at Tesla (and, after leaving, wrote a book about the company, leading to clashes with Elon Musk). While working at the messaging app Kik, he met Chris Best, Kik’s chief technology officer and his future Substack co-founder. The two saw that media companies were overly reliant on social media for distribution, and that profits were flowing to the likes of Facebook rather than to the creators of content. They wanted to build “a game where people would happily pay for good media,” scaling up the preëxisting achievements of writers such as Andrew Sullivan and Ben Thompson, whose small digital publications thrived on a subscription model. Substack would help writers publish their content and charge their readers while managing the messy back-end business, in exchange for ten per cent of writers’ revenue.

McKenzie courts for Substack such writerly talents as Bill Bishop, Matthew Yglesias, and Bari Weiss, whose publication The Free Press remains among the most popular and best-earning offerings on the platform. He recounts a boozy literary party sponsored by his company and quotes liberally, and redundantly, from his own old speeches and blog posts. The Substack team fends off acquisition offers from Jack Dorsey’s Twitter and Musk’s X, choosing to prioritize their independence. They also navigate debates over free speech from critics who complain that Substack hosts, and thus profits from, hateful content including pro-Nazi newsletters. McKenzie’s justification is ultimately the same as that of the social networks that he argues against: Substack is a neutral platform empowering its users, not an arbiter of truth. He writes, “When a platform decides what its uses are and aren’t allowed to see, it effectively positions itself as a centralized police force with the moral authority to decide what’s good and what’s bad.”

Such big-tent branding has helped Substack to become an unqualified success, at least in the eyes of its investors, and has made “Substacking” a cultural buzzword, much as “tweeting” dominated the early twenty-tens. It’s not just reporters who have Substacks now; celebrities (Pamela Anderson), musicians (Patti Smith), and traditional publications (including The New Yorker) do, too. (I, full disclosure, have my own accounts.) The rescued “media” of McKenzie’s title encompasses not just journalism but a broader realm of entertainment, with Substack providing a monetizable layer between creators and their fans. The company is, in essence, a crowdfunding e-commerce site, belonging to the same category as Kickstarter, Patreon, Gumroad, and OnlyFans. But it has out-evolved its ancestors and bested its competitors in its relevance to public discourse and in its direct commodification of online parasocial relationships. McKenzie predicts that “new companies will emerge” from such subscription platforms, but thus far Substack has only encouraged further atomization as audiences gravitate toward the loudest, most charismatic voices. The result is not a revived traditional media industry—few Substacks employ editors, for example—so much as a new form of public square in which anyone can shout.

“How to Save the Media” belongs to the genre of instructive founder’s autobiography, in which the heroic entrepreneur inevitably endures some brief trials on his path to power and riches, and offers the business lessons learned along the way. If mass social platforms driven by advertising are what’s wrong with the internet, McKenzie argues, then a platform driven by subscriptions can save it. Substack does allow thousands more writers (and podcasters and miscellaneous creators) to sustain careers in an otherwise barren industry landscape; it is now considered normal to charge your followers’ credit cards the cost of a fancy caffeinated beverage each month for the privilege of receiving your reporting, recipes, or ramblings. Yet as the company has grown, Substack has also come to look more like its stated enemies: it added a Twitter-esque feed of algorithmically recommended short posts, called Notes; its app has become a multimedia hub. McKenzie criticizes social media for how it “turns publishers into digital characters who compete for attention on crowded feeds,” but aspiring writers now hustle to make themselves known as characters on Substack, too. The writer Emily Sundberg, whose newsletter “Feed Me” is one of McKenzie’s highlighted triumphs, observed, in an influential 2024 essay, that “if you blacked out the names of many of the writers I come across on Substack today, I wouldn’t be able to tell them apart.” She went on to pinpoint the Substack generic style: “lists, random thoughts, and (easy to write) roundups of ‘what I’ve been doing’ do really well on this site.”

Another new book, “Content Machines,” by the Carleton University professor Sarah Brouillette, is less optimistic than McKenzie’s about digital platforms’ influence on publishing. In the online marketplace, Brouillette argues that writers have become mercenaries, “a node in a network of needy users” who must “invest their own time and money in design and sales if they want to succeed.” The book proceeds through chapters on such phenomena as the user-generated fiction platform Wattpad, BookTok and the popularity of the romance genre, Audible’s many algorithm-gaming offerings, self-publishing advice gurus, and autofiction’s relationship to social media. In each case, she analyzes how the structures and forces of the various internet platforms shape the style of the writing hosted on them. A roving analyst in addition to a well-read academic, Brouillette pays close attention to the trappings of Wattpad conventions (known as WattCon) and to such textual specimens as “How to Write a Book in 48 Hours,” by the self-publishing coach Dale L. Roberts, which suggests such hacks as using talk-to-text programs or “outsourcing” work to others. She concludes that writing on the internet, particularly in spaces where it’s simple to charge money for it, tends to push writers toward the confessional, the self-helpy, and the soothing.

Though Substack is not one of Brouillette’s subjects, much of what she describes applies equally to the platform—like, say, “a new kind of labor regime that turns people’s daily online creativity into an agglomerated mass of possibly monetizable material.” As content creators struggle to compete for attention and subscription dollars, they end up finding their way to the same solutions, relying on “established patterns,” Brouillette writes, echoing Sundberg’s observation; the goal is less to produce great writing than to “maximize your work’s efficiency.” Social media is blamed for raising a generation of self-promoting narcissists and fuelling a precipitous decline in attention spans and intellectual engagement. But in the new writer economy a “desperation for attention” is practically “an industry command,” Brouillette writes. The platform may not save journalism as a whole, but it certainly helps prolong the careers of those willing to play the “game,” as McKenzie put it, of cultivating their personal brands. ♦

items.title: Susan Collins Was Doomed by Her Moderation
items.description: All summer and fall, Susan Collins’s campaign dotted Maine’s roads with red signs bearing the self-assured slogan “Susan Collins: Our Senator.”
items.author: Rebecca Traister
paragraphs: All summer and fall, Susan Collins’s campaign dotted Maine’s roads with red signs bearing the self-assured slogan “Susan Collins: Our Senator.”

Indeed, Collins has been senator for a very long time, first winning office after a 1996 campaign in which she promised that, if elected, she’d serve only two terms. “Twelve years is long enough to be in public service and make a contribution,” a 43-year-old Collins said at the time. “Then come home and let someone else take your place.”

Now 73, Collins will be coming home to Maine in January. Her place in Washington will be taken by Troy Jackson, a union man, logger, and former president of the state senate, who beat her soundly on Tuesday night. The response has been ecstasy verging on disbelief, so long has Collins been a fixture in Maine’s political firmament.

“OMG I don’t have words,” said Deqa Dhalac, former state legislator and mayor of South Portland, by text early Wednesday morning. “I believed in Troy’s vision and I was asking myself: is Maine gonna listen this time and send Susan to retire?”

One person who worked on Chellie Pingree’s 2002 campaign to unseat Collins told me how, 24 years ago, there had been an understanding about the fleeting opportunity of beating a senator during their first reelection bid: “You have to beat her now,” he remembered being told, “or she’ll wind up there for 30 years.” Pingree, running in the wake of 9/11, had not been able to take Collins out, and the 30-year prophecy came true.

As the news of Collins’s long-awaited defeat spread through the Portland watch party late on Tuesday, Pingree herself — who had just won her tenth term in Congress and was celebrating the victory of her daughter Hannah as the state’s new governor — described how it felt to watch the people around her, many in “Solidarity” T-shirts, hugging each other. “This is a sea change for Maine,” said Pingree, “and people will spend many hours breaking down how something this dramatic could happen.”

Amidst all the history made on Tuesday night, Collins’s defeat feels momentous in a very specific way: a blaring signal of the desire for generational change, the rejection of purported moderation as some inherent political virtue, and an electrifying reminder that people at the bottom can still find a way to wrest power back from those at the top.

The Maine result is shocking because Collins has cultivated an aura of vampiric invincibility, a reputation rooted mostly in the 8.6 percent margin she posted in 2020 after trailing Democrat Sara Gideon in polls leading up to Election Day. That surprise win — in the same cycle in which Maine voters chose Joe Biden over Donald Trump by nine points — burnished Maine voters’ grim belief that this woman would rule in deathless perpetuity.

But prior to 2020, Collins’s victories weren’t supernatural feats; she won repeatedly because a lot of people liked her. A startling number of Maine Democrats, even liberal Democrats, have voted for Collins in the past. This summer, Troy Jackson told me he was pretty sure he had voted for her years ago; Jackson’s predecessor on the ticket, Graham Platner, has said that he had voted for her as well.

“It’s hard to explain to people outside of Maine,” the writer Shay Stewart-Bouley said. “‘Why did you all keep voting for her?’ But I moved here as a Black woman from Chicago 24 years ago, and I asked around, and everybody rocked with her back then.”

Collins was hailed as the last of a dying breed, a throwback to the misty memories of bipartisanship. Now the last Republican Senator left in New England, and a practitioner of a kind of politics often described as moderate, Collins was celebrated for her occasional willingness to vote across the aisle and broker compromise with her Democratic colleagues, especially the women. In 2015, a Morning Consult poll pegged Collins’s approval rating at 78 percent, making her the second-most popular senator, behind only Bernie Sanders. As strange as that may sound, she was understood to share a quality with the senator from Vermont: independence.

Independence is important to Maine, a state where a third of voters are unenrolled in either party and with a history of elected officials who defied their parties’ leadership to take stands they believed in. Collins’s role model was four-term Republican senator Margaret Chase Smith, the first woman ever to serve in both houses of Congress and an odd duck who supported much of the New Deal, advocated for the U.S. to get into Vietnam and to use nuclear weapons against the Soviet Union, voted for the establishment of Medicare and Medicaid, and delivered a legendary 15-minute “Declaration of Conscience” address against McCarthyism.

To be persuasively independent, in the spirit of Smith, is to possess a set of values, however zany or mismatched they may be. Collins’s early career showed flashes of ideological commitments, especially to abortion and gay rights. The beginning of her end was her fealty to Trump, a president she proclaimed she would not support, then whose bidding she mostly did.

But independence is different from moderation, and moderation was much more Collins’s calling card, the thing she was no longer capable of plausibly performing. Tom Allen, a former Democratic Congressman who ran against Collins and lost in 2008, said, “Five terms — 30 years — is a problem, especially for someone trying to walk down the middle in this political environment. It’s much more polarized than when I ran against her.”

Polarization implies equivalent moves toward the margins, but most of the movement toward a radical edge has thus far come from Collins’s Republican Party, which has grown increasingly open in its bigotry and drive toward authoritarian control. Collins’s former Senate colleague and longtime rival, Olympia Snowe, understood this and got out while the getting was good, retiring in 2013. It is perhaps the ultimate indignity for Collins that Snowe remains a respected figure in Maine while Collins will be remembered as a politician who steadily nudged her moral center closer to her party’s ever more acidic resentments.

This is what made her brand of moderation untenable. It was advertised as a form of political collegiality, an impulse to compromise in the service of functional government, but as the years wore on and her party became ever more hellbent in its plan to strip Americans of voting rights, reproductive care, and health care, it grew harder to pretend that civility had anything to do with it, or that there was anything moderate or functional about finding middle ground with a party whose a state police force kidnaps people and puts them in concentration camps and in July murdered a father in her own state.

“Susan Collins may be the same,” said Bouley, “but politics has changed, and Maine has changed.” She noted rising costs, the ever-widening gap between rich and poor, and demographic changes, both the blue-tilting urbanites moving in since COVID and the growth of a Somali immigrant population. “Yes, Maine is still predominantly white,” said Bouley, “but it went from 98 percent white to 92 percent white, and that’s a big deal with such a small population. Not only does Collins not represent those communities, she hasn’t made any effort to connect with them in any way.”

During this campaign, Collins’s veneer of civility slipped. As the conservative outlet the Maine Wire stoked racist fears of voter fraud by Somali Americans, Collins commented that “only Americans should be voting in American elections” and cheerfully posed, with Joe Manchin, alongside a prop sword that a conservative journalist had recently wielded outside a Lewiston mosque.

For Collins, moderation was perhaps never about finding some moral middle ground between political poles. Rather, hers was a politics of deference to hierarchies in which no ideas are better than other ideas and the highest calling is simply the preservation of entrenched systems through an ideologically blank commitment to “working across the aisle.”

What Collins seems to stand for most intensely is the protection of institutional power. She voted to acquit both Bill Clinton and Donald Trump of impeachment charges when they were president, only voting to convict Trump after January 6, when he was not in office. She proudly argued that she made decisions on judicial and cabinet appointments, including Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, based not on ideology but on a candidate’s qualifications and her belief that presidents had the right to select the people they wanted to select by dint of being presidents. She excused her worst sleights of hand — in which she would vote an egregious appointee or piece of legislation out of the committees where she had power, then vote against them when on the floor where her vote didn’t matter — with claims about the propriety of the full senate body being able to deliberate.

But passive commitment to simply letting those in power wield it without meaningful check or balance, to preserving the institutional norms and authority for which she had such reverence, ironically hastened the corrosion of those institutions. The destruction of everything from Medicaid to the Supreme Court to USAID to the Kennedy Center to the White House itself leaves old-timey institutionalists with no institutions left to defend. They all failed so profoundly that the moderate approach Collins clung to for so long no longer looks rational at all.

In her last desperate bid to retain her seat, Collins revealed more than she should have about her sneering disdain for those people without institutional power or resumes for her to evaluate. She was open in mocking Jackson’s socioeconomic background, kicking off her campaign against him with a cruel aside about the mother of his children being his second cousin. And at the end, she deployed retired Maine broadcaster Bill Green — long a cozy, moderate presence himself, who in 2020 cut an ad about Collins that many credit with saving her skin — to drop the hammer on Jackson by noting that he’s the kind of guy you’d call if you needed a cord of wood, unqualified for the complex work of senatoring.

Green’s ad may have again sealed the deal in this election, this time in reverse. It exposed the emptiness and elitism of those whose snug, homey moderation was perhaps never about values or belief in anything other than money and power. A view in which simply being “our senator” was argument enough to justify remaining a senator.

On Tuesday, those people — the loggers and the immigrants, the ones whose hospitals are closing, who cannot even imagine the kinds of dollars that have flowed through Collins’s campaigns coffers in her 30 years in office — found in themselves a willingness to do what Collins never could: to change the shape of who has seniority and authority, to sacrifice their senator’s power in order to get their own back.

items.title: Talarico, Ossoff, El-Sayed: Watch Every Big Democratic Victory Speech
items.description: Tuesday’s election results were so stunningly good for Democrats that it’s hard to take it all in. In addition to retaking both the House and the Senate, Democrats scored a slew of once unthinkable wins (most notably, finally and decisively turning Texas blue)
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Tuesday’s election results were so stunningly good for Democrats that it’s hard to take it all in. In addition to retaking both the House and the Senate, Democrats scored a slew of once unthinkable wins (most notably, finally and decisively turning Texas blue). There were also so many firsts that it’s difficult to count.

Since all of this news broke overnight and no networks aired candidates’ victory speeches in full, many are still catching up on all the Democratic joy. Below, we’ve rounded up of all the big speeches so you can get to know America’s new leaders — or just bask in this unfamiliar feeling of victory.
James Talarico: “We just took back Texas … In this state, power belongs to the people.”
Talarico is the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Texas since 1988.
Gina Hinojosa: “We shocked the world.”
Hinojosa will be the first Latina governor of Texas.
Abdul El-Sayed: Parents who’ve struggled to explain Trump’s hate, tell your kids “the bad guys lost.”
Michigan’s El-Sayed is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
Jon Ossoff: Americans “rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence” of Trump.
The Georgia senator was the only Democratic Senate incumbent defending a seat in a state Trump won in 2024.
Keisha Lance Bottoms: “You’ve shown that no amount of money will ever — never, ever, ever — overcome the power of the people.”
Bottoms, who won the Georgia governor’s race, is the first Black woman elected governor of any state.
Annie Andrews: “You have shown … that we will not bow down.”
Andrews defeated Darline Graham, the late senator Lindsey Graham’s sister, flipping a Senate seat Republicans have held since 1998.
Troy Jackson: “Trump and the billionaires need to understand one thing … I don’t owe them a damn thing!”
Jackson defeated Susan Collins, who has represented Maine in the U.S. Senate for nearly 30 years.
Chris Pappas: “I want to thank the guy next to me, my amazing husband.”
New Hampshire’s Pappas is the first openly gay man to win a Senate seat.
Adam Hamilton: “The people in Kansas … are saying what’s happening in Washington is not okay.”
Hamilton is the first Democrat Kansas has elected to the U.S. Senate since 1932.
Amy Acton: “Ohio has chosen unity and decency over division and hate. The healing begins today.”
Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected governor of Ohio.
Sherrod Brown: “We will fight to end these tariffs. We will end this war.”
Brown reclaimed a U.S. Senate seat he held for 18 years before his 2024 defeat. His opponent Jon Husted’s butt was, incredibly, a major theme of Trump’s closing midterms message.
Rob Sand: Democrats, “you’ve had a hard few years here in Iowa. But balanced government has been restored.”
Sand won the Iowa governorship, a position held by Republicans for 16 years.
Josh Turek: “I will fight to end this war in Iran. I will fight to end these chaotic tariffs.”
Turek flipped Iowa’s U.S. Senate seat, giving the state its first Democratic senator in nearly two decades.
Roy Cooper: “We told Washington loud and clear that North Carolinians will always matter more than the billionaires and the insiders.”
The former governor flipped a U.S. Senate seat in North Carolina, which backed Trump in the last three presidential elections.
Peggy Flanagan: “We will rip ICE apart!”
Minnesota’s Flanagan is the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate. She may share the distinction with Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola, whose race has not been called.
Deb Haaland: We “proved that Democrats are entrusted to fight for our home. For New Mexico. Not New America.”
Haaland was elected governor of New Mexico. She will be the nation’s first Native American woman governor.
