In late November, a breakthrough might inspire you to reallocate your time, energy, money, and resources. This is your green light to invest in your creative side hustle or a promising romantic connection.

For you, the whole month is building toward the full moon in your sign on Nov. 24. But first, you should lay the groundwork. In early November, you need to adjust your priorities. Cut out whatever’s been draining your energy, and focus on habits and activities that fill your cup.
An old passion project or romantic connection could find its worth again ahead of Sagittarius season (beginning on Nov. 22). If you feel hopeful, dive in.

Finally, the full moon brings surprising clarity on what needs to change within in order for you to manifest the life you really want. Don’t underestimate what can click into place when you let go. Only worry about what you can control.

Don’t be surprised when the passion, connection, and spark you thought was lost makes a dramatic return. The Scorpio new moon on Nov. 9 creates space for you to get clear on your values, hidden desires, and what will truly make you happy. This kind of self-reflection could be a powerful magnet for love.

However, don’t expect to figure out all the answers at once. Clarity will come gradually and certain outcomes will remain uncertain. On Nov. 24, try not to worry about the missing pieces when the full moon lights up your psychological sector. Choose your next step and see it through.

Unresolved feelings have been churning in the background, creating a moody start to the month. However, when you are committed to building bridges — not burning them — you may finally make progress. Lead with honesty and speak with care.

The second half of the month revives the fire in your social life, but concerns about your budget and schedule could hinder your ability to live in the moment. Don’t be irresponsible, but stay as flexible as possible. Your friendships are worth their weight in gold.

Confusion turns into clarity this month. Mark your calendar for Nov. 13, when Mercury retrograde switches gears, alleviating the pressure you feel to dissect the subliminal meaning of every text or email. In order to get conversations moving again, you don’t necessarily need to find the perfect words for expressing yourself. Start by recognizing that your voice has value, even if others disagree with your perspective.

Around mid-month, your focus shifts toward pursuing your life’s purpose. On Nov. 25, calculating Mars enters your sign, boosting your energy, discipline, and drive. Forge your own way rather than adhering to other people’s standards. Your journey is yours alone.

Venus, your ruling planet, is in retrograde from Oct. 3 - Nov. 14. Your attention has been focused on the hard work of examining who you are, what you want, and whether you’re willing to ask for it. However, don’t expect immediate progress once this phase wraps up. Acknowledge where self-doubt still keeps you stuck.

A deep hunger for meaningful conversation kicks in during the second half of the month. Whether you engage in thoughtful debates, pick up a new book, or listen to a podcast that blows your mind, prepare for your outlook to radically change — or at least you’ll plant new seeds.

November opens with a deep personal reset. The new moon rises in your sign on Nov. 9, setting the stage for new goals, intentions, and ideas around how you want to show up in the world. You can reinvent yourself at any moment, even on a random Wednesday, if you’re tired of holding back.

Your self-awareness sharpens on Nov. 13. Mercury travels forward in your sign, dissolving the intense air of mystery you’ve been projecting that’s kept some people at arm’s length. If you are emerging from an extended period of solitude, be wary of rushing into trust, consistency, and comfort. Nothing worth having is built overnight. People will treat you more warmly if you act with confidence and generosity.
Sagittarius (Nov. 21-Dec. 20)
You’ve been bravely confronting your fears for months, and you’ve finally earned a break. Relax and release the negativity!

The real shift comes on Nov. 22, when the sun reinvigorates your sign. Suddenly, you’re back to your best self. You don’t need to force optimism, and adventures seem to be looking for you, not the other way around. Pursue what makes you feel alive. That said, your partner may ask where they fit into your solo exploration.
If relationships don’t steal your focus at the end of the month, your career might take to the spotlight. Move with a plan.
Capricorn (Dec. 21-Jan. 18)

Any uncertainty surrounding your career or public image will resolve in the first two weeks of the month. A relationship with a boss or mentor may move in a positive new direction, or you might find yourself getting involved with a community that shares your values. Either way, welcome the support!

As a hard-working Capricorn, you struggle to accept that rest can be productive. Everyone needs to recharge, and when Sagittarius season begins on Nov. 22, it’s your turn. Use introspection as a healing practice. As a result of your quiet time, you may be inspired to make a change in your lifestyle. Once your energy returns, set things into motion as soon as possible.
Aquarius (Jan. 19-Feb. 17)

It’s difficult to plan your life when you are questioning the very principles that have long underpinned your definition of success. Give yourself grace for the slow progress made this autumn. You may be stumbling toward something more valuable than you realize: a renewed sense of passion and purpose. Once Mercury and Venus station direct on Nov. 13 and 14, follow your heart with unwavering loyalty. Share your inspiration and the ideas that have motivated you with your friends or followers.

If you’re single or casually dating, a sudden peak in your love life could coincide with the flirtatious Gemini full moon on Nov. 24. Just keep in mind that you are in an important season of building. Enjoy what feels light and playful, but be cautious of entering a serious commitment until you are more certain of what you are able to invest.

If a new course of study or philosophical idea calls your name, go all in. You may discover a belief or intellectual field that resonates with where you are now rather than who you used to be. Before you hand over your credit card, however, wait for the hazy retrograde energy to settle around Nov. 14.

If you are itching for a bigger life during the second half of the month, the right move is to follow your feelings rather than your fears. Be discerning about who you team up with this month. Make sure they share your enthusiasm and seriousness about building in a new direction.
For more, check out your tarot reading.

items.title: Exclusive: Lisa Rinna's No. 1 Holiday Party Survival Tip: "I Don't Say Goodbye"
items.description: Lisa Rinna’s Unapologetic Guide To Surviving Holiday Party Season
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Lisa Rinna’s Unapologetic Guide To Surviving Holiday Party Season
The Bravo legend is serving up her best winter style tips — with a side of exit strategy.
This holiday season, Lisa Rinna is trading Beverly Hills for Manhattan. And she’s *very* excited. “It’s going to be our first Christmas in New York,” she gushes over Zoom.

With a new ZIP code comes a whole new set of holiday plans, which so far include watching the Thanksgiving Day parade from her apartment and leaning into her signature main-character dressing — but for the winter chill. “You feel more elevated here for Christmas than you do on the West Coast. We have 80-degree Christmases in L.A.,” says the Real Housewives of Beverly Hills alum, who’s tapped to star in the upcoming Off-Broadway revival of Neil Simon’s Rumors from Jan. 9 through Feb. 28. “New York just makes you want to up the ante.”

Rinna is already ahead of schedule. In her new campaign for Express, “Holiday, Hamlin Style,” launching today, she test-drives festive classics like high-shine sequins, glamorous Santa-red gowns, and cozy knits. The shoot was a full family affair, featuring her husband, Harry Hamlin; daughter Delilah Belle Hamlin; and Delilah’s boyfriend, Mick Maio. “To get to work with your family, pinch me,” she says of the shoot. She’s especially thrilled about sharing the lens with her partner: “A couple of weeks ago, I was like, ‘We need to make Harry into a supermodel now.’ Everybody else is. I literally put that out in the universe.”

Naturally, working alongside her loved ones sparked a little holiday nostalgia. The project took her back to her own traditions, particularly matching with her family in Christmas sweaters. (As true Bravo fans know, Rinna loves a matching moment — whether they’re in red flannel pajamas or Santa hats.) It even inspired a possible outfit idea for this year.

Ahead, the reality-TV icon shares her one foolproof holiday ’fit, her secret to tricking everyone into matching, and how to navigate awkward party small talk (and when to deploy the perfect Irish exit).
How To Feel Festive In 2 Seconds

Holiday dressing practically comes with its own maximalist dress code — think sequins; velvets; bows; and enough reds, greens, and metallic golds to make you look like you’re twinning with the tree. But according to Rinna, getting into the holiday spirit doesn’t require a head-to-toe disco ball look. All it takes is a cozy knit to pull off an instant seasonal vibe shift.

“When I was with Delilah, we were wearing the sweaters — laughing and dancing around,” she says of her favorite piece from the campaign. “You put on a Christmas sweater — a cute one — and it makes you feel like Christmas.”
How To Get Your Entire Crew To Match

With a household full of working models — daughters Amelia and Delilah, plus husband Harry — getting everyone to agree on a single style aesthetic can be a challenge. But individual tastes go out the window in December.

“Because [the girls are] three years apart, I never matched them except for Christmas,” says Rinna, adding, “As long as it’s not really a really, really bad Christmas sweater — which is a funny idea actually now that I think about it — they’ll pretty much wear whatever I bring to the table.”
How To Guarantee A Major Style Moment

Finding a bold way to make a statement in the winter is easy. But if she had to pick her go-to festive uniform, it would be a sharp pantsuit. “I love a red suit, a green suit, a holiday-inspired gold suit,” she says. Her only rule? Make sure it fits right. “If it’s tailored properly, everybody looks great in it,” she promises.

On the flip side, there is one style choice she’d encourage everyone to ditch this season. “Unless it’s soft and cozy, anything that’s an uncomfortable fabric, we can retire it,” she says. Consider this your permission to permanently shelf any scratchy sequins or stiff velvets.
How To Trust Your Own Fashion Instincts

While Rinna is a legendary tastemaker, she’s no longer the only fashionista in the family. To say her daughters have an impact on her wardrobe would be an understatement. “A thousand bajillion percent,” she says of how much they inspire her.

Because her daughters have completely different styles — Delilah loves vintage, shopping for bold patterns and jewelry at flea markets; Amelia prefers classic, opting for more tomboyish choices and very few prints and accessories — Rinna has plenty of fresh mood board ideas to draw from.

But there’s a difference between borrowing ideas from her kids and asking them for validation. When it’s time to actually pull together a look, she shuts out the noise and trusts her own gut (and her stylist’s expertise). “I don’t ever show anybody [my outfits],” Rinna says. “I don’t think you need anybody’s opinion.”
How To Master The Party Exit Strategy

Between the endless small talk and the risk of bumping into a frenemy, holiday parties can be a lot. Luckily, Rinna has a straightforward approach to getting through them. Her first rule is basic: Know when to leave. And when you’re ready, you just... go. “I don’t say goodbye,” she says. “I just slip out.”
How To Survive The Social Drama

And if you bump into someone wearing the exact same ’fit? Embrace it. “I like to accidentally match with somebody else. I think that’s fun,” she says. What she won’t do, though, is suffer through an uncomfortable conversation just for the sake of being polite. She’d rather skip out on an event entirely than sit there faking niceties.
She also has one major rule passed down to her daughters: Keep it cute. “Don’t drink too much. Ever,” she explains. “Don’t get sloppy. Don’t get messy.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: How To Shop Sephora's Holiday Savings Event Like A Beauty Editor
items.description: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: All linked products are independently selected by our editors. If you purchase any of these products, we may earn a commission.

The holidays have arrived early at Sephora, and by that, we mean the retailer’s highly anticipated savings event is back for 2026. Whether you’re eyeing a bevy of sparkly gift sets or looking to replenish your favorite luxe serum, Sephora’s Holiday Savings Event is the perfect opportunity to do just that.

If you’ve shopped Sephora’s sales before, you probably know the drill: Depending on your Beauty Insider membership tier — Insider, VIB, or Rouge, determined by how much you spend annually — you can score 10%, 15%, or 20% off, respectively. The sale is now open to all Beauty Insider tiers, and new this year, Rouge members can share the love (aka the sale's top discount) with up to five friends, each of whom will receive a one-time-use coupon for 20% off. The event wraps up for everyone on November 9, and to redeem your discount, simply enter promo code ALLONSALE at checkout; your savings will automatically reflect your membership tier. (One more perk worth knowing: All Beauty Insider members get 30% off Sephora Collection products from October 30 through November 9, no code required.)

As with previous years, there are a few exclusions and limits to keep in mind as you plan your Sephora haul. Shoppers are limited to two Dyson items (choose wisely), three Shark Beauty items, and three The Ordinary products.
Now that you know the rules of the road, onto the fun part: Keep scrolling for the most worthwhile items to add to your cart during the sale.

Rhode entered Sephora doors only last year, and you know what that means: All your dewy skincare essentials are available to shop during the Holiday Savings Event. If you can only choose one product, make it the Glazing Milk essence, which is perfect for adding a light veil of hydration as the weather cools down.

This blockbuster advent calendar by Sephora Collection is 30% off during the entire duration of the Holiday Savings Event, bringing the price tag down to just $42. With a value of $190 in products, this is a serious steal that we predict won't stay in stock for long.

We previously reviewed Shark’s FlexFusion styler, and it surpassed our expectations with flying colors. This year, we're eyeing the Glam —Shark's newest hair innovation, which includes curling barrels, a smoothing brush, finishing tool, straightener, and a concentrator nozzle to achieve a variety of looks in a limited edition steel blue colorway.

If we had a beauty crystal ball, we would forecast that this Danessa palette will be quite the hot commodity for holiday makeup looks this season. Create endless dazzling looks using the entire assortment, or pop out each six-pan palette, remove the magnetic logo mirror in the center, and take it on the go. (Genius!)

If you love niche, luxury fragrance, here's a name you've probably never heard of — for now. From the brains of Melanie Bender (whose resume includes executive roles at Rhode, Versed, and Merit) and Joe Cloyes and Greg Gonzalez (founders of Youth To The People) comes Lore. The collection of five hyper-sensorial, unique fragrances ranges from fruity with a hint of smoky mezcal (Disfruta) to Lovely And A Little Twisted, a milky rose that's utterly addictive. Best of all: They all clock in at $92 for a full-size bottle — easily half of comparable designer brands — and that's before your sale discount.

Summer Fridays' hydrating, nonslip hydrogel eye patches are soaked in skin-loving ingredients to soothe and depuff tired eyes, making them a great option to stock up on ahead of the holiday travel season.

There’s stiff competition in the world of tinted lip butters, balms, and treatments, but EADEM has carved out a niche as the ultimate IYKYK status lippie. This cozy set comes with five full-size balms in the brand’s most beloved flavors, working out to just $17.60 each — a steal for a formula that feels a little more special than your everyday lip balm. Consider it the perfect gift to split with your besties (or, you know, keep all to yourself). Shopping on a tighter budget? There’s also a trio of Le Chouchou minis for $39.

Patrick Starrr’s ONE/SIZE setting spray is goated for a reason: It locks makeup in place for hours on end while delivering a soft-matte finish that can withstand even the longest holiday parties. This holiday duo costs the same as the full-size spray alone, so you’re essentially getting the mini for free. Consider it a no-brainer for makeup maximalists and anyone whose glam needs to stay put from morning to midnight.

This time two years ago, celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips' brand, m.ph, was still waiting in the wings. This year, however, is a different story. The versatile complexion palette is already a Sephora bestseller, and thanks to a recent restock (and long-awaited shade expansion, you can snag yours at a discount during the sale.

items.title: Civic life | Psyche
items.description: That feeling of values crumbling has a name: civic grief
paragraphs: That feeling of values crumbling has a name: civic grief
Fairness, dignity and shared obligation are precious. Grieving their loss is a first step toward doing something about it
A deep sense of ease – what the Danes call ‘tryg’ – is a collective responsibility that allows individuals to flourish
The people most drawn to ideological thinking and authoritarianism aren’t aware of what makes them so susceptible
Historically, trust in institutions freed us to do extraordinary things. They can be flawed, but we lose them at our peril
At a time of rising intolerance, the century-old work of C E M Joad reminds us what tolerance really is and why we need it
Some people watch history pass by. Others high in ‘historical consciousness’ truly live it – and seem to benefit as a result
Social media utterances aren’t enough. Burke’s stand against colonial injustice shows we must confront our own complicity
When political regimes fail us, don’t turn to optimism. It’s disappointment that holds the radical potential for change
Many dismiss utopian ideas. But imagining a better world is a vital political skill for tackling today’s challenges
To protect our descendants from catastrophe, we must overcome the emotional hurdles that make it easy for us to look away
The science of protest reveals successful tactics and common weak points. Those who want change should take it onboard

items.title: How psychology’s classic studies misled us about the self | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk
items.author: Jack W Klein; William B Swann
paragraphs: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk responses to their immediate environment. Lacking an enduring web of preferences, attitudes and proclivities, the contents of the H vacuus character would be filled by whatever situation they find themselves in. As a result, their behaviour would vary dramatically as they moved from one situation to the next.

Scrutiny of H vacuus would reveal a host of curious behaviours. Their attitudes towards others would be shaped by random factors that unconsciously influence their thoughts. They might feel ‘warmer’ toward others when they handle a hot cappuccino, and ‘colder’ when clasping an iced latte. Their political decisions would hinge on seemingly innocuous details. For instance, turnout in their elections would surge if they were affirmed as being ‘voters’, rather than merely people who vote. And on morality, their views on topics from abortion to pornography could depend on something as mundane as whether they had washed their hands, making them feel ‘cleansed’ and in the mood for judging others.

Given the inherent fluidity of H vacuus, trying to predict their behaviour beyond the present moment would be pure folly. H vacuus would be so mercurial that when they wed, they would effectively be marrying a stranger. In the end, being the pawns of powerful environmental forces would compromise their ability to effectively plan and adapt. Others would recognise the impossibility of holding them responsible for their actions, as they could refuse to accept responsibility for their behaviour by claiming: ‘I was just responding to the situation!’ At the end of the day, religious, ethical and judicial systems would be largely irrelevant.

In light of the many challenges facing H vacuus, it may be surprising to learn that this fictitious creature is based on an implicit assumption about human nature suggested by the work of numerous influential behavioural scientists. This assumption is that if you were to peer into the contents of people’s selves, you would discover little that isn’t susceptible to the random influences of the situation. Indeed, the peculiarities of H vacuus life described above – including the ideas about ‘warm’ attitudes, election turnout and moral cleansing – are based on claims that have been made about real humans.

We label this view of human psychology the empty-self metaphor. Although it has fostered an erroneous understanding of human nature, the empty-self metaphor has inspired a large following. These followers embrace an optimistic view in which human foibles can be readily vanquished through systematic manipulation of the social environment. However alluring it may be, we suggest that it is time to replace this Panglossian view with one that acknowledges the importance of enduring psychological structures.

The empty-self view has a long history in psychology, arguably tracing its origins to the behaviourist movement at the beginning of the 20th century. The behaviourists were almost entirely focused on ‘the situation’, eschewing speculation about what they considered the ‘black box’ of the mind. This emphasis on the situation was influential with founding social psychologists, who defined social psychology as the study of how individual thoughts, feelings and behaviours ‘are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of other human beings’.

An emphasis on the power of the situation, and its propensity to overwhelm or displace personal agency, has dominated social psychology ever since. Examples abound. In the 1970s, the author of self-perception theory argued that, rather than beliefs guiding behaviour (as common sense might imply), situations cause behaviour, and people generally infer their own beliefs by taking note of how they behave. Others made the corollary argument that personalities effectively do not exist. In fact, the term ‘fundamental attribution error’ was coined to describe an allegedly flawed tendency to attribute someone’s behaviour to their personality. Elsewhere, including in sociology, impression management research and the dramaturgical movement suggested that all the world’s a stage, with people portraying whatever character best suits a given scene. This focus on the situation reached a fever pitch with the ‘situationists’, who explicitly placed the influence of the situation on human behaviour far above any possible internal motivations.

Although situationism has lost some of its lustre, the empty-self metaphor has remained at least implicitly popular within certain circles. This is particularly true in the field of social priming, which deals with the impact of seemingly inconsequential environmental cues on human behaviour. In examples of this kind of research, seeing words related to old age seemed to make university students walk more slowly, and plotting dots on paper further apart appeared to make people feel more distant from their family.
Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has lost force

In recent years, however, the evidential tide has turned against the empty self. Social priming and other areas of social psychology have struggled in the wake of the ‘replication crisis’ – the unfortunate realisation that a surprising number of psychological findings could not be independently replicated. Many such findings are likely to have been false positives, stemming from tendentious statistical decision-making and other questionable research practices. The authors of one report found that when a number of social priming studies were carried out again, only 17 per cent of the findings were successfully replicated. A much smaller proportion of empty-self-style research has been dismissed as simply fraudulent – such as the celebrated finding that people are more honest when filling out forms if they sign at the beginning, rather than at the end.

In our own research, we’ve compared studies that were or were not premised on the empty-self assumption that behaviour is unexpectedly shaped by subtle, seemingly irrelevant environmental factors, as opposed to pre-existing beliefs and dispositions. We found that studies reflecting an empty-self view were far less likely to hold up.

Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has also lost force. Take, for instance, Stanley Milgram’s obedience studies, in which participants were asked to administer electric shocks to someone until the victim seemed to be unconscious or dead. These classic studies have been taken as evidence that authority can override individual will. However, subsequent research has found that personal traits associated with diligence and helpfulness predicted an increased willingness to administer the electric shocks. This reframes the experiment as demonstrating not mindless obedience, but often wilful collaboration – participants who gave the shocks were ostensibly helping an experimenter in the service of ‘science’.

Consider also the Stanford prison experiment, led by Philip Zimbardo, where students acting as guards in a fake prison (with others acting as prisoners) appeared to succumb to their temporary role, becoming belligerent. Attributing this behaviour to the roles the students were assigned is jeopardised by several design flaws, including a selection bias that likely caused dispositionally authoritarian individuals to be overrepresented in the study. The upshot is that participants’ unique, personal identities seem to have mattered far more than the authors of these classic examples of situational influence would have us believe.

The idea that the human mind is so fickle should have attracted more scepticism than it has often received. First and foremost, it is at odds with other evidence. The entire field of personality psychology – which investigates the unique qualities of people that persist across situations – informs us that the self is not empty at all. Measures of personality such as the Big Five traits (openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism) are remarkably stable and predictive of behaviour and long-term life outcomes. In fact, research suggests that the average effects of personality and situations on behaviour are similar in magnitude. Elsewhere, there is ample evidence for an enduring self: for example, self-esteem is largely steady over the lifespan, and attempts to break habits frequently fail, highlighting that personal tendencies impede many people’s efforts at self-change.

It is not difficult, though, to understand the appeal of the empty-self metaphor. The idea that our thoughts and behaviours are dictated by banal aspects of daily life, such as the temperature of our coffee, offers a tantalising glimpse at ‘hidden’ causes of behaviour. This is probably why social priming occupied a full chapter of Daniel Kahneman’s bestselling book Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), why mentalists like Derren Brown attract large TV audiences by showing how the ‘power of psychology’ can be used to control and befuddle, and why exciting ‘counterintuitive’ findings are published in top journals.

The empty-self metaphor also lends itself to an admittedly admirable progressive agenda (popular among social psychologists) that is focused on addressing inequality in the social environment and avoiding victim-blaming. If the plight of the have-nots is primarily attributable to the harsh social conditions that society unwittingly thrusts upon them, then the obvious solution is to change those social conditions. Ultimately, the empty-self metaphor teases the provocative possibility that society could be righted if only we determine how to control the social environment. But reality is much messier.
There is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us

The good news is that psychology appears to be slowly moving toward increased acceptance of what’s called ‘interactionism’: the view that the person and the situation interactively dictate behaviour. Many people have heard of nudging, in which subtle changes to the presentation of choices can systematically influence behaviour (eg, placing fruits and vegetables more conspicuously, to increase healthy consumption). The idea of nudging has proven enormously popular, with multiple governments around the world setting up ‘nudge units’, but initial results were lacklustre. Happily, research has moved to second-generation, interactionist nudges that tailor the intervention to the beliefs and preferences of the individual. For example, recent research suggests that personalised nudges to make healthier food purchases might be more effective than generic ones.

Interactionism likewise paves a more realistic path forward for social change. Rather than assuming that one size fits all, an interactionist approach acknowledges that individual differences inform the way people respond to social situations. Any social movement to reduce harmful behaviour or improve wellbeing needs to meet people where they are at. That means acknowledging that different individuals will respond to the same policies and political messages differently, and in accordance with their own perspectives.

Rebuking the empty-self view recognises that, far from being the dithering shells that psychology studies have often suggested we are, most of us are loyal to a reasonably clear and coherent self-concept. We do not ‘marry strangers’, nor do our relationships hinge on irrelevant details of the moment. On the contrary, there is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us. Although imputing this degree of agency and stability to the self may lack the intoxicating simplicity of Homo vacuus, we are confident that it will pave the way to a deeper understanding of Homo sapiens.

items.title: The self-making world of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck | Aeon Essays
items.description: The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was 65 when his great treatise on the transformation of life was published. With Philosophie zoologique (1809), translated a century later as Zoological Philosophy, Lamarck intended to establish an entirely new scien
items.author: Jessica Riskin
paragraphs: The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was 65 when his great treatise on the transformation of life was published. With Philosophie zoologique (1809), translated a century later as Zoological Philosophy, Lamarck intended to establish an entirely new science, one built on the idea that all living beings are constantly transforming themselves, from the tiniest microbes to the most complex mammals, gaining new forms and new abilities. It wasn’t the bodily structures of organisms that determined their ways of life, Lamarck said, but just the opposite: their ways of life in response to their circumstances gave rise to their changing bodily forms. ‘Can there be any consideration in natural history more important,’ he demanded, ‘or deserving of greater attention, than the one I have just set forth?’ (My translation.)

But if you’ve heard anything at all about Lamarck, it’s probably how wrong he was about one animal in particular, the giraffe, and how this giraffe fiasco epitomises his wrongness about everything. Lamarck suggested that, by stretching to reach leaves in high tree branches, giraffes slightly elongated their necks, creating tiny changes that were then handed down to their offspring, accumulating over many generations to produce the long necks we see today. Around the turn of the 20th century, Lamarck’s giraffe idea became a laughing stock when biologists roundly rejected the notion that bodily changes undergone in the course of an individual lifetime could be inherited in the next generation.

It wasn’t only his ideas about long-necked mammals that came under attack. Lamarck’s interest in giraffes was just a passing mention in the midst of his voluminous writings, which set out a revolutionary, field-founding theory: organisms, he claimed, transform themselves and, in doing so, they remake the world. That idea has drawn scorn for more than two centuries.

Though Lamarck is often overlooked, his science was foundational to modern biology and informed the theory of evolution that Charles Darwin later developed. Darwin followed Lamarck in believing in the agency of living beings to transform themselves and their environment. But most people don’t know about Lamarck’s influence on Darwin because, around the turn of the 20th century, Darwin’s followers expurgated every trace of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist version of evolution, rendering living beings the objects of random variation and outside forces. For the neo-Darwinists, living things played no direct role in the evolutionary process. Evolution happened through random genetic variation and external environmental pressures. For Darwin’s followers, organisms were just as passive as they had been for the creationists, who saw them as products of divine will.

Throughout the history of modern biology, most powerful figures in science and politics have ridiculed and repressed Lamarck’s radical idea that organisms have agency in the evolutionary process. In mainstream biology today, a neo-Darwinian view of living things as passive still largely dominates, though research in several areas has been challenging its reign.

This is the story of how Lamarck’s radical idea was cast aside by mainstream science, and why it was overlooked for so long. It is also the story of a surprising reversal: in recent decades, some biologists have begun turning back toward Lamarck’s view of life.

While many people think of giraffes when they hear Lamarck’s name, few know that he coined the word ‘biology’, in 1802. He needed a name to designate a new science he thought should exist: a science of all living beings, and only living beings. At the time, there was no such field. There were broader sciences, such as natural history, which included inanimate things like rocks, rivers and mountains; and there were narrower sciences, such as botany or zoology, which covered subsets of the living world. But Lamarck thought there should be a science of life. At the heart of his new science, he developed the first theory of what we now call ‘evolution’, although he didn’t call it that. He simply referred to ‘change’.

Lamarck lived and worked in the Jardin des plantes (Garden of Plants) in Paris from 1788 until his death, aged 85, in 1829. His life was tumultuous, to say the least. He lived through the French Revolution, then under Napoleon, then during the Bourbon Restoration. He survived the Reign of Terror, as well as the withering disdain of Napoleon and his circle of scientific advisors, and the return of the monarchy; he also outlived three wives and four of his eight children. In the last decade of his life, he was blind and frail but carried on working with the help of his daughter Rosalie. At the end of his long career, he had identified and named more than 6,000 species, and for more than two decades had taught a legendary course in the Garden of Plants, drawing students from all over the world. The course grew so famous that even fictional characters attended it, such as the lovelorn young Amaury, hero of Sainte-Beuve’s autobiographical novel Volupté: The Sensual Man (1834).

By daring to usurp God’s monopoly on Creation and reassign it to mortal beings, Lamarck provoked the ire of the mighty and powerful. He wrote that life originated in spontaneous generation, brought about by natural forces such as electricity and heat acting upon inanimate matter. This led to the emergence of the simplest organisms: single-celled protozoa and algae. From that point, a property intrinsic to living matter exerted itself, a tendency to complexify, which Lamarck named ‘the power of life’. As organisms grew more complex, another cause of transformation came into play: their responsiveness to the environment. In the simplest beings, this responsiveness was rudimentary – an irritability or sensitivity, and reflexive reaction. But in birds and mammals, Lamarck argued, it rose to the level of ‘acts of will’, through which creatures could form ‘habits’ and ‘ways of life’ in response to their circumstances. By means of these behaviours, they directed their inner fluids toward the limbs and organs they used most. (Darwin would later propose a similar idea. In 1868, he suggested that parts of the body threw off particles of inheritance, called ‘gemmules’, which were modified by an animal’s behaviours and could carry the modifications into its offspring.)
He imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life

Not only did living beings create and transform themselves, according to Lamarck’s picture of things, they also made and re-made the inanimate world. Plants played the primary role in this process, he thought, because they could invent themselves out of just sunlight, air and water. He described experiments to confirm this miraculous capacity. For instance, carve a hollow into the side of a turnip and suspend the vegetable in a window by its root, Houdini-style: nothing up its sleeves! Keep the hollow filled with water, and you’ll see that the turnip will grow a whole flowering plant. It has created itself literally from thin air. Plants, by bringing together the primitive elements into combinations, originated the cosmic relay chain, then handed off their work to animals. By eating, digesting and engaging in their other functions and behaviours, animals produced more elaborate compounds, and so they shared with plants the defining ability of all living beings to build, compose and create.

Having begun his career in botany, in 1793 Lamarck was obliged to move, reluctantly, into zoology. This was in the midst of the Revolution, during the transitional moment when the main botanical garden in Paris – the King’s Garden – became the republican Garden of Plants under the auspices of a new National Museum of Natural History. The committee in charge of this transformation did not assign Lamarck to a chair in botany as he wanted, but instead to the lowliest chair in zoology: the Professorship of Insects and Worms. He would later tell his students that he’d been, at first, disappointed: if he couldn’t carry on studying botany, then why not charismatic megafauna, like lions? But then he’d had two hopeful thoughts. First, his assigned creatures constituted nine-tenths of the animal world, so he hadn’t been relegated to an unimportant corner of zoology. And, second, he imagined the simplest animals might reveal to him the foundation of animal life. Contemplating his insects and his worms with this faint gleam of hope, he created a new taxonomic category, ‘invertebrates’, and set to work studying them.

The invertebrates, he told his students in 1800, ‘conduct us insensibly toward the inconceivable limit of animalisation’, toward those beings ‘barely endowed with animality’ with whom ‘nature perhaps began’. For Lamarck, this essence of animal life was the power of generation and regeneration: the ability to produce living matter, including new bodily tissues and new organisms. The simplest animals had the most widespread generative faculties. For instance, the Genevan naturalist Abraham Trembley had shown that, if you cut up polyps (freshwater hydras) into lots of pieces, they regenerate an entire animal from each part. Other invertebrates, too, had incredible powers of generation. Insects could metamorphose. Crustaceans could grow new legs. Sea stars, new rays. Snails, a new head. The invertebrates far outnumber the vertebrates, Lamarck explained, thanks to this generative ability. Their number is unknowably vast because of the ‘infinite smallness’ of the smallest among them. These animals display a ‘frightening fecundity’, he wrote; it seems that ‘matter animalises itself from every direction.’ Lamarck marvelled at the tiny coral polyps that were identified as the chief producers of the great calcareous mountain chains and enormous banks of chalk found all over Earth. These minuscule animals create islands, fill bays and gulfs, clog ports and ‘completely transform the coastlines’.

The invertebrates became the basis of Lamarck’s idea that living organisms held a monopoly on creative agency. Religious faith, Lamarck acknowledged, could be a consolation for a ‘good man who persuades himself of it’ but was ‘absolutely foreign’ to his own study of living nature. Souls were not physically knowable, whereas the dynamic, creative action of living beings was everywhere apparent. Life, to Lamarck, now became the manifest capacity to create in the face of all nature’s forces of destruction.

The incessant creative activity of each organism was far from solitary. Living beings collaborated as they worked to form the world and fend off destruction, and Lamarck took a great interest in this collaborative action. For instance, one spring day in 1798, having brought his family to a country house he briefly owned outside Paris, he noticed a swallow’s nest in one of the windows. Shortly afterwards, a local child destroyed the nest, leaving the pair of swallows homeless just as the female was about to lay her eggs. Immediately, 10 or 12 other swallows gathered around the wreckage. The birds were so agitated and noisy that at first Lamarck assumed they were quarrelling, but he soon realised it was just the opposite. They had organised themselves to rebuild the nest collaboratively. He watched in amazement as some remained by the construction site while others came and went with twigs. Swallows generally take eight to 12 days to build their nest, Lamarck observed, but these worked so diligently that they finished it the following morning.
The seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. They hadn’t become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey

As evidence of animals’ power of creation and self-transformation, Lamarck cited many examples in which the increased use of a body part had apparently developed and shaped it: the webbed feet of water birds from pushing against the water; the hooked talons of eagles from clasping branches; shorebirds’ long, skinny legs and necks. Lamarck reckoned that shorebirds dislike the water yet have to wade out to catch their prey. Sinking into the mud, they stretch their legs in distaste, straining to keep their body above water, and craning their necks. This behaviour over many generations resulted in stilt-like legs and snaky necks.

When a seal arrived in the menagerie of the natural history museum in June 1809, Lamarck watched the animal with fascination. Its obvious kinship with land mammals confirmed his idea that all mammals, and indeed all life, had originated in the water. He noticed that the seal used its hind limbs as a paddle when swimming. Yet the legs hadn’t fully joined together to become a fin because the seal also used them for seizing prey. The distinctive combination of uses for the hind limbs had produced a structure that could work either like a paddle or like a hand.

Lamarck had set Aristotle’s ancient Scale of Nature not just in motion but in a great commotion. For two millennia, since the time of Aristotle, natural philosophers had imagined every being ranked from simplest to most complex in a fixed, unchanging order. Each form of life had its appointed place in the hierarchy. But now Lamarck announced that, rather than being arrayed along the Scale of Nature, living beings were themselves ever making and remaking the order of life by their own incessant activity, and in many directions at once.

Lamarck’s idea of self-making and world-making organisms gained him powerful enemies. His nemesis was the palaeontologist Georges Cuvier, a favourite of Napoleon. Cuvier was a devout Lutheran who categorically rejected the idea that living forms changed over time and instead upheld the fixity of species. His central anatomical principle, the principle of correlation of parts, was an assertion of rational design: he claimed that one could infer all the parts of a creature from any single part because they all implied one another by rational necessity. Cuvier also insisted that animals’ habits and behaviours followed from their structures – they behaved as they were designed to behave – whereas Lamarck said it was just the opposite: animal structures resulted from their habits and behaviours. This same commitment to fixity shaped how Cuvier read the fossil record.

Cuvier believed in extinctions and was a leading figure in establishing their reality. But he assumed that creatures went extinct because catastrophes, like floods and fires, eliminated them, and then those creatures were replaced by newly created ones. This idea supported the doctrine of special creation: that God had created each species for its place in nature. Cuvier’s science was perfectly suited to Napoleon’s purposes. It was a scientific doctrine of revolutionary change that was also profoundly conservative, each revolution imposed from the outside, each a return to the same ultimate authority, and the whole thing guaranteed by Napoleon’s own scientific experts rather than the Church. Cuvier’s science was cutting-edge, but at the same time, it bolstered an authoritarian order. It was emphatically not the science of the materialist, atheist revolutionaries; but nor was it the older science of the Catholic Church. Cuvier translated the authority of religion into science – a powerful modern concoction.
Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world

It’s no surprise, then, that Napoleon loathed Lamarck, who challenged Cuvier’s model of science. This hatred was dramatically apparent on a freezing day in November 1809 when the members of the National Institute stood shivering as they awaited the emperor in a salon of the Tuileries Palace to present their new works. We have the story from the astronomer François Arago, who was present as a new member of the Institute at the age of 23. Standing near young Arago was Lamarck, 65 and frail, holding a copy of his Philosophie zoologique. Napoleon at last entered the room and marched up to Arago as he would to a new conscript, fixing him with a stare and barking: ‘You’re very young! What’s your name?’ Before Arago could answer, his neighbour on the right, eager to be noticed, replied: ‘His name is Arago!’ Napoleon: ‘What science do you cultivate?’ Arago’s left-hand neighbour piped up with: ‘He cultivates astronomy!’ While Arago ruefully reflected that Napoleon must take him for a mute or an imbecile, the emperor turned to Lamarck, who presented his magnum opus. Growling that he was accepting it only ‘out of consideration for your white hair’, Napoleon snatched the book and, without looking at it, thrust it into the hands of an aide, while Lamarck, with tears of humiliation rolling down his cheeks, tried to explain what was in it.
Had Napoleon known what was in the book, he would certainly have liked it even less. Rather than consolidating power, Lamarck’s theory distributed it throughout the living world.

After Lamarck died, Cuvier emerged as the victor who wrote the history, quite literally. While director of the National Institute, he wrote Lamarck’s official ‘eulogy’, which is surely the nastiest eulogy ever written, dismissing Lamarck’s theory as poetry rather than science. This set the tone for assessments of Lamarck’s ideas for a long time to come.

Following Cuvier, many others ridiculed Lamarck’s science. Because it emerged in the midst of the French Revolution and replaced God with the creative agency of living organisms, it smelled to contemporaries of atheism, revolution and regicide. These ill odours promised trouble not only for Lamarck and Lamarckism but for evolutionary theory more generally.

Darwin struggled over his relations with Lamarck. He drew, importantly, on Lamarck’s theory in formulating his own, but he also insisted on the distinctness of the two. As he wrote to his geologist friend Charles Lyell in 1863, he knew that an association with Lamarckism would be ‘very injurious’ to his theory’s reputation. Still, Darwin did retain various forms of agency within the evolving organism, including Lamarck’s principle that animal behaviours produced heritable effects on their bodies, which Darwin called ‘the inherited effects of use and disuse’. Natural selection, he believed, worked in conjunction with these other factors. But after Darwin died, his followers around the turn of the 20th century eliminated all traces of Lamarckism from their neo-Darwinist theory, rendering organisms as passive as they had been at the hands of Cuvier’s divine creator. The eradication of Lamarckism became the defining feature of neo-Darwinism.

A founding figure in this movement was the German biologist August Weismann. In the 1880s, he began to draw a sharp distinction between somatic (body) cells and germ (reproductive) cells. He said that no changes taking place in the somatic cells could ever be transmitted to the germ cells. This is the so-called Weismann barrier, eliminating the possibility of ‘inheritance of acquired characters’. In a rather cruel series of experiments, Weismann chopped the tails off several generations of mice in order to show that their offspring had perfectly healthy tails. He himself acknowledged that this result had no real bearing on Lamarck’s theory: neither Lamarck nor Darwin had ever claimed that amputations were inherited, only internally generated changes. But Weismann reckoned it would defeat popular belief in the inheritance of acquired characteristics. The mouse-tail experiments remain rhetorically powerful, and still appear in biology textbooks today.

Weismann emphasised that his approach to science rested on the assumption of a divine presence behind the whole process. He assured his readers that his biology didn’t just leave room for a ‘Universal Cause’ but actually demanded one. He wrote of a ‘Final Cause’ operating ‘behind’ the mechanism of the universe. All agency lay with this remote, divine presence and none with the evolving, mortal beings themselves. Therefore, Weismann said his science was ‘absolutely opposed’ to materialism.
There’s a eugenic logic in the idea that living beings are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces

The ‘Weismann barrier’ – the exclusion of Lamarckian inheritance – became the central principle of neo-Darwinism. After the identification of the structure of the DNA molecule in 1953, Francis Crick restated the Weismann barrier as the ‘central dogma of molecular biology’: DNA transcription runs only in one direction, from DNA through RNA to protein, never in the reverse, from which Crick drew the implication that acquired characteristics could never be inherited. Nothing a living being did could make a difference to the machinery of inheritance.

Denying the agency of organisms has not been a purely intellectual mistake. It has had implications reaching far beyond the debates of scientists. For one thing, there’s a eugenic logic built into the idea that living beings, including humans, are the passive objects of genetic programming and outside forces. Essentially all the neo-Darwinists of the early through middle decades of the 20th century were fervent eugenicists. Crick is an example. ‘Let us take up this whole question of eugenics,’ he exhorted his colleagues at a London conference in 1963. ‘I do not see why people should have the right to have children,’ he observed. He mused that it would be a fairly simple matter for a government to sterilise the whole population by putting some chemical in the food supply and then reverse the effect only for those people ‘licensed to bear children’. These were not fringe views; eugenic theories and programmes were mainstream in neo-Darwinist biology for much of the 20th century, and some still linger today.

Additionally, the idea of the fundamental passivity of organisms has helped inform two centuries of environmental destruction, as it has encouraged people to regard the living world as raw material to manipulate and exploit for economic and imperial gain. Lamarck, who witnessed the Industrial Revolution firsthand, warned of this in his last work. He pointed out deforestation and its consequences, and he lamented that people were selfish and shortsighted, waging wars and plundering nature for riches, annihilating their own means of conservation. He concluded despairingly: ‘It looks as if man were destined to exterminate himself after making the globe uninhabitable.’

From the start, Lamarck’s science of self-making, world-creating living beings antagonised the powerful. In contrast, the dominant tradition in evolutionary biology from the end of the 19th century, largely abiding still today, renders living organisms as the objects of external forces, posing no threat to gods or monarchs or other worldly powers. Evolutionary science became the reductive account of an essentially passive living world. By this standard, Lamarck’s vision of a world continually in the making, shaped by its own mortal inhabitants, wasn’t even wrong: it just wasn’t science. But science, like living beings, is always changing. Evolutionary biology today is full of exhilarating unrest.

Lamarck’s ideas have been making a comeback in several areas of biology. For instance, the study of epigenetic inheritance – involving structures outside the DNA that influence gene expression – has demonstrated, throughout every kind of organism, that characteristics acquired in an individual lifetime can indeed be inherited. Many of the examples that scientists have been finding involve the responses of various kinds of animals to climate change. An example is the spiny chromis, a slender damselfish inhabiting the coral reefs of the Pacific. In 2015, marine biologists showed that its metabolism responds to the higher water temperatures brought on by climate change by transforming in myriad ways, and that these changes are inherited from generation to generation. The spiny chromis isn’t alone. In 2020, scientists found that the reef-building coral that provides the damselfish’s home also responds to changing ocean temperatures and salinity with epigenetic changes that it passes on to its offspring.

German evolutionary geneticists have found that wild guinea pigs subjected to heat-stress show heritable alterations in their livers, which play a crucial role in metabolic regulation; and biologists in the United States and Kenya have shown that the metabolisms of baboons also heritably change in response to differences in their food supply. In fact, it seems increasingly apparent that all kinds of living beings respond to their changing environments with heritable epigenetic transformations. These might provide means of rapid adaptation that precedes, and perhaps shapes, slower genetic changes.
Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous

Another area of current interest is the role of animal behaviour in directing natural selection. Martha Muñoz, an ecologist and evolutionary biologist at Yale University in Connecticut, studies a kind of lizard in the Dominican Republic called the anole, which is closely related to the iguana. Muñoz has shown that, as these lizards moved from the coast up into the mountains, reaching as high as 3,000 metres, they adapted to the much colder temperatures by being ‘behaviourally nimble’, for example, by basking on the sun-drenched boulders. Rather than showing physiological differences that would give them greater cold tolerance, they have rapidly evolved shorter legs and flatter skulls, enabling them to hide from predators in the crevices of the rock. ‘Far from being passive vessels at the mercy of their circumstances,’ Muñoz told the journal Science in 2022, ‘organisms can influence evolution directly.’ Her research confirms that ‘behaviour is one of the major architects of evolution’ and that ‘organisms can influence natural selection.’

The theory of ‘niche construction’ offers another example. The central principle of this theory is that organisms contribute to shaping their environments, creating the ecological niches that exert selective pressures on them. Bird nests, beaver dams, termite mounds, worm and mole burrows, spiderwebs, beehives – the evidence of organisms creating their own environments is ubiquitous. John Odling-Smee, the scholar who coined the term ‘niche construction’, wrote in 2024 that biologists should rethink what the theory of evolution should be about: not just natural selection acting upon organisms in given environments but ‘the coevolution of organisms with their environments’.

Neo-Darwinism, with its passive model of living beings, has been teetering on its throne. One current movement, known as the extended evolutionary synthesis, seeks to widen the evolutionary picture beyond the neo-Darwinist focus on random genetic variation and natural selection, in part by including behavioural and even cultural elements. Many animals have something like what we call culture in humans, and this includes cultural forms that are inherited and passed down. Lamarck knew this. He wrote that intelligent animals – birds and mammals – could create new habits and ways of life that would be maintained over generations. There is overwhelming and definitive evidence that all kinds of animals – birds, primates, whales, fish, insects – learn from one another and have cultural traditions that are handed down from generation to generation. Communication and social learning make a crucial difference to survival and reproduction, and therefore to evolution. Animals communicate vitally important things to one another including information about food, predators, songs, migration routes and where to find a mate. To give just one example, humpback whales develop different approaches to hunting from one community to another – one in the Northeast Pacific, another in the Gulf of Maine – and teach these to their offspring.

These innovative humpback whales, along with the nimble mountain lizards of the Dominican Republic and legions of other living things – all of them, in fact – exemplify what Lamarck knew and mainstream evolutionary biology has long denied. Living beings are active, self-making, and world-making. They are creators, even the humblest of them. The implication, deeply unpopular with autocrats from Napoleon onward, can be a source of hope: neither creativity nor transformative power can ultimately be controlled or monopolised.

items.title: AnOther Loves: Shades for the Morning After
items.description: From Tom Ford’s earliest days to Haider Ackermann’s seductive reinvention of the house, sunglasses have always been part of the uniform. These styles offer two new ways to hide
items.author: George Pistachio
paragraphs: From Tom Ford’s earliest days to Haider Ackermann’s seductive reinvention of the house, sunglasses have always been part of the uniform. These styles offer two new ways to hide

“You know, one always looks better in photographs with sunglasses on,” Tom Ford said as a camera approached him at Haider Ackermann’s debut for his namesake house. He promptly put on a pair. Sunglasses, after all, have been part of the label almost from the beginning: when Ford founded it in 2005, eyewear was among its earliest propositions, arriving two years before his menswear. It is fertile territory for Ackermann, whose Tom Ford is increasingly becoming a conversation with Mr Ford rather than a cosplay. These two styles pictured above offer different ways to disappear. The Bronson is a hefty acetate pilot with pink-tinted lenses; the Brady, rather more dramatically, is a gold metal wraparound with a single smoke-mirror lens stretched across the face. Both carry the little metal T, one of the house’s earliest and most enduring signatures, but beyond that, their shapes have history of their own. The pilot began as practical equipment in the 1930s, developed to protect aviators’ eyes from glare at altitude, before Hollywood helped turn them into something much cooler. The Brady belongs to an exhibitionist branch of this shady family tree: shield sunglasses appeared in the futuristic fashions of Courrèges, Cardin and Yves Saint Laurent in the late 1960s, then returned with vengeance around the turn of the millennium. Before his debut, Ackermann described Ford as the night and himself as “more the morning after” – in that case, keeping these sunglasses on feels commonsensical.
The Brady and Bronson sunglasses by Tom Ford are available to buy now

items.title: Meet the Witches in Harley Weir and Dilara Fındıkoğlu’s New Zine
items.description: On a Monday morning in late October, I received two missed calls from Harley Weir. I’d not spoken to the photographer since I last interviewed her over a year ago. Strangely, just minutes before, I’d been asked by my editor to speak to her again – this time ab
items.author: Dominique Sisley
paragraphs: On a Monday morning in late October, I received two missed calls from Harley Weir. I’d not spoken to the photographer since I last interviewed her over a year ago. Strangely, just minutes before, I’d been asked by my editor to speak to her again – this time about Witch, a new zine made in collaboration with fashion designer Dilara Fındıkoğlu, exploring ancient magic and the innate power of women. When I called Weir back, she was apologetic, admitting that she’d accidentally dialled me from her pocket (“it was a butt dial!”). A coincidence – though given the subject, an eerily well-timed one.

Witch feels a natural extension of Weir’s long-standing preoccupations. Her photographs have always been imbued with an earthy, almost primordial mysticism, documenting the feminine body in its various states of transformation. Her vision of womanhood is complex: tender, sexual, at times even grotesque. “People have historically been afraid of the natural woman,” Weir explains over Zoom when we catch up properly a few days later. “Her affinity with nature, her intuition, the ability to create life, which is a magical, crazy, unexplained thing that can’t really be controlled or understood.” In the background, the photographer’s newborn daughter gurgles.

We’re soon joined on the call by Fındıkoğlu. Friends as well as collaborators, the pair share a fascination with feminine power, and the fears that have long surrounded it. In Witch, this interest comes into sharp focus. Shot over five days across Romania, the zine takes us inside dimly lit rooms crammed with candles, tarot cards and religious icons. In its portraits, Fındıkoğlu’s intricate corsetry – equal parts armour and adornment – lends the women a ceremonial, otherworldly presence. “The idea came about in conversation with creative director Matthew Scorțe, who is Romanian and told me tales of witches from his hometown,” says Weir, “and who better to team up with than Dilara, queen of the witches?” Fındıkoğlu, lighting up a Vogue and flicking her long, jet-black hair out of her face, elaborates: “We were trying to redefine the word ‘witch.’ Everyone is afraid of it because it’s associated with something evil, something dangerous. But we wanted to show that these powers are completely natural and that we all carry them within us.”

Alongside the images, Witch features conversations with seven women from Romania, conducted by Weir and Fındıkoğlu. Among them are a practising Roma witch, a trans activist and sex worker, a journalist, and a body-modification artist. Each has her own relationship with the figure of the witch – for some, it represents a serious spiritual tradition; for others, a symbol of independence. “Many witches in Romania are highly paid; they’re doing well,” says Weir. “They’re still thriving. It’s not like it’s this hidden thing over there.”

For Fındıkoğlu, the idea of the witch speaks to something more universal. “I think we’ve become so obsessed with understanding and rationalising everything that we’ve lost touch with the mystery of being human,” she says. “I feel like we’re already otherworldly beings in so many ways. There’s so much magic within us that we don’t even recognise. Why is the word magic understood as something we can‘t achieve?”
Below, in an extract from the zine, four of the women featured in Witch reflect on their own experiences.
Mihaela Minca is a practising Roma witch who describes herself as belonging to the “most ancient lineage” of witches on Romanian soil

“We, Roma people – who are born and raised in Romania – are living history. Our legacy is passed down through trauma and blood. Witchcraft is both an innate birthright and a sacred gift. However, all women possess this magical power within themselves. The importance is to express, embody and use it. When she does, she becomes a very powerful woman. Magic lives in the heart of every woman on this earth.

“In the Roma community, women are traditionally expected to live in closed circles, suppressing their opinions and living without a voice. Fortunately, the witch lineage that I’m a part of gave me a platform to express myself.”
Antonella is a Romanian Roma trans woman, sex worker, tarot reader and activist who has campaigned for trans visibility and rights in her home country

“I’ve been working in the sex industry for the past 20 years. I’ve experienced a lot of street violence, harassment, violation and discrimination. I always try to see the good in everything [...] Sunshine will find its way onto your path.

“Seeing nobody talking about trans women [in Romania], I stepped forward as a political candidate. [Because of] heavy backlash from churches and conservative movements asking how a ‘hooker’ could run, I didn’t win, but it was something new for Romania and provided a platform for the trans community. I also wrote about my life because I wanted to leave something behind, and this started my trans activism in Romania. It stirred a lot of protest, but ultimately a lot of movement.
“My past will never heal. Maybe I don’t want my wounds to heal. These wounds, both emotional and physical, have made me the powerful woman that I am today.”
Andra Mureșan is a Romanian journalist whose work investigates violence against women, sexual abuse and the growing threat of image-based abuse

“I report on deepfake abuse and sexual violence in Romania […] I see women constantly being blamed, even though society is the one at fault. Over the last year, I struggled to stay focused on my purpose as a journalist. My last article documented two sexually abused women who were ignored and blamed by the police, judges and prosecutors. I realised then that my writing is my weapon.

“When I was little, I used to see a witch as a fictional character. Then, as I got older, I understood the history of it more [...] the witch trials, and how this affected our rights as women […] Our rights are never guaranteed to stay the way they are today. If our rights are dismantled, we’ll have to come together [and use] our power as ‘witches’.”
Maria is a Romanian body-modification artist and science student whose experiments with piercing explore the limits of the body and conventional ideas of feminine beauty

“I’ve had every weird haircut and possible piercing [...] I’ve had people yell at me on the street or even hiss like vampires. I guess, as women, we’re used to it and just brush it off. [...] I always liked a more alternative style, and what I did to my body felt beautiful to me. I do think it makes men uncomfortable because they feel like they’re losing power. We’re born into rules we never chose, and while breaking them threatens their power, other women also judge us for stepping out of line.

“Doing whatever you want is liberating, but so is facing negative reactions without letting them break you. It’s freeing to realise you’ve moved past the anxiety of keeping yourself boxed in. Breaking free gives me an adrenaline rush and makes me happy. It’s sad seeing people stay stuck instead of doing the work to free themselves.”
Harley Weir and Dilara Fındıkoğlu’s Witch is released on 31 October, published by IDEA

items.title: All power to a former gasholder that’s Amsterdam’s hottest new cultural hub
items.description: Culture has long claimed abandoned industrial structures, drawn to their atmospheric voids and the freedom found in their decay. In 1990s Amsterdam, one such structure, a 19th-century gas holder in Westerpark, was revered as a ‘temple to techno’. Now, after ho
items.author: Harriet Thorpe
paragraphs: Culture has long claimed abandoned industrial structures, drawn to their atmospheric voids and the freedom found in their decay. In 1990s Amsterdam, one such structure, a 19th-century gas holder in Westerpark, was revered as a ‘temple to techno’. Now, after hosting one-off events for years, Gashouder (Dutch for 'gas holder') has opened as a permanent cultural venue for live and electronic music, performance and art with capacity for 3,500 revellers.

Gashouder’s new chapter balances its restoration as a heritage-listed ‘Rijksmonument’ with a subterranean extension that enables its functional, long-term operation. Arriving through historic red-brick arches, visitors now descend into the old gasholder’s futuristic new concrete ‘underworld’ that directly mirrors the perimeter of the concert hall above.

Amsterdam-based interdisciplinary studio Inside Outside designed the architecture and interiors of this underworld as an experiential and flexible 21st-century system driven by the venue's 19th-century geometry. 'We love restoring historic industrial buildings, but we also want to lift them up with an extra layer that gives them new life,' says Aura Luz Melis, partner at Inside Outside.

Radial strips of light echoing the former steel skeleton guide visitors towards a central gathering space lit with a glowing lamp by Lumus Instruments, inspired by the gasholder’s former flame. A series of curved sliding and demountable walls of aluminium and polycarbonate shift into five different event configurations, dividing the functions of the bar, toilets, backstage and merchandise kiosk.

Glitches in this sci-fi scenography reveal the raw roughness of the steel sheet-pile retaining wall, almost at one with the texture of the earth. Meanwhile, sections of glossy, reflective PVC flooring contrast with ‘ghost’ sections of matte-black corrugated steel, energising the space, alongside lighting informed by the minimalist experimentalism of the 20th century’s avant-garde Zero art movement.

Founded by Dutch designer Petra Blaisse in 1991, Inside Outside has pioneered shifting interior atmospheres through textile design, landscape, light and perspectives. Rather than being superfluous or aesthetic, those ‘layers’ are in fact 'functional, flexible and demountable', explains Melis, and over the past ten years she’s seen their work become even more relevant as cultural institutions seek to be less extractive and more resourceful.

A staircase twists up to the expansive concert hall, which has a soaring 14.5m ceiling height. The exposed architecture dates back to 1881 and was technically restored by architect André van Stigt of Buro van Stigt. Inside Outside printed new acoustic panels with a grainy, to-scale photograph of the building’s brick walls, camouflaging them abstractly into the historic atmosphere.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

For Lennart Rottier, founder of Universe Building and co-owner of Gashouder and the wider Cultuurpark Westergas (together with Duncan Stutterheim), the roof and the bricks are essential to the performances, forging a moment of connection between time, creativity and place. The venue’s programming plugs a gap in Amsterdam’s music scene for mid-career artists, and has an alternative edge inspired by its rave history, yet you’ll also find the National Ballet and Royal Orchestra on the agenda.

Rottier hopes the industrial architecture will challenge these more traditional art forms, while attracting younger audiences to them. 'The monument determines our direction, the heritage determines our values,' he explains, proud of the place-making vision that’s been forged under an owner-developer-operator model in collaboration with the municipality.

This means that the cultural experience of the Gashouder starts at the entrance to the 23-hectare Westerpark, and in the village of 19th-century red-brick ‘Hollandsche Neorenaissance’ buildings hosting bars, restaurants, clubs and galleries.

Inside Outside’s collaboration extends across the park with a scheme of lighting, wayfinding and bike parking (80 per cent of Gashouder visitors arrive by bike) set to unfold in 2028. Amidst the trees, the authentic silhouette of Gashouder sculpturally looms, preserving its original power, before revealing its futuristic underworld that equips it for the next century.
Gashouder, Klönneplein 1, 1014 DD Amsterdam, gashouder.nl

Harriet Thorpe is a writer, journalist and editor covering architecture, design and culture, with particular interest in sustainability, 20th-century architecture and community. After studying History of Art at the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) and Journalism at City University in London, she developed her interest in architecture working at Wallpaper* magazine and today contributes to Wallpaper*, The World of Interiors and Icon magazine, amongst other titles. She is author of The Sustainable City (2022, Hoxton Mini Press), a book about sustainable architecture in London, and the Modern Cambridge Map (2023, Blue Crow Media), a map of 20th-century architecture in Cambridge, the city where she grew up.

items.title: 11 satin accessories to add opulence to any outfit
items.description: With the breakneck pace of contemporary fashion – where a trend can take over the feed and then disappear within weeks, even days – it is rare for a runway piece to retain its cachet beyond the season. There are, of course, exceptions, most usually in the real
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: With the breakneck pace of contemporary fashion – where a trend can take over the feed and then disappear within weeks, even days – it is rare for a runway piece to retain its cachet beyond the season. There are, of course, exceptions, most usually in the realm of accessories, which tend to have greater staying power. Such was the case with Prada’s ‘Wish’ bag, which, despite being from S/S 2026 (which means it was first shown in September 2025) and there having been two more Prada womenswear shows held in between, was named as the ‘hottest product’ of Q3 2026 by the Lyst Index last week. The index, which collates search and social-media data to assess brand buzz, also saw Prada take the top spot as the quarter’s ‘hottest brand’ (it knocked Parisian powerhouse Chanel into number two).
11 of the best satin accessories for autumn/winter

Crafted from duchesse satin, in an array of Prada-esque hues – from sky blue to topaz and ivy green – the ‘Wish’ bag is a riff on the classic drawstring dust bag, and fits into a wider adoption of the fabric in recent seasons. Synonymous with luxury and wealth – satin was first developed during in 12th-century China from silk filaments – the lustrous fabric made its journey westwards during the Renaissance, adopted by monarchs and merchants to denote status. On the runway, designers have given it a more quotidian spin: at Celine’s S/S 2027 menswear show, colourful satin cummerbunds wrapped around simple cashmere sweaters and trousers, while at Prada’s S/S 2026 show, opulent satin opera gloves were teamed with uniform-style shirts and trousers. Creative directors Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons said it was about removing clothing from its usual ‘hierarchies’, positing a ‘new elegance’ for a world in flux.

It is in this spirit that we have collated 11 of the best satin accessories as we enter a season of dressing up – these are pieces that, with their innate elegance, can be worn to elevate even the simplest of outfits. Like a plissé satin belt by Valentino Garavani that denotes old-world glamour but could equally be worn over a T-shirt and jeans, or colourful clutch bags from Saint Laurent and Alaïa, which instantly transform the everyday.
Discover 11 of the best satin accessories to add opulence to any outfit.

These 1980s-inflected power pumps from Saint Laurent are crafted from brown satin and feature a razor-thin plexiglass and satin spike heel. Elongated towards a squared ‘vamp’ heel, their dramatic silhouette is an apt reminder of Anthony Vaccarello‘s knack for after-dark glamour (the designer left the house after a decade last month).

Pieter Mulier’s ‘Le Teckel’ handbag is one of the defining successes of his tenure, which culminated in January 2026 after five years at the house (his next role is at Versace). This clutch version of the elongated style is the perfect contemporary evening bag, crafted from smooth yellow satin.

Vivid flashes of colour have become a calling card of Michael Rider’s collections for Celine, which marry a preppy sensibility with the bourgeois codes for which the Parisian house is known. This silk-satin scarf comes in scarlet-red – one of Rider’s signature hues, utilised by the designer since his debut in the summer of 2025.

Last month, Prada’s ‘Wish’ pouch – a play on the humble dust bag, remade in satin or leather – was named Lyst’s hottest product of Q3 (the platform uses search data and social media data to measure ‘buzz’).
